library.name: Pantrix UI
library.description: A design system and adaptive UI library for Compose Multiplatform: one Kotlin codebase for Android, iOS, the desktop (JVM) and the web (Wasm and JS). It is built directly on Compose Foundation, with **no Material dependency**, and one theme follows each platform's own conventions: its touch targets, its focus rings, its component geometry.

modules.description: Pantrix UI's components for Compose Multiplatform, with no Material dependency.

modules.description: Pantrix UI's theme, tokens, adaptive window and platform services for Compose Multiplatform.

modules.name: material3
modules.description: The bridge between Pantrix UI's theme and Material 3's, in both directions.

pages.title: Colours
pages.summary:
The theme's colours: `PantrixTheme.colors`. A component asks for a colour by its job, not by its name: the main action is `primary`, an error `danger`, a card's ground `surface`. The theme says which colour that job is; going from the light theme to the dark changes the component's colour, and not its code.

The examples of the roles, the grounds and the lines read their colours from `PantrixTheme.colors` and write no colour code: they change with the theme when it is switched from light to dark in "Settings". The palette does not look at the theme: its scales are the same in both.
features: **Six roles.** `primary` is the brand's role: the main action, and what is selected. `success`, `info`, `warning` and `danger` convey a status; `neutral` is the role with no hue of its own, for what should not draw the eye.

**A role's four colours.** Each role is a `PantrixColor`: `color` is the role at full strength and `container` the role softened; `onColor` and `onContainer` are the colours of the text and icons drawn on them.
**Two grounds.** `background` is the app's backdrop; `surface` is the ground of a raised or grouped area: a card, a sheet, a dialog, a menu.

**Text colours.** On the grounds the main text is written in `textPrimary`, supporting text in `textSecondary` and the text of what cannot be used in `textDisabled`. `textInverse` is the text on a fill of the theme's opposite tone.
**Edges and lines.** `border` is a box's soft edge, `borderHover` that edge under a pointer, `borderStrong` the mark of a control that is nothing but its mark, and `divider` the line between items.

**Disabled, focus, scrim.** `disabledContainer` and `disabledContent` are the fill of a control that cannot be used and what is drawn on it; `focusRing` is the ring around what has keyboard focus, and `scrim` the dimming laid behind a modal.
**Content colour.** A fill tells everything inside it which colour is written on it: text and icons that are given no colour take it. `contentColorFor` finds a fill's pair in the theme.
**Chart colours.** `chart` holds the colours a chart tells its series apart by, in the order they are handed out. They are no role: they do not say what a series is, only tell it from the others.
**Palette.** `PantrixPalette` gives each of eighteen colours in eleven steps. The roles pick their steps from it; components read the roles, not the palette.

**Your own colours.** `PantrixColors` is a `data class`: `PantrixColors.Light` and `PantrixColors.Dark` are the two ready-made sets, `copy` changes a single role of a set, and `PantrixTheme(colors = …)` gives the set to the theme.

examples.name: ColorsRoles
examples.title: Six roles
examples.description:
Each row is a role, and each box one of that role's fills. On the left, `color` is the role at full strength: a solid button's fill. On the right, `container` is the role softened: the fill of a soft button or of a tinted area. The two lines inside a box are written in the colour that reads on that fill: `onColor` on `color`, `onContainer` on `container`.

None of the colours is written here: all of them are read from `PantrixTheme.colors`. Switch the theme to dark in "Settings": the same six roles come back, in the colours that read on a dark ground.

examples.name: ColorsGroundsAndText
examples.title: Grounds and text colours
examples.description:
The theme has two grounds. `background` is the app's backdrop, behind everything. `surface` is the ground of a raised or grouped area: a card, a sheet, a dialog, a menu. Text is written in the same colours on both: the main text in `textPrimary`, supporting text in `textSecondary`, the text of what cannot be used in `textDisabled`. What is not text, such as an icon nothing else gives a colour, is drawn in `onSurface`.

The box below is a fill of the theme's opposite tone: the text on it is `textInverse`, white in the light theme and all but black in the dark. A tooltip is drawn this way: its fill is `onSurface`, its text `textInverse`.

examples.name: ColorsBordersAndDividers
examples.title: Edges and lines
examples.description:
`border` is the edge of a box: a text field's, a chip's. It is soft by design: stronger than `divider` and far quieter than text. `borderHover` is that edge under a pointer, a notch stronger. `borderStrong` is the mark of a control that is nothing but its mark: a checkbox's box, a radio button's ring, a switch that is off. It is at 3:1 against what it stands on (WCAG 1.4.11), so that the control is seen before it is chosen. The empty box of the checkbox below is drawn in it.

`border` is below that 3:1. A product that has to meet it for the edges of its fields gives its theme a stronger colour here.

`divider` is the line between items or sections, lighter than `border`: it separates, and is no control's edge. A `PantrixHorizontalDivider` that is given no colour is drawn in it on the theme's grounds.

examples.name: ColorsDisabledFocusAndScrim
examples.title: Disabled, focus ring and scrim
examples.description:
The fill of a control that cannot be used is `disabledContainer`, and the text and icon on it are `disabledContent`: the disabled button beside the box is drawn in those two. Disabled text that stands on no fill is `textDisabled`: a disabled checkbox's label.

`focusRing` is the colour of the ring around the component that has keyboard focus. The edge of the box here is drawn in that colour and at the ring's width (`PantrixTheme.platform.focusRingWidth`). `scrim` is the dimming laid over the app behind a modal, a dialog or a sheet: the text of the last box lies under it.

examples.name: ColorsContentColor
examples.title: The content colour a fill provides
examples.description:
A fill tells everything inside it which colour is written on it. Filled with a role's colour, a `PantrixSurface` provides the one the theme pairs with it as the content colour: `onColor` for `color`, `onContainer` for `container`. The icon, the text and the line in the first two boxes were given no colour; all three took that one. The line is thirty per cent of it.

The theme's own grounds provide no content colour. The third box is filled with `surface`: each component in it is drawn in its own default, the text in `textPrimary`, the icon in `onSurface`, the line in `divider`.

The fill of the last box is in none of the theme's roles. The theme cannot know what reads on it: the content colour is the caller's to give, with `contentColor`.

appNames.name: ownColors
appNames.description: The "app's own colour" of the examples: a purple that is in none of the theme's roles. It is there to show what changes when a component is given `colors`; given one of the theme's roles, nobody could tell whether the colour came from the component's tone or from the parameter.

examples.name: ColorsChart
examples.title: Chart colours
examples.description:
`chart` holds the colours a chart hands out to its series: the first series takes the first, the second the second. With more series than colours, `chartColor(index)` starts again at the first. The default sets have ten.

Three things decided them. Each stands out on both of the theme's grounds as far as a line or a bar needs to be seen: at least 3:1. The light set and the dark set carry the same hues in the same order: when the theme turns, a series changes its shade and not its colour. And the order was built so that two colours next to each other stay apart for an eye that does not tell red from green, or blue from yellow; that is why some steps are one lighter or one darker than their neighbour's.

Even so, colour alone does not carry ten series, to any eye: a chart of many series marks them by more than colour. For your own brand's colours, `PantrixTheme.colors.copy(chart = listOf(…))` is enough.

examples.name: ColorsPalette
examples.title: The palette's scales
examples.description:
`PantrixPalette` holds the raw scales the theme's colours are picked from: eighteen colours, each in eleven steps, from left to right 50, 100, 200 and on by hundreds to 900, then 950. `PantrixPalette.all` gives them all, with their names.

In the default themes a role's `color` is its scale's 600 or 700 in the light theme and its 400 in the dark; its `container` is the 100 in the light theme and the 900 in the dark, the 800 for `neutral`. There the `primary` role is from the `Blue` scale, `success` from `Green`, `info` from `Cyan`, `warning` from `Amber` and `danger` from `Red`; the `neutral` role, the grounds, the text and the lines are from `Slate`. The whites of the light theme are no step of any scale: `surface`, `textInverse` and the roles' `onColor`.

A component does not read the palette: it reads the roles. The palette is for picking steps when a theme's roles are built.

examples.name: ColorsOwnRole
examples.title: A role of your own, built from the palette
examples.description:
When a colour is needed that is in none of the theme's six roles, a role is built from the palette: a `PantrixColor`, with its four colours. Here it is from the `Violet` scale, at the steps of the theme's own roles: 600 with white on it in the light theme, 400 with 950 on it in the dark. That way the colour stands out from the ground in both themes, and the text on it reads. An app knows for itself whether its theme is dark; in this app `LocalDemoDarkTheme` says so.

A role built this way is used as the theme's roles are: `buttonColors(variant)` makes a button's colours from it. The "app's own colour" examples on the other pages are in this purple.

appNames.name: LocalDemoDarkTheme
appNames.description: Whether the app's theme is dark right now: the system's mode while the setting is "System", and the setting itself otherwise.

examples.name: ColorsOwnBrand
examples.title: A theme that changes the brand's colour
examples.description:
The brand's colour is the `primary` role, and the theme gives it. `PantrixColors` is a `data class`, so `copy` changes a single role; `PantrixTheme(colors = …)` gives the new set to what is inside it. The buttons, the checkbox and the switch here were given no colour: they read `primary` and are drawn in the purple the theme gives.

For the whole app the same is done in the outermost theme. `focusRing` is a colour of its own: it does not change when `primary` does, and is given as well where that is wanted.

appNames.name: ownColors
appNames.description: The "app's own colour" of the examples: a purple that is in none of the theme's roles. It is there to show what changes when a component is given `colors`; given one of the theme's roles, nobody could tell whether the colour came from the component's tone or from the parameter.

examples.name: ColorsOwnComponentContent
examples.title: Your own component's content colour
examples.description:
The app's own component finds its content colour from the theme too. `Pill` takes a fill and asks with `contentOn` for the colour of what it draws on it: the colour paired with the fill where it is a role's (what `contentColorFor` finds), `textPrimary` where it is the theme's ground, and the component's own default where the theme does not know the colour. `ProvidePantrixContentColor` gives that colour to what is inside: the text and the icon were given no colour, and both took it.

The line underneath asks `contentColorFor` directly: on success's fill it gives `onColor`.

examples.name: ColorsTwoSets
examples.title: Pantrix's two sets
examples.description: Pantrix's own two sets: `rememberPantrixColors(darkTheme)` gives the light or the dark one, whatever the app's brand. The two are also read as `PantrixColors.Light` and `PantrixColors.Dark`: an app builds its own set from them with `copy`. Here two sections take the two sets; each draws its ground with its own `surface`.

pages.title: Typography
pages.summary:
The theme's type scale: `PantrixTheme.typography`. Nine styles, largest to smallest. A text asks for its size by its job, not in points: a page's title is `display`, a card's title is `title`, a button's label is `label`. The theme says what size and weight that job is set in.

The metrics on this page are not written by hand. The line above each specimen reads the style's name and its metrics from the `TextStyle` in the theme: `size / line height · weight · letter spacing`. When the type scale or the typeface changes, this page changes with it by itself.
features: **Nine styles.** `display`, `headline` and `title` for headings; `callout`, `body`, `label`, `footnote` and `caption` for text; `code` for identity-bearing text.

**Text given no style is `label`.** `PantrixText`, `PantrixLink` and `PantrixAutoText` are set in the base text, `LocalPantrixTextStyle`, when they are given no `style`. The theme starts it at `label`: the style of a control's label. A part gives its own base text with `ProvidePantrixTextStyle`. Compose Foundation's `BasicText` does not read this value: a `BasicText` given no style is set in the system's typeface.

**A style named by its role.** `TypeRole` is a role of the scale; `PantrixTheme.typography[TypeRole.Body]` is its style. A component's style names the role without holding a typeface: text fields are set in `TextFieldStyle.textRole`, `body` on Android and iOS, `label` on the desktop and the web.

**The scale and the typeface are separate.** `buildPantrixTypography(fontFamily = …)` keeps the scale and changes the typeface: a brand's family is passed, and the sizes and the weights stay the same.

**Three families.** `fontFamily` is the family of the text, `headingFontFamily` that of `display`, `headline` and `title`, and `monoFamily` that of `code`. A heading family that is not given is the text's; a monospace family that is not given is `FontFamily.Monospace`.

**Pantrix's own typeface.** `rememberPantrixTypography()` gives the scale in Plus Jakarta Sans, loaded from the library's own resources. It is what is used when the app's theme is given no typography.
**Weights.** The library's typeface is one variable font: its weight axis runs from 200 to 800.

**An app's typeface.** `PantrixTypeface` names a typeface by its font files; each file, with its weight, is a `PantrixFont`. `rememberPantrixTypography(typeface)` gives the scale in that typeface; `codeTypeface` has code written in a typeface of its own.

**Fallback fonts.** In a browser, Compose draws a character none of the app's fonts has in a Noto font it fetches from Google's servers. A `PantrixTypeface`'s `fallbacks` are the fonts of such characters: they are read with the typeface, and nothing is fetched. The library's typeface carries Pantrix Symbols for the marks of a Mac's keys (`⌘ ⇧ ⌥`).

**In a browser.** A browser fetches the typeface, and draws text in a fallback face until it arrives. `PantrixTypefaceGate` draws the app after the typeface has come; `rememberPantrixTypography(typeface)` stays in the old typeface while it is changed, and changes once when the new one has come. `areTypefacesLoaded(…)` says when it has.
**A section's typeface.** `PantrixTheme(typography = …)` gives that typography to every component inside it: to the whole app, or to one section of it alone.
**A style is a look, not a role.** Text set in a heading style is not a heading to a screen reader: that is what the `role` parameter of `PantrixText` says, `TextRole.Heading(level)`.
**The system's font size.** The scale's sizes, line heights and letter spacings are given in sp: when the system's font size is raised, the text grows with it.

examples.name: TypographyHeadings
examples.title: Headings
examples.description:
The scale's three heading styles. `display` is the page's title, typically one per screen. `headline` is a section's heading. `title` is the title of a card, a panel or a dialog.

The line above each specimen reads the style's name and its metrics from the theme. All three are set in the heading family given when the scale is built (`headingFontFamily`).
examples.code:
val type = PantrixTheme.typography
TypeSpecimen(name = "display", style = type.display, text = "Design system")
TypeSpecimen(name = "headline", style = type.headline, text = "Recent orders")
TypeSpecimen(name = "title", style = type.title, text = "Payment method")

@Composable
private fun TypeSpecimen(
    name: String,
    style: TextStyle,
    text: String
) {
    Column(verticalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.xs)) {
        PantrixText(
            text = "$name · ${style.metrics()}",
            style = PantrixTheme.typography.caption,
            color = PantrixTheme.colors.textSecondary
        )
        PantrixText(text = text, style = style)
    }
}

private fun TextStyle.metrics(): String = "${fontSize.formatted()} / ${lineHeight.formatted()} · " +
    "${fontWeight.label()} · letter spacing ${letterSpacing.formatted()}"

private fun TextUnit.formatted(): String {
    if (isUnspecified) return "-"
    val hundredths = (value * 100).roundToInt()
    val sign = if (hundredths < 0) "-" else ""
    val whole = abs(hundredths) / 100
    val fraction = abs(hundredths) % 100
    val number = when {
        fraction == 0 -> "$whole"
        fraction % 10 == 0 -> "$whole.${fraction / 10}"
        else -> "$whole.${fraction.toString().padStart(2, '0')}"
    }
    return if (isEm) "$sign$number em" else "$sign$number"
}

private fun FontWeight?.label(): String = when (val weight = this?.weight) {
    null -> "-"
    100 -> "Thin"
    200 -> "ExtraLight"
    300 -> "Light"
    400 -> "Normal"
    500 -> "Medium"
    600 -> "SemiBold"
    700 -> "Bold"
    800 -> "ExtraBold"
    900 -> "Black"
    else -> "$weight"
}

examples.name: TypographyTextStyles
examples.title: Text styles
examples.description:
The five styles for text, largest to smallest, each with the kind of text it meets where it is used. `callout` is emphasised body: a lead paragraph, the description of an empty screen. `body` is body text: a paragraph, a description, what is typed in a field. `label` is a control's label: a button, a tab, the name of a form field. `footnote` is supporting text: a form's help text, the explanation of an error. `caption` is metadata: a time, a counter, a detail in a table cell.

The body specimen has every letter of the alphabet, and its paragraph runs over several lines: that is where the line height shows.
examples.code:
val type = PantrixTheme.typography
TypeSpecimen(
    name = "callout",
    style = type.callout,
    text = "You have no orders yet. When you place your first order, it will appear here."
)
TypeSpecimen(
    name = "body",
    style = type.body,
    text = "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog. " +
        "This paragraph shows how the line height holds over more than one line."
)
TypeSpecimen(name = "label", style = type.label, text = "Add to cart")
TypeSpecimen(name = "footnote", style = type.footnote, text = "Your password must be at least 8 characters long.")
TypeSpecimen(name = "caption", style = type.caption, text = "Updated 2 minutes ago · 3 / 5")

            color = PantrixTheme.colors.textSecondary

}

examples.name: TypographyCode
examples.title: Code and the monospace family
examples.description:
`code` is the style of identity-bearing text: an order number, an event name, a fragment of code. It is set in a monospace family.

The family is the `monoFamily` parameter of `buildPantrixTypography`. For a single identifier inside a sentence, only the style's family is taken and not the whole style: the number in the second line is set in the family of `code`, at the sentence's own size.

examples.name: TypographyNoStyle
examples.title: Text given no style
examples.description:
The first text is given no style and the second is given `label`: the two are drawn the same. A `PantrixText` that is given no `style` is set in the theme's `label` style; so are `PantrixLink` and `PantrixAutoText`.

`label` is the style of a control's label. A paragraph, a heading or a footnote asks for its style explicitly: `style = PantrixTheme.typography.body`.
examples.code:
PantrixText(text = "Style not given: Add to cart", tagKey = "no_style")
PantrixText(text = "Style label: Add to cart", style = PantrixTheme.typography.label, tagKey = "label_style")
PantrixText(
    text = "label · ${PantrixTheme.typography.label.metrics()}",
    style = PantrixTheme.typography.caption,
    color = PantrixTheme.colors.textSecondary
)

examples.name: TypographyBaseOfAPart
examples.title: The base text of a part
examples.description:
A part gives the style of the text in it that is given none itself: `ProvidePantrixTextStyle`. Here a part of paragraphs is set in `body`. A part inside it gives only the weight: what it gives goes over the one around it, and the size and the line height it does not give stay as they are. Text given a style is still in its own style.

A section's base text is told by `LocalPantrixTextStyle`: the last line reads it.
examples.code:
ProvidePantrixTextStyle(PantrixTheme.typography.body) {
    PantrixText(text = "In this part, text given no style is set in the body.", tagKey = "part_body")
    ProvidePantrixTextStyle(TextStyle(fontWeight = FontWeight.Bold)) {
        PantrixText(text = "A part inside it changes only the weight.", tagKey = "part_bold")
    }
    PantrixText(
        text = "Text given a style is set in its own style.",
        style = PantrixTheme.typography.footnote,
        tagKey = "part_footnote"
    )
    PantrixText(
        text = "This section's base text: ${LocalPantrixTextStyle.current.metrics()}",
        style = PantrixTheme.typography.caption,
        color = PantrixTheme.colors.textSecondary
    )
}

examples.name: TypographyWeights
examples.title: Weights
examples.description:
A style can be changed in place: `copy(fontWeight = …)` keeps the style's size and line height and changes its weight. Here is the `body` style in seven weights.

The typeface here is not taken from the theme but from the library itself, with `rememberPantrixTypography()`: it is one variable font whose weight axis runs from 200 to 800, and each of the seven weights here is one point on that axis. `Thin` and `Black` lie outside the axis: they are drawn in the nearest weights, `ExtraLight` and `ExtraBold`.
examples.code:
val body = rememberPantrixTypography().body
val weights = listOf(
    "ExtraLight" to FontWeight.ExtraLight,
    "Light" to FontWeight.Light,
    "Normal" to FontWeight.Normal,
    "Medium" to FontWeight.Medium,
    "SemiBold" to FontWeight.SemiBold,
    "Bold" to FontWeight.Bold,
    "ExtraBold" to FontWeight.ExtraBold
)
Column {
    weights.forEach { (name, weight) ->
        PantrixText(text = "$name · The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog", style = body.copy(fontWeight = weight))
    }
}

examples.name: TypographyOwnFont
examples.title: Your own typeface
examples.description:
The app's own typeface: `buildPantrixTypography(fontFamily = …)` keeps Pantrix's scale and changes the typeface. Here the family is Poppins, from the app's own font files; `PantrixTheme(typography = …)` gives it to every component inside it.

The line above each specimen shows that the metrics stay the same: the size, the line height, the weight and the letter spacing are the scale's, and only the letters themselves change.

appNames.name: Poppins
appNames.description: Poppins from the app's own files: seven weights, each a file of its own. It has no SemiBold: a text of that weight is drawn in a neighbouring one. Its licence, the SIL Open Font License 1.1, is beside the files: `files/licenses/poppins_ofl.txt`. The marks of a Mac's keys are drawn in the library's fallback.

examples.name: TypographyHeadingFamily
examples.title: Headings in another family
examples.description:
Headings and text can be in separate families. `headingFontFamily` is the family of `display`, `headline` and `title` alone; the rest is set in `fontFamily`. Here the heading is in Poppins and the paragraph under it in Plus Jakarta Sans.

Unless `headingFontFamily` is given, the headings are set in `fontFamily` too.

appNames.name: PlusJakartaSans
appNames.description: Plus Jakarta Sans from the app's own files: seven weights, each a file of its own.

appNames.name: Poppins
appNames.description: Poppins from the app's own files: seven weights, each a file of its own. It has no SemiBold: a text of that weight is drawn in a neighbouring one. Its licence, the SIL Open Font License 1.1, is beside the files: `files/licenses/poppins_ofl.txt`. The marks of a Mac's keys are drawn in the library's fallback.

examples.name: TypographyOfTheApp
examples.title: The app's three typographies
examples.description:
This app has three typographies: the library's own (`rememberPantrixTypography()`), and Plus Jakarta Sans and Poppins from the app's own files. All three are the same scale. The first two are the same typeface as well: the library's own typeface is Plus Jakarta Sans too, and only the font files differ. The one whose letters are different is Poppins. Here each stands in a theme of its own, one under another; the one that says "selected" is the app's typography right now.

The "Typeface" choice in "Settings" and the menu in the top bar switch the whole app to another one. The choice is a state: when it changes the theme is recomposed, and every page is drawn in the new typeface.

appNames.name: LocalDemoSettings
appNames.description: The app's settings, for every screen inside it: the buttons in the top bar and the "Settings" page read and change them from here. Outside the app, on a page drawn by itself in a test, they are the default settings.

appNames.name: TypographyStyle
appNames.description: Says where the app's typography comes from.

appNames.name: defaultTypography
appNames.description: The typography of the choice `style`: Pantrix's scale, in the typeface that is chosen.

examples.name: TypographyByRole
examples.title: A style by its role
examples.description: The scale's nine roles, by their jobs: `TypeRole` says what a text is, `typography[role]` gives its style. A component's style says its text the same way, by a role: when the theme changes, it is not the style but the role's style that changes.
examples.code:
val typography = PantrixTheme.typography
TypeRole.entries.forEach { role ->
    PantrixText(text = role.name, style = typography[role], tagKey = "role_${role.name.lowercase()}")
}

examples.name: TypographyFromFiles
examples.title: A typeface from its files
examples.description:
A typeface is built from its files: each `PantrixFont` is a font file and its weight, and a `PantrixTypeface` is a list of them. `rememberPantrixFontFamily` reads the files and gives a family. The marks of keys Poppins lacks (`⌘K`) are drawn in the fallback, the library's Pantrix Symbols: `fallbacks`.

On the web, until the files arrive the text is drawn in another typeface. `areTypefacesLoaded(…)` says whether the files have been read, `isPantrixTypefaceLoaded()` the same of the library's own typeface. `PantrixTypefaceGate` draws its content only once the typeface has been read: at the app's root, so that the text is not seen in another typeface for a moment.

examples.name: TypographyCodeTypeface
examples.title: The code's own typeface
examples.description:
The code's typeface is given apart from the text's: `rememberPantrixTypography(typeface, codeTypeface)` builds the scale in `typeface` and the `code` style in `codeTypeface`. Without it, code is written in `FontFamily.Monospace`. A brand gives its own monospaced typeface here; this demo carries only two families, so the code is written in Poppins.

An app that keeps its typefaces in a list asks with the list whether they have all arrived: `areTypefacesLoaded(list)`.

appNames.name: PlusJakartaSans
appNames.description: Plus Jakarta Sans from the app's own files: seven weights, each a file of its own.

appNames.name: Poppins
appNames.description: Poppins from the app's own files: seven weights, each a file of its own. It has no SemiBold: a text of that weight is drawn in a neighbouring one. Its licence, the SIL Open Font License 1.1, is beside the files: `files/licenses/poppins_ofl.txt`. The marks of a Mac's keys are drawn in the library's fallback.

pages.title: Spacing
pages.summary: The spacing scale: a screen's gaps and paddings are built from these seven steps. The components' own spacing is in their styles; the scale is for the screen's own layout: a card's padding, the gap between two lines, a column's margin.
features: **Steps.** `none` 0, `xs` 4, `sm` 8, `md` 12, `lg` 16, `xl` 24, `xxl` 32dp. `PantrixTheme.spacing` is the nearest theme's scale.
**Density.** The theme multiplies the scale by the density (`scaled`): at the compact density each step is 0.85 times, at the spacious density 1.15 times; `none` stays nought.
**Your own scale.** `PantrixTheme(spacing = PantrixSpacing(…))` changes some of the steps or all of them; a step not given keeps its default. `rememberPantrixSpacing()` is the library's own scale.

examples.name: SpacingSteps
examples.title: Seven steps
examples.description: The scale's seven steps, as the theme gives them: each bar is a step wide. A density scales the steps; on the "Density" page the same bars grow shorter or longer inside a compact or a spacious theme.

examples.name: SpacingOwnScale
examples.title: Your own scale
examples.description: The same card on two scales. The card itself reads only the scale's steps, by name: its padding is `lg`, the gap between its lines `sm`, the space before its button `md`. The left one is on the library's own scale (`rememberPantrixSpacing()`); the theme on the right changes two steps, `PantrixSpacing(sm = 12.dp, lg = 24.dp)`, and the card gets roomier without doing anything else.

pages.title: Shapes
pages.summary: The shape scale: how round the corners are, from square to fully round. A component's style names not a shape but a step of the scale (`ShapeRole`); how round the step is, the brand gives.
features: **Steps.** `xs` 2, `sm` 4, `md` 8, `lg` 12, `xl` 16dp; the two ends, `none` (square) and `full` (fully round), are the same on every brand. `PantrixTheme.shapes` is the nearest theme's scale.
**Ready scales.** `PantrixShapes.Sharp` squares every step off, `PantrixShapes.Pill` makes every step fully round. `rememberPantrixShapes()` is the library's own scale.

**Role and shape.** `ShapeRole` is a step of the scale; `ShapeSpec.Fixed` is a single shape off the scale. Both are a `ShapeSpec`, and `toShape()` turns it into a `Shape` on the nearest theme's scale.

examples.name: ShapesScale
examples.title: The scale
examples.description: The scale's seven shapes, as the theme gives them: the brand's five steps between the two ends.

examples.name: ShapesPresets
examples.title: Sharp and pill
examples.description: The same three components on three scales: the library's own (`rememberPantrixShapes()`), `PantrixShapes.Sharp` and `PantrixShapes.Pill`. The components were given no shape: each reads the step its style names from the theme's scale. That is why the card, the text field and the tag change their corners with the brand.

examples.name: ShapesRoleAndFixed
examples.title: A role's shape and a fixed one
examples.description: The app's own box takes its shape from the scale too. A `ShapeRole` is a step's name: `ShapeRole.Large.toShape()` is the nearest theme's `lg`, and changes with the brand. A shape off the scale is given with `ShapeSpec.Fixed`: here a ticket with cut corners, the same on every brand. Both are a `ShapeSpec`: a component's style is given one the same way.

pages.title: Elevation
pages.summary: The elevation scale: how far a surface stands out from what is under it, by its shadow. A card, a menu, a dialog stands at a step of this scale; the app's own surface takes its step from here too.
features: **Steps.** `none` 0, `sm` 1, `md` 2, `lg` 4, `xl` 8dp. `PantrixTheme.elevation` is the nearest theme's scale.
**Your own scale.** `PantrixTheme(elevation = PantrixElevation(…))` changes the steps; a step not given keeps its default. `rememberPantrixElevation()` is the library's own scale.
**Density.** Density does not scale shadows: a compact screen is a screen with less air, not one with shallower shadows.

examples.name: ElevationSteps
examples.title: Five steps
examples.description: The scale's five steps: each square is a `PantrixSurface` at one step's elevation.

examples.name: ElevationOwnScale
examples.title: Your own scale
examples.description: The same two surfaces on two scales. The surfaces read their elevation by name, `md` and `xl`. Those on the left are on the library's own scale (`rememberPantrixElevation()`); the theme on the right doubles the steps, and the surfaces stand out more.

pages.title: Motion
pages.summary: Durations and easings: how long a transition lasts and how it speeds up and slows down. Every animation of the library takes its duration from here; an animation of the app's own that does too follows the system's "reduce motion" setting by itself.
features: **Durations.** `fast` 100, `normal` 200, `slow` 350 milliseconds. `PantrixTheme.motion` is the nearest theme's.

**Easings.** `standardEasing` is the curve of most transitions, `emphasizedEasing` that of a transition meant to be noticed. `PantrixEasing` carries three curves: `Standard`, `Emphasized`, `Linear`; `curve` is Compose's `Easing`.

**Less motion.** While `reduceMotion` is true, `duration(ms)` gives nought: transitions are skipped, a spinner or a skeleton stops. The theme reads it from the system (`rememberSystemMotion()`, `systemReduceMotion()`).

examples.name: MotionDurationsAndEasings
examples.title: Durations and easings
examples.description: Three durations and three easings. Press "Play": the upper three dots go with the same easing in `fast`, `normal` and `slow` time, the lower three in the same time with three easings. The duration is taken with `duration(…)`: where the system has reduced motion, the dots move to their place without waiting.

examples.name: MotionReduced
examples.title: Less motion
examples.description: Less motion. The theme reads its motion from the system: `rememberSystemMotion()` puts the system's "reduce motion" setting (`systemReduceMotion()`) in `reduceMotion`. The switch gives the same to an inner theme by hand, `PantrixMotion(reduceMotion = true)`: the spinner and the skeleton stop, and the durations go to nought.

pages.title: Density
pages.summary: The interface density: how much air a screen has. The density multiplies the components' heights, paddings and gaps, the theme's spacing scale and the page margins together; lines, borders, icons and shadows stay as they are.
features: **Three densities.** `Compact` 0.85, `Comfortable` 1, `Spacious` 1.15 times (`scale`). The default is `Comfortable` (`rememberPantrixDensity()`); a screen used with a mouse can take the compact density.

**A whole theme.** `PantrixTheme(density = …)` gives the density to everything in it: a settings screen or a data table can be compact, a welcome screen spacious. `PantrixTheme.density` is the nearest theme's.
**Touch target.** The spacious density enlarges the touch target; the compact density does not shrink it.
**Your own measure.** The app's own measure can be multiplied by the density too: `scaledForDensity(scale)`.

examples.name: DensityThree
examples.title: Three densities
examples.description: The same form at three densities. Choose a density: the inner theme gives it to the text field, the checkbox, the buttons and the space between them together. Text and icons stay the same size; what changes is the air between them.

examples.name: DensityOwnMeasure
examples.title: Your own measure too
examples.description: The app's own row follows the density too: its height is 56dp, and `scaledForDensity(PantrixTheme.density.scale)` multiplies it by the nearest theme's density. The middle theme is at the library's default (`rememberPantrixDensity()`); the left one is compact, the right one spacious.

pages.title: Component styles
pages.summary: A component's measures and form are its style: its height, its padding, its corners, its icon's size. Each style has a preset on each platform; on top of it come the brand's, the theme's and a section's, in that order. A component's own parameter comes before all of them.
features: **The whole app.** `PantrixTheme(styles = pantrixStyles(…))` gives the styles to everywhere in it. A style's override is built by its key: `ButtonStyle.override(all = …, ios = …)`; each names only the fields it changes.
**A section.** `ProvidePantrixStyles(styles) { … }` gives the styles to what is in it alone, on top of the outer ones.
**By platform.** `override`'s `android`, `ios`, `desktop` and `web` parameters are that platform's override, on top of `all`.
**The brand's paths.** `ComponentTokenOverrides` says a brand's changes by path: `"button.shape"`, `"icon.size"`. A preset carries them; `PantrixTheme(componentOverrides = …)` gives them too.
**Reading.** `PantrixTheme.style(ButtonStyle)` is a style as it holds at that place: the preset, the brand, the theme, the section and the density together.

**Your own component.** A `PantrixStyle` and its `PantrixStyleKey` put the app's own component in the same order: it has a preset by platform, is overridden in a theme and in a section, and scales with the density.

examples.name: ComponentStylesForTheApp
examples.title: The app's styles
examples.description: Styles for the whole app: the outer `PantrixTheme` is given `styles = pantrixStyles(…)`. Here an inner theme does the same for a section: the buttons' corners are small (`ShapeRole.Small`), the icons 28dp. No component was given a parameter; the second row is the same components with their styles unchanged.

examples.name: ComponentStylesForAPart
examples.title: A section and a platform
examples.description: A section and a platform. `ProvidePantrixStyles` gives the styles to what is in it alone, on top of the outer styles. An override is given by platform too: the card's corners are small on every platform (`ShapeRole.Small`) and large on iOS (`ShapeRole.Large`); the one of the platform you opened this page on is drawn.

examples.name: ComponentStylesBrandPaths
examples.title: The brand's paths
examples.description: A brand's changes are said by path: the first part is the style's name, the rest the field. `ComponentTokenOverrides` carries them as shapes and measures; a brand's preset (`DesignPreset`) gives them this way too. Here the buttons are medium round by `"button.shape"`, the icons 16dp by `"icon.size"`. `PantrixTheme.style(ButtonStyle)` reads the style in force.

examples.name: ComponentStylesOwnComponent
examples.title: Your own component's style
examples.description:
The app's own component takes a style too. `PromoStyle` is a `PantrixStyle`: each of its fields has a "not given" value, `merge` takes what is given on top, and `scaled` multiplies its air by the density (`scaledForDensity`). Its companion object is its `PantrixStyleKey`: it holds the preset on each platform (`PlatformPresets`) and reads the brand's paths (`"promo.padding"`). The component takes its style with `PantrixTheme.style(PromoStyle)`, and its shape with `toShape()`.

The upper box is at its preset; the lower one's section turns it into a pill with `PromoStyle.override(…)`.

pages.title: Nested theme
pages.summary:
A theme inside another: where a part of the screen is to look different, that part is wrapped in a second `PantrixTheme`, and only what changes is given. The inner theme takes every setting it is not given from the outer one; what it is given is its own.

The examples write the theme's values at that point, line by line. A line that differs from the outer theme's ends with "(changed)": what the inner theme changed, and what it took from the outer one, is read there.
features: **Only what is given changes.** The platform the app told its theme, the density, the language and its strings, the styles and the place events are reported to are the outer theme's in the inner one too.

**A dark or a light part.** A theme that is not given `darkTheme` is as dark as the theme around it, and keeps that theme's colours. Told to be dark inside a light theme, it takes the dark colours of the preset the outer theme is built on, or Pantrix's own dark set where there is no preset.
**Its own colours.** A part that is given `colors` is drawn with that set: it can be a set with a single role changed.

**The density is applied once.** `density` scales the spacing and the heights by the inner theme's density: not on top of the outer one's, but in its place. `Compact` does not make the touch target smaller.
**Language and reading direction.** In a part that is given `locale`, what the components say by themselves is in that language, and the reading direction is that language's.
**Events.** The components of a part that is given no `analytics` report their events to the place the outer theme gives.

**Preset.** `PantrixTheme(preset = …)` puts a part in a brand's look: the colours, the typography, the shapes and the component overrides are the preset's, and the rest the outer theme's. The part is as dark as the theme around it, whatever the system says.

**The dark the reader chose.** `rememberPantrixColors(preset, darkTheme)` gives the preset's light or dark set. The outermost theme makes Android's bars and iOS's status bar, keyboard and controls follow its own dark; an app that sets its bars itself gives it `followSystemBars = false`.
**A theme draws no ground.** A dark part's ground is drawn by a `PantrixSurface` or a card put inside the theme.
**A theme is not a layout.** What is inside it is laid out by the layout the theme stands in: as if the theme were not there.
api: com.pantrixui.foundation.theme.PantrixTheme(DesignPreset, PantrixColors, PantrixTypography, PantrixDensity, PantrixShapes, PantrixMotion, PantrixSpacing, PantrixElevation, PantrixPlatform, PantrixWindow, PantrixLayouts, ComponentTokenOverrides, PantrixStyles, PantrixLocale, PantrixStrings, TestTagPolicy, PantrixAnalytics, PantrixHaptics, PantrixDiagnostics, Boolean, @Composable () -> Unit)

com.pantrixui.foundation.theme.PantrixTheme(Boolean, PantrixColors, PantrixTypography, PantrixDensity, PantrixShapes, PantrixMotion, PantrixSpacing, PantrixElevation, PantrixPlatform, PantrixWindow, PantrixLayouts, ComponentTokenOverrides, PantrixStyles, PantrixLocale, PantrixStrings, TestTagPolicy, PantrixAnalytics, PantrixHaptics, PantrixDiagnostics, Boolean, @Composable () -> Unit)

examples.name: NestedThemeOppositeColors
examples.title: A part in the opposite colours
examples.description:
A part in the opposite colours to what is around it: dark in a light theme, light in a dark one. The inner theme is given only `darkTheme`; the density, the touch target and the language are the outer theme's. Look at the lines: only "Colours" has changed.

A theme draws no ground. The part's ground is drawn by the `PantrixSurface` inside it: in the inner theme's `surface` colour. The text, the checkbox and the lines read their colours from the inner theme too.

Turn the switch off: the part is told to be as dark as what is around it, the theme keeps the outer theme's colours, and no line changes.

examples.name: NestedThemeEvents
examples.title: Events that go to the outer theme
examples.description:
The outer theme was given only an `analytics` that counts the components' events. The lines are written inside it: the colours, the density and the language come from the app's theme, and none of them has changed.

The part inside it is a theme too, and it was given only `darkTheme`. Press "Save": the event goes from inside the part's theme to the outer theme's counter. The part's theme gives no `analytics`; it takes the outer one's.

examples.name: NestedThemeDensePart
examples.title: A compact part: only the density changes
examples.description:
The same controls, first at the page's density and then in a `Compact` part: for a compact table or a toolbar. The inner theme is given only `density`. Density scales the air: the spacing and the heights. The colours and the language are the outer theme's.

The density is applied once, not on top of the outer one: even while the app's density is "Spacious", the compact part's spacing is the spacing of `Compact`. Change the density in "Settings" and look at the lines.

The touch target stands apart: `Spacious` makes it larger, `Compact` does not make it smaller. The platform's value is a floor; in a compact part too, the place a finger presses gets no smaller.

examples.name: NestedThemeOtherLanguage
examples.title: A part in another language: the components' own texts change
examples.description:
A part in the language the app does not speak: English while the app is Turkish, Turkish while it is English. The inner theme is given only `locale`: what the components say by themselves ("Loading", "Close") is in that language. In the lines, the language and the component's own text have changed; the colours, the density and the rest are the outer theme's.

The theme does not translate the texts the app writes itself: the names of the lines stayed in the app's language.

examples.name: NestedThemeRightToLeft
examples.title: A right-to-left part
examples.description:
The reading direction comes from the language: the theme tells what is inside it the direction of the language it is given. `PantrixLocale.Arabic` is written from right to left; in this part the row starts on the right, and the "First" button stands there. The row and the buttons were given no direction: a component does not look at the language, it reads the direction from where the theme says it, Compose's `LocalLayoutDirection`.

The part's content is in a `Column` inside the theme. Because a theme is not a layout, it is the layouts inside it that read the direction: the column starts its rows from the right, and the row its buttons. The line at the bottom writes the theme's language and the reading direction at that point.

examples.name: NestedThemeOwnColors
examples.title: A part in its own colour
examples.description:
A theme that is given `colors` gives that set to what is inside it. Here the outer theme's colours are taken and only the `primary` role is replaced, by the app's own purple: `PantrixTheme.colors.copy(primary = …)`. The buttons and the chip in the part were given no colour; whatever reads `primary` gets the purple.

The density, the language and the rest are the outer theme's: the controls in the two rows differ only in their colours.

appNames.name: ownColors
appNames.description: The "app's own colour" of the examples: a purple that is in none of the theme's roles. It is there to show what changes when a component is given `colors`; given one of the theme's roles, nobody could tell whether the colour came from the component's tone or from the parameter.

examples.name: NestedThemeNoLayoutOfItsOwn
examples.title: A theme is not a layout
examples.description:
What the inner theme holds is laid out by the layout the theme stands in: the theme puts no box in between. "Next" and "Finish" are inside a theme, but they are children of the same `Row` as "Back"; they stand side by side, and the `Row` gives the gaps between them.

Only the inner theme's two buttons are compact.

examples.name: NestedThemePreset
examples.title: A brand's preset
examples.description:
A brand's look in one place: a `DesignPreset` gives its colours (light and dark), its type, its shapes and its component settings. `PantrixTheme(preset = Harbor)` puts the section in that brand; the rest, the language, the density, the events, is the outer theme's. The section is as dark as what is around it: on a dark page it is drawn in the brand's dark colours.

The brand's colours are read outside a theme too: `rememberPantrixColors(Harbor)` gives the brand's set as the system is light or dark, for the colour of a system bar or a notification. The line underneath is its primary colour.

appNames.name: Poppins
appNames.description: Poppins from the app's own files: seven weights, each a file of its own. It has no SemiBold: a text of that weight is drawn in a neighbouring one. Its licence, the SIL Open Font License 1.1, is beside the files: `files/licenses/poppins_ofl.txt`. The marks of a Mac's keys are drawn in the library's fallback.

examples.name: NestedThemeChosenDark
examples.title: The dark the reader chose
examples.description:
The reader chooses the dark or the light theme in the app's own setting: the preset's set in that dark is taken with `rememberPantrixColors(Harbor, darkTheme = dark)` and given to the theme. Whatever the system's mode says, the part is as dark as was chosen.

The outermost theme, at the app's root, makes what the system draws follow that choice too: Android's bars' icons, iOS's status bar, keyboard and controls. The theme here stands inside, and leaves the bars alone. An app that paints its bars itself gives its outermost theme `followSystemBars = false`.

appNames.name: Poppins
appNames.description: Poppins from the app's own files: seven weights, each a file of its own. It has no SemiBold: a text of that weight is drawn in a neighbouring one. Its licence, the SIL Open Font License 1.1, is beside the files: `files/licenses/poppins_ofl.txt`. The marks of a Mac's keys are drawn in the library's fallback.

examples.name: NestedThemeLocals
examples.title: The theme's locals
examples.description: Each of the theme's values is a `CompositionLocal`: `PantrixTheme.spacing` reads `LocalPantrixSpacing`, `PantrixTheme.colors` reads `LocalPantrixColors`. The lines read the same values straight from the locals. A preview or a test can also give one local on its own: the button underneath was drawn with `LocalPantrixShapes provides PantrixShapes.Pill`. In an app, the way to change a section is still a nested theme: a theme fits the values it gives to each other and scales the spacing by the density; a single local does not.

pages.title: Button
pages.summary: The button that starts an action: save, send, delete. It is the most pressed component of a screen, and on every platform it is drawn in that platform's own geometry: its corners are fully rounded on Android, desktop and the web, and medium rounded on iOS.
features: **Six variants.** `variant` says how prominent the button is: the one primary action on a screen is `Solid`, secondary actions are `Outline`, `Soft` and `Subtle`, tertiary actions are `Text`, and an action that cannot be undone is `Destructive`.

**Five sizes.** `size` picks the height, the padding and the label's text style together: from 24dp to 56dp, in steps of 8dp. The height is a minimum height: when the system's text size is made larger, the button grows with its label.
**Icons.** `leadingIcon` stands before the label and `trailingIcon` after it, and both take the label's colour.
**Loading.** `loading` shows a spinner in place of the leading icon and stops presses until the action is done.

**Form.** A press on a button given a `form` validates the form first: while a field is invalid `onClick` is not called, and that field takes the focus. While the form is being submitted, the button shows as loading by itself.

**In any role.** The default colour is the theme's `primary` role, and for `Destructive` the `danger` role; `PantrixColor.buttonColors(variant)` gives the same variant in another role, and `ButtonColors` gives it in a colour entirely its own.
**Content of its own.** There is a second `PantrixButton` that takes content instead of a label: a counter, two lines, a badge. In that one `contentDescription` is required.
**Accessibility.** `contentDescription` is read in place of the label, not after it: give one only where the label does not say what the button does, as a "+" does not.
api: com.pantrixui.components.elements.button.PantrixButton(String, () -> Unit, Modifier, ButtonVariant, ButtonSize, Boolean, Boolean, Boolean, (@Composable () -> Unit)?, (@Composable () -> Unit)?, ButtonStyle?, Shape, ButtonColors, String?, FormState?, String?, MutableInteractionSource?)

com.pantrixui.components.elements.button.PantrixButton(() -> Unit, String, Modifier, ButtonVariant, ButtonSize, Boolean, Boolean, Boolean, ButtonStyle?, Shape, ButtonColors, FormState?, String?, MutableInteractionSource?, @Composable RowScope.() -> Unit)

examples.name: ButtonVariants
examples.title: Variants
examples.description: `variant` picks the button's colour and how prominent it is. A screen has one `Solid`: the eye goes to it first. `Outline`, `Soft` and `Subtle` are secondary actions; `Text` is a tertiary action with no surface, like "Cancel". `Destructive` says the action cannot be undone, and is never the only button of a dialog.

examples.name: ButtonSizes
examples.title: Sizes
examples.description:
`size` picks one of five heights: 24, 32, 40, 48 and 56 dp. The default is `Medium`. The two ends are for particular places: `ExtraSmall` in a dense table row or beside a field, `ExtraLarge` for the single action a phone screen is built around.

The height is the button's minimum height. When the system's text size is made larger and the label becomes taller than the button, the button grows with it and the label is not cut.

examples.name: ButtonIcons
examples.title: Buttons with icons
examples.description: `leadingIcon` stands before the label and `trailingIcon` after it. The icon is given no colour: it takes the button's content colour by itself. Since it is decoration, its `contentDescription` is null; a screen reader reads the label alone.
examples.code:
FlowRow(
    horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.sm),
    verticalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.sm)
) {
    PantrixButton(
        text = "New folder",
        onClick = {},
        leadingIcon = { PantrixIcon(imageVector = PantrixIcons.Folder, contentDescription = null) },
        tagKey = "new_folder"
    )
    PantrixButton(
        text = "Continue",
        onClick = {},
        variant = ButtonVariant.Soft,
        trailingIcon = { PantrixIcon(imageVector = PantrixIcons.ArrowForward, contentDescription = null) },
        tagKey = "continue"
    )
    PantrixButton(
        text = "Refresh",
        onClick = {},
        variant = ButtonVariant.Outline,
        leadingIcon = { PantrixIcon(imageVector = PantrixIcons.Refresh, contentDescription = null) },
        tagKey = "refresh"
    )
}

examples.name: ButtonLoadingAndDisabled
examples.title: Loading and disabled
examples.description:
`loading` shows a spinner in place of the leading icon and stops presses until the action is done: the same action does not start twice. Press "Save": it shows as loading for two seconds, then the app's snackbar lets you know.

`enabled = false` draws the button faded, and the button takes no press. The two are not the same thing: a loading button says an action is under way, a disabled one that the action cannot be done right now.

examples.name: ButtonFullWidth
examples.title: Full width
examples.description: `fullWidth` stretches the button to the width of the space it is in: the submit button under a form, the two buttons of a sheet. Here the column is 360dp at most, and the buttons fill it.

examples.name: ButtonRolesAndOwnColors
examples.title: In another role and in a colour of its own
examples.description:
A variant's colours come from the theme's `primary` role, and `Destructive`'s from the `danger` role. `PantrixColor.buttonColors(variant)` gives the same variant in another role: the top row is four variants in the `success` role.

The colour of the button in the bottom row is in none of the theme's roles: `ButtonColors` takes the fill, the content's colour and, if wanted, the edge directly.
examples.code:
val success = PantrixTheme.colors.success
val own = ownColors()
FlowRow(
    horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.sm),
    verticalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.sm)
) {
    listOf(ButtonVariant.Solid, ButtonVariant.Soft, ButtonVariant.Outline, ButtonVariant.Text).forEach { variant ->
        PantrixButton(
            text = "Approve",
            onClick = {},
            colors = success.buttonColors(variant),
            tagKey = "confirm_${variant.name.lowercase()}"
        )
    }
}
PantrixButton(
    text = "Join the campaign",
    onClick = {},
    colors = ButtonColors(container = own.color, content = own.onColor),
    tagKey = "own_colors"
)

appNames.name: ownColors
appNames.description: The "app's own colour" of the examples: a purple that is in none of the theme's roles. It is there to show what changes when a component is given `colors`; given one of the theme's roles, nobody could tell whether the colour came from the component's tone or from the parameter.

examples.name: ButtonShapeAndStyle
examples.title: Shape and style
examples.description: `shape` changes the corners of one button: one of the theme's shapes, or any `Shape`. `style` changes the button's geometry: here, with `pressedScale`, a button that shrinks while it is pressed. Only the fields that are given change; the rest comes from the theme's and the platform's style.
examples.code:
FlowRow(
    horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.sm),
    verticalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.sm)
) {
    PantrixButton(text = "Square", onClick = {}, shape = PantrixTheme.shapes.none, tagKey = "square")
    PantrixButton(text = "Slightly rounded", onClick = {}, shape = PantrixTheme.shapes.sm, tagKey = "rounded")
    PantrixButton(text = "Fully rounded", onClick = {}, shape = PantrixTheme.shapes.full, tagKey = "pill")
    PantrixButton(
        text = "Shrinks when pressed",
        onClick = {},
        variant = ButtonVariant.Soft,
        style = ButtonStyle(pressedScale = 0.94f),
        tagKey = "press_scale"
    )
}

examples.name: ButtonOwnContent
examples.title: Content of its own
examples.description:
The `PantrixButton` that takes content instead of a label: the content is a row (`RowScope`) and is drawn in the button's content colour. Here a counter beside the label goes up with every press.

In this form `contentDescription` is required: whatever is in the button, a screen reader reads one sentence, "Like, 12 likes".

examples.name: ButtonSubmitsAForm
examples.title: A button that submits a form
examples.description:
A button given a `form` is the form's submit button. A press validates the form first: while the field is empty `onClick` is not called, and the field shows its error and takes the focus. If the form is valid, `form.submit` runs, and while it does the button shows as loading by itself: `loading` is not given separately.

Leave the field empty and press "Invite", then type a name and try again.

pages.title: Icon Button
pages.summary: A button that is only an icon: close, refresh, search. It is square, as tall as a `PantrixButton` of the same size, and fully round by default. As it has no label, `contentDescription` says what it does.
features: **Six variants.** `variant` picks the button's colours: they are `PantrixButton`'s variants. The default is `ButtonVariant.Text`: it has no surface, and is for the actions in a toolbar.
**Five sizes.** `size` picks the button's side and its icon's size together: the button from 24dp to 56dp, its icon from 16dp to 32dp.
**Touch target.** As much room as the platform's minimum touch target is kept around the button: a button that is drawn small can be pressed with a finger too.
**Shape.** It is fully round on every platform; `shape` gives it one of the theme's shapes, or any `Shape`.
**Description.** `contentDescription` is the name a screen reader reads, and it names the action, not the icon: "Close", not "cross".

**A button without a description.** Null is given only to a button that repeats what something a screen reader and the keyboard already reach does. Such a button is hidden from the reader and is no stop for the keyboard; a mouse and a finger still press it.
**Its own content.** There is a second `PantrixIconButton` that takes content in place of an icon: an icon with a badge, an animated icon. A screen reader hears the description alone.

**Colours.** By default `colors` is the variant's colours in the `primary` role, and for `Destructive` in the `danger` role; `PantrixColor.buttonColors(variant)` gives them in another role, and `ButtonColors` in a colour entirely its own.
**Disabled.** `enabled = false` draws the button faded, and the button takes no press. A variant with no fill stays without one when disabled.
api: com.pantrixui.components.elements.iconbutton.PantrixIconButton(ImageVector, String?, () -> Unit, Modifier, ButtonVariant, ButtonSize, Boolean, Shape, ButtonColors, String?, MutableInteractionSource?, ButtonStyle?)

com.pantrixui.components.elements.iconbutton.PantrixIconButton(String?, () -> Unit, Modifier, ButtonVariant, ButtonSize, Boolean, Shape, ButtonColors, String?, MutableInteractionSource?, ButtonStyle?, @Composable () -> Unit)

examples.name: IconButtonPlain
examples.title: At its plainest
examples.description:
The least it takes: an icon, a description that says what it does, and the action to run when it is pressed. Its variant is `Text` and its size `Medium`: a round button of 40dp with no fill.

Press the button: the line under it says how many times it was pressed. As it has no fill, the button's circle shows while it is pressed and while the keyboard focus is on it.
examples.code:
var refreshed by rememberSaveable { mutableIntStateOf(0) }
PantrixIconButton(
    imageVector = PantrixIcons.Refresh,
    contentDescription = "Refresh",
    onClick = { refreshed += 1 },
    tagKey = "refresh"
)
PantrixText(
    text = "Times refreshed: $refreshed",
    color = PantrixTheme.colors.textSecondary,
    tagKey = "refreshed"
)

examples.name: IconButtonVariants
examples.title: Variants
examples.description:
`variant` picks the button's colours; all six are `PantrixButton`'s variants. `Solid` is the main action on a screen, `Outline`, `Soft` and `Subtle` are secondary actions, and `Destructive` says the action cannot be undone.

The default is `Text`: it has no surface, and only its icon is drawn. It is for the actions in a toolbar.

examples.name: IconButtonSizes
examples.title: Sizes
examples.description:
`size` picks one of five sizes: the button is a square of 24, 32, 40, 48 or 56 dp, and its icon is 16, 20, 24, 28 or 32 dp. The default is `Medium`. Beside a `PantrixButton` of the same size, the two are the same height.

The room around the small buttons is the touch target: a button is drawn small but takes up as much room as the platform's minimum touch target. That is 48dp on Android, 44dp on iOS, and 32dp on desktop and the web when they are used with a mouse.

examples.name: IconButtonShapeAndStyle
examples.title: Shape and style
examples.description:
An icon button is fully round on every platform. `shape` changes that: the second button has the theme's medium roundness (`shapes.md`), and the third has square corners (`shapes.none`).

`style` changes the button's dimensions: an icon button reads only the sizes of `ButtonStyle`. The last button is still `Medium`, but its icon is drawn at 16dp instead of 24dp. Only the field that is set changes, and the rest comes from the theme's style.
examples.code:
Row(
    horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.sm),
    verticalAlignment = Alignment.CenterVertically
) {
    PantrixIconButton(
        imageVector = PantrixIcons.Folder,
        contentDescription = "Fully round button",
        onClick = {},
        variant = ButtonVariant.Soft,
        tagKey = "pill"
    )
    PantrixIconButton(
        imageVector = PantrixIcons.Folder,
        contentDescription = "Slightly round button",
        onClick = {},
        variant = ButtonVariant.Soft,
        shape = PantrixTheme.shapes.md,
        tagKey = "rounded"
    )
    PantrixIconButton(
        imageVector = PantrixIcons.Folder,
        contentDescription = "Square-cornered button",
        onClick = {},
        variant = ButtonVariant.Soft,
        shape = PantrixTheme.shapes.none,
        tagKey = "square"
    )
    PantrixIconButton(
        imageVector = PantrixIcons.Folder,
        contentDescription = "Button with a small icon",
        onClick = {},
        variant = ButtonVariant.Soft,
        style = ButtonStyle(medium = ButtonSizeStyle(iconSize = 16.dp)),
        tagKey = "small_icon"
    )
}

examples.name: IconButtonDisabled
examples.title: Disabled
examples.description: `enabled = false` draws the button faded, and the button takes no press. A variant with a fill takes the theme's disabled fill; `Text` and `Outline`, which have no fill, stay without one when disabled, and do not turn into a grey shape.

examples.name: IconButtonRolesAndOwnColors
examples.title: In another role and in a colour of its own
examples.description:
A variant's colours come from the theme's `primary` role, and `Destructive`'s from the `danger` role. `PantrixColor.buttonColors(variant)` gives the same variant in another role: the first two buttons are in the `success` and `danger` roles.

The last button's colour is in none of the theme's roles: `ButtonColors` takes the fill and the icon's colour directly. The icon is given no colour of its own: it takes the button's content colour by itself.
examples.code:
val colors = PantrixTheme.colors
val own = ownColors()
Row(horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.sm)) {
    PantrixIconButton(
        imageVector = PantrixIcons.Check,
        contentDescription = "Approve",
        onClick = {},
        colors = colors.success.buttonColors(ButtonVariant.Soft),
        tagKey = "approve"
    )
    PantrixIconButton(
        imageVector = PantrixIcons.Close,
        contentDescription = "Reject",
        onClick = {},
        colors = colors.danger.buttonColors(ButtonVariant.Outline),
        tagKey = "reject"
    )
    PantrixIconButton(
        imageVector = PantrixIcons.Star,
        contentDescription = "Add to collection",
        onClick = {},
        colors = ButtonColors(container = own.color, content = own.onColor),
        tagKey = "own_colors"
    )
}

appNames.name: ownColors
appNames.description: The "app's own colour" of the examples: a purple that is in none of the theme's roles. It is there to show what changes when a component is given `colors`; given one of the theme's roles, nobody could tell whether the colour came from the component's tone or from the parameter.

examples.name: IconButtonOwnContent
examples.title: Its own content: an icon with a badge
examples.description:
The `PantrixIconButton` that takes content in place of an icon: here an icon with a badge at its corner. The content is drawn in the button's content colour.

What is in the button is a picture of what the description says: a screen reader hears the description alone. So the badge's count is written in the description, "Inbox, 3 unread"; the badge itself is not read. "New message" raises the count, and a press on the icon button resets it.

examples.name: IconButtonWithoutADescription
examples.title: A button without a description
examples.description:
`contentDescription = null` is given only to a button that repeats what something else already does. Here the whole card is pressed and opens the order; the arrow at its end does the same thing and is a sign for the eye alone.

Such a button is hidden from screen readers and is no stop for the keyboard: a stop on something the reader will never read is worse than no stop at all. A mouse and a finger still press it. A button that is the only way to its action always has a description.

pages.title: Button Group
pages.summary:
A few actions of the same rank, drawn as one control or side by side with the same gap between them: a toolbar, a stepper, the two buttons under a dialog.

The group chooses nothing and none of its buttons stays selected. Where one of several options stays selected, use a segment button: it says which one is selected.
features: **Attached or apart.** With `attached` on, which is its default, the buttons touch: the group has one shape, one edge around it and a line between each two buttons. With it off, the same buttons stand with a gap between them, each with its own shape and edge.
**Row or column.** `orientation` lays the buttons out side by side or one under another. In a column they are all as wide as the widest.

**Width.** In a row each button is as wide as what it says. In a narrow space the short ones stay whole and the long ones share what is left; with `equalWidth` they all share the group's width equally.
**A label or an icon alone.** `GroupButton` has two constructors: a label, with or without an icon before it; or an icon alone. For a button that is an icon alone, `contentDescription` is required.
**Each button is a button.** Tab stops at each of them, a screen reader says the name and the role of each, and each draws its own focus ring and reports its own press.
**A button's own state.** `enabled`, `loading`, `variant` and `colors` can be given to each `GroupButton` separately. The group's `variant`, `size`, `colors` and `enabled` are for all the buttons.
**Touch target.** An attached group reserves the platform's touch target once, around itself; each of its buttons is at least that long along the group.

**Automation.** The buttons are named inside the group's tag: `ButtonGroup_clipboard.Button_copy`. A button that is an icon alone is tagged as an `IconButton`, and a button without a key by its index.

examples.name: ButtonGroupToolbar
examples.title: An attached toolbar
examples.description:
Its shortest form: a list of buttons. The group is attached and its variant is `Outline`: there is one edge around it and a line between each two buttons, and the corners are only at the group's two ends.

The first button has an icon before its label; the last is an icon alone and says what it does with `contentDescription`. Each button is a button in its own right: Tab stops at each of them, and a screen reader says the name of each. Press a button: the line below names the last action.
examples.code:
var last by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf<String?>(null) }
PantrixButtonGroup(
    buttons = listOf(
        GroupButton(text = "Copy", onClick = { last = "Copy" }, icon = PantrixIcons.Copy, tagKey = "copy"),
        GroupButton(text = "Paste", onClick = { last = "Paste" }, tagKey = "paste"),
        GroupButton(
            icon = PantrixIcons.MoreHorizontal,
            contentDescription = "More actions",
            onClick = { last = "More actions" },
            tagKey = "more"
        )
    ),
    tagKey = "clipboard"
)
PantrixText(
    text = last?.let { "Last action: $it" } ?: "No action pressed yet",
    style = PantrixTheme.typography.footnote,
    color = PantrixTheme.colors.textSecondary,
    tagKey = "clipboard_result"
)

examples.name: ButtonGroupStepper
examples.title: A stepper of icons alone
examples.description:
A stepper made of icons alone, in the `Soft` variant. A button that is an icon alone is written with the second constructor of `GroupButton`, and there `contentDescription` is required: a button is never decoration.

`enabled` is given to each button separately: at the lower limit the minus button cannot be pressed, and the plus button can.

examples.name: ButtonGroupDescribedLabels
examples.title: Labels read by their description
examples.description: Two buttons that change the text size. Their labels are "A-" and "A+": enough for someone who sees them, but they mean nothing in a screen reader. So each has a `contentDescription`, and the screen reader reads the description alone, not the label: "Make text smaller", "Make text larger".

examples.name: ButtonGroupVariants
examples.title: Variants
examples.description: `variant` is the variant of every button that has none of its own; when it is not given, it is `Outline`. In the variants that have an edge, `Outline` and `Subtle`, there is one edge around the group and the lines between the buttons are in its colour. In those without an edge, only the lines between the buttons are drawn.
examples.code:
listOf(
    ButtonVariant.Outline,
    ButtonVariant.Subtle,
    ButtonVariant.Soft,
    ButtonVariant.Solid,
    ButtonVariant.Text
).forEach { variant ->
    PantrixButtonGroup(
        buttons = listOf(
            GroupButton(text = "Previous", onClick = {}, tagKey = "previous"),
            GroupButton(text = "Next", onClick = {}, tagKey = "next")
        ),
        variant = variant,
        tagKey = "variant_${variant.name}"
    )
}

examples.name: ButtonGroupSizes
examples.title: Sizes
examples.description: `size` is the size of every button in the group, so that they all line up: here `Small`, `Medium` and `Large`. When it is not given, it is `Medium`.
examples.code:
listOf(ButtonSize.Small, ButtonSize.Medium, ButtonSize.Large).forEach { size ->
    PantrixButtonGroup(
        buttons = listOf(
            GroupButton(text = "Cut", onClick = {}, tagKey = "cut"),
            GroupButton(text = "Copy", onClick = {}, tagKey = "copy"),
            GroupButton(text = "Paste", onClick = {}, tagKey = "paste")
        ),
        size = size,
        tagKey = "size_${size.name}"
    )
}

examples.name: ButtonGroupColumn
examples.title: A column of actions
examples.description:
`orientation = Orientation.Vertical` lays the buttons out one under another: they are all as wide as the widest. In an attached column the corners are at the top and the bottom of the group, and the lines between the buttons are horizontal.

The action that deletes carries its own variant: on that button the `variant` of `GroupButton` takes the place of the group's.
examples.code:
PantrixButtonGroup(
    buttons = listOf(
        GroupButton(text = "Rename", onClick = {}, tagKey = "rename"),
        GroupButton(text = "Duplicate", onClick = {}, tagKey = "duplicate"),
        GroupButton(text = "Delete", onClick = {}, variant = ButtonVariant.Destructive, tagKey = "delete")
    ),
    orientation = Orientation.Vertical,
    tagKey = "record"
)

examples.name: ButtonGroupApartAndEqual
examples.title: Apart and of equal width
examples.description:
The two actions under a dialog. With `attached = false` they stand apart, each with its own shape and edge, with the style's gap between them. With `equalWidth = true` they share the group's width equally; here the group is 360dp wide at most.

`loading` is the button's own state: when "Delete" is pressed it shows as loading for a short while and cannot be pressed in the meantime. "Cancel" stops the loading.

examples.name: ButtonGroupNarrowRoom
examples.title: In a narrow space
examples.description:
The same three buttons, twice, in a space 280dp wide. In a row each button is as wide as what it says; where there is not enough room the short ones stay whole and the long one takes what is left, its label cut off with an ellipsis.

The second group has `equalWidth = true`: the three buttons share the width equally, and the long label is cut off sooner.
examples.code:
PantrixButtonGroup(
    buttons = listOf(
        GroupButton(text = "Save", onClick = {}, tagKey = "save"),
        GroupButton(text = "Exit without saving and delete the draft", onClick = {}, tagKey = "discard"),
        GroupButton(text = "Cancel", onClick = {}, tagKey = "cancel")
    ),
    modifier = Modifier.width(280.dp),
    tagKey = "narrow"
)
PantrixButtonGroup(
    buttons = listOf(
        GroupButton(text = "Save", onClick = {}, tagKey = "save"),
        GroupButton(text = "Exit without saving and delete the draft", onClick = {}, tagKey = "discard"),
        GroupButton(text = "Cancel", onClick = {}, tagKey = "cancel")
    ),
    modifier = Modifier.width(280.dp),
    equalWidth = true,
    tagKey = "narrow_equal"
)

examples.name: ButtonGroupRoleColors
examples.title: In a role's colours
examples.description: `colors` draws the group's buttons in the given colours instead of a variant's `primary` colours. Here `PantrixColor.buttonColors(ButtonVariant.Outline)` gives the outlined button colours of the `success` role. In an attached group the colour given for the edge is the colour of the group's one edge and of the lines between the buttons.
examples.code:
PantrixButtonGroup(
    buttons = listOf(
        GroupButton(text = "Approve", onClick = {}, icon = PantrixIcons.Check, tagKey = "approve"),
        GroupButton(text = "Approve all", onClick = {}, tagKey = "approve_all")
    ),
    colors = PantrixTheme.colors.success.buttonColors(ButtonVariant.Outline),
    tagKey = "review"
)

examples.name: ButtonGroupOwnColors
examples.title: In its own colour
examples.description:
The first group's colour is in none of the theme's roles: `ButtonColors` takes the fill, the content's colour and the edge directly.

In the second group only one button has a colour of its own. On that button the `colors` of `GroupButton` take the place of the group's colours and of its own variant; the button still stands inside the group's edge.
examples.code:
val own = ownColors()
PantrixButtonGroup(
    buttons = listOf(
        GroupButton(text = "Add to collection", onClick = {}, icon = PantrixIcons.Star, tagKey = "collect"),
        GroupButton(text = "Share", onClick = {}, tagKey = "share")
    ),
    colors = ButtonColors(container = own.container, content = own.onContainer, border = own.color),
    tagKey = "own_colors"
)
PantrixButtonGroup(
    buttons = listOf(
        GroupButton(text = "Edit", onClick = {}, tagKey = "edit"),
        GroupButton(
            text = "Feature",
            onClick = {},
            colors = ButtonColors(container = own.color, content = own.onColor),
            tagKey = "feature"
        )
    ),
    tagKey = "one_own_button"
)

appNames.name: ownColors
appNames.description: The "app's own colour" of the examples: a purple that is in none of the theme's roles. It is there to show what changes when a component is given `colors`; given one of the theme's roles, nobody could tell whether the colour came from the component's tone or from the parameter.

examples.name: ButtonGroupShapeAndStyle
examples.title: Shape and style
examples.description:
In an attached group `shape` is the shape of the whole group: each button carries only the corners at its own end. In a group whose buttons stand apart it is the shape of each button. The first group was drawn in the theme's slightly rounded shape (`shapes.sm`).

`style` changes the group's geometry: in the second group `ButtonGroupStyle(gap = 16.dp)` widens the gap between the buttons that stand apart. The buttons' sizes come from the button's own style, not from the group's.
examples.code:
PantrixButtonGroup(
    buttons = listOf(
        GroupButton(text = "Print", onClick = {}, tagKey = "print"),
        GroupButton(text = "Export", onClick = {}, tagKey = "export"),
        GroupButton(text = "Share", onClick = {}, tagKey = "share")
    ),
    shape = PantrixTheme.shapes.sm,
    tagKey = "less_round"
)
PantrixButtonGroup(
    buttons = listOf(
