        GroupButton(text = "Back", onClick = {}, tagKey = "back"),
        GroupButton(text = "Next", onClick = {}, tagKey = "forward")
    ),
    attached = false,
    style = ButtonGroupStyle(gap = 16.dp),
    tagKey = "wide_gap"
)

examples.name: ButtonGroupDisabled
examples.title: A disabled group
examples.description: The group's `enabled = false` disables every button: none of them takes a press, and their labels and the group's edge are drawn faded.
examples.code:
PantrixButtonGroup(
    buttons = listOf(
        GroupButton(text = "Undo", onClick = {}, tagKey = "undo"),
        GroupButton(text = "Redo", onClick = {}, tagKey = "redo")
    ),
    enabled = false,
    tagKey = "locked"
)

pages.title: Link
pages.summary: A link on its own: not a word inside a sentence, but a text by itself. It runs an action or opens a web page: the "Forgot my password" under a sign-in form, the "Privacy policy" at the bottom of a page. It is underlined, and in the theme's `primary` colour.
features: **Two overloads.** A link that takes `onClick` runs an action. One that takes `url` opens the address with the platform's `UriHandler`: in the browser, or in the app that handles the address.

**Underlined.** A link is not told apart by its colour alone: someone who cannot tell the two colours apart knows it by the line under it. A link that stands in no sentence and is known by its place takes `underline = LinkUnderline.OnHover`: it is underlined under a pointer and while it holds the focus, and always where the platform is used by touch.

**Its own colour.** `color` sets the text, the underline, and the tint that appears under the link while a pointer is over it or it is pressed. Left out, it is the theme's `primary` colour, on a fill too: there the caller gives the colour that reads.
**Text style.** Left out, `style` is the theme's `label` style, the style of a `PantrixText` given none: a link beside a text is as large as that text.

**Touch target.** It is never shorter than the platform's minimum touch target: 48dp on Android, 44dp on iOS, and 32dp on desktop and the web when they are used with a mouse. It is as wide as its text, and starts where a text above it starts.
**Disabled.** `enabled = false` draws the link in the theme's disabled text colour, and the link takes no press. It keeps its underline: it reads as a link that cannot be followed, not as plain text.

**Mouse and keyboard.** While a pointer is over the link and while it is pressed, a faint tint in the link's colour appears under its text. The link takes the keyboard focus too: with the focus, that tint is in the focus ring's colour.
**Analytics.** Every click is reported to the theme's `analytics` as the `Link` component's `click` event. The event says whether the link opens an address, and never the address itself.
**Automation.** `tagKey` sets the test tag: a link given `tagKey = "forgot_password"` has the tag `Link_forgot_password`.
api: com.pantrixui.components.elements.link.PantrixLink(String, () -> Unit, Modifier, TextStyle, Color, Boolean, String?, LinkUnderline)
com.pantrixui.components.elements.link.PantrixLink(String, String, Modifier, TextStyle, Color, Boolean, String?, LinkUnderline)

examples.name: LinkRunsAnAction
examples.title: A link that runs an action
examples.description:
At its plainest: a text and an `onClick` that runs when it is pressed. The link is written underlined, in the theme's `primary` colour. Press "Forgot my password": the app's snackbar lets you know.

It is given a `tagKey`: automation finds this link by the tag `Link_forgot_password`.
examples.code:
val snackbars = LocalPantrixSnackbars.current
val scope = rememberCoroutineScope()
PantrixLink(
    text = "Forgot my password",
    onClick = { scope.launch { snackbars?.show(message = "Reset link sent") } },
    tagKey = "forgot_password"
)

examples.name: LinkOpensAnAddress
examples.title: A link that opens an address
examples.description: The second overload takes `url` in place of `onClick`. When it is pressed the address is opened with the platform's `UriHandler`: in the browser, or in the app that handles the address. Its look and its other parameters are the same as the first overload's.
examples.code: PantrixLink(text = "Privacy policy", url = "https://example.com/privacy", tagKey = "privacy_policy")

examples.name: LinkOwnColor
examples.title: In its own colour
examples.description: `color` is the link's own colour: it sets its text, its underline, and the tint that appears under it when a pointer comes over it or presses it. The first link's colour is the app's own purple, which is in none of the theme's roles; the second's is the theme's `danger` role.
examples.code:
val snackbars = LocalPantrixSnackbars.current
val scope = rememberCoroutineScope()
val own = ownColors()
Row(horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.xl)) {
    PantrixLink(
        text = "Campaign terms",
        onClick = { scope.launch { snackbars?.show(message = "Campaign terms opened") } },
        color = own.color,
        tagKey = "campaign_terms"
    )
    PantrixLink(
        text = "Delete my account",
        onClick = {},
        color = PantrixTheme.colors.danger.color,
        tagKey = "delete_account"
    )
}

appNames.name: ownColors
appNames.description: The "app's own colour" of the examples: a purple that is in none of the theme's roles. It is there to show what changes when a component is given `colors`; given one of the theme's roles, nobody could tell whether the colour came from the component's tone or from the parameter.

examples.name: LinkOnAFill
examples.title: On a fill
examples.description:
A link does not look at the content colour around it: given no colour, it is in the theme's `primary` colour on a fill too. Where the fill is `primary` itself, that colour cannot be read; the caller gives the colour that reads there with `color`, here the role's `onColor`.

The `PantrixText` beside it is given no colour: it takes the fill's content colour by itself.

examples.name: LinkTextStyle
examples.title: Beside a text, and its text style
examples.description:
A link given no `style` is in the theme's `label` style, like a `PantrixText` given no style: in the top row the two stand side by side, at the same size.

The link below is given `style = PantrixTheme.typography.footnote`: the small link under a form. Though its text is smaller, the link is never shorter than the platform's touch target; it is as wide as its text, and starts where the row above it starts.

examples.name: LinkRowOfLinks
examples.title: Links in a row
examples.description:
Links that do not stand in a sentence: the row at a page's foot. Where they stand already says they are links; with `underline = LinkUnderline.OnHover` they are underlined only under a pointer and while they hold the keyboard's focus.

Where the platform is used by touch there is neither: on Android and iOS these links too are underlined always. A link inside a sentence stays at the default, `LinkUnderline.Always`: its colour alone does not reach whoever cannot tell it apart.

examples.name: LinkTouchTarget
examples.title: Touch target
examples.description:
The area a link takes up is painted here. It is at least as tall as the platform's touch target: 48dp on Android, 44dp on iOS, and 32dp on desktop and the web when they are used with a mouse. It is as wide as its text.

The second link is in the `caption` style: the text is smaller, and the area stays as tall. A touch just beside a short link reaches it too.
examples.code:
val area = PantrixTheme.colors.neutral.container
Row(horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.xl)) {
    PantrixLink(text = "Help", onClick = {}, modifier = Modifier.background(area), tagKey = "help_body")
    PantrixLink(
        text = "Help",
        onClick = {},
        modifier = Modifier.background(area),
        style = PantrixTheme.typography.caption,
        tagKey = "help_caption"
    )
}

examples.name: LinkDisabled
examples.title: Disabled
examples.description:
`enabled = false` draws the link in the theme's disabled text colour, and the link takes no press. It keeps its underline: without it, it would read as plain text. Press "Resend code": the link is disabled for five seconds.

The second link is given a `color` as well. A disabled link is in the theme's disabled colour whatever is given.

appNames.name: ownColors
appNames.description: The "app's own colour" of the examples: a purple that is in none of the theme's roles. It is there to show what changes when a component is given `colors`; given one of the theme's roles, nobody could tell whether the colour came from the component's tone or from the parameter.

examples.name: LinkReportsItsClick
examples.title: Reporting a click
examples.description:
Every click is reported to the theme's `analytics` as an event: its component is `Link` and its action `click`. The event's `external` value says whether the link ran an action (`false`) or opened an address (`true`); the address itself is not in the event.

The two links here are inside a theme that is given only `analytics`: the last event to arrive is written under them. Press one.

pages.title: Text
pages.summary:
A text in the theme's type scale: a paragraph, a heading, a label. `style` says how the text is set, and `role` what a screen reader hears it as: they are two things, and neither stands in for the other.

The text is set in the size its style says; what does not fit its room is cut. A text that has to get smaller to fit is `PantrixAutoText`.
features: **Type scale.** `style` takes one of the theme's nine styles: eight from `display` down to `caption`, largest to smallest, and the monospace `code`. A text given no style is set in the `label` style.

**Role.** `role` says what the text is: prose (`Paragraph`, the default), a heading (`Heading`), a label (`Label`) or decoration (`Decorative`). A user who moves from heading to heading with a screen reader does not stop at a text that is set like a heading but not marked as one.

**Colour.** In order: `color`, the style's own colour, the content colour of where the text stands, the theme's `textPrimary`. On the page, on a surface and on a card a text is drawn in `textPrimary`; on a fill it takes the colour that reads there by itself.
**Lines and overflow.** `maxLines` says the most lines the text takes, and `minLines` the least. What does not fit is cut as `overflow` says: with an ellipsis by default.
**Alignment.** `textAlign` aligns the lines within the text's own width.
**Selectable text.** With `selectable` the user can select the text and copy it.

**Styled text.** There is a second `PantrixText` that takes an `AnnotatedString`: parts of a sentence that are bold, coloured or of another size, links, and an icon placed inside the line with `inlineContent`.
**Automation.** A text given a `tagKey` carries the tag `Text_<tagKey>`. A text given no key is not tagged.
api: com.pantrixui.components.elements.text.PantrixText(String, Modifier, TextStyle, Color, TextAlign?, Int, Int, TextOverflow, Boolean, TextRole, Boolean, ((TextLayoutResult) -> Unit)?, String?)

com.pantrixui.components.elements.text.PantrixText(AnnotatedString, Modifier, TextStyle, Color, TextAlign?, Int, Int, TextOverflow, Boolean, TextRole, Boolean, Map<String, InlineTextContent>, ((TextLayoutResult) -> Unit)?, String?)

examples.name: TextWithoutAStyle
examples.title: A text given no style
examples.description:
The least there is to write: the text alone. Given no style, it is set in the theme's `label` style; given no colour, it is drawn in the theme's `textPrimary` colour. The second line is the same text with the `label` style given outright: the two are the same.

`label` is the style of a control's label. Giving a paragraph `body`, or a heading `title` or `headline`, is up to you: the third line is set in `body`.
examples.code:
PantrixText(text = "Your order is on its way", tagKey = "no_style")
PantrixText(text = "Your order is on its way", style = PantrixTheme.typography.label)
PantrixText(text = "Your order is on its way", style = PantrixTheme.typography.body)

examples.name: TextTypeScale
examples.title: Type scale
examples.description:
The theme's nine styles, largest to smallest: each line is set in its own style and says what that style is for. A style carries the type's size, its line height, its weight and its letter spacing together.

`code` is set in a monospace face. The styles' metrics are written on the "Typography" page, read from the theme.
examples.code:
val typography = PantrixTheme.typography
PantrixText(text = "display: the page's title", style = typography.display)
PantrixText(text = "headline: a section heading", style = typography.headline)
PantrixText(text = "title: the title of a card, a panel, a dialog", style = typography.title)
PantrixText(text = "callout: emphasised body text, the description of an empty screen", style = typography.callout)
PantrixText(text = "body: body text, a paragraph, a description", style = typography.body)
PantrixText(text = "label: a control's label, a text given no style", style = typography.label)
PantrixText(text = "footnote: supporting text, the description under a field", style = typography.footnote)
PantrixText(text = "caption: a small detail, a time, a counter", style = typography.caption)
PantrixText(text = "code: order_id = 8F2A-19C4", style = typography.code)

examples.name: TextRoles
examples.title: Roles
examples.description:
`role` says what the text is; `style` says how it looks. `TextRole.Heading` reports the text to a screen reader as a heading: a user who moves from heading to heading with the screen reader stops at it. `level` is the heading's depth: 1 for the page's title, 2 for its sections. A text set large and bold but given no role is plain prose to a screen reader.

`Paragraph` and `Label` are read as they are. A `Decorative` text is hidden from the screen reader and its words are never read: it is for text that repeats what something else already says. Here the large "%72" is a picture of the sentence under it; the screen reader reads only the sentence.
examples.code:
val typography = PantrixTheme.typography
PantrixText(
    text = "Account",
    style = typography.headline,
    role = TextRole.Heading(level = 1),
    tagKey = "heading_account"
)
PantrixText(
    text = "Storage",
    style = typography.title,
    role = TextRole.Heading(level = 2),
    tagKey = "heading_storage"
)
PantrixText(text = "%72", style = typography.display, role = TextRole.Decorative, tagKey = "share")
PantrixText(text = "72 per cent of the storage is full.", style = typography.body)
Row(horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.sm)) {
    PantrixText(text = "Plan", role = TextRole.Label)
    PantrixText(text = "Monthly, 50 GB", color = PantrixTheme.colors.textSecondary)
}

examples.name: TextColours
examples.title: Colour, and the colour of where it stands
examples.description:
On the page, a text given no colour is drawn in the theme's `textPrimary` colour. `color` changes that: `textSecondary` for a secondary detail, the `danger` role's colour for an error.

On a fill, still no colour is given. When a `PantrixSurface` is filled with a role's colour, the text inside takes the colour that reads on that fill by itself: `primary.onColor` in the first box, `success.onContainer` in the second. The theme's own surface is not a fill but a ground: the text in the third box is drawn in `textPrimary` again.

examples.name: TextMaxLinesAndOverflow
examples.title: Maximum lines and overflow
examples.description: The same paragraph three times, in a column at most 320dp wide. The first takes as many lines as it wants. The second stays at two lines with `maxLines = 2`, and what does not fit ends in an ellipsis: the default of `overflow` is `TextOverflow.Ellipsis`. The third is one line and, with `TextOverflow.Clip`, is cut without an ellipsis.
examples.code:
val paragraph = "Your order has been shipped. It will reach the delivery address tomorrow between 09:00 and 18:00; the courier " +
    "will call you before coming to the door."
Column(
    modifier = Modifier.widthIn(max = 320.dp),
    verticalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.md)
) {
    PantrixText(text = paragraph, style = PantrixTheme.typography.body)
    PantrixText(text = paragraph, style = PantrixTheme.typography.body, maxLines = 2, tagKey = "two_lines")
    PantrixText(
        text = paragraph,
        style = PantrixTheme.typography.body,
        maxLines = 1,
        overflow = TextOverflow.Clip,
        tagKey = "clipped"
    )
}

examples.name: TextMinLines
examples.title: Minimum lines
examples.description: `minLines` makes even a short text take the room of that many lines. The titles of the two boxes that stand side by side are set with `minLines = 2` and `maxLines = 2`: one fits on one line and the other is longer than two, but both take two lines of room. So the prices under them line up, and the boxes are the same height.

examples.name: TextAlignment
examples.title: Alignment
examples.description: `textAlign` aligns the lines within the text's own width. That is why the texts are given `fillMaxWidth()`: a text only as wide as its words has no room to align them in.
examples.code:
PantrixText(text = "Aligned to the start", modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(), textAlign = TextAlign.Start)
PantrixText(text = "Centred", modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(), textAlign = TextAlign.Center)
PantrixText(text = "Aligned to the end", modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(), textAlign = TextAlign.End)

examples.name: TextSelectable
examples.title: Selectable text
examples.description:
With `selectable = true` the user can select the text and copy it. It is for text that will be taken somewhere else: an order number, an IBAN, an error code. A screen reader reads it as it reads any other text.

Try to select the number on the second line; the label above it cannot be selected.
examples.code:
PantrixText(text = "Order number", style = PantrixTheme.typography.footnote, role = TextRole.Label)
PantrixText(
    text = "PX-2026-0001-8F2A-19C4",
    style = PantrixTheme.typography.code,
    selectable = true,
    tagKey = "order_number"
)

examples.name: TextAnnotated
examples.title: Styled text
examples.description:
The `PantrixText` that takes an `AnnotatedString`: parts styled differently inside one text. Its style, its colour, its lines and its role are the same as a plain text's.

In the first line the decimal part of the amount is set at `0.6.em`: an `em` is a share of the size of the text around it. In the second line one part is bold, and one is in the `danger` role's colour. The third line has a link; it is underlined, because someone who cannot tell colours apart cannot see a link that differs from its sentence by colour alone. Press the link: the app's snackbar reports it.

examples.name: TextInlineContent
examples.title: An icon inside the line
examples.description:
`inlineContent` puts something that is not text inside the line. A place is kept in the text with `appendInlineContent`; `inlineContent` says, for that place's key, what is drawn there and how much room it takes. Here there is an icon in the middle of the sentence: it stands on the same line as the words.

The second value of `appendInlineContent` is what stands for that place in the text: a screen reader reads the icon by this word.

pages.title: Auto Text
pages.summary:
Text that gets smaller to stay in view: an amount, a title, a name. It is as large as its style says while it fits its room; when it does not, it goes down to the largest size in which all of it is in view, and it grows back as it is shortened.

In everything else it is `PantrixText`: the theme's type scale, the colour of where it sits, the role it tells a screen reader.
features: **One line.** The text is one line unless told (`maxLines = 1`), and is fitted to the width it is given.

**More than one line.** With a larger `maxLines` the text wraps first, and is set smaller when its lines run out. The lines of a text that is set smaller are as much closer: the line height follows the text's size.
**Text that fits its box.** `maxLines = Int.MAX_VALUE` leaves the lines to the height: the text is fitted to the width and the height it is given, both at once.

**The smallest size.** At `minFontSize` the text stops shrinking, and what does not fit is cut as `overflow` says. It is the theme's `footnote` size unless given; it is given in `sp`, or in `em` as a share of the style's size.

**A room to fit.** The text has to be given a width: `fillMaxWidth()`, a `weight` or a size; and a height too, where it may take any number of lines. A text that is offered all the width it wants never shrinks.
**Styled text.** There is a second `PantrixAutoText`, which takes an `AnnotatedString`. A span's size given in `em` shrinks with the text; one given in `sp` is kept as it is.
**In the first frame.** The size is found while the text is laid out: the first frame already shows the text fitted.
**Automation.** A text that is given a `tagKey` carries the tag `AutoText_<tagKey>`. A text without a key is not tagged.
api: com.pantrixui.components.elements.autotext.PantrixAutoText(String, Modifier, TextStyle, TextUnit, Color, TextAlign?, Int, Int, TextOverflow, Boolean, TextRole, Boolean, ((TextLayoutResult) -> Unit)?, String?)

com.pantrixui.components.elements.autotext.PantrixAutoText(AnnotatedString, Modifier, TextStyle, TextUnit, Color, TextAlign?, Int, Int, TextOverflow, Boolean, TextRole, Boolean, Map<String, InlineTextContent>, ((TextLayoutResult) -> Unit)?, String?)

examples.name: AutoTextFitsItsRoom
examples.title: Text that fits its room
examples.description:
The same name three times, each with less room than the one before, in the `title` style. While it has room enough, the text is as large as its style says. When it has not, it goes down, on one line, to the largest size in which all of it is in view. If it still does not fit at its smallest size, the theme's `footnote` size, it stops shrinking, and what does not fit is cut with an ellipsis.

The text gets its room from `modifier`: here a width. The grey ground shows that room.
examples.code:
val name = "Selim Karaosmanoğlu"
val room = PantrixTheme.colors.neutral.container
PantrixAutoText(
    text = name,
    modifier = Modifier.width(320.dp).background(room),
    style = PantrixTheme.typography.title,
    tagKey = "name_wide"
)
PantrixAutoText(
    text = name,
    modifier = Modifier.width(160.dp).background(room),
    style = PantrixTheme.typography.title,
    tagKey = "name_narrow"
)
PantrixAutoText(
    text = name,
    modifier = Modifier.width(72.dp).background(room),
    style = PantrixTheme.typography.title,
    tagKey = "name_narrowest"
)

examples.name: AutoTextBalance
examples.title: A balance that shrinks on one line
examples.description:
A balance in the largest style. "Add digit" makes the amount longer: the amount is as large as its style says while it fits the line, and when it does not, it gets as small as it takes to stay on one line; "Delete digit" lets it grow back. The pale line under it is the same text without the shrinking, a `PantrixText`: it is cut when it does not fit.

The decimal part and the currency are half the amount's size. Their size is given in `em`: it is a share of the text around it, so it shrinks with the amount when the amount shrinks, and stays half of it on every platform.

examples.name: AutoTextTwoLines
examples.title: A heading on two lines at the most
examples.description:
A heading fitted to two lines at the most: `maxLines = 2`. The text first wraps onto two lines; when two lines are not enough it is set smaller, and its lines come as much closer. `minFontSize` is the theme's `body` size: the heading is never set smaller than that, and if it still does not fit there it is cut with an ellipsis.

It is a heading even when it shrinks: with `role = TextRole.Heading(level = 2)` a screen reader is told so. The column is 420dp wide at the most, and the heading fills it.
examples.code:
Column(modifier = Modifier.widthIn(max = 420.dp)) {
    PantrixAutoText(
        text = "Your credit card statement is ready: pay by the twenty-eighth",
        modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(),
        style = PantrixTheme.typography.headline,
        minFontSize = PantrixTheme.typography.body.fontSize,
        maxLines = 2,
        role = TextRole.Heading(level = 2),
        tagKey = "statement_title"
    )
}

examples.name: AutoTextInABox
examples.title: A paragraph that fits its box
examples.description:
A paragraph fitted to a box of a set height. `maxLines = Int.MAX_VALUE` leaves the lines to the box's height: the text is set in the largest size that fits the 96dp box in width and in height at once, and never larger than its style's size. Narrow the window: the text gets smaller as the box gets narrower.

The box's ground and its padding are in the text's own `modifier`; the text is fitted to the room the padding leaves.
examples.code:
PantrixAutoText(
    text = "A design system exists so that the same decision is not made again on every screen: it is made once " +
        "and looks the same everywhere.",
    modifier = Modifier
        .fillMaxWidth()
        .height(96.dp)
        .background(PantrixTheme.colors.neutral.container)
        .padding(PantrixTheme.spacing.sm),
    style = PantrixTheme.typography.title,
    textAlign = TextAlign.Center,
    maxLines = Int.MAX_VALUE,
    tagKey = "quote"
)

examples.name: AutoTextMinFontSize
examples.title: The smallest size
examples.description:
The same text three times, in the same 200dp room; only `minFontSize` differs. The text stops shrinking when it gets down to that size: the smaller the smallest size, the further the text can shrink and the more of it is in view.

The first one's smallest size is `16.sp`. The second is given none: it is the theme's `footnote` size. The third one's is `0.4.em`: `em` is a share of the style's own size, here four tenths of the `title` size.
examples.code:
val airport = "Sabiha Gökçen International Airport"
val room = Modifier.width(200.dp).background(PantrixTheme.colors.neutral.container)
PantrixAutoText(
    text = airport,
    modifier = room,
    style = PantrixTheme.typography.title,
    minFontSize = 16.sp,
    tagKey = "min_16sp"
)
PantrixAutoText(text = airport, modifier = room, style = PantrixTheme.typography.title, tagKey = "min_default")
PantrixAutoText(
    text = airport,
    modifier = room,
    style = PantrixTheme.typography.title,
    minFontSize = 0.4.em,
    tagKey = "min_em"
)

examples.name: AutoTextInTiles
examples.title: In boxes side by side, on a fill
examples.description:
A number in each of two boxes side by side, in the `headline` style. The boxes share the width by `weight`, and each number is fitted to its own box: the short one stays as large as its style says, and the long one shrinks.

No colour is given. Like `PantrixText`, the text takes the content colour of where it sits: in the box filled with `primary` it is written in the colour that reads on that fill.

pages.title: Icon
pages.summary:
A square icon, drawn in one colour. It mostly finds its colour itself: it takes the content colour of where it sits, and inside a button it is drawn in the same colour as the button's label.

An icon is not a picture: its source's own colours are not used, and all of it is painted in one colour. A photo, an illustration or a logo to be drawn in its own colours is a `PantrixImage`.
features: **Three sources.** A vector (`imageVector`), a bitmap (`bitmap`) or any `painter`: all three are drawn at the same size and in one colour.
**Size.** `size` is the icon's width and height; left out, it is the size in the theme's `IconStyle`, 24dp on every platform. The icon is drawn at this size whatever the source's own size.

**Colour.** An icon given no `tint` takes the content colour of where it sits: a button's label colour, a disabled control's faded colour. Where nothing gives a colour it is drawn in the theme's `onSurface` colour.

**Screen reader.** `contentDescription` is a decision made for every icon: given words, a screen reader reads them; where a label beside the icon already says what it is, null is given and the icon is hidden from the reader.
**The library's icons.** `PantrixIcons` holds the components' own icons and a few for an app's screens: drawn on a 24-unit grid with a 2-unit stroke, round at its ends and corners.

**Right to left.** The six icons that point back or forward mirror in a right-to-left layout: `ChevronBack`, `ChevronForward`, `FirstPage`, `LastPage`, `ArrowBack` and `ArrowForward`. The others are drawn the same in every language.
**Automation.** An icon given a `tagKey` carries the tag `Icon_<tagKey>`. An icon given no key is not tagged.

examples.name: IconDecorativeAndNamed
examples.title: A decorative icon and a named one
examples.description:
The least it takes: a vector and `contentDescription`. The description has no default, and is written for every icon.

In the first row a label beside the icon says what it is. The icon is decoration: it was given `contentDescription = null` and is hidden from screen readers, and a reader says only "Saved". The icon in the second row stands alone and carries the meaning itself: its description is "Warning", and a reader reads it out. A description says what the icon means, not what it looks like.

examples.name: IconSizes
examples.title: Sizes
examples.description:
`size` is the icon's width and height: 16, 20, 24, 32 and 48 dp. The icon in the middle was given no size: it is the size in the theme's icon style, 24dp on every platform.

An icon is drawn at this size whatever its source's own size. Its stroke is relative to its grid, 2 units in 24: it grows thicker and thinner with the icon.

examples.name: IconTintAndContentColour
examples.title: Tint and the colour of where it sits
examples.description:
The first row: an icon given no colour is drawn on the page in the theme's `onSurface` colour; `tint` gives it a role's colour.

None of the icons in the second row was given a `tint`. Each took the content colour of where it sits: on a surface filled with `primary`, the colour that reads on that fill; inside a button, the label's colour; in a disabled button, that button's faded colour.
examples.code:
val colors = PantrixTheme.colors
val spacing = PantrixTheme.spacing
Row(horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(spacing.lg)) {
    PantrixIcon(imageVector = PantrixIcons.Info, contentDescription = null)
    PantrixIcon(imageVector = PantrixIcons.Info, contentDescription = null, tint = colors.info.color)
    PantrixIcon(imageVector = PantrixIcons.Success, contentDescription = null, tint = colors.success.color)
    PantrixIcon(imageVector = PantrixIcons.Warning, contentDescription = null, tint = colors.warning.color)
    PantrixIcon(imageVector = PantrixIcons.Error, contentDescription = null, tint = colors.danger.color)
}
FlowRow(
    horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(spacing.md),
    verticalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(spacing.sm),
    itemVerticalAlignment = Alignment.CenterVertically
) {
    PantrixSurface(color = colors.primary.color) {
        PantrixIcon(
            imageVector = PantrixIcons.Inbox,
            contentDescription = null,
            modifier = Modifier.padding(spacing.sm),
            tagKey = "on_a_fill"
        )
    }
    PantrixButton(
        text = "Refresh",
        onClick = {},
        leadingIcon = { PantrixIcon(imageVector = PantrixIcons.Refresh, contentDescription = null) },
        tagKey = "refresh"
    )
    PantrixButton(
        text = "Refresh",
        onClick = {},
        enabled = false,
        leadingIcon = { PantrixIcon(imageVector = PantrixIcons.Refresh, contentDescription = null) },
        tagKey = "refresh_disabled"
    )
}

examples.name: IconSources
examples.title: Three sources: vector, bitmap, painter
examples.description:
Three sources, at the same size and in the same colour: a vector, a bitmap and a `painter`. The bitmap here is drawn in code; in an app it comes from a resource or from an image loader.

The third icon's source is Compose Multiplatform's multicoloured logo. `PantrixIcon` paints it in one colour and brings it to its own size. The one beside it is the same source drawn with `PantrixImage`: a picture keeps its own colours.

examples.name: IconRightToLeft
examples.title: Icons that mirror in right-to-left layouts
examples.description:
The icons that point back or forward follow the reading direction: they mirror in a right-to-left layout. The search lens and the play triangle do not: they are drawn the same in every language.

Both rows are written with the same six icons in the same order. The second row is in a right-to-left layout: the icons run from right to left and the arrows point the other way, while the search and play icons are drawn as they are.

examples.name: IconGallery
examples.title: All the icons
examples.description:
All the icons in `PantrixIcons`, with their names. A name is as it is written in code: `PantrixIcons.Check`. The ones with "mirrors" written under them are flipped in a right-to-left layout; that is read from the icon itself, from its `autoMirror` field.

As their names are written under them, the icons are decoration and are hidden from screen readers.
examples.code:
FlowRow(
    horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.sm),
    verticalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.lg)
) {
    ALL_ICONS.forEach { icon ->
        Column(
            modifier = Modifier.width(104.dp),
            verticalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.xs),
            horizontalAlignment = Alignment.CenterHorizontally
        ) {
            PantrixIcon(imageVector = icon, contentDescription = null, tagKey = icon.name)
            PantrixText(
                text = icon.name,
                style = PantrixTheme.typography.caption,
                textAlign = TextAlign.Center,
                maxLines = 1
            )
            if (icon.autoMirror) {
                PantrixText(
                    text = "mirrors",
                    style = PantrixTheme.typography.caption,
                    color = PantrixTheme.colors.textSecondary
                )
            }
        }
    }
}

private val ALL_ICONS = listOf(
    PantrixIcons.Check,
    PantrixIcons.Close,
