    PantrixIcons.File,
    PantrixIcons.Copy,
    PantrixIcons.Eye,
    PantrixIcons.EyeOff,
    PantrixIcons.Pause,
    PantrixIcons.Play
)

examples.name: IconStyleOverride
examples.title: A default size by style
examples.description: An icon's size is not a parameter but its style: `IconStyle` carries the size of an icon that is given none. `ProvidePantrixStyles` changes it for a part of the tree; `PantrixTheme`'s `styles` parameter for the whole app. Here the first icon takes its size from the style, the second is given a `size`: the parameter comes before the style.

pages.title: Image
pages.summary:
A picture: a photo, an illustration, a logo. What sets it apart from `PantrixIcon` is its colours: an icon is painted in the one colour of where it sits, and a picture keeps its own.

It does not load the picture itself: it takes a ready-made `Painter`, an `ImageVector` or an `ImageBitmap`.
features: **Three sources.** A `Painter`, an `ImageVector` or an `ImageBitmap`: there is a `PantrixImage` for each, and their other parameters are the same.
**Its own colours.** A picture is not painted in the content colour around it. Only `colorFilter` changes its colours.
**Saying something, or decorating.** `contentDescription` describes the picture for screen readers. A picture that only decorates says so with `contentDescription = null`, and is hidden from them.
**Size.** `modifier` gives the size. Given none, the picture is its source's own size.
**Fitting.** `contentScale` says how the picture fits the area it is given. The default is `Fit`: the whole picture shows, with its proportions kept.
**Alignment.** `alignment` says where in the area the picture stands; the default is its centre.
**Transparency.** `alpha` draws the picture faded.
**Sampling.** In the overload that takes an `ImageBitmap`, `filterQuality` says how the bitmap is sampled when it is drawn larger or smaller than its own size.
**Automation.** A picture carries a test tag only when it is given a `tagKey`: `Image_logo` for `tagKey = "logo"`.
api: com.pantrixui.components.elements.image.PantrixImage(Painter, Modifier, String?, ColorFilter?, Alignment, ContentScale, Float, String?)
com.pantrixui.components.elements.image.PantrixImage(ImageVector, Modifier, String?, ColorFilter?, Alignment, ContentScale, Float, String?)
com.pantrixui.components.elements.image.PantrixImage(ImageBitmap, Modifier, String?, ColorFilter?, Alignment, ContentScale, Float, FilterQuality, String?)

examples.name: ImagePlain
examples.title: A picture
examples.description:
At its plainest: a `Painter` and a size. The picture is drawn in its own colours and fits the area it is given, keeping its proportions.

It is given no description: this picture is decoration, and is hidden from screen readers.
examples.code:
PantrixImage(
    painter = painterResource(Res.drawable.compose_multiplatform),
    modifier = Modifier.size(96.dp),
    contentDescription = "Compose Multiplatform logo"
)

examples.name: ImageOwnSize
examples.title: At its own size
examples.description:
A picture given no size is its source's own size: this illustration is a square of 450dp. Where the place it stands in is narrower, it fits that place, keeping its proportions.

Press the button: the picture appears; press it again and it is hidden.

examples.name: ImageDescribedAndDecorative
examples.title: A picture that says something and a decorative one
examples.description:
`contentDescription` describes the picture for screen readers: the one on the left is read as "Compose Multiplatform logo". The one on the right is given `null`: it says it is decoration, and is hidden from screen readers. A picture that says something is given a description; one that only decorates is given `null`.

A picture carries a test tag only when it is given a `tagKey`: the left one's tag is `Image_logo`, and the right one has no tag.

examples.name: ImageContentScale
examples.title: Fitting
examples.description:
`contentScale` says how the picture fits the area it is given. The three areas are the same size, 120 by 72 dp; the picture is square.

`Fit` (the default) shows the whole picture, with room left at the sides. `Crop` fills the area, and the top and the bottom, which overflow, are cut off. `FillBounds` stretches the picture to fill the area, and its proportions are lost.

The other values can be given too: `Inside` only shrinks a picture larger than the area, and `None` does not scale the picture at all.

examples.name: ImageAlignment
examples.title: Alignment
examples.description:
`alignment` says where in the area the picture stands; the default is its centre. Here the picture fits the area with `Fit` and room is left at the sides: `CenterStart` rests the picture against the side where a line starts, and `CenterEnd` against the side where it ends.

In a picture cropped with `Crop`, `alignment` picks which part shows.

examples.name: ImageColorFilterAndAlpha
examples.title: Colour filter and transparency
examples.description: A picture keeps its own colours; `colorFilter` changes them. In order: the picture itself, the picture painted in a single colour with `ColorFilter.tint`, in greyscale with a colour matrix that brings its saturation down to zero, and faded with `alpha = 0.4f`.

examples.name: ImageFromAVector
examples.title: From a vector: how it differs from an icon
examples.description:
The second overload takes an `ImageVector` and draws the vector's own colours: the first picture is a multicoloured illustration.

`PantrixIcons.Star` is an icon drawn in black. `PantrixImage` draws it as it is, black; in the dark theme it is hard to tell from the ground. The `PantrixIcon` beside it paints the same vector in the content colour of where it sits. A mark in one colour is drawn with `PantrixIcon`, and an illustration with colours of its own with `PantrixImage`; where a picture has to be painted, it is given a `colorFilter`, as the last one is.
examples.code:
Row(
    horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.xl),
    verticalAlignment = Alignment.CenterVertically
) {
    PantrixImage(
        imageVector = vectorResource(Res.drawable.compose_multiplatform),
        modifier = Modifier.size(48.dp),
        contentDescription = "Compose Multiplatform logo"
    )
    PantrixImage(
        imageVector = PantrixIcons.Star,
        modifier = Modifier.size(48.dp),
        contentDescription = "Star, as a picture",
        tagKey = "star_image"
    )
    PantrixIcon(
        imageVector = PantrixIcons.Star,
        contentDescription = "Star, as an icon",
        size = 48.dp,
        tagKey = "star_icon"
    )
    PantrixImage(
        imageVector = PantrixIcons.Star,
        modifier = Modifier.size(48.dp),
        contentDescription = "Star, as a tinted picture",
        colorFilter = ColorFilter.tint(ownColors().color)
    )
}

appNames.name: ownColors
appNames.description: The "app's own colour" of the examples: a purple that is in none of the theme's roles. It is there to show what changes when a component is given `colors`; given one of the theme's roles, nobody could tell whether the colour came from the component's tone or from the parameter.

examples.name: ImageFromABitmap
examples.title: From a bitmap, and sampling
examples.description:
The third overload takes an `ImageBitmap` and has a parameter of its own: `filterQuality` says how the bitmap is sampled when it is drawn larger or smaller than its own size.

The bitmap here is a checkerboard of eight by eight pixels, enlarged to 96dp. The one on the left is given `FilterQuality.None`: the pixels stay sharp. The one on the right has the default: the pixels blend into each other at their edges.

examples.name: ImageShapeAndGround
examples.title: Shape and ground
examples.description:
A picture has no parameter for a shape, a ground or a padding: `modifier` gives all three. Here `clip` cuts the area, `background` paints the area that was cut, and `padding` brings the picture in from the edges.

The one on the left is a circle (`shapes.full`), the one on the right a square with round corners (`shapes.lg`).
examples.code:
Row(horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.xl)) {
    PantrixImage(
        painter = painterResource(Res.drawable.compose_multiplatform),
        modifier = Modifier
            .size(72.dp)
            .clip(PantrixTheme.shapes.full)
            .background(PantrixTheme.colors.neutral.container)
            .padding(PantrixTheme.spacing.md),
        contentDescription = "Compose Multiplatform logo"
    )
    PantrixImage(
        painter = painterResource(Res.drawable.compose_multiplatform),
        modifier = Modifier
            .size(72.dp)
            .clip(PantrixTheme.shapes.lg)
            .background(PantrixTheme.colors.neutral.container)
            .padding(PantrixTheme.spacing.md),
        contentDescription = "Compose Multiplatform logo"
    )
}

examples.name: ImageBehindContent
examples.title: Behind content, as decoration
examples.description:
Like a faded logo behind a heading: the picture covers the surface with `fillMaxSize()`, `ContentScale.Crop` cuts off what overflows, and `alpha` leaves it faded behind the text.

Its description is `null`: it is decoration, and a screen reader reads the text alone.
examples.code:
PantrixSurface(
    modifier = Modifier.widthIn(max = 360.dp).fillMaxWidth().height(120.dp),
    color = PantrixTheme.colors.primary.container,
    shape = PantrixTheme.shapes.lg
) {
    PantrixImage(
        painter = painterResource(Res.drawable.compose_multiplatform),
        modifier = Modifier.fillMaxSize(),
        contentScale = ContentScale.Crop,
        alpha = 0.25f,
        contentDescription = null
    )
    PantrixText(
        text = "Compose Multiplatform",
        modifier = Modifier.align(Alignment.Center),
        style = PantrixTheme.typography.title
    )
}

pages.title: Avatar
pages.summary:
The picture of a person or a thing: a photograph, the initials of a name, or an icon standing for either. It stands beside the name in a list's row, at the start of a comment, at the top of a profile.

An avatar is drawn and not pressed. One that opens a profile goes inside what takes the press: a button, a list's row.
features: **Initials, an icon or neither.** Where `initials` are given they are drawn; where they are not, the `icon` is; with neither, the avatar is a plain shape filled with its tone's colour.

**Photograph.** Pantrix loads no pictures. `image` is a slot: the app puts the picture there with its own loader, from a resource, or as a drawing of its own. The picture is drawn over the initials: the letters show while it loads and when it cannot be loaded.

**Six tones.** `tone` fills the avatar with the colour of one of the theme's roles; `colors` gives a colour that no role has. A tone says nothing by itself: a screen reader reads the description, not the colour.

**Size.** `size` or `modifier` gives the avatar its size. The initials and the icon are a share of the avatar: they keep their proportion at every size. The style's size is 40dp on Android and iOS, and 32dp on desktop and the web.
**Shape.** An avatar is a circle on every platform; `AvatarStyle(shape = ...)` changes its corners.
**As written.** Initials are not put in upper case. The first two letters are kept, without the spaces between them.

**Screen reader.** With a `contentDescription` the avatar is read as an image by that name. Given null, it is hidden: that is right for an avatar with its name written beside it. The initials are never read out.
**Font scale.** The initials keep their share when the system's text size is made larger, too: an avatar does not grow with the text around it.

examples.name: AvatarPlain
examples.title: At its plainest
examples.description:
The least it takes: a description and initials. Its tone is `Neutral`, and its size the style's.

An avatar that stands alone takes its name from its description: a screen reader reads it as an image named "Ayşe Yılmaz". The letters "AY" are not read out; they are what the description shortens.
examples.code: PantrixAvatar(contentDescription = "Ayşe Yılmaz", initials = "AY", tagKey = "ayse")

examples.name: AvatarBesideAName
examples.title: Beside a name
examples.description:
An avatar that stands beside its name has no description: `contentDescription = null`. The name is written beside it; a screen reader does not read the same name twice, and the avatar is hidden from it.

Initials are drawn as they are written, and are not put in upper case: the "ik" in the last row stays in lower case.

examples.name: AvatarTones
examples.title: Tones
examples.description:
`tone` fills the avatar with the colour of one of the theme's roles, and writes the letters in the colour that reads on it. The default is `Neutral`: a grey with no meaning at all.

In every tone the avatar is drawn in the role's solid colour, not in its pale `container`: a small circle of that colour is lost on a light page. A tone says nothing by itself; what a colour is to mean has to be in the words beside it.

examples.name: AvatarSizes
examples.title: Sizes
examples.description:
`size` is the avatar's width and height: 24dp in a comment, 32dp in a dense row, 40dp in a row, 56dp on a card, 72dp on a profile. The size can be given by `modifier` too; it then takes the place of `size`.

The initials are four tenths of the avatar and the icon six tenths: the proportion stays the same whatever the size, and no second style is needed.

examples.name: AvatarInitials
examples.title: Initials
examples.description:
Initials are drawn as they are written. They are not put in upper case: `i` becomes `İ` in Turkish and `I` in other languages, and an avatar is not the place to get a name wrong. The first avatar was given "ik", and so it stayed.

The first two letters of what is given are kept, without the spaces between them: the avatar given "Ayşe Yılmaz" writes "Ay", and the one given "D K" writes "DK". How a name is shortened is the app's to say, not the avatar's: the app gives the letters to draw.

examples.name: AvatarPhoto
examples.title: A photograph that comes later
examples.description:
A profile whose photograph comes later. The avatar is given its `image` slot from the start, but the slot draws nothing until "Load photo" is pressed: until then the initials show. When the photograph comes it covers the letters. An image loader does the same while it loads, or when it fails.

The slot is as large as the avatar and is cut to its shape. The "photograph" here is a gradient with no size of its own; for a picture that is not square, ask for `ContentScale.Crop`. What the picture says of itself is not read: the avatar's description stands for both.

examples.name: AvatarIconAndEmpty
examples.title: An avatar with an icon, and an empty one
examples.description:
An avatar without initials draws its `icon`: a person, a group, a company. Like the letters, the icon is drawn in the colour that reads on the tone.

The second is given neither letters nor an icon: it is a plain circle filled with its tone's colour. Its description still says its name.

examples.name: AvatarRoundedShape
examples.title: An avatar with corners
examples.description:
An avatar is a circle on every platform. `style` changes the style of this avatar alone: `AvatarStyle(shape = ...)` takes the corners to a step of the theme's shape scale. Here a folder's avatar and a company's are drawn with corners, by `ShapeRole.Medium`.

Only the field that is set changes: the size and the letters' share come from the theme's style.
examples.code:
val rounded = AvatarStyle(shape = ShapeRole.Medium)
Row(horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.sm)) {
    PantrixAvatar(
        contentDescription = "Documents",
        icon = PantrixIcons.Folder,
        tone = AvatarTone.Info,
        style = rounded
    )
    PantrixAvatar(
        contentDescription = "Pantrix A.Ş.",
        initials = "PX",
        tone = AvatarTone.Primary,
        style = rounded,
        tagKey = "company"
    )
}

examples.name: AvatarTransparentLogo
examples.title: A transparent logo
examples.description: A picture that is transparent in places shows what is under it. Such a picture is given alone, without initials or an icon: behind this logo there is only the tone's colour.

examples.name: AvatarOwnColors
examples.title: A colour of its own
examples.description:
`colors` gives the avatar a fill of the given colour, not of a tone: a team's own colour, say, or a label's. The first avatar's colour is in none of the theme's roles; both its fill and the colour of its letters are given, because only whoever gives a fill the theme does not know can tell what reads on it.

The second is given a fill alone, and that fill is one of the theme's own colours, `success.container`. The letters take the colour the theme pairs with that fill, without it being given.
examples.code:
val own = ownColors()
Row(horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.sm)) {
    PantrixAvatar(
        contentDescription = "Design team",
        initials = "DT",
        colors = AvatarColors(container = own.color, content = own.onColor),
        tagKey = "team"
    )
    PantrixAvatar(
        contentDescription = "Support team",
        initials = "ST",
        colors = AvatarColors(container = PantrixTheme.colors.success.container),
        tagKey = "support_team"
    )
}

appNames.name: ownColors
appNames.description: The "app's own colour" of the examples: a purple that is in none of the theme's roles. It is there to show what changes when a component is given `colors`; given one of the theme's roles, nobody could tell whether the colour came from the component's tone or from the parameter.

pages.title: Badge
pages.summary: A small mark that stands on something else: a count, or just a dot. It tells of unread messages, of notifications that are waiting, of whether a person is online. By itself it says nothing; it is read together with the icon or the avatar it sits on.
features: **A count or a dot.** With a `count` the badge is a pill that writes the number; without one, a dot. A number of one digit sits in a circle.
**A count that overflows.** A number above `maxCount` is written "99+", and the pill stops growing there.
**Zero is a count too.** Zero is drawn as "0": taking the badge away when there is nothing left to count is the caller's to do. A number below zero is drawn as "0" as well.
**Six tones.** `tone` fills the badge from one of the theme's roles; `colors` gives a colour that no role has.
**On the corner of something.** `PantrixBadgedBox` sets the badge on a corner of its content; on round content it sets it on the circle, not on the box (`BadgeOverlap.Circular`).

**Screen reader.** Without a `contentDescription` the badge is hidden from screen readers: a lone "3" read out says nothing, and the number is said by the description of the element the badge sits on.
**Font scale.** The number is set in the theme's `caption` style and grows with the system's text size, and the pill with it.

examples.name: BadgeDotAndCount
examples.title: Dot and count
examples.description: Without a `count` the badge is a dot; with one it is a pill that grows wider with its number. A number of one digit is a full circle, and the pill is never narrower than it is tall.

examples.name: BadgeMaxCount
examples.title: A count that overflows
examples.description: A number above `maxCount` is not written; the limit and a plus are written in its place: the default limit is 99. The pill stops growing there, and does not cover the icon it sits on. The last badge's limit is 9.

examples.name: BadgeTones
examples.title: Tones
examples.description: `tone` fills the badge with the colour of one of the theme's roles, and writes the number in the colour that reads on it. The default tone is `Danger`: a badge mostly tells of something that needs looking at. The top row has a number in every tone, and the one under it a dot in every tone.

examples.name: BadgeOnAnIcon
examples.title: On the corner of an icon
examples.description:
`PantrixBadgedBox` sets the badge on a corner of its content: by default the top corner on the side where lines end.

The badge is hidden from screen readers; the icon's own description says the number ("Inbox, 5 unread"). When the number gets down to zero no badge is put there at all: it is the caller that does this, not the badge. Raise the number with the buttons: past 99 it reads "99+", and the pill grows away from the icon.
examples.code:
var unread by rememberSaveable { mutableIntStateOf(START_UNREAD) }
Row(
    horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.lg),
    verticalAlignment = Alignment.CenterVertically
) {
    PantrixBadgedBox(badge = { if (unread > 0) PantrixBadge(count = unread, tagKey = "unread") }) {
        PantrixIcon(
            imageVector = PantrixIcons.Inbox,
            contentDescription = if (unread > 0) "Inbox, $unread unread" else "Inbox",
            tagKey = "inbox"
        )
    }
    PantrixButton(
        text = "+1",
        onClick = { unread += 1 },
        variant = ButtonVariant.Outline,
        size = ButtonSize.Small,
        tagKey = "one_more"
    )
    PantrixButton(
        text = "+50",
        onClick = { unread += MANY },
        variant = ButtonVariant.Outline,
        size = ButtonSize.Small,
        tagKey = "many_more"
    )
    PantrixButton(
        text = "Mark as read",
        onClick = { unread = 0 },
        variant = ButtonVariant.Text,
        size = ButtonSize.Small,
        tagKey = "read"
    )
}

private const val START_UNREAD = 5

private const val MANY = 50

examples.name: BadgeOnAvatars
examples.title: On avatars
examples.description:
On round content the badge stands on the circle, not on the corner of the box: `overlap = BadgeOverlap.Circular`. `alignment` says which corner; the status dot is at the bottom, on the side where lines end.

The status dots are made larger with `BadgeStyle(dotSize = 12.dp)`: large enough to be made out on an avatar. The avatar's description says what the dot means ("İbrahim Öztürk, online"); the dot is hidden from screen readers.

examples.name: BadgeOwnColors
examples.title: A colour and a description of its own
examples.description:
`colors` gives the badge a fill of the given colour, not of a tone: here the app's own purple, which is in none of the theme's roles. Only the fields that are set change; the tone still decides the rest.

These badges stand alone, not on an icon. So they say what they mean themselves: each is given a `contentDescription`, and a screen reader reads "4 new offers".

appNames.name: ownColors
appNames.description: The "app's own colour" of the examples: a purple that is in none of the theme's roles. It is there to show what changes when a component is given `colors`; given one of the theme's roles, nobody could tell whether the colour came from the component's tone or from the parameter.

examples.name: BadgeBesideText
examples.title: Beside a text
examples.description: A badge can stand on a text too. `PantrixBadgedBox` keeps the baseline of its content: with `alignByBaseline` the "new" label stands on the same line as the title beside it, and the dot on the label's corner.

pages.title: Chip
pages.summary:
A chip is a compact action, a filter that goes on and off, or an item the user put in and can take out again: a recipient, a tag, an applied filter.

There are two forms of `PantrixChip`. The one that takes `onClick` is an action or only shows a value, and can carry a remove button. The one that takes `selected` and `onSelectedChange` is a filter: it is on or off.
features: **Action.** A chip given `onClick` is a button, and its name is its label. `leadingIcon` puts an icon before the label.

**Filter.** A filter that is on is drawn filled and carries a tick in the icon's place: it is not colour alone that says it is on. A screen reader hears a checkbox that is selected or not. The chip does not change by itself: it is whatever `selected` says.

**Remove button.** `onRemove` puts a cross at the chip's end: it is a target of its own, and a screen reader reads it with the label, "Remove Ayşe Yılmaz". The chip does not take itself out; `onRemove` does.

**A chip that only shows a value.** A chip given `onClick = null` shows a value, and a filter given `onSelectedChange = null` is read-only: they take no press and no focus, but still tell a screen reader their names.
**Long label.** A label too long for its room ends in an ellipsis; the icon and the cross stay whole.
**Disabled.** With `enabled = false` neither the chip nor its cross can be pressed; the chip is drawn in the theme's disabled colours.
**Colours and style.** `colors` changes only the colours it gives, and `style` only the dimensions it gives.
**Platform.** On Android it is 32dp tall with medium rounded corners; on iOS it is a pill of 32dp, and on desktop and the web one of 30dp. The platform's touch target is reserved around it.
**Automation.** A chip given a `tagKey` carries the tag `Chip_<tagKey>`, and its cross `ChipRemove_<tagKey>`. A press is reported as a `Chip` event, and the event never carries the label's text.
api: com.pantrixui.components.elements.chip.PantrixChip(String, (() -> Unit)?, Modifier, ImageVector?, (() -> Unit)?, Boolean, ChipStyle?, ChipColors?, String?, MutableInteractionSource?)
com.pantrixui.components.elements.chip.PantrixChip(String, Boolean, ((Boolean) -> Unit)?, Modifier, ImageVector?, Boolean, ChipStyle?, ChipColors?, String?, MutableInteractionSource?)

examples.name: ChipActions
examples.title: An action chip
examples.description:
The first form: a chip that takes `onClick` is a button that does something when it is pressed, and its name is its label. Its shortest form is the first chip: a label and an `onClick`. In the second, `leadingIcon` stands before the label. The third is disabled with `enabled = false`: it is drawn faded and takes no press.

Press a chip: the line below says which one was pressed last.
examples.code:
var last by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf<String?>(null) }
FlowRow(horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.sm)) {
    PantrixChip(label = "Share", onClick = { last = "Share" }, tagKey = "share")
    PantrixChip(
        label = "Add to calendar",
        onClick = { last = "Add to calendar" },
        leadingIcon = PantrixIcons.Calendar,
        tagKey = "calendar"
    )
    PantrixChip(label = "Archive", onClick = { last = "Archive" }, enabled = false, tagKey = "archive")
}
PantrixText(
    text = last?.let { "Last action: $it" } ?: "No action pressed yet",
    style = PantrixTheme.typography.footnote,
    color = PantrixTheme.colors.textSecondary,
    tagKey = "last_action"
)

examples.name: ChipFilters
examples.title: A selectable chip: filters
examples.description:
The second form: a chip that takes `selected` and `onSelectedChange` is a filter that goes on and off. The chip changes nothing by itself: `onSelectedChange` reports the value the user asks for, and here the screen's state keeps the keys of the filters that are on.

A filter that is on is drawn filled and carries a tick at its start; it is not colour alone that shows it is on. In the filter that has an icon, "Favourites", the tick takes the icon's place and the chip's width does not change. The filters are in a row that scrolls sideways; the line below says how many are on.

examples.name: ChipRecipients
examples.title: Removable chips: recipients
examples.description:
`onRemove` puts a cross at the chip's end. The cross is a button in its own right: a screen reader says "Remove Ayşe Yılmaz", so the crosses of a row can be told apart. The chip does not take itself out; it is the code here that takes the recipient out of the list.

A press on the chip itself opens the recipient; a press on the cross does not. Recipients that do not fit in the row go on to the next one. "Restore" puts them all back.

examples.name: ChipValuesOnly
examples.title: Chips that only show a value
examples.description:
Two chips that cannot be pressed. "Members only" is a filter and was given `onSelectedChange = null`: it is read-only and takes no press and no focus, but still tells a screen reader its name and that it is on. With `onClick = null`, "Draft" only shows a value: it is one item for a screen reader.

Neither of them is disabled: they are drawn in their own colours, and simply have nothing to press.

examples.name: ChipLongLabelAndWideChip
examples.title: A long label and a wide chip
examples.description:
A label too long for its room ends in an ellipsis. The icon and the cross take their room first and the label is given what is left: a long label gets shorter, while its icon and its cross stay whole. The first chip cannot be pressed but can be removed: a chip given `onClick = null` still carries its cross when `onRemove` is given.

The second chip is wider than it needs to be, 220dp: its icon and its label are in the middle, as in a button, and its cross is at the end.
examples.code:
PantrixChip(
    label = "Third-quarter reports as they were sent to the board, with all their attachments",
    onClick = null,
    leadingIcon = PantrixIcons.Folder,
    onRemove = {},
    tagKey = "long"
)
PantrixChip(
    label = "Kotlin",
    onClick = null,
    modifier = Modifier.width(220.dp),
    leadingIcon = PantrixIcons.Star,
    onRemove = {},
    tagKey = "wide"
)

examples.name: ChipDisabled
examples.title: Disabled chips
examples.description:
With `enabled = false` the chip cannot be pressed, and it says so to a screen reader too. A disabled chip is drawn in the theme's disabled colours: a filter that is on takes the disabled fill; a chip without a fill stays without one, and its label fades. Along with the chip, its cross cannot be pressed either.

The last chip was given `colors`, but it was drawn like the others all the same: so that a disabled chip looks the same everywhere in a product, it uses the theme's colours and not its own.
examples.code:
val own = ownColors()
FlowRow(
    horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.sm),
    verticalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.sm)
) {
    PantrixChip(label = "In stock", selected = true, onSelectedChange = {}, enabled = false, tagKey = "disabled_on")
    PantrixChip(label = "On sale", selected = false, onSelectedChange = {}, enabled = false, tagKey = "disabled_off")
    PantrixChip(
        label = "Selin Çağlar",
        onClick = {},
        leadingIcon = PantrixIcons.Person,
        onRemove = {},
        enabled = false,
        tagKey = "disabled_recipient"
    )
    PantrixChip(
        label = "My collection",
        selected = true,
        onSelectedChange = {},
        enabled = false,
        colors = ChipColors(selectedContainer = own.color, selectedContent = own.onColor),
        tagKey = "disabled_own_colors"
    )
}

appNames.name: ownColors
appNames.description: The "app's own colour" of the examples: a purple that is in none of the theme's roles. It is there to show what changes when a component is given `colors`; given one of the theme's roles, nobody could tell whether the colour came from the component's tone or from the parameter.

examples.name: ChipOwnColors
examples.title: Its own colours
examples.description:
Two chips whose colours were given by the caller. The first is a filled action: its fill, its label and its icon were given, and its edge was removed with `Color.Transparent`. The second is a filter, and only the colours it is drawn in while it is on were given: while it is off it is drawn in the theme's. Press the filter to turn it off and see the difference.

`ChipColors` changes only the colours that are given; one that is left out is decided by the theme's role.
examples.code:
val own = ownColors()
var inCollection by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf(true) }
Row(horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.sm)) {
    PantrixChip(
        label = "New season",
        onClick = {},
        leadingIcon = PantrixIcons.Star,
        colors = ChipColors(
            container = own.container,
            content = own.onContainer,
            icon = own.onContainer,
            border = Color.Transparent
        ),
        tagKey = "new_season"
    )
    PantrixChip(
        label = "My collection",
        selected = inCollection,
        onSelectedChange = { inCollection = it },
        colors = ChipColors(selectedContainer = own.color, selectedContent = own.onColor),
        tagKey = "my_collection"
    )
}

appNames.name: ownColors
appNames.description: The "app's own colour" of the examples: a purple that is in none of the theme's roles. It is there to show what changes when a component is given `colors`; given one of the theme's roles, nobody could tell whether the colour came from the component's tone or from the parameter.

examples.name: ChipShapeAndStyle
examples.title: Shape and style
examples.description: `style` changes the geometry of this chip alone; the fields that are not given come from the theme's and the platform's style. The first chip has no style and its shape is the platform's: medium rounded on Android, fully rounded on the others. The second's corners are slightly rounded with `ShapeRole.Small`, and the third's are fully rounded with `ShapeRole.Full`. The last is 40dp tall and has 20dp of room at each side of its label.
examples.code:
FlowRow(
    horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.sm),
    verticalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.sm),
    itemVerticalAlignment = Alignment.CenterVertically
) {
    PantrixChip(label = "No style", onClick = {}, tagKey = "plain")
    PantrixChip(label = "Slightly rounded", onClick = {}, style = ChipStyle(shape = ShapeRole.Small), tagKey = "rounded")
    PantrixChip(label = "Fully rounded", onClick = {}, style = ChipStyle(shape = ShapeRole.Full), tagKey = "pill")
    PantrixChip(
        label = "Tall",
        onClick = {},
        style = ChipStyle(height = 40.dp, horizontalPadding = 20.dp),
        tagKey = "tall"
    )
}

pages.title: Divider
pages.summary:
A thin line that separates content: between the rows of a list, the sections of a card, the groups of a toolbar. It is drawn horizontal or vertical; a horizontal one can carry a label, like the "or" between two ways in on a sign-in screen.

It is three composables: `PantrixHorizontalDivider`, `PantrixVerticalDivider`, and `PantrixDivider`, which takes its orientation in `orientation`.
features: **Horizontal and vertical.** A horizontal line is as wide as its container, a vertical one as tall.

**Label.** `label` puts a text on a horizontal line. `align` says where the text sits: at the start, in the centre or at the end. At the start or the end, a short stretch of line stays on the label's side.
**Thickness.** `thickness` is how thick the line is; its default is 1dp.
**Indent.** `startIndent` leaves a gap before a horizontal line and above a vertical one. It is not used on a labelled line.

**The colour of where it stands.** A line that is given no colour is the theme's `divider` on the theme's own grounds. On a fill, where that colour would not read, it is a share of the colour that is written there: on a role's surface, in a filled card, between the rows of a menu that has a colour of its own.

**Its own colour.** `color` draws the line in the colour it is given. It does not change the label's colour: the label is `textSecondary` on the theme's grounds, and the colour that is written there on a fill.
**Screen reader.** A line without a label is decorative and hidden from screen readers. A labelled line's label is read.
**Right to left.** `DividerAlign.Start` and a horizontal line's `startIndent` go by the side a line starts on: in a right-to-left interface that is the right.

examples.name: DividerBetweenRows
examples.title: Between rows
examples.description: At its plainest: a `PantrixDivider` with no parameters. It is horizontal, as wide as its container, 1dp thick and in the theme's `divider` colour. It is decorative: a screen reader reads only the rows.
examples.code:
Column(verticalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.md)) {
    PantrixText(text = "Profile")
    PantrixDivider()
    PantrixText(text = "Security")
    PantrixDivider()
    PantrixText(text = "Notifications")
}

examples.name: DividerWithALabel
examples.title: Labelled
examples.description:
`label` puts a text on the line: the line runs on both sides of the text. On a sign-in screen, the "or" between two ways in is written like this.

The label is in the theme's `label` style and its secondary text colour. A labelled line is not decorative: a screen reader reads the label.

examples.name: DividerLabelAlign
examples.title: Where the label sits
examples.description: `align` says where along the line the label sits; its default is `Center`. `Start` and `End` move the label to one side, but not right up to the edge: a short stretch of line stays on that side.
examples.code:
PantrixHorizontalDivider(label = "Start", align = DividerAlign.Start)
PantrixHorizontalDivider(label = "Centre", align = DividerAlign.Center)
PantrixHorizontalDivider(label = "End", align = DividerAlign.End)

examples.name: DividerThickness
examples.title: Thickness
examples.description: `thickness` is how thick the line is: 1dp (the default, `DefaultThickness`), twice that and four times that, in that order. On a labelled line the lines on both sides of the text are that thick too.
examples.code:
PantrixHorizontalDivider(thickness = DefaultThickness)
PantrixHorizontalDivider(thickness = DefaultThickness * 2)
PantrixHorizontalDivider(thickness = DefaultThickness * 4)
PantrixHorizontalDivider(label = "Labelled", thickness = DefaultThickness * 2)

examples.name: DividerStartIndent
examples.title: Indent
examples.description:
`startIndent` leaves a gap before the line: the line starts level with the text, not under the icon. Here the icon is 24dp and the gap to the text 16dp; the indent is the sum of the two, 40dp.

The line at the end of the list has no indent (`DefaultStartIndent`, 0dp): the list ends there.

`startIndent` is not used on a labelled line. On a vertical line the gap is above the line.

examples.name: DividerVertical
examples.title: Vertical
examples.description:
`PantrixVerticalDivider` is as tall as its container, so it is put where the height is known. In the top row the row gives the height: `Modifier.height(IntrinsicSize.Min)` brings the row down to the height of the text in it, and the line is as tall. In the bottom row the height was given to the line itself: `PantrixTheme.spacing.xl`, 24dp at the default density.

A vertical line carries no label and is hidden from screen readers.

examples.name: DividerByOrientation
examples.title: Its orientation as a parameter
examples.description:
`PantrixDivider` takes its orientation as a value: `DividerOrientation.Horizontal` draws a `PantrixHorizontalDivider`, `DividerOrientation.Vertical` a `PantrixVerticalDivider`. Where the orientation depends on a condition, one call covers both.

Here the lines inside the two columns are horizontal, and the one between the columns is vertical. `label` and `align` apply to a horizontal line only.

examples.name: DividerOwnColor
examples.title: In its own colour
examples.description:
`color` draws the line in the colour it is given: the top one in the app's own purple, which is in none of the theme's roles; the bottom one in the theme's `danger` role.

`color` paints the line alone. The label of the bottom line is still in the theme's secondary text colour.
examples.code:
PantrixHorizontalDivider(color = ownColors().color, thickness = 2.dp)
PantrixHorizontalDivider(color = PantrixTheme.colors.danger.color, label = "Actions that cannot be undone")

appNames.name: ownColors
appNames.description: The "app's own colour" of the examples: a purple that is in none of the theme's roles. It is there to show what changes when a component is given `colors`; given one of the theme's roles, nobody could tell whether the colour came from the component's tone or from the parameter.

examples.name: DividerOnAFill
examples.title: On a fill
examples.description:
No line here was given a colour. The theme's `divider` colour is for the theme's own grounds; on a fill the line is a share of the colour that is written there (thirty per cent of it), and the label is that colour itself.

The surface at the top is in the theme's `primary` colour: the line comes from the role's `onColor`. The one below is a filled card (`CardVariant.Filled`): the line comes from the card's content colour.

examples.name: DividerRightToLeft
examples.title: Right to left
examples.description: `DividerAlign.Start` and `startIndent` go by the side a line starts on, not by the left. This example turns the reading direction to right-to-left inside itself: the label sits on the right, and the second line's indent is on the right.

pages.title: Spinner
pages.summary: A spinning arc that says something is in progress: while a page loads, while a save is under way. It does not say how much of the work is done and takes no progress value; it only says to wait.
features: **Size.** `size` is one side of the spinner; the spinner is square. If it is not given, it is the style's size: 18dp on every platform.
**Thickness grows with size.** The arc's thickness is a ninth of the size: a 16dp spinner inside a button and a 48dp one on an empty page read at the same weight.

**Colour.** Without `color`, the spinner is in the content colour of where it sits, as in a solid button. Where there is no content colour it is in the theme's `primary` colour: the theme's own grounds give no content colour, so on the page, on a surface and in a card the spinner spins in the brand's colour.
**Screen reader.** `contentDescription` is announced as a polite live region (`LiveRegionMode.Polite`). Its default is "Loading" in the theme's language.

**Where it is already said.** Inside something that says by itself that it is loading, `contentDescription = null` is given. `PantrixButton`'s `loading` does this for the spinner it puts inside the button.
**Reduced motion.** When the system asks for reduced motion the arc does not spin; it keeps still.

**Style.** `SpinnerStyle` holds the size of a spinner that is given none. A brand changes it with the `spinner.size` value, a theme with `styles`, and a part of the tree with `ProvidePantrixStyles`. The app's density does not scale it.
**Automation.** `tagKey` builds the test tag: a spinner given `tagKey = "orders_loading"` has the tag `Spinner_orders_loading`.

examples.name: SpinnerPlain
examples.title: On its own
examples.description:
At its plainest: no parameter is given. The spinner is the style's size (18dp), and is announced to a screen reader as "Loading".

No colour is given either. The example stands on the theme's ground, and the ground gives no content colour: the spinner spins in its own default, the brand's colour.
examples.code: PantrixSpinner()

examples.name: SpinnerSizes
examples.title: Sizes
examples.description:
`size` is the spinner's side: here 16, 24, 32 and 48 dp. The arc's thickness grows with the size, so they all read at the same weight.

The second one's size is not a number but a step of the theme's spacing scale: `PantrixTheme.spacing.xl`, 24dp. A size taken from the scale scales with the app's density; one given as a number does not.

examples.name: SpinnerInOtherColors
examples.title: Colours
examples.description: `color` draws the arc in the colour it is given. In order: the theme's `success` and `danger` roles, the secondary text colour, and the app's own purple, which no role of the theme has.

appNames.name: ownColors
appNames.description: The "app's own colour" of the examples: a purple that is in none of the theme's roles. It is there to show what changes when a component is given `colors`; given one of the theme's roles, nobody could tell whether the colour came from the component's tone or from the parameter.

examples.name: SpinnerOnAFill
examples.title: On a fill
examples.description:
A spinner that is given no colour takes the content colour of where it sits. The first surface is in the theme's `primary` colour: the spinner spins in the role's `onColor`. The second is in the `success` role's `container`: the spinner is in `onContainer`. Neither is given a `color`.

The button's spinner is the button's own: `loading = true` puts it in place of the leading icon, in the button's content colour.

examples.name: SpinnerLoadingAPage
examples.title: While a page loads
examples.description:
A large spinner in the centre, standing in for the content until it arrives: `size = PantrixTheme.spacing.xxl`, 32dp.

`contentDescription` says what is loading: a screen reader says "Loading orders" in place of "Loading". `tagKey` is given too: automation finds the spinner by the tag `Spinner_orders_loading`. Press the button: the content arrives and the spinner goes.

examples.name: SpinnerBesideItsText
examples.title: Beside a text that says it is loading
examples.description: A spinner that is given `contentDescription = null` says nothing to a screen reader. The text beside it already says the work is in progress: the spinner need not say it as well.

examples.name: SpinnerStyleOverride
examples.title: Default size from the style
examples.description:
`SpinnerStyle` holds the size of a spinner that is given none. `ProvidePantrixStyles` changes it for a part of the tree; the same change is given to the whole app through `PantrixTheme`'s `styles` parameter.

The first spinner takes its size from the style: 28dp here. The second is given `size`: the parameter takes precedence over the style.

pages.title: Skeleton
pages.summary:
A pale block that stands in for content that has not arrived yet: the lines of a paragraph that is loading, an avatar's circle, an image's rectangle. It shows the shape and the place of the content to come ahead of time; a light band moving across it says something is loading.

It is two components: `PantrixSkeleton` is a single block, `PantrixSkeletonText` the lines of a paragraph. The placeholder for a whole card is a component of its own: `PantrixCardSkeleton`.
features: **The caller gives the size.** `PantrixSkeleton` has no size of its own: it is given with `modifier`, the size of the content it stands in for.
**Shape.** `shape` is the block's corners. Its default is the theme's smallest rounding (`shapes.xs`); in place of an avatar, `shapes.full` draws a circle.
**Lines.** `PantrixSkeletonText` draws as many lines as `lines` says. The last line is shorter than the others: the block reads as a paragraph. `lineHeight` is the height of the lines.
**Band.** A lighter band moves across the block, from one end to the other and back. When the system asks for reduced motion the band keeps still, and the block is in its own colour alone.

**Colours.** `SkeletonColors` is two colours: the block's own (`base`) and the band that moves across it (`highlight`). A colour that is left out stays the theme's role: `disabledContent` and `divider`.
**On a fill.** A skeleton does not look at the content colour around it: on a fill that is not one of the theme's grounds, the caller gives its colours.
**Screen reader.** Every skeleton says its `contentDescription`; the default is "Loading" in the theme's language. `PantrixSkeletonText` says it once for all its lines.
**Announcing once.** In a placeholder made of several skeletons the parts are given `contentDescription = null`, and the parent around them says once that it is loading.

examples.name: SkeletonParagraph
examples.title: In place of a paragraph
examples.description:
At its plainest: three lines standing in for a paragraph that is loading. `lines` is the number of lines; the last line is shorter than the others, so the block reads as a paragraph.

The band that moves across them says something is loading; when the system asks for reduced motion the band keeps still. A screen reader says "Loading" once for the three lines.
examples.code: PantrixSkeletonText(lines = 3, modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth())

examples.name: SkeletonOwnColors
examples.title: In its own colour
examples.description:
`colors` puts the skeleton in the colours it is given, not the theme's. There are two: `base` is the block's own colour, `highlight` the band that moves across it. Here both are pale versions of the app's own purple: they show whatever the ground is. When the system asks for reduced motion the band keeps still and only `base` shows.

Only a colour that is set changes; one that is left out stays the theme's role.
examples.code:
val own = ownColors()
PantrixSkeletonText(
    lines = 3,
    modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(),
    colors = SkeletonColors(base = own.color.copy(alpha = 0.35f), highlight = own.color.copy(alpha = 0.15f))
)

appNames.name: ownColors
appNames.description: The "app's own colour" of the examples: a purple that is in none of the theme's roles. It is there to show what changes when a component is given `colors`; given one of the theme's roles, nobody could tell whether the colour came from the component's tone or from the parameter.

examples.name: SkeletonShapes
examples.title: A single block and its shape
examples.description:
`PantrixSkeleton` is a single block and has no size of its own: `modifier` gives it its size, that of the content it stands in for. `shape` is the block's corners.

In order: an avatar's circle (`shapes.full`), an image's rectangle (`shapes.md`), a button's pill, and a line that is given no shape. The default shape is the theme's smallest rounding: `shapes.xs`.

examples.name: SkeletonLineHeight
examples.title: Line height
examples.description: `lineHeight` is the height of each line; its default is `PantrixTheme.spacing.md`, 12dp. It is chosen to suit the size of the text it stands in for: 8dp at the top for small text, the default in the middle, and 20dp at the bottom for a heading. The space between the lines does not change.
examples.code:
PantrixSkeletonText(lines = 2, modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(), lineHeight = PantrixTheme.spacing.sm)
PantrixSkeletonText(lines = 2, modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth())
PantrixSkeletonText(lines = 2, modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(), lineHeight = 20.dp)

examples.name: SkeletonAnnouncedOnce
examples.title: A row announced once
examples.description:
An avatar and two lines: the skeleton of a list row. If both parts said "Loading", a screen reader would say it twice for the same row.

The parts are given `contentDescription = null`. The row as a whole says once that it is loading, in the theme's own string: `PantrixTheme.strings.loading`.

examples.name: SkeletonOnAFill
examples.title: On a fill
examples.description:
A skeleton does not look at the content colour around it: on a fill that is not one of the theme's grounds, the caller gives its colours. The surface here is in the `info` role's `container`.

`base` is a pale version of the colour written on that surface (`onContainer`), and `highlight` is the surface's own colour: the band looks like an opening that passes through the lines.

examples.name: SkeletonUntilContentArrives
examples.title: Until the content arrives
examples.description:
A skeleton resembles the content it stands in for: a circle of the same size in place of the avatar, two lines in place of two lines of text. Press the button: the content arrives and takes the skeleton's place. The caller decides which of the two is drawn.

While it loads, the circle has no description; the lines beside it say "Loading" once. The lines' tag (`tagKey`) is what a test waits on: once `SkeletonText_profile` is gone, the content has arrived.

pages.title: Text Field
pages.summary:
Text the user types: a name, an email address, a note of a few lines. Its label sits above the box and stays there: it does not cover the placeholder, and can be read while typing too. The box may have supporting text or an error's message under it, icons at its two ends, a button at its end that empties the field, and a character count below.

The field is built on a `TextFieldState`: it holds the text, the selection and what the keyboard is still composing together. So the keyboard is never handed a text that has moved on: that is what loses characters and makes the caret jump with some keyboards. For code that keeps its text as a `String` there is another `PantrixTextField` that takes a `value` and an `onValueChange`, and for a form's field one that takes a `field`.
features: **Three overloads.** In the one that takes a `state`, the text is read from the state: `state.text` where it is used, and `snapshotFlow { state.text.toString() }` to follow it as it is typed. The one that takes a `value` and an `onValueChange` keeps the text with the caller, and `onValueChange` does the filtering. The one that takes a `field` gets its value, its error and its name from its field in the form.

**Label and placeholder.** `label` is written above the box and is the field's name for a screen reader; a press on the label puts the caret in the box too. `placeholder` shows while the field is empty. A field with no label gets its name from `contentDescription`.

**Supporting text and error.** `supportingText` is written under the box. `error` turns the border, the label, the supporting text and the caret to the `danger` role; the supporting text is then the message that says what to put right, and a screen reader announces it as the error.

**Icons and the clear button.** `leadingIcon` stands before the text and `trailingIcon` after it. While the field is not empty, `showClearButton` shows a button that empties it: the button leaves the caret in the field and is no stop for Tab.
**Length limit.** With `maxLength` an edit that would pass the limit is turned down whole, and the count is written under the box ("12/120"); `showCharacterCount = false` hides the count.

**Several lines.** With `lineLimits = TextFieldLineLimits.MultiLine(...)` the box grows with its text and Enter starts a new line. Where the field is given a height, the box fills it and text that does not fit scrolls inside the box.

**Keyboard and transformations.** `keyboardOptions` picks the keyboard's type and its action key, and `onKeyboardAction` is called when that key is pressed. A field a number is typed in that has an action asks for its keyboard with `numberKeyboardOptions`: an iPhone's number pad has no action key. `inputTransformation` changes what is typed, or turns it down, before it enters the field; `outputTransformation` says how the text is shown, without changing it. `contentType` tells the platform what the field holds, so that the platform can fill it in.

**Focus, disabled and read-only.** The box's border is what shows the focus: in the `primary` colour and thicker, and no ring is drawn as well. A field under a dialog or a sheet keeps its focus, but is drawn at rest and without its caret. A field with `enabled = false` takes no focus; a `readOnly` one can be focused, and its text selected and copied.

**Style and colours.** `style` (`TextFieldStyle`) changes the box's shape, its dimensions and its border, and `colors` (`TextFieldColors`) its colours: only the fields that are given. A disabled field is in the theme's disabled colours whatever is given.

**Text size.** What is typed and the placeholder are set in the style's `textRole`: `body` (16sp) on Android and iOS, as in Material 3 and on iOS; `label` (14sp) on the desktop and the web, as on a page used with a pointer. A select's box and the page jump field are set in it as well.

**Reading direction.** Each paragraph takes its direction from its own first letter: an email address typed into an Arabic form reads `ada@`, not `@ada`. The text is aligned with the layout, and stays on its label's side.

examples.name: TextFieldPlain
examples.title: At its plainest
examples.description:
The least there is to write: a `TextFieldState` and a label. The state is created with `rememberTextFieldState()`, and what is typed is read from it; the line below shows `name.text` as it is typed.

The label sits above the box and stays there; a press on the label puts the caret in the box too. The box's border is what shows the focus. `tagKey` sets the field's test tag: `TextField_<tagKey>`.
examples.code:
val name = rememberTextFieldState()
PantrixTextField(
    state = name,
    modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(),
    label = "Name",
    tagKey = "name"
)
PantrixText(
    text = if (name.text.isEmpty()) "Nothing typed yet" else "Typed: ${name.text}",
    color = PantrixTheme.colors.textSecondary
)

examples.name: TextFieldSearch
examples.title: A search field without a label
examples.description:
A search field that has no label: `contentDescription` tells a screen reader its name. The placeholder says the same, so the screen reader does not read it as well: the field is not named twice while it is empty.

`leadingIcon` stands before the text. A slot does not size what is put in it; the icon takes the size in the field's style: `PantrixTheme.style(TextFieldStyle).iconSize`. While the field is not empty, `showClearButton` shows the button that empties it; the button leaves the caret in the field.

`keyboardOptions` makes the keyboard's action key "Search", and `onKeyboardAction` is called when that key is pressed. Type something and press the keyboard's "Search" key, or Enter: the app's snackbar says what was searched for.
examples.code:
val snackbars = LocalPantrixSnackbars.current
val scope = rememberCoroutineScope()
val query = rememberTextFieldState()
PantrixTextField(
    state = query,
    modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(),
    placeholder = "Search orders",
    leadingIcon = {
        PantrixIcon(
            imageVector = PantrixIcons.Search,
            contentDescription = null,
            size = PantrixTheme.style(TextFieldStyle).iconSize
        )
    },
    showClearButton = true,
    keyboardOptions = KeyboardOptions(imeAction = ImeAction.Search),
    onKeyboardAction = { scope.launch { snackbars?.show(message = "Searched for: ${query.text}", tagKey = "searched") } },
    contentDescription = "Search orders",
    tagKey = "search"
)

examples.name: TextFieldIcons
examples.title: Leading and trailing icons
examples.description:
`leadingIcon` stands before the text and `trailingIcon` after it: in a right-to-left layout they change places. Both take the secondary text colour; a text put in a slot, like the "kg" in the second field, is drawn in that colour too.

The clear button stands before `trailingIcon` and is no stop for Tab: a stop after every field would double the presses it takes to get through a form. A screen reader still reaches the button as a button.
examples.code:
val iconSize = PantrixTheme.style(TextFieldStyle).iconSize
PantrixTextField(
    state = rememberTextFieldState(),
    modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(),
    label = "Username",
    leadingIcon = { PantrixIcon(imageVector = PantrixIcons.Person, contentDescription = null, size = iconSize) },
    tagKey = "username"
)
PantrixTextField(
    state = rememberTextFieldState("72"),
    modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(),
    label = "Weight",
    trailingIcon = { PantrixText(text = "kg") },
    showClearButton = true,
    keyboardOptions = KeyboardOptions(keyboardType = KeyboardType.Number),
    tagKey = "weight"
)

examples.name: TextFieldSupportingTextAndError
examples.title: Supporting text and error
examples.description:
`supportingText` stands under the box, in a small type. With `error = true` the border, the label, the supporting text and the caret turn to the `danger` role; the supporting text is then the message that says what to put right, and a screen reader announces it as the error. Type a few letters: as long as the password is shorter than eight characters the field is in error, and says how many characters are missing.

This field keeps its text as a `String`, not in a `TextFieldState`: `value` is shown, and `onValueChange` is asked for every change. The password is drawn as dots by `visualTransformation`. It is kept with `remember` and not with `rememberSaveable`: saved state may be written to disk. The password field that has a button to show its text is `PantrixSecureTextField`.
examples.code:
var password by remember { mutableStateOf("") }
val missing = 8 - password.length
val tooShort = password.isNotEmpty() && missing > 0
PantrixTextField(
    value = password,
    onValueChange = { password = it },
    modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(),
    label = "Password",
    supportingText = if (tooShort) "Characters missing: $missing" else "At least 8 characters",
    error = tooShort,
    showClearButton = true,
    keyboardOptions = KeyboardOptions(keyboardType = KeyboardType.Password),
    visualTransformation = PasswordVisualTransformation(),
    contentType = ContentType.NewPassword,
    tagKey = "password"
)

examples.name: TextFieldHeldAsString
examples.title: A field whose text is held as a String
examples.description:
The `PantrixTextField` that takes a `value` and an `onValueChange`: the field shows `value`, and asks `onValueChange` for every change the user makes. A change the callback does not take is not shown: filtering is done there, and this overload takes no `inputTransformation`. The text asked for has to come back as `value` by the next frame, or the field shows the old text and the caret jumps: keep the text in state that the callback writes at once; where the text lives in a flow, pick the overload that takes a `state`.

This overload takes its lines through `singleLine`, `minLines` and `maxLines`, and is one line unless told otherwise. The field here is given an address of two lines, as if pasted from somewhere else: the field shows the line break as a space, and the second line is not cut off; the text that is held stays as it is.
examples.code:
var address by remember { mutableStateOf("Bağdat Cad. No: 12\nKat 3, Daire 8") }
PantrixTextField(
    value = address,
    onValueChange = { address = it },
    modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(),
    label = "Address (one line)",
    supportingText = "The line break in the text shows as a space",
    showClearButton = true,
    tagKey = "address_line"
)

examples.name: TextFieldValueLinesAndAction
examples.title: Lines and the action key in the String overload
examples.description:
The overload that keeps its text as a `String` takes its lines through `singleLine`, `minLines` and `maxLines`, not through `lineLimits`. The first field is two lines tall and grows to four; past that, the text scrolls inside it.

The keyboard's action key, too, is answered by `keyboardActions` and not by `onKeyboardAction`: it says what to do for the action `keyboardOptions` names. Type something in the second field and press the keyboard's action key: the app's snackbar says what was typed.
examples.code:
val snackbars = LocalPantrixSnackbars.current
val scope = rememberCoroutineScope()
var message by remember { mutableStateOf("") }
var nickname by remember { mutableStateOf("") }
PantrixTextField(
    value = message,
    onValueChange = { message = it },
    modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(),
    label = "Message",
    singleLine = false,
    minLines = 2,
    maxLines = 4,
    tagKey = "message"
)
PantrixTextField(
    value = nickname,
    onValueChange = { nickname = it },
    modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(),
    label = "Nickname",
    keyboardOptions = KeyboardOptions(imeAction = ImeAction.Done),
    keyboardActions = KeyboardActions(
        onDone = { scope.launch { snackbars?.show(message = "Nickname: $nickname") } }
    ),
    tagKey = "nickname"
)

examples.name: TextFieldSeveralLines
examples.title: Several lines and a character count
examples.description:
`lineLimits = TextFieldLineLimits.MultiLine(minHeightInLines = 3)` starts the box three lines tall; the box grows with its text, and Enter starts a new line. Tab does not type a tab, it moves the focus on: otherwise a keyboard would have no way forward out of the field.

With `maxLength = 120` an edit that would pass the limit is turned down whole: typing stops at the limit, and a paste that does not fit is not put in at all. Characters are counted as `String.length` counts them, so an emoji can count as two. The count is written under the box, opposite the supporting text. Text set in code is not cut: where it is over the limit, the user can still make it shorter.
examples.code:
PantrixTextField(
    state = rememberTextFieldState(),
    modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(),
    label = "Note for the courier",
    placeholder = "The doorbell does not work, please knock",
    supportingText = "Passed on to the courier",
    maxLength = 120,
    lineLimits = TextFieldLineLimits.MultiLine(minHeightInLines = 3),
    tagKey = "note"
)

examples.name: TextFieldFixedHeight
examples.title: A field given a height
examples.description:
A height given to the field is the whole field's: `Modifier.height(160.dp)`. The label stays at the top, and the supporting text and the count at the bottom; the box fills the height they leave, and text that does not fit scrolls inside the box. No part of the field runs outside the height it is given.

Press the clear button: with its text gone, the box is still the same height.
examples.code:
PantrixTextField(
    state = rememberTextFieldState(INSTRUCTIONS),
    modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth().height(160.dp),
    label = "Delivery instructions",
    supportingText = "The field's height is fixed: the text scrolls inside the box",
    showClearButton = true,
    maxLength = 400,
    lineLimits = TextFieldLineLimits.MultiLine(),
    tagKey = "instructions"
)

private const val INSTRUCTIONS = "The building's street door is kept locked: ring the bell twice.\n" +
    "If nobody answers, leave it at the guard's booth.\n" +
    "If the parcel is heavy, take the lift: third floor.\n" +
    "There is a dog at the door: it barks but does not bite.\n" +
    "I am at home after six in the evening.\n" +
    "If you cannot reach me, call the caretaker."

examples.name: TextFieldTransformations
examples.title: Input and output transformations
examples.description:
`inputTransformation` sees every change the user makes before it enters the field: the one here turns a change down whole if it holds anything but digits. With `maxLength`, the transformation runs first and the limit applies to what it lets through.

`outputTransformation` says how the text is shown, without changing it: the number's spaces are only drawn. Type "5321234567": the box shows "532 123 45 67", while `phone.text`, which the line below reads, has no spaces.

examples.name: TextFieldNumberAndAction
examples.title: A field of numbers and the action key
examples.description:
A field a number is typed in, with something to do once it is typed, asks for its keyboard with `numberKeyboardOptions`: it gives the keyboard's type and its action key together. On Android the keyboard of numbers has an action key. An iPhone's number pad has none: ten digits and a key that takes one back. There a number typed in a field that asked for `KeyboardType.Number` cannot be sent; `numberKeyboardOptions` asks for the keyboard of numbers and punctuation in its place: it opens on its digits and has an action key.

Type a quantity and press the keyboard's action key, or Enter: the app's snackbar says the quantity. The keyboard on an iPhone also has signs and, a press away, letters: the field turns those down (`inputTransformation`).

examples.name: TextFieldProfileForm
examples.title: Fields bound to a form
examples.description:
The `PantrixTextField` that takes a `field` gets its value, its error and its name from its field in the form. No `tagKey` is given: the field's `id` is the automation key (`TextField_<id>`). When the focus leaves an empty field, the rule's message takes the place of the supporting text; that is when the error first shows.

In a field given `form`, the keyboard's action key submits the form. In the first field the "Next" key moves the focus to the next field; in the second the action key submits the form through the "Save" button, and where a field is in error the focus goes to it. Leave both fields empty and press "Save".
examples.code:
val snackbars = LocalPantrixSnackbars.current
val scope = rememberCoroutineScope()
val form = rememberFormState()
PantrixTextField(
    field = form.field("full_name", initial = "", Rules.notBlank("Enter your name")),
    modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(),
    form = form,
    label = "Full name",
    supportingText = "As it appears on your card",
    keyboardOptions = KeyboardOptions(capitalization = KeyboardCapitalization.Words, imeAction = ImeAction.Next),
    contentType = ContentType.PersonFullName
)
PantrixTextField(
    field = form.field("email", initial = "", Rules.matches(EMAIL, "Enter a valid email address")),
    modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(),
    form = form,
    label = "Email",
    placeholder = "name@example.com",
    showClearButton = true,
    keyboardOptions = KeyboardOptions(keyboardType = KeyboardType.Email),
    contentType = ContentType.EmailAddress
)
PantrixButton(
    text = "Save",
    onClick = {
        scope.launch { form.submit { snackbars?.show(message = "Details saved", tagKey = "profile_saved") } }
    },
    form = form,
    tagKey = "save_profile"
)

private val EMAIL = Regex("""\S+@\S+\.\S+""")

examples.name: TextFieldDisabledAndReadOnly
examples.title: Disabled and read-only
examples.description:
`enabled = false` draws the field in the theme's disabled colours: the field takes no focus, cannot be typed into, and a screen reader is told it is disabled.

`readOnly = true` only stops the text being changed: the field can be focused, and its text selected and copied.
examples.code:
PantrixTextField(
    state = rememberTextFieldState("Pantrix A.Ş."),
    modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(),
    enabled = false,
    label = "Disabled",
    supportingText = "Set by your organisation",
    tagKey = "company"
)
PantrixTextField(
    state = rememberTextFieldState("SIP-2026-0914"),
    modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(),
    readOnly = true,
    label = "Read-only",
    supportingText = "Cannot be changed; can be selected and copied",
    tagKey = "order_no"
)

examples.name: TextFieldOwnColors
examples.title: Its own colours
examples.description:
The colours given with `colors` are used, and those left out stay the theme's roles. The first field's colours are not written as fixed values but taken from the theme's `success` role: they are right in the dark theme too. The box's fill is the role's soft tone; the text and the icon are in the colour that reads on that tone; the border and the caret are the role's own colour. The label, the supporting text and the error colour are not given: they stay as the theme has them.

The second field is given only two colours, both the app's own purple: the border while the field has the focus, and the caret. Press the field, type something and select it: the selection's handles and its highlight take the caret's colour too.
examples.code:
val success = PantrixTheme.colors.success
PantrixTextField(
    state = rememberTextFieldState("PANTRIX10"),
    modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(),
    label = "Discount code",
    supportingText = "Code valid: 10% off",
    leadingIcon = {
        PantrixIcon(
            imageVector = PantrixIcons.Check,
            contentDescription = null,
            size = PantrixTheme.style(TextFieldStyle).iconSize
        )
    },
    showClearButton = true,
    colors = TextFieldColors(
        container = success.container,
        border = success.color,
        hoveredBorder = success.color,
        focusedBorder = success.color,
        text = success.onContainer,
        icon = success.onContainer,
        cursor = success.color
    ),
    tagKey = "coupon"
)
val own = ownColors()
PantrixTextField(
    state = rememberTextFieldState(),
    modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(),
    label = "Invitation code",
    placeholder = "PX-0000",
    colors = TextFieldColors(focusedBorder = own.color, cursor = own.color),
    tagKey = "own_colors"
)

appNames.name: ownColors
appNames.description: The "app's own colour" of the examples: a purple that is in none of the theme's roles. It is there to show what changes when a component is given `colors`; given one of the theme's roles, nobody could tell whether the colour came from the component's tone or from the parameter.

examples.name: TextFieldOwnStyle
examples.title: Its own style
examples.description:
`style` is this call's own style: only the fields it sets change, and the rest comes from the theme's and the platform's style.

The first field is a fully round box: `TextFieldStyle(shape = ShapeRole.Full)`. The second takes the same style but holds several lines: the curve of a fully round box would run into the first line of its text, so the field is drawn with `ShapeRole.Large`. In the third, `height` raises the box's least height; the one line stands in the middle of the box.
examples.code:
PantrixTextField(
    state = rememberTextFieldState(),
    modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(),
    placeholder = "Search products",
    showClearButton = true,
    style = TextFieldStyle(shape = ShapeRole.Full),
    contentDescription = "Search products",
    tagKey = "pill"
)
PantrixTextField(
    state = rememberTextFieldState(),
    modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(),
    label = "Comment",
    lineLimits = TextFieldLineLimits.MultiLine(minHeightInLines = 2),
    style = TextFieldStyle(shape = ShapeRole.Full),
    tagKey = "pill_comment"
)
PantrixTextField(
    state = rememberTextFieldState(),
    modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(),
    label = "Title",
    style = TextFieldStyle(height = 56.dp),
    tagKey = "tall"
)

examples.name: TextFieldInteractions
examples.title: Watching the interactions from outside
examples.description:
`interactionSource` hoists the field's interactions: its focus, its hover and its presses. Without one, the field keeps a source of its own. The line below reads from the same source: press the field, then bring the pointer over the box.

It is the box that reports the pointer: a pointer over the label or over the supporting text does not count.
examples.code:
val interactions = remember { MutableInteractionSource() }
val focused by interactions.collectIsFocusedAsState()
val hovered by interactions.collectIsHoveredAsState()
PantrixTextField(
    state = rememberTextFieldState(),
    modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(),
    label = "Subject",
    supportingText = "The pointer counts only while it is over the box",
    interactionSource = interactions,
    tagKey = "observed"
)
PantrixText(
    text = "Focused: ${if (focused) "yes" else "no"} · Pointer over it: ${if (hovered) "yes" else "no"}",
    color = PantrixTheme.colors.textSecondary
)

pages.title: Filled Text Field
pages.summary:
A text field whose label is inside its box. The label rests in the text's place while the field is empty and without the focus; it moves up to its own line above the text when the field takes the focus or something is typed. The box is filled and has no outline at rest; it is outlined in the `primary` colour with the focus, and in the `danger` colour in error.

Underneath it is `PantrixTextField`'s text field, with another decoration around it: the two take the same things and can stand in for each other. It is built on a `TextFieldState`, and has an overload that takes a `value` and an `onValueChange`, and one that takes a form's field.
features: **The label inside the box.** At rest `label` is in the text's place and in the text's size; with the focus, or while there is a text, it shrinks and moves up to its own line. In a field with no label the text stands in the middle of the box.
**Placeholder.** `placeholder` shows while the label is out of its place: while the field is empty and has the focus. In a field with no label it shows whenever the field is empty.

**Fill and outline.** At rest the box is filled and has no outline. With the focus and in error the fill turns to the surface's colour and the box is outlined; it takes an outline under a pointer too. A disabled field has no fill.

**Supporting text and error.** `supportingText` is written under the box. `error` turns the outline, the supporting text and the caret to the `danger` role, and a screen reader is told; the label keeps its own colour.

**Several lines.** With `lineLimits = TextFieldLineLimits.MultiLine(...)` the box is as tall as its least lines, grows to its most, and from there scrolls its text inside it: the bar at its end shows how far.

**Icons, clear button, count.** `leadingIcon` stands before the label and the text, and `trailingIcon` after them. `showClearButton` shows the button that empties the field; `maxLength` limits the length and writes the count.
**Keyboard and transformations.** `keyboardOptions`, `onKeyboardAction`, `inputTransformation`, `outputTransformation` and `contentType` are the same as the text field's.

**Three overloads.** In the one that takes `state` the text is read from the state. The one that takes `value` and `onValueChange` keeps the text with its caller; it has no scroll bar. The one that takes `field` takes its value, its error and its name from its field in the form.

**Style and colours.** `style` (`FilledTextFieldStyle`) changes the box's shape and dimensions, and `colors` (`FilledTextFieldColors`) its colours: only the fields that are set. A disabled field has no fill and is in the theme's disabled text colour whatever is given.
**Text size.** What is typed, the resting label and the placeholder are set in the style's `textRole`: `body` (16sp) on Android and iOS, `label` (14sp) on the desktop and the web.

**Automation.** With `tagKey` the field is named `FilledTextField_<tagKey>`, and its clear button `FilledTextFieldClear_<tagKey>`. The field reports that it took the focus and that it was cleared, and never its text.
