pages.title: Form
pages.summary: A form's fields, its rules and its submission. Not the components themselves but the state that holds them together: which field is in error, what waits while it is submitted and what Enter does are known not by each component but by the form.
features: **Fields.** `rememberFormState()` sets up a form's state, `form.field(id, initial, rules…)` one of its fields. A field's `id` is its name in the form and the automation tag of the component bound to it: a component in a form needs no `tagKey`.

**Bound components.** The text fields, the checkbox, the radio group, the switch, Select, MultiSelect, and the date and time fields take a `field`: they show its value, call `onValueChange` when it changes and `onFocusLost` when the focus leaves, and write the error under their box. A component that is none of them is bound to a field by hand.

**Rules.** A `Rule` gives a value's error, or null. `Rules` carries the most common ones: `notBlank`, `required`, `mustBeTrue`, `minLength`, `maxLength`, `matches`, and `satisfies` for a rule that looks at something else. A field's rules are tried in turn; the first that fails gives the error.

**When an error shows.** A field that is not touched shows no error: the error shows when the focus leaves the field, or when the form is submitted. A touched field is checked again at every change, and an error that is put right goes at once.

**Submitting.** `form.submit { … }` checks every field first; where one fails, the focus goes to the first field in error and the block does not run. While the block runs `isSubmitting` is true: a button given the `form` looks loading for that time and takes no second press.

**Enter.** In a text field given a `form`, the keyboard's action key submits the form: with the work of the button given the `form`, or the work given with `RegisterSubmit`. Where there are several buttons the last to register wins.

**By hand.** `validateAll()` checks every field and counts it touched, `focusFirstError()` gives the focus to the first field in error, `isValid` says whether the form passes without showing any error, and `reset()` takes the form back to its start. `field.reset(value)` gives a field a new starting value: a saved address that comes from a server.

examples.name: FormSignUp
examples.title: A sign-up form
examples.description:
A sign-up form with every rule of `Rules`: the name is not left blank (`notBlank`), the e-mail fits a pattern (`matches`), the password is at least eight and at most sixty-four characters (`minLength`, `maxLength`), the second password looks at the first (`satisfies`), the birthday and the country are not passed over (`required`), and the terms are accepted (`mustBeTrue`).

Press "Open account" without typing anything: all the errors show at once and the focus goes to the first field in error. Fill a field in: its error goes as you type. Once the form is valid the button looks loading while it is submitted; Enter in the last field does the same.
examples.code:
val report = LocalExampleEvents.current
val scope = rememberCoroutineScope()
val form = rememberFormState()
val name = form.field("name", initial = "", Rules.notBlank("Type your name"))
val email = form.field(
    "email",
    initial = "",
    Rules.notBlank("Type your e-mail address"),
    Rules.matches(EMAIL, "This is not an e-mail address")
)
val password = form.field(
    "password",
    initial = "",
    Rules.minLength(8, "The password must be at least 8 characters"),
    Rules.maxLength(64, "The password can be at most 64 characters")
)
val again = form.field(
    "password_again",
    initial = "",
    Rules.notBlank("Type the password again"),
    Rules.satisfies<String>("The passwords are not the same") { it == password.value }
)
val birthday = form.field<PantrixDate?>("birthday", initial = null, Rules.required("Type your birthday"))
val country = form.field<String?>("country", initial = null, Rules.required("Choose a country"))
val terms = form.field("terms", initial = false, Rules.mustBeTrue("Accept the terms"))
Column(
    modifier = Modifier.widthIn(max = 400.dp),
    verticalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.md)
) {
    PantrixTextField(field = name, modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(), form = form, label = "Name")
    PantrixTextField(
        field = email,
        modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(),
        form = form,
        label = "E-mail",
        keyboardOptions = KeyboardOptions(keyboardType = KeyboardType.Email)
    )
    PantrixSecureTextField(
        field = password,
        modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(),
        form = form,
        label = "Password",
        supportingText = "At least 8 characters"
    )
    PantrixSecureTextField(
        field = again,
        modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(),
        form = form,
        label = "Password, again"
    )
    PantrixDateTextField(field = birthday, form = form, label = "Birthday", maxDate = rememberToday())
    PantrixSelect(
        field = country,
        options = COUNTRIES,
        modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(),
        label = "Country",
        placeholder = "Choose"
    )
    PantrixCheckbox(field = terms, label = "I accept the terms of use")
    PantrixButton(
        text = "Open account",
        onClick = {
            scope.launch {
                form.submit {
                    delay(SUBMIT_MILLIS)
                    report("Account opened: ${email.value}")
                }
            }
        },
        modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(),
        form = form,
        tagKey = "sign_up"
    )
}

private val COUNTRIES = listOf(
    SelectOption("TR", "Türkiye"),
    SelectOption("DE", "Germany"),
    SelectOption("NL", "the Netherlands"),
    SelectOption("GB", "United Kingdom")
)

private val EMAIL = Regex("[^@\\s]+@[^@\\s]+\\.[^@\\s]+")

private const val SUBMIT_MILLIS = 1_200L

pages.title: Date Picker
pages.summary: Choosing a day or a stretch of days from a calendar turned a month at a time. The calendar is the choice itself: it stands in the page, or is put in a popover, a dialog or a sheet. It does not keep the choice; the chosen day comes to `onSelect`.
features: **Navigation.** The arrows turn the month; pressing the title shows the years in place of the days, and choosing a year turns the calendar to the same month of it. Where the chosen day is not on show, the calendar goes to its month.
**Days that cannot be chosen.** The days outside `minDate` and `maxDate`, and those `isDateEnabled` leaves out, are drawn faint and cannot be pressed; the arrows do not go past the ends.

**Stretch.** The first press chooses the stretch's first day and the second its last; a press on a day before the first starts the stretch again there. While the last is chosen, the days to the one under the pointer are shown in a lighter colour.
**Keyboard.** The calendar is one Tab stop. The arrows walk a day or a week, Page Up and Page Down a month, with Shift a year, Home and End to the week's first and last day; Enter and Space choose.

**Screen reader.** Each day is read in full with the day of the week ("Saturday, October 17, 2026"); chosen, today, and the start, the middle and the end of a stretch are said. When the month changes, the new month is announced politely.
**Week.** It starts on the language's day: Sunday in English, Monday in Turkish, Saturday in Arabic; `firstDayOfWeek` changes it.

**Today.** The ringed day is the today of the screen's clock and turns by itself at midnight. The screen's clock is `LocalPantrixClock`, the device's by default (`PantrixClock.System`); another place's day is given by `today`, or for a whole screen by `LocalPantrixClock`.
**Platform.** A day's room is the platform's least touch target on a phone (48dp on Android, 44pt on iOS), and 36dp on the desktop and the web. In a narrow place the days shrink until they fit.
**Date type.** Days are `PantrixDate`s, and no date library is needed; docs/guide/date-time/DATE_TIME_GUIDE.md turns them into `kotlinx-datetime`'s or `java.time`'s.
api: com.pantrixui.components.date.datepicker.PantrixDatePicker(PantrixDate?, (PantrixDate) -> Unit, Modifier, PantrixDate?, PantrixDate?, ((PantrixDate) -> Boolean)?, Int?, Boolean, PantrixDate, DatePickerStyle?, DatePickerColors?, String?)

examples.name: DatePickerAnotherToday

pages.title: Date Text Field
pages.summary: A text field for a day: the day is typed in digits, or chosen from a calendar that the button at the box's end opens. The label stands above the box; the field is drawn as a `PantrixTextField`.
features: **Digits alone.** The field takes digits alone; as each part is whole its mark comes by itself: in Turkish `18102026` becomes `18.10.2026`, in American English `10182026` becomes `10/18/2026`. A phone opens its keyboard of digits. Backspace after a mark deletes the digit before it.

**A pasted day.** A day written out is read as it is written: in the field's order first, and else with the year first, as in ISO 8601. In Turkish `2026-10-18` becomes `18.10.2026` too; a year of two digits is one of the hundred years around today (`18.10.26`, 2026). A text not read so comes in as its digits.

**Format.** `format` gives the order of the parts and the mark between them; by default it comes from the theme's language and region: Turkish and German `GG.AA.YYYY`, Britain and Arabic `DD/MM/YYYY`, the US `MM/DD/YYYY`, a language not known ISO 8601 (`YYYY-MM-DD`). While empty the field shows the pattern; a screen reader hears it as the order of the parts ("Day, Month, Year").

**Value.** `onValueChange` is called each time the field's day changes: a whole day the calendar takes, or null where the field holds nothing, half a day, digits that make no day or a day it does not take. A half-typed day stays on the screen while `value` is null; another day from outside is written into the field.

**Its own error.** The field writes what is typed wrong under the box itself: a date not finished, once the field is left, a day the calendar has not (31 February), a day outside `minDate` and `maxDate`, a day `isDateEnabled` does not take. The app's `error` comes first; its message is `supportingText`.

**Calendar.** It opens with the button, with Alt+↓ on the desktop and the web, by pressing the box of a read-only field, and with Enter or Space. `presentation` says what it opens in: by default a sheet in a narrow window and a popover under the box in a wider one; or in every window a popover, a sheet or a dialog; the same on every platform. Pressing a day in the calendar takes the day and closes the calendar; Escape and pressing outside close it with nothing changed. Opened with the keyboard the focus goes to the chosen day, or else to today; once it closes it is back on the field.

**Three overloads.** The one with `value` and `onValueChange`; the one with `state` (`rememberDateTextFieldState()`): `date` is the field's day, setting it puts the day in the field, `text` tells a half-typed field from an empty one; the one with `field` binds to a form's field.
**Date type.** Days are `PantrixDate`s; to convert them to `kotlinx-datetime` or `java.time`, docs/guide/date-time/DATE_TIME_GUIDE.md.

examples.name: DateTextFieldDelivery
examples.title: A delivery day on a weekday
examples.description: A delivery day on a weekday within the next month. In the calendar the weekends are faint. A Saturday typed is not taken and the field says "This day cannot be chosen"; a day past the month says the bounds.
examples.code:
var delivery by remember { mutableStateOf<PantrixDate?>(null) }
val today = rememberToday()
PantrixDateTextField(
    value = delivery,
    onValueChange = { delivery = it },
    label = "Delivery day",
    supportingText = "Delivered on weekdays only",
    minDate = today.plusDays(1),
    maxDate = today.plusMonths(1),
    isDateEnabled = { it.dayOfWeek <= FRIDAY },
    tagKey = "delivery"
)

private const val FRIDAY = 5

val today = rememberToday()
Column(verticalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.sm)) {

        label = "Report day",
        format = DateFieldFormat.Iso,
        tagKey = "report_day"

            state.date != null -> "Day: ${state.date}"

        style = PantrixTheme.typography.body
    )
    PantrixButton(
        text = "Write today",
        onClick = { state.date = today },
        variant = ButtonVariant.Outline,
        tagKey = "write_today"
    )
}

pages.title: Time Picker
pages.summary: Choosing a time from columns: the hours, the minutes, and by a clock of twelve hours the half of the day. The picker is the choice itself: it stands in the page, or is put in a popover, a dialog or a sheet. It does not hold the choice; the chosen time comes to `onSelect`.
features: **Choosing.** A press on a value gives a whole time, and the other column stays as it is. With nothing chosen yet, an hour comes with its first minute that can be chosen, and a minute with the first such hour. The chosen value scrolls to the middle of its column.

**Times that cannot be chosen.** The minutes outside `minTime` and `maxTime`, and the hours none of whose minutes are between them, are drawn faint and cannot be pressed. Where `maxTime` comes before `minTime`, the times that can be chosen run past midnight; by a clock of 24 hours the column of the hours starts at `minTime`'s hour.
**Minute step.** `minuteStep` sets how far apart the minutes are: with 15, 00, 15, 30 and 45.

**12 or 24 hours.** `is24Hour` gives the picker its shape: `true` 22:00 with two columns, `false` 10:00 PM with a column of the half of the day (AM/PM, ÖÖ/ÖS, ص/م). It is 24 hours in every language by default. To write the time on a screen by the same clock, `strings.time(hour, minute, is24Hour = …)`.

**Keyboard.** Each column is one Tab stop. The arrows choose a value on, Page Up and Page Down six hours or fifteen minutes, Home and End the first and the last value; typing digits goes to the value they write ("1" then "4" is hour 14). ← and → move between the columns.
**Screen reader.** Each column is read by its name and each value as a button; the chosen time is announced politely.
**Platform.** A row is the platform's least touch target on a phone (48dp on Android, 44pt on iOS), and 36dp on the desktop and the web.

**Time type.** Times are `PantrixTime`s; a day and a time become a moment on the device's clock with `PantrixDate.at`. For turning them into `kotlinx-datetime`'s or `java.time`'s, see docs/guide/date-time/DATE_TIME_GUIDE.md.

examples.code:
var call by remember { mutableStateOf<PantrixTime?>(PantrixTime(OPENS, 0)) }
val strings = PantrixTheme.strings
Column(verticalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.sm)) {
    PantrixTimePicker(
        selected = call,
        onSelect = { call = it },
        minTime = PantrixTime(OPENS, 0),
        maxTime = PantrixTime(LAST_CALL, HALF_HOUR),

        tagKey = "call"

        text = call?.let { "Call at: ${strings.clock(it.hour, it.minute)}" } ?: "Choose a time for the call",
        style = PantrixTheme.typography.body
    )
}

private const val HALF_HOUR = 30

private const val OPENS = 9

private const val LAST_CALL = 17

pages.title: Time Text Field
pages.summary: A text field for a time of day: the time is typed in digits, or chosen from a time picker that the button at the box's end opens. The label stands above the box; the field is drawn as a `PantrixTextField`.
features: **Digits alone.** The field takes four digits at most; once the hour is whole the colon comes by itself: `1430` becomes `14:30`. A first digit that cannot start an hour is an hour of one digit: `930` becomes `09:30`. A phone opens its keyboard of digits.
**A pasted time.** A time written out is read as it is written: `14:30`, `14.30`, `1430`, or with a half of the day, `2:30 PM`, `ÖS 2:30`. A second written after the minute is let go.

**Twelve hours.** With `is24Hour = false` the hours are typed 01 to 12, and the half of the day stands in the box beside the digits as a button: a press, or Space while it has the focus, turns it, and on desktop and the web A and P do too. The default is 24 hours, as the picker's.

**Value.** `onValueChange` is called each time the field's time changes: a whole time the field takes, or null while the field is empty, half typed, or holds digits that make no time. A half-typed time stays on the screen while `value` is null; another time from outside is written into the field, its second kept until the hour and minute are typed over.

**Its own error.** The field writes what is wrong under the box itself: an unfinished time on leaving the field, a time the clock has not (25:00), a time outside `minTime` and `maxTime`. Where `minTime` is after `maxTime` the times run past midnight, as a night shift's. The app's `error` comes first; its message is `supportingText`.

**Picker.** It opens with the button, with Alt+↓ on the desktop and the web, by pressing the box of a read-only field, and with Enter or Space; `presentation` chooses what it opens in: by default a sheet in a narrow window and a popover in a wider one; or in every window a popover, a sheet or a dialog. Every press in the picker writes the time into the field at once and the picker stays open, so the hour is chosen first and then the minutes; Enter on a value, Escape and pressing outside close it. Opened with the keyboard the focus goes to the chosen hour, or else to the current one. `minuteStep` sets only the picker's minutes; a minute in between can be typed.

**Three forms.** The form that takes `value` and `onValueChange`; the form that takes a `state` (`rememberTimeTextFieldState()`): `time` is the field's time, `text` tells a half-typed field from an empty one; the form that takes a `field` is bound to a form's field.
**The time type.** Times are `PantrixTime`; to put one together with a day, and to turn it into other libraries' types, see docs/guide/date-time/DATE_TIME_GUIDE.md.

pages.title: Elastic Date Picker
pages.summary: A range of time that can move with the clock: a dashboard is filtered by it, and "the last 15 minutes" is still the last 15 minutes at the next refresh. Elastic UI's `EuiSuperDatePicker`, built again on Pantrix.
features: **Field.** The quick menu's calendar at the start, the range's name in the middle ("Last 15 minutes", "Today"), Refresh beside it. A press on the name shows the two ends (start → end) and opens the start's panel. A range with no name shows its two ends straight away.

**Quick menu.** The last or the next amount of a unit, ‹ and › that move the range by its own length, the ranges `commonlyUsed` offers by name (by default Elastic UI's eight) and those `recentlyUsed` holds. A choice there is handed over at once.

**An end.** Three tabs: Absolute (a calendar, the times by the half hour and a moment to type), Relative (an amount, a unit, the moment it falls on, rounding to the unit), Now. Moving to a tab makes the end what that tab shows. Apply at the end of the moment's field on Absolute and Relative takes the edit and closes the panel; Now's button makes the end now and does the same.

**An edit that waits.** The field is painted in the success colour, a mark appears at its end and the button beside it says Update. An end before the start paints the field in the danger colour and Update takes nothing. With `updateButton = None` each edit is handed over at once.

**One press.** With a panel open, a press on the other end, on Update or anywhere else on the page closes the panel and does what it presses, as in Elastic UI. A press on the open end's button closes its panel.

**Popover, sheet or dialog.** `presentation` says what each panel opens in; the same on every platform. The default is a sheet in a narrow window and a popover in a wider one. The panels have no title over them.
**Close-set panels.** As Elastic UI's: an end's panel is as wide as its calendar and the times beside it, the quick menu 400dp; the fields, tabs and buttons in them are 8dp lower than a form's.

**Auto refresh.** `autoRefresh` and `onAutoRefreshChange`: "Refresh every" in the quick menu, and how often at the field's end; `minAutoRefresh` the shortest. Each turn waits for `onRefresh`, and one that fails stops the refresh.
**Time window.** `timeWindowButtons`: ‹ and › move the range by its length, and zoom out, and zoom in where asked for, widen and narrow it by `zoomFactor`.
**The field's layout.** `layout`: the range, the quick menu's button alone, or auto refresh alone.
**The quick menu's parts.** `customQuickPanels` for panels of its own, `quickMenu` for an order of its own.
**Time zone and disabled words.** `utcOffset` is the moments' difference, `timeZoneName` the name in the panels; `disabledText` the words of a picker that takes no choice.
**Screen reader.** Each end is a button by its name and its words ("Start date, ~ 15 minutes ago"); an edit that waits is announced politely.

**Time.** The ends are `PantrixTimePoint`s; `PantrixTimeRange.resolve()` makes them two `Instant`s by now, and `toDateMath()` writes them in Elasticsearch's date math. More in docs/guide/date-time/DATE_TIME_GUIDE.md.

            value = from,

            modifier = Modifier.weight(1f),
            label = "from",
            error = start == null,
            showCharacterCount = false,
            tagKey = "from"
        )
        PantrixTextField(
            value = to,
            onValueChange = { to = it },
            modifier = Modifier.weight(1f),
            label = "to",
            error = end == null,
            showCharacterCount = false,
            tagKey = "to"
        )
    }
    PantrixButton(
        text = "Apply",
        onClick = { if (start != null && end != null) range = PantrixTimeRange(start, end) },
        variant = ButtonVariant.Outline,
        enabled = start != null && end != null,
        tagKey = "read"
    )
}

pages.title: Card
pages.summary:
A container for one subject: a header, a body and actions on a surface of their own, with media edge to edge above them. An order, an article, a group of settings.

A card is as wide as its widest part. Given a width, usually with `fillMaxWidth()`, its media spans that width and its actions sit against the card's end edge.
features: **Three variants.** `variant` says how the card is set apart from what it stands on: `Elevated` by a shadow, `Filled` by a fill, `Outlined` by a hairline.

**Slots.** `header` stands above the body and `footer` below it; `media` is drawn above them all, edge to edge, and takes none of the card's padding. The lines of the body have the theme's small spacing (`spacing.sm`) between them.

**Height.** A card given a height is filled by its body: the `footer` stands at the card's foot, and a child of the body given a `weight` takes the room between. The cards of a row are of one height this way.
**One button.** Given `onClick`, the whole card is one button: a screen reader hears one target. A button in the `footer` keeps its own press.
**A card that cannot be pressed.** A card that has `onClick` and whose `enabled` is false gives its content the theme's disabled colour; a child that sets a colour of its own keeps it.

**Content colour.** On the theme's `surface`, that is, in an `Elevated` and an `Outlined` card, the card gives its content no colour: each child is drawn in its own default. A `Filled` card, and a card given a role's fill, gives the colour that reads on that fill.
**Colours of its own.** `CardColors` gives the fill, the content's colour and the edge; one that is left out stays the variant's.

**Platform.** The corners and the shadow depend on the platform (`CardStyle`): a medium corner and a 2dp shadow on Android, a large corner and no shadow on iOS, a small corner and a 1dp shadow on desktop and the web.

**Skeleton.** `PantrixCardSkeleton` stands in for a card whose data has not arrived: the card's own surface, with bars in it where the header, the lines and the buttons will be. It is announced to a screen reader once, for the whole card.
**Automation.** `tagKey` gives the card the tag `Card_<tagKey>`; a press is reported as a `Card` event, along with the card's variant.

examples.name: CardPlain
examples.title: At its plainest
examples.description:
Its shortest form: a `PantrixCard` and its body. No variant was given, so it is `Elevated`. The lines of the body stand one under another, with the theme's small spacing between them.

The first card was given no width: it is as wide as its widest line. The second was given `fillMaxWidth()` and fills the space it is in.

examples.name: CardVariants
examples.title: Three variants
examples.description: `variant` picks how the card is set apart from what it stands on. `Elevated` is in the theme's `surface` colour and is lifted by a shadow; on iOS it has no shadow, and the surface colour alone sets the card apart. `Filled` is not lifted and is set apart by the neutral role's fill: it is for a card on a surface that is already raised. `Outlined` is edged by a hairline in the theme's `divider` colour: it is for dense lists of cards, where many shadows become noise.

examples.name: CardSlots
examples.title: Media, header and actions
examples.description:
The card's three slots. `media` stands at the very top, above the header too, and takes none of the card's padding: it reaches the card's edges, and the card cuts its corners. `header` is above the body and is usually the card's title. `footer` gathers the actions in a row at the card's end edge; the main action stands last.

Since the card was given a width, the media spans that width and the actions sit against the end edge.

examples.name: CardsOfOneHeight
examples.title: Of one height in a row
examples.description:
The cards of a row are as tall as the tallest: the row is given `height(IntrinsicSize.Min)`, and each card `weight(1f)` and `fillMaxHeight()`. A card given a height is filled by its body: the `footer` stands at the card's foot, the button of the plan with the short summary too. A child of the body given `Modifier.weight(1f)` takes the room between and pushes the price down to the button.

A card given no height is as tall as what it holds, and its `footer` stands right under its body.

examples.name: CardAsAButton
examples.title: The whole card as one button
examples.description:
Given `onClick`, the whole card is one button. That is the accessible way to build a card that opens something: a screen reader hears one target, with the card's text or, if one is given, with `contentDescription`. Press the first card: the app's snackbar lets you know.

The second card's `enabled` is false: it cannot be pressed and gives its content the theme's disabled colour; this colour of its text is what says that it cannot be pressed. A card without `onClick` ignores `enabled`.

examples.name: CardOwnColors
examples.title: In its own colours
examples.description:
With `colors` the card takes the given colours, not its variant's; a field that is left out stays the variant's.

The first card was given only a fill, and that fill is the colour of one of the theme's roles: the theme itself pairs it with the colour that reads on it. The second card's fill is in none of the theme's roles; it is the app's own purple, and the theme cannot know what reads on it, so `content` is given too. On the third card, which is `Outlined`, only the edge changed.

appNames.name: ownColors
appNames.description: The "app's own colour" of the examples: a purple that is in none of the theme's roles. It is there to show what changes when a component is given `colors`; given one of the theme's roles, nobody could tell whether the colour came from the component's tone or from the parameter.

examples.name: CardShapePaddingAndStyle
examples.title: Shape, padding and style
examples.description:
`shape` changes the corners of one card and wins over the style's corners. `contentPadding` is the room around the header, the body and the actions; its default is `spacing.lg`, and the second card was given `spacing.sm`.

`style` changes the card's geometry: on the last card, a deeper shadow with `CardStyle(elevation = 8.dp)`. Only the field that is given changes, and it changes on every platform: this card has a shadow on iOS too.

examples.name: CardSkeleton
examples.title: Until the data arrives: the skeleton
examples.description:
Press "Refresh": for two seconds the two cards are replaced by their skeletons. `PantrixCardSkeleton` is not drawn to look like a card: it is built from the card's own shape, fill, shadow, padding and spacing. Its bars take the room of what they stand in for: when the data arrives the card's height does not change, and nothing below it moves.

The skeleton cannot know what is in the card: `showHeader`, `lines`, `footerButtons` and `mediaHeight` are given to match the card it stands in for. The first card has a header, one line and two buttons: `lines = 1`, `footerButtons = 2`.

The fill and the content colour of the "Campaign" card were given by the caller. Its skeleton takes the card's colours with `colors` too; its bars are drawn in the colour given with `skeletonColors`.

appNames.name: ownColors
appNames.description: The "app's own colour" of the examples: a purple that is in none of the theme's roles. It is there to show what changes when a component is given `colors`; given one of the theme's roles, nobody could tell whether the colour came from the component's tone or from the parameter.

examples.name: CardSkeletonList
examples.title: A loading list
examples.description:
A loading list: the skeletons of two outlined cards. `mediaHeight` stands in for the media the card will show, `lines` for the lines of the body, and `footerButtons` for the actions.

A skeleton that stands alone is announced to a screen reader once, for the whole card: with the theme's word, "Loading". Inside something that already says it is loading, this announcement is turned off: here the list says once that it is loading, and the skeletons were given `contentDescription = null`.

pages.title: Surface
pages.summary:
The plainest container: it paints a colour in a shape and clips its content to that shape, with an optional 1dp border and a shadow. A panel, a coloured band, the ground of a slide.

Its real work is the content colour. The library's rule is this: a fill says what colour is written on it; the theme's own grounds do not. A `PantrixText` and a `PantrixIcon` inside a surface painted with a role's fill take the colour that reads on that fill without being told.
features: **Fill.** `color` is the surface's colour; left out, it is the theme's `surface`.
**On a role's fill.** The content is drawn in `onColor` on the role's `color`, and in `onContainer` on its `container`.
**On the grounds.** On the theme's `surface` and its `background` the surface gives no content colour: each component draws in its own default, a text in `textPrimary` and an icon in `onSurface`.
**On a colour the theme does not know.** On a fill no role has, the surface gives no colour either; the colour that reads on it is given with `contentColor`.
**A ground inside a fill.** A ground-coloured surface that stands on a fill is a ground again: the colour the fill gave its content ends there.
**Shape.** `shape` sets the corners; its default is the theme's `md` shape. The content is clipped to that shape.
**Border.** When `border` is given a colour, a 1dp line is drawn around the surface.
**Shadow.** `elevation` puts a shadow under the surface; its default is zero.
**The content is in a box.** `content` is a `BoxScope`: the children stand one on top of another and are placed with `Modifier.align`. The surface has no padding of its own.

examples.name: SurfacePlain
examples.title: At its plainest
examples.description: The least there is to write: a `PantrixSurface` with its content. Its colour is the theme's `surface` and its shape is the theme's `md` shape; it has no border and no shadow. The surface takes as much room as its content and has no padding of its own: the padding comes from the text inside.

examples.name: SurfaceOnARole
examples.title: On a role's fill
examples.description: Where `color` is a role's fill, the surface gives its content the colour paired with that fill: `onColor` on the role's `color`, `onContainer` on its `container`. The icon and the text in the rows are given no colour; both take what the surface gives.

examples.name: SurfaceOnGrounds
examples.title: On the grounds and on a colour the theme does not know
examples.description:
On the theme's own grounds, `surface` and `background`, the surface gives no content colour: each component draws in its own default, a text in `textPrimary` and an icon in `onSurface`.

It is the same on a fill no role has: the theme cannot know what reads on that colour. The third surface is painted in the app's own purple, and its content is again drawn in its own defaults. The fourth is given `contentColor`: on a fill like this it is the caller who says what colour reads on it.

appNames.name: ownColors
appNames.description: The "app's own colour" of the examples: a purple that is in none of the theme's roles. It is there to show what changes when a component is given `colors`; given one of the theme's roles, nobody could tell whether the colour came from the component's tone or from the parameter.

examples.name: SurfaceGroundOnAFill
examples.title: A ground inside a fill
examples.description: A ground-coloured surface on a fill is a ground again. The outer surface gives its content `onColor`; the inner one is the theme's `surface` and does not pass that colour on: the text inside it is drawn in `textPrimary` again, and the icon in `onSurface`. The colour the fill gave would not read on that ground.

examples.name: SurfaceReadContentColor
examples.title: Reading the content colour
examples.description: The content colour is carried by `LocalPantrixContentColor`; something you draw yourself can read it too. The dot here is a `Box`, and takes its colour from there. On the grounds the value is `Color.Unspecified`: there the dot picks its own default.

examples.name: SurfaceShapes
examples.title: Shape and clipping
examples.description:
`shape` is the surface's corners: one of the theme's shapes, or any `Shape`. The square surfaces show five of the theme's shapes; the default is `md`.

The content is clipped to the surface's shape. The band inside the bottom surface is a rectangle from edge to edge; its corners were cut by the surface's `xl` shape.

examples.name: SurfaceBorder
examples.title: Border
examples.description: When `border` is given a colour, a 1dp line that follows the surface's shape is drawn around it; without one there is no border. A panel's border is usually the theme's `divider` colour. The thickness does not change: only the colour is given.

examples.name: SurfaceElevation
examples.title: Shadow
examples.description: `elevation` puts a shadow under the surface, following its shape. Here are the five steps of the theme's elevation scale: `PantrixTheme.elevation`, from 0dp to 8dp. The shadow is drawn outside the surface's bounds: it needs room around the surface.

examples.name: SurfaceBox
examples.title: The content is in a box
examples.description: `content` is a `BoxScope`: the children are not laid out one under another, they stand one on top of another, and each picks its place with `Modifier.align`. To lay them out one under another, put a `Column` inside.

pages.title: Scaffold
pages.summary:
The layout of a screen: a top bar, a bottom bar and a side bar around the content, and the app's snackbars over the content. It measures the bars and the window's insets, and gives the content the padding it needs to keep clear of them.

It fills a bounded space, usually the window: a scrolling parent has no height to give it. That is why each example on this page is in a box of a given height, and all but "The window's insets" have `windowInsets` at zero: the box is not the window, and the insets of the system bars are in the app's own scaffold. That scaffold is a real use too: the app's shell (`App.kt`, `shell/DemoNavigation.kt`) puts its navigation in a bottom bar in a narrow window and in a sidebar in a wide one.
features: **Three bars.** `topBar`, `bottomBar` and `sideBar`. The side bar runs the scaffold's full height along the start edge, on the right in a right-to-left layout; the top and the bottom bar span the remaining width.

**The content's padding.** The content reaches under the bars. The `padding` given to `content` is, on each edge, the bar's size or the window inset of an edge without a bar, whichever is larger. It is passed to a list as `contentPadding`: the list scrolls under the bars.

**Window insets.** Each slot is given, as `insets`, the insets of the window edges it touches: a bar extends its fill behind the system bar and keeps its content in the safe area. Insets a parent has consumed are not given again.

**Keyboard.** `windowInsets` is the system bars and the display cutout, and the keyboard is not among them: a screen with text fields adds `Modifier.consumeWindowInsets(padding).imePadding()` to its content.

**Focus.** In content that scrolls beneath a bar, what takes the focus is brought to the edge of the scrolling area, and that edge is behind the bar. The content says what it keeps free at its ends with `Modifier.scrollPadding`: the focus stays between the bars.

**Adaptive navigation.** The second `PantrixScaffold`, the one that takes `navigation`, moves the navigation according to its own width: along the bottom edge while the scaffold is narrower than 600dp, and along the start edge from that width on. The threshold is changed with `ScaffoldStyle`.
**A foldable on a table.** On a device held half open with its fold lying across, the navigation stays at the bottom whatever the width.

**The system's vertical bar.** On the iPhone Duo's outer screen the system keeps a column along the right edge for bars that stand upright, with the status bar at its top. A scaffold that reaches that column puts the navigation at the column's bottom (`ScaffoldNavigationPlacement.VerticalBar`): an upright `PantrixNavigationBar` is drawn there. A `PantrixTopBar` inside it hands its back button and its actions to the column's top too, under the status bar, and its title stays where it is. It does so only in a window that stands upright and has no fold: on the inner screen and on its side the status bar stays alone in the column, and the navigation and the buttons are where they always are. Of two scaffolds one inside the other, the outer one holds the column.
**Snackbars.** A scaffold given `snackbars` shows them over the content, between the bars, and provides them to everything inside it as `LocalPantrixSnackbars`.

**Colour.** `containerColor` is drawn behind everything, the system bars included. On the theme's own grounds the scaffold provides no content colour; on a role's fill it provides the colour paired with that fill.

**Order.** A keyboard and a screen reader go from the side bar to the top bar, the buttons in the vertical bar, the content, the bottom bar and the snackbars. The bars and the snackbars are drawn over the content.
api: com.pantrixui.components.container.scaffold.PantrixScaffold(Modifier, (@Composable (insets: PaddingValues) -> Unit)?, (@Composable (insets: PaddingValues) -> Unit)?, (@Composable (insets: PaddingValues) -> Unit)?, PantrixSnackbarState?, @Composable () -> Unit, Color, Color, WindowInsets, @Composable (padding: PaddingValues) -> Unit)

com.pantrixui.components.container.scaffold.PantrixScaffold(@Composable (placement: ScaffoldNavigationPlacement, insets: PaddingValues) -> Unit, Modifier, (@Composable (insets: PaddingValues) -> Unit)?, PantrixSnackbarState?, @Composable () -> Unit, Color, Color, WindowInsets, ScaffoldStyle?, @Composable (padding: PaddingValues) -> Unit)

examples.name: ScaffoldTopBar
examples.title: Top bar and the content's padding
examples.description:
A top bar and a list that scrolls under it. `topBar` is given `insets` and passes them on to the bar. The content fills the whole scaffold, the space under the bar too: the `padding` that comes to `content` was passed to the list as `contentPadding`, so the first row starts below the bar and the list passes under the bar as it scrolls. Once the list has left its start, the bar draws a line along its bottom edge (`scrolled`).

The scaffold is inside the page, so it was given a height and `windowInsets` was set to zero; on a screen neither is written.

examples.name: ScaffoldBottomBar
examples.title: Bottom bar
examples.description:
`bottomBar` spans the remaining width below the content: here it is a `PantrixNavigationBar` with three destinations. Which destination is open is the screen's state; the bar only reports the one that was pressed.

The content keeps clear of both bars with `padding`: the top padding is the height of the top bar, and the bottom padding that of the bottom bar. The line in the middle shows the values the scaffold gave.

examples.name: ScaffoldFocusBetweenTheBars
examples.title: Focus in a list that scrolls beneath the bars
examples.description:
While the content scrolls beneath the bars, what takes the focus by the keyboard does not stay behind a bar. Compose brings what takes the focus to the list's edge, and since the list reaches under the bars that edge is behind a bar. Here every item says how much the list keeps free at its ends (`Modifier.scrollPadding`): what takes the focus is brought inside that, between the two bars.

The padding is the share the scaffold gave and the room of a focus ring (`PantrixTheme.platform.focusRingReach`). In a column the ring asks for its own room; in a lazy list it cannot, so the list adds that room to its `contentPadding` and tells its items the same value.

Move down by pressing Tab on a keyboard and up by pressing Shift with Tab: every button is shown with its ring between the two bars.

examples.name: ScaffoldSideBar
examples.title: Side bar
examples.description:
`sideBar` runs the scaffold's full height along the start edge: here it is a `PantrixNavigationRail`. The top bar spans the width that is left beside it and does not reach over it. In a right-to-left layout the side bar is on the right.

A keyboard and a screen reader come to the side bar first, then to the top bar, then to the content.

examples.name: ScaffoldAdaptiveNavigation
examples.title: Navigation that moves with the width
examples.description:
The `PantrixScaffold` that takes `navigation` chooses the place of the navigation itself, and tells the navigation where it is (`placement`): along the bottom edge while the scaffold is narrower than 600dp, and along the start edge from that width on. The navigation draws the same destinations as a navigation bar at the bottom and as a rail along the start edge.

The width is the scaffold's own, not the window's: a scaffold in a box goes by the width of the box. If the box is narrower than 600dp the navigation is at the bottom; otherwise it is along the start edge. Pick "Narrow": the box becomes 360dp wide and the navigation moves down to the bottom. In a narrow window the box does not reach 600dp whichever is picked, and the navigation stays at the bottom.

The content stays in the same composition while the navigation moves: press the counter, then change the width; the number is still there.

examples.name: ScaffoldOwnThreshold
examples.title: The width at which the navigation moves
examples.description: The width at which the navigation moves to the start edge is in the scaffold's style: `ScaffoldStyle.sideNavigationMinWidth`, 600dp on every platform. This scaffold was given 280dp through `style`: if the box is 280dp or wider the navigation is along the start edge, even in a window narrower than 600dp.

examples.name: ScaffoldVerticalBar
examples.title: In the system's vertical bar
examples.description:
On the iPhone Duo's outer screen, from iOS 27.1 on, the system keeps a column along the right edge for bars that stand upright: the status bar at its top and the app's bars below it. Pick "Cover": the faint strip is where the status bar is. The scaffold reaches that column, so it puts the navigation at the column's bottom and tells it `ScaffoldNavigationPlacement.VerticalBar`; an upright `PantrixNavigationBar` is drawn there. The `PantrixTopBar` in the content hands its back button and its two actions to the column's top, under the status bar, and its title stays where it is. The app's own shell stands the same way on the Duo's outer screen.

In the upright bar the destinations have their icons alone, as UIKit's tabs in that column: rest on an icon or press it long, and its name shows in a tooltip. Turn "Labels" on: the names are written under the icons too (`showLabels`). The other windows have no column: the navigation is at the bottom or at the start edge by the width, and the buttons are in the top bar. On the Duo's inner screen and on its side the system keeps the column too, but the scaffold leaves it to the status bar, and this is how it stays.

The scaffold is as tall as the outer screen, 678dp; the place in the column is measured by the window, and the scaffold starts at the window's top.

examples.name: ScaffoldSnackbars
examples.title: Snackbars
examples.description:
A scaffold given `snackbars` shows them over the content and inside the padding it gives the content: between the bars. It provides the same state to everything inside it as `LocalPantrixSnackbars`; a screen does not take the state as a parameter to show a snackbar. The button here is a separate composable inside the scaffold, and reads the state from there.

Press "Archive": the snackbar appears inside the scaffold in this box, not in the app's window. Its place depends on the platform: in the middle of the bottom edge on Android, at the top on iOS, and in the bottom end corner on desktop and the web. A scaffold given no `snackbars` keeps the `LocalPantrixSnackbars` of the layout around it: the boxes in the other examples see the app's.

examples.name: ScaffoldInsets
examples.title: The window's insets
examples.description:
In a window `windowInsets` is not written: the scaffold reads the insets of the system bars and the display cutout itself. This box has no system bar, so two insets were given by hand: 28dp at the top and 20dp at the bottom; a caption stands where each bar would be.

Each bar is given the inset of the edge it touches as `insets`. The top bar and the bottom bar pad their content by it: their fill reaches behind the inset, and the title and the destinations stay clear of it. The content's padding grows to match: the values in the line in the middle are the bar's height plus the window's inset.

examples.name: ScaffoldColors
examples.title: Ground and content colour
examples.description:
`containerColor` is the scaffold's ground; its default is the theme's `background`. On the theme's own grounds the scaffold provides no content colour: each component draws in its own default. The upper scaffold was painted with a role's fill, and itself gave the text inside it the colour paired with that fill.

The colour of the lower one is not in the theme but is the app's own purple: the theme cannot know what reads on it, so that is given with `contentColor`.

appNames.name: ownColors
appNames.description: The "app's own colour" of the examples: a purple that is in none of the theme's roles. It is there to show what changes when a component is given `colors`; given one of the theme's roles, nobody could tell whether the colour came from the component's tone or from the parameter.

pages.title: Page Scaffold
pages.summary: A screen inside an app's shell: its name and what it can do at its top, and under them what it shows. The shell is built once with a `PantrixScaffold`, its navigation along the bottom of a narrow window and down the side of a wide one; this frames each of its screens. The pages on this page stand inside a bordered surface, so that their edges show. The card's window picker shows the same page narrow and wide.
features: **Bar.** The page draws its own `PantrixTopBar`, the scaffold none: as the page changes, the title goes with it. The bar holds `title`, `subtitle`, a back button where `onBack` is given, and the actions. The bar's title starts where the content does, at the page's margin. When the content scrolls under the bar, a line is drawn along the bar's bottom edge.

**The title in a wide page.** With `titlePlacement = PageTitlePlacement.Adaptive` there is no bar from Expanded on: the title is written large at the top of the content, the subtitle under it, and the actions beside it are buttons with their labels. In a narrower page they are in the bar.
**Large title.** With `largeTitle` the title is written large under the bar, and goes up into the bar as the content scrolls; the same on every platform.
**Under the title.** `header` stands under the title and scrolls with the content: a description, a notice. `stickyHeader` stays under the bar: tabs, a search, filters. The line is under it then.

**Actions.** `actions` are laid out by the room: buttons with their labels in a wide page, the primary one filled; icons in a Compact one, their names in a tooltip and for a screen reader. What has no room, and in a Compact page what has no icon, is in the "…" menu, in the order given. `onAction` is told the key of the one pressed. `trailing` stands after them all the time: the app's own buttons.

**Scroll.** With `PageScroll.Page` the title, `header` and the content scroll together. With `PageScroll.None` the content fills the room under the bar and scrolls itself, and takes the room it is to leave with `contentPadding`. A list's page is a `PantrixLazyPageScaffold`: its title and its `header` are the list's first rows.

**Width.** By default (`PageWidth.Full`) the page takes its whole width, in a wide window too: cards, a table, a dashboard. `PageWidth.Content` keeps a page that is read to the theme's content width, in line with the title.

**Room and keyboard.** The page reads the room of the `PantrixScaffold` around it itself (`LocalPantrixScaffoldPadding`) and hands none of it on: a page inside a page does not leave the same room again. The page ends above the keyboard; a field that takes the focus is not left behind a bottom bar.

**The window's title.** The page names the tab on the web, the window on the desktop, after itself (`PantrixWindowTitle`); the app adds its own name with `LocalPantrixWindowTitleFormat`. A page inside a page, as the examples on this page are, leaves the title to the outer one.

**Screen reader, event and tags.** The title is the page's heading and the pane's name. A page given a `tagKey` reports a `show` event each time it opens, with its tag, not its title; what is put inside it is in `TestScope(tagKey)`.

examples.name: PageScaffoldOrders
examples.title: A page of an admin
examples.description: The orders page of an admin panel. `titlePlacement = PageTitlePlacement.Adaptive`: choose "Wide" in the card's picker, and the title and the actions go down to the top of the content and the bar goes; in "Narrow" they are in the bar and the actions turn into icons. "Archive" has no icon: in a narrow page it is in the "…" menu. The key of the action pressed is written in the page.

examples.name: PageScaffoldProducts
examples.title: Tabs under the bar, a list that scrolls itself
examples.description: The tabs stand under the bar (`stickyHeader`), the list scrolls itself (`scroll = PageScroll.None`) and takes the room the page leaves with `contentPadding`: its last row inside the room, the margin inside the rows. Scroll the list: the line shows under the tabs. Press the back button and the subtitle counts.

examples.name: PageScaffoldInbox
examples.title: A large title and a list
examples.description: A list's page: `PantrixLazyPageScaffold`. Its rows are composed as they come into view; `header` is the list's first row. `largeTitle = true`: the title is written large under the bar, and goes up into the bar as the list scrolls. `trailing` puts the app's own button at the end of the bar. `width = PageWidth.Content`: a list that is read keeps to the theme's content width in a wide window.

examples.name: PageScaffoldInShell
examples.title: Inside a shell, with measures of its own
examples.description: A page inside a shell: the `PantrixScaffold` has a bottom bar, the page reads its room itself and leaves its last row above the bar. `padding` is that even when it is not given (`LocalPantrixScaffoldPadding.current`); it is written out here. `style` changes the page's margin and the room between its sections.

examples.name: PageScaffoldWindowTitle
examples.title: The window's title
examples.description: The window's title is given without a page too: `PantrixWindowTitle` says the screen's name, and `LocalPantrixWindowTitleFormat` how it is written as the window's. Turn the switch on: on the web the tab's title, on the desktop the window's, becomes "Reports — Admin"; turn it off and this page's comes back. Android and iOS show their user no window's title.

pages.title: Showcase Scaffold
pages.summary: A screen that stands outside the app's shell: sign in, sign up, a password reset, an invitation, a welcome, a page not found. A showcase stands on one side, a picture, a quote or slides, and the form on the other. In a narrow room only the form is left. The screens on this page stand inside a bordered surface; the card's window picker shows the same screen narrow and wide.
features: **Showcase.** `showcase` stands beside the form once the scaffold is as wide as `showcaseFrom`, Expanded by default; `showcaseSide` says which side it stands on. In a narrower room it is not composed at all: its slides do not turn and its pictures are not loaded. The scaffold goes by its own width, not the window's.

**The showcase's background.** `showcaseBackground` fills the showcase to its edges, a picture or a gradient, under the system's bars; what `showcase` holds keeps clear of them. `scrim` deepens the background so that what is written on it reads. The showcase is drawn in its own colours (`ShowcaseScaffoldColors`).

**Form.** `content` is the form, in the middle of its side and no wider than the style's form width. `header` stands above it, a heading; `footer` under it, a way to sign up. `formLayout` keeps the three together in the middle of the side's height, or apart: the header at the top, the footer at the foot.

**Bars.** `topBar` is a row across the top of the form's side, a logo at its start and a language at its end; `bottomBar` a row across its foot, a line of copyright. They stay where they are as the form scrolls between them. Where the showcase is not shown, a line parts each bar from the form; a bar with nothing in it takes no room. Each knows whether the showcase is shown (`showcaseShown`): the logo the showcase carries in a wide window moves to the start of the top bar in a narrow one.

**Frame.** With `ShowcaseFrame.Adaptive`, from Large on, the scaffold is a card in the middle of `backdrop`; a card with no showcase is the form's width and as tall as what it holds. In a narrower window, and with `ShowcaseFrame.Edge` at every width, it reaches the window's edges.
**Foldable.** At an upright fold the showcase is in one half and the form in the other; the two meet at the fold. At a fold lying across only the form is left.

**Room and keyboard.** The scaffold stands outside the shell, so it keeps clear of the system's bars and the display's cut-out itself (`windowInsets`). Only the form's side scrolls; it ends above the keyboard, and a field that takes the focus stays in view.

**What it remembers.** The form and the showcase are each composed in one place whatever the layout: what is typed in a field and a slide's place stay as a phone is turned on its side or the window widens into a card. Type in a field and switch the window picker from "Narrow" to "Wide".

**The window's title, screen reader, event and tags.** `title` is not drawn: it is the window's and the tab's name, and the screen's name for a screen reader. The form is read first, and takes the focus first, wherever the showcase stands. A screen given a `tagKey` reports a `show` event each time it opens; what is put in it is inside `TestScope(tagKey)`.

examples.name: ShowcaseScaffoldAdmin
examples.title: Signing in to an admin panel
examples.description: An admin panel's sign-in screen. The showcase is navy and reaches the edges (`frame = ShowcaseFrame.Edge`): the logo at the top, a customer's words in the middle, the figures and the copyright line at the bottom. The language menu stands at the end of the form side's top bar (`topBar`); the chosen language has a check beside it (`PantrixMenuItem`'s `selected`). Switch the window picker to "Short" or "Wide": the showcase comes beside the form. In "Narrow" the showcase goes; the logo moves to the start of the top bar and the copyright line into the bottom bar (`bottomBar`), each looking at whether the showcase is shown (`showcaseShown`), and a line parts each bar from the form. "Sign in" is enabled once both fields are filled.

appNames.name: said
appNames.description: A text written in two languages, as it reads in the app's current language: for the shell's own texts, and in an example for a text the translation files do not know because it has no letters in it, as a percentage. The text's two languages stand side by side where it is used; whoever changes a button's name sees both together.

appNames.name: DemoIcons
appNames.description: The sample app's own icons: for the sections in the navigation and the buttons on the top bar. The library's icons (`PantrixIcons`) are as many as a component library cannot do without; an app's home, grid or settings icon is its own.

appNames.name: LocalExampleEvents
appNames.description: Where an example tells its card what happens in it: a button pressed, a row chosen, a dialog closed. The card writes the last thing told under the example, on its "Last event" line.

examples.name: ShowcaseScaffoldSlides
examples.title: Signing in beside slides
examples.description: Slides that turn in the showcase (`PantrixCarousel`): each a heading and a sentence. With `showcaseFrom = WindowWidthClass.Medium` the showcase is shown from 600 dp on, in "Medium" too. In "Book" the showcase is in one half and the form in the other, and they meet at the fold; in "Tabletop" only the form is left. In "Narrow" the showcase is not composed at all: its slides do not turn.

appNames.name: DemoIcons
appNames.description: The sample app's own icons: for the sections in the navigation and the buttons on the top bar. The library's icons (`PantrixIcons`) are as many as a component library cannot do without; an app's home, grid or settings icon is its own.

examples.name: ShowcaseScaffoldSignUp
examples.title: Signing up on a picture
examples.description: Signing up on a picture. A gradient stands where the picture would: the showcase's background (`showcaseBackground`) and what the card stands on (`backdrop`). The showcase is at the end (`showcaseSide = ShowcaseSide.End`); `scrim = ShowcaseScrim.Bottom` deepens the background towards its foot so that the line at the bottom reads. The showcase stands in the card with corners of its own (`showcaseInset`). In "Wide" the layout is a card, which `ShowcaseFrame.Adaptive` draws from Large on; in "Short" it reaches the edges.

appNames.name: DemoIcons
appNames.description: The sample app's own icons: for the sections in the navigation and the buttons on the top bar. The library's icons (`PantrixIcons`) are as many as a component library cannot do without; an app's home, grid or settings icon is its own.

examples.name: ShowcaseScaffoldReset
examples.title: Password reset
examples.description: A screen with no showcase: the form alone. In "Wide" the form is a card of its own width in the middle of the backdrop; in a narrower window it reaches the edges. `footer` is the way back to signing in.

appNames.name: DemoIcons
appNames.description: The sample app's own icons: for the sections in the navigation and the buttons on the top bar. The library's icons (`PantrixIcons`) are as many as a component library cannot do without; an app's home, grid or settings icon is its own.

examples.name: ShowcaseScaffoldNotFound
examples.title: A page not found
examples.description: A page not found, with `formLayout = ShowcaseFormLayout.Spread`: the logo at the top, the words in the middle of the side, the help link under them and the copyright line in the bottom bar (`bottomBar`). The showcase is a large "404" in the theme's neutral colour: a colour that is the theme's brings the colour of what is written on it with it.

appNames.name: DemoIcons
appNames.description: The sample app's own icons: for the sections in the navigation and the buttons on the top bar. The library's icons (`PantrixIcons`) are as many as a component library cannot do without; an app's home, grid or settings icon is its own.

pages.title: Accordion
pages.summary:
Sections whose content folds away under their headers, so that a long page can be read a part at a time.

Which sections are open is the screen's state: the accordion is given the keys of the open sections (`expanded`), and when a header is pressed it reports back the new set that is to be open (`onExpandedChange`). The accordion changes nothing by itself. That is what lets a screen open the section a link points at, keep what was open across a rotation, or close everything from a button of its own.
features: **Three variants.** `variant` says how the sections are told apart: `Plain` puts a line between them, `Bordered` puts one edge around them all, `Separated` makes each section a card of its own.
**One section or many.** Any number of sections stay open at once; with `singleExpanded`, opening one closes the one that was open.

**The parts of a header.** The header of an `AccordionSection` has its `title`, with `subtitle` under it, `icon` before it and `trailing` at its end. `trailing` is a part of the header's button and is read with it: a count, a badge; a control of its own does not belong there.
**Keys.** Each section's `key` is the same in every language, and no two sections of an accordion have one key.
**A closed section is not composed.** A section's content is composed only while the section is open; what it kept with `rememberSaveable` is there again when the section is opened again.
**Disabled.** The accordion's `enabled` keeps every header from being pressed, and a section's own `enabled` only that section's; open or closed, the section stays as it is.

**Screen reader.** A header is a button and a heading that carries its section's name. A screen reader is offered what a press does, to expand the section or to collapse it, and is told whether the section is open. The chevron is a picture of that, and is not read.

**Platform.** A header is a row of a list: 56dp on Android, 44dp on iOS and the web, 40dp on desktop; it is never lower than the platform's touch target, and grows with a long title and a large type. The corners are the card's.

**Colour.** `AccordionColors` gives the fill, the text's colour and the lines. The variants that have no fill stand on what is behind them: on a fill, they are written in the colour that fill gives what stands on it.

**Automation.** With `tagKey` the accordion is `Accordion_<tagKey>`, a header in it `Accordion_<tagKey>.Header_<key>` and what it opens `Accordion_<tagKey>.Content_<key>`. A press is reported as `expand` or `collapse`, with the section's key.

examples.name: AccordionQuestions
examples.title: Frequently asked questions: a line between them
examples.description:
The plainest form, questions and answers. The keys of the open sections are the screen's state and are kept with `rememberSaveable`; the accordion takes them as `expanded` and, when a header is pressed, reports the new set with `onExpandedChange`. Any number of sections stay open at once.

No variant is given: `Plain`, a line between the sections and nothing around them. A long title that does not fit on one line runs onto a second, and the header grows with it. The last section's `enabled` is false: it cannot be pressed, is written in the disabled text's colour and stays closed.

examples.name: AccordionOrders
examples.title: Inside one edge, with a count at a header's end
examples.description:
`AccordionVariant.Bordered` puts the sections inside one edge; there is still a line between them.

The `icon` before the title is drawn in the title's colour, and a screen reader passes over it. The count at the header's end is given with `trailing`: it stands between the title and the chevron, is a part of the header's button, and a screen reader reads it with the title. Here it is written in small type and is given no colour.

examples.name: AccordionSettings
examples.title: Each section a card, only one open at a time
examples.description:
`AccordionVariant.Separated` makes each section a card of its own, with a gap between them. With `singleExpanded` only one section stays open at a time: opening one closes the one that was open. It is for pages where two open sections would push the rest off the screen.

`subtitle` is the second line, under the title, and gives the section's summary: flip the switches, and the subtitle of "Notifications" changes between "On" and "Off".

examples.name: AccordionRemembers
examples.title: A section that closes keeps what was typed
examples.description:
A closed section's content is not composed at all; yet the section keeps, even while it is closed, everything that was saved to be restored. The field keeps its text with `rememberTextFieldState()`, and that state is saved.

Type something into the "Delivery note" section, close the section and open it again: when the section closes the field leaves the screen, and when it opens again what you typed is there.

examples.name: AccordionControlled
examples.title: Opening and closing from outside
examples.description: Since the open sections are the screen's state, they change from outside the accordion too. The two buttons above press no header; they only change the set: one puts every key into it, the other empties it. The accordion draws the new set.
examples.code:
var open by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf(emptySet<String>()) }
Row(horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.sm)) {
    PantrixButton(
        text = "Open all",
        onClick = { open = setOf("monday", "tuesday", "wednesday") },
        variant = ButtonVariant.Outline,
        size = ButtonSize.Small,
        tagKey = "accordion_open_all"
    )
    PantrixButton(
        text = "Close all",
        onClick = { open = emptySet() },
        variant = ButtonVariant.Text,
        size = ButtonSize.Small,
        tagKey = "accordion_close_all"
    )
}
PantrixAccordion(
    sections = listOf(
        AccordionSection(key = "monday", title = "Monday") { PantrixText(text = "09.00 Weekly planning") },
        AccordionSection(key = "tuesday", title = "Tuesday") { PantrixText(text = "14.00 Design review") },
        AccordionSection(key = "wednesday", title = "Wednesday") { PantrixText(text = "No meetings") }
    ),
    expanded = open,
    onExpandedChange = { open = it },
    variant = AccordionVariant.Bordered,
    tagKey = "week"
)

examples.name: AccordionDisabled
examples.title: All disabled
examples.description: With `enabled = false` no header can be pressed and every section is held as it is: an open one stays open and a closed one closed. The headers are written in the disabled text's colour. A section's own `enabled` does the same for that section alone.

examples.name: AccordionOwnColors
examples.title: In its own colours
examples.description: `colors` gives the accordion the colours set there in place of the theme's: here, cards in a colour the theme does not have. The fill is given with `container`; the headers and the content take the `content` colour, and the line is given separately, with `divider`. A colour that is left out stays the theme's.

appNames.name: ownColors
appNames.description: The "app's own colour" of the examples: a purple that is in none of the theme's roles. It is there to show what changes when a component is given `colors`; given one of the theme's roles, nobody could tell whether the colour came from the component's tone or from the parameter.

examples.name: AccordionOnAFill
examples.title: On a fill
examples.description: The `Plain` and `Bordered` variants have no fill of their own: they stand on what is behind them. Here the accordion is inside a surface painted with a role's fill, and is given no colours: the titles, the subtitle and the chevron are written in the colour that fill gives what stands on it, and the lines are drawn in a share of that colour. The theme's line would not read on this fill.

examples.name: AccordionOwnStyle
examples.title: In its own style
examples.description: `style` changes the accordion's geometry; only the fields that are given change, and the rest comes from the platform's style. Here the header's least height is set to 64dp and the gap between the cards to 16dp; the corners are not a step of the brand's shape scale but a fixed 20dp: `ShapeSpec.Fixed`.

pages.title: Tabs
pages.summary:
A row of tabs that switches between views of the same content: one is selected, and an indicator slides to the one selected next.

The tabs are only the row; the app draws the selected view itself, below the row. Which tab is selected is the screen's state too: the row is given its index (`selectedIndex`), and reports back the one the user chose (`onSelect`). The row selects nothing by itself.
features: **Indicator.** The style's `indicator` marks the selected tab: a line under it, a line over it, a pill behind it, or its colour alone. The indicator slides when the selection changes; in a theme with reduced motion it takes its place at once.

**A shared row, or one that scrolls.** The tabs share the row's width. With `scrollable` each is as wide as its label and the row scrolls sideways: it opens on the selected tab, and brings each tab selected after that to its middle.
**Icon and badge.** `TabItem.icon` stands before the label and `TabItem.badge` after it: a count or a dot. Where the tab is narrow it is the label that is cut, and the badge stays whole.
**Disabled tab.** A press does nothing on a tab whose `enabled` is false, the arrow keys skip it, and it is drawn in the theme's disabled text colour whatever colour is given.

**Keyboard.** The row is one stop for the Tab key, on the selected tab. The arrow keys select the next and the previous tab, the other way round in a right-to-left layout; Home and End the first and the last. While a tab has the focus, the focus goes with the selection.
**Screen reader.** Each tab is a tab that says whether it is selected, and together they are one group. The badge's description is read after the label, as a part of the tab.
**Platform.** A tab's least height is 48dp on Android, 44dp on iOS, and 40dp on the desktop and the web; a tab is never shorter than the platform's touch target.
**Colour.** The row has no fill of its own: it sits on the page or on a surface. `TabsColors` gives the colours of the selected tab and of the others, of the indicator, and of the hairline below.

**Automation.** With a `tagKey` the row is `Tabs_<tagKey>` and its tabs are `Tabs_<tagKey>.Tab_<key>`. A selection is reported with the tab's index and whether a press or a key made it; never with its label.

examples.name: TabsPlain
examples.title: Views of a profile
examples.description:
At its plainest: three tabs that share the row's width equally, and the selected view below them. The selected tab's index is the screen's state; it is kept with `rememberSaveable`, and is not lost when the screen rotates.

The tabs do not draw the view: the text below them is chosen here, with `when`. The default indicator is the line under the selected tab.

examples.name: TabsBadges
examples.title: Tabs with badges
examples.description:
`TabItem.badge` puts a `TabBadge` after the label: a number where `count` is given, a dot where it is not. The "Activity" tab shows the number of unseen transactions; when the tab is opened the number goes to zero and the badge goes away. The dot on "Settings" says an update is waiting.

A screen reader reads the badge's `contentDescription` after the tab's name: "Activity, 3 new transactions". A number alone says nothing of what it counts; that is why the description has no default, and giving null is a decision.

examples.name: TabsIndicators
examples.title: The selected tab's indicator
examples.description:
The style says what marks the selected tab: `TabsStyle(indicator = ...)`. The four rows show the same selection, each with the name of its indicator written above it; press another tab in one of them, and all four change together.

`Underline` is the default on every platform: a line along the selected tab's bottom edge. `Top` puts the same line along the top edge, for a row that sits below what it switches. `Pill` puts a pill in the primary role's pale fill behind the selected tab, and does not draw the hairline under the row: it is how iOS draws its segmented control, and here it picks a chart's period. `None` draws no indicator; the selected tab is marked by its colour alone.
examples.code:
var period by rememberSaveable { mutableIntStateOf(1) }
val caption = PantrixTheme.typography.caption
val quiet = PantrixTheme.colors.textSecondary
PantrixText(text = "Underline", style = caption, color = quiet)
PantrixTabs(tabs = PERIODS, selectedIndex = period, onSelect = { period = it }, tagKey = "underline")
PantrixText(text = "Top", style = caption, color = quiet)
PantrixTabs(
    tabs = PERIODS,
    selectedIndex = period,
    onSelect = { period = it },
    style = TabsStyle(indicator = TabIndicator.Top),
    tagKey = "top"
)
PantrixText(text = "Pill", style = caption, color = quiet)
PantrixTabs(
    tabs = PERIODS,
    selectedIndex = period,
    onSelect = { period = it },
    style = TabsStyle(indicator = TabIndicator.Pill),
    tagKey = "period"
)
PantrixText(text = "None", style = caption, color = quiet)
PantrixTabs(
    tabs = PERIODS,
    selectedIndex = period,
    onSelect = { period = it },
    style = TabsStyle(indicator = TabIndicator.None),
    tagKey = "none"
)

private val PERIODS = listOf(
    TabItem(label = "Day", tagKey = "day"),
    TabItem(label = "Week", tagKey = "week"),
    TabItem(label = "Month", tagKey = "month")
)

examples.name: TabsScrollable
examples.title: Categories with icons in a row that scrolls
examples.description:
More categories than the row has room for, each with its icon. With `scrollable = true` each tab is as wide as its label and the row scrolls sideways. The selected tab comes to the middle of the row, so that the tabs on both sides of it can be seen and pressed.

The count on "Inbox" is over the largest number that is written: "99+". The last category is disabled: it cannot be pressed, and the arrow keys skip it.
examples.code:
var category by rememberSaveable { mutableIntStateOf(0) }
PantrixTabs(
    tabs = CATEGORIES,
    selectedIndex = category,
    onSelect = { category = it },
    scrollable = true,
    tagKey = "categories"
)

private val CATEGORIES = listOf(
    TabItem(
        label = "Inbox",
        icon = PantrixIcons.Inbox,
        tagKey = "inbox",
        badge = TabBadge(contentDescription = "More than 99 unread messages", count = 128)
    ),
    TabItem(label = "Starred", icon = PantrixIcons.Star, tagKey = "starred"),
    TabItem(label = "Folders", icon = PantrixIcons.Folder, tagKey = "folders"),
    TabItem(label = "People", icon = PantrixIcons.Person, tagKey = "people"),
    TabItem(label = "Calendar", icon = PantrixIcons.Calendar, tagKey = "calendar"),
    TabItem(label = "Search", icon = PantrixIcons.Search, tagKey = "search"),
    TabItem(label = "Archive", icon = PantrixIcons.Folder, enabled = false, tagKey = "archive")
)

examples.name: TabsWithAPager
examples.title: With pages that are swiped
examples.description: The app changes the selection as much as the user does. Here the selected tab is a pager's page: swipe the page sideways, and the indicator slides to the new tab. When a tab is pressed the tabs only report which one; it is the code in `onSelect` that turns the page.

examples.name: TabsNoSelection
examples.title: With no tab selected
examples.description: When `selectedIndex` is an index outside the tabs, no tab is selected and no indicator is drawn: the app is in a place that is no tab's view. Press the button: the selection goes. Press a tab: it comes back.
examples.code:
var view by rememberSaveable { mutableIntStateOf(0) }
PantrixTabs(
    tabs = listOf(
        TabItem(label = "Feed", tagKey = "feed"),
        TabItem(label = "Explore", tagKey = "explore"),
        TabItem(label = "Saved", tagKey = "saved")
    ),
    selectedIndex = view,
    onSelect = { view = it },
    tagKey = "home"
)
PantrixButton(
    text = "Open search results",
    onClick = { view = -1 },
    variant = ButtonVariant.Outline,
    size = ButtonSize.Small,
    tagKey = "tabs_open_search"
)
PantrixText(
    text = if (view < 0) "Search results are open: no tab is selected" else "A tab's view is open",
    color = PantrixTheme.colors.textSecondary
)

examples.name: TabsOwnColors
examples.title: In its own colours
examples.description:
With `colors` the row takes the colours it is given, not the theme's. The first row is given the colour of the selected tab and of the line; the tabs that are not selected and the hairline below stay in the theme's colours. The badge of the "Pending" tab, too, is filled with the colour it is given and not with its tone's.

The second row is a row of pills, and only the pill's fill is given. That fill is the colour of one of the theme's roles, so the theme pairs the selected label's colour with it. On a fill no role has, `selectedContent` is given as well.
examples.code:
val own = ownColors()
var order by rememberSaveable { mutableIntStateOf(0) }
var period by rememberSaveable { mutableIntStateOf(0) }
PantrixTabs(
    tabs = listOf(
        TabItem(
            label = "Pending",
            tagKey = "pending",
            badge = TabBadge(
                contentDescription = "2 pending orders",
                count = 2,
                colors = BadgeColors(container = own.color, content = own.onColor)
            )
        ),
        TabItem(label = "Shipped", tagKey = "shipped"),
        TabItem(label = "Delivered", tagKey = "delivered")
    ),
    selectedIndex = order,
    onSelect = { order = it },
    colors = TabsColors(selectedContent = own.color, indicator = own.color),
    tagKey = "orders"
)
PantrixTabs(
    tabs = PERIODS,
    selectedIndex = period,
    onSelect = { period = it },
    style = TabsStyle(indicator = TabIndicator.Pill),
    colors = TabsColors(indicator = PantrixTheme.colors.success.container),
    tagKey = "success_pill"
)

private val PERIODS = listOf(
    TabItem(label = "Day", tagKey = "day"),
    TabItem(label = "Week", tagKey = "week"),
    TabItem(label = "Month", tagKey = "month")
)

appNames.name: ownColors
appNames.description: The "app's own colour" of the examples: a purple that is in none of the theme's roles. It is there to show what changes when a component is given `colors`; given one of the theme's roles, nobody could tell whether the colour came from the component's tone or from the parameter.

pages.title: Top Bar
pages.summary:
The bar at the top of a screen: the screen's name, with a navigation icon at its start and actions at its end.
