The bar is as wide as what holds it and as tall as its style says; it is taller only where what it holds needs it, as a title set larger does. On a screen it usually stands in the `topBar` slot of `PantrixScaffold`. The bars on this page do not stand at the top edge of a screen, so each is inside a surface with a border: that is how their bounds show.
features: **Title and subtitle.** `title` is the screen's name, on one line; `subtitle` is written under it, smaller: a count, a state. Either is cut short when it does not fit the room between the navigation icon and the actions, and does not run under them. Their text styles are given with `titleStyle` and `subtitleStyle`; unless given, they are the theme's `title` and `footnote` styles.

**Platform.** The title stands at the start on Android, desktop and the web, and in the middle of the bar on iOS. A title in the middle is in the exact middle of the bar while it fits there; when it does not, it moves away from the wider side. The bar is 54dp tall on Android and iOS, 56dp on desktop and the web.

**Navigation icon and actions.** `navigationIcon` stands before the title: a back button, or a button that opens a menu. `actions` is a row after the title: icon buttons for what the screen can do, the most used first.

**Back button.** `PantrixBackButton` draws the platform's icon: an arrow on Android, desktop and the web, a chevron on iOS; both turn round in a right-to-left layout. A screen reader calls it "Back" in the theme's language.
**Line over scrolled content.** While `scrolled` is true a line is drawn along the bar's bottom edge. The line is inside the bar's height; nothing moves as it comes and goes.

**Collapsing title.** A bar given a `state` writes its title large while it is open, in a band under the row; as the content scrolls up the band closes and the title comes into the row. The content hands the bar its scroll with `Modifier.topBarScroll(state)`.
**Insets.** `insets` is the room the bar keeps clear at its edges: for the status bar and a cutout. The bar's fill runs behind them.

**Colour.** The bar is the theme's `surface`, with the title in `textPrimary` and the subtitle in `textSecondary`. `TopBarColors` gives the fill, the colour of the content and the line; on a bar with a fill, all of it is written in one colour.

**Reading order.** A screen reader and the Tab key go through the bar in the order it reads: the navigation icon, the title and the subtitle under it, the actions. The title is the screen's heading for a screen reader.

**Automation.** With a `tagKey` the bar is tagged `TopBar_<tagKey>`, and the large title of a collapsing bar `TopBar_<tagKey>.Title_large`. The back button is an icon button: it carries the tag `IconButton_<tagKey>`, and its press is reported as an icon button's.

examples.name: TopBarPlain
examples.title: Title only
examples.description: The least there is to write: `title` alone. With no navigation icon, a title at the start begins at the bar's own inset; on iOS the title is in the middle.

examples.name: TopBarConversation
examples.title: Back button, actions and content scrolling under the bar
examples.description:
A conversation screen: a back button, two actions and a list that scrolls under the bar. `navigationIcon` puts a `PantrixBackButton` before the title; the subtitle says how many times the back button has been pressed. `actions` puts two icon buttons after the title: drawn as they are, in the brand's colour.

Scroll the list: as soon as it leaves its top, a line appears along the bar's bottom edge (`scrolled`), and it stays for as long as the list can scroll back. The line is inside the bar's height; nothing moves as it comes and goes.

examples.name: TopBarSubtitle
examples.title: Subtitle
examples.description: `subtitle` puts a line of smaller text under the title: a count, a state. The navigation icon here is not a back button but an icon button that opens a menu.

examples.name: TopBarOwnType
examples.title: Title and subtitle in text styles of their own
examples.description: The title and the subtitle can each be given a text style: `titleStyle` and `subtitleStyle`. Unless given, they are the theme's `title` and `footnote` styles; here `callout` and `caption` are given. Where the style has no colour of its own, the text stays in the bar's colour. A larger style makes the bar as tall as its line needs.

examples.name: TopBarLongTitle
examples.title: A title that does not fit is cut short
examples.description: The title does not run under the navigation icon or the actions: a title too long for the room left between them is cut short. The bar here is at most 360dp wide; the title does not fit between the back button and the star, and its end is cut off.

examples.name: TopBarTitlePlaces
examples.title: Where the title stands: at the start and in the middle
examples.description:
Where the title stands follows the platform: at the start on Android, desktop and the web, in the middle of the bar on iOS. Here the same bar is drawn twice, and the place is given with `style`: `TopBarStyle(titleAlignment = ...)`. Both show, whichever platform you are on.

A title in the middle is in the middle of the bar whatever stands beside it: the back button does not push it aside.

examples.name: TopBarBackIcons
examples.title: The back button's icon
examples.description:
`PantrixBackButton` takes the icon it draws from the bar's style: `TopBarStyle.backIcon`. The platform's own icon is an arrow on Android, desktop and the web, a chevron on iOS. Here each of the two bars is given an icon with `style`; a back button in a bar's `navigationIcon` uses the style that bar was given.

Both turn round in a right-to-left layout: flip the reading direction from the "Typeface and direction" menu in the app's top bar and look.

examples.name: TopBarBackDisabled
examples.title: With nowhere to go back to
examples.description: On the first screen of a flow there is nowhere to go back to: the `enabled` of `PantrixBackButton` is false and the button cannot be pressed. Move on with the button at the end: the back button is enabled from the second step on.

examples.name: TopBarCollapsing
examples.title: A large title that collapses as the list scrolls
examples.description:
A collapsing title: the state is the app's and is kept with `rememberPantrixTopBarState()`; the list hands the bar its scroll with `Modifier.topBarScroll(state)`. While the bar is open the title is written large, in the theme's `headline` style, in a band under the row. The large title stands at the bar's start on every platform; the title in the row stands where the platform has it, in the middle on iOS.

Scroll the list up: first the band closes and the title comes into the row, and only then does the list scroll. The bar opens again only once the list is back at its top. Left between its two heights by a finger, it goes on to the nearer; after a mouse wheel it goes on the way the wheel was last turned. A screen reader reads the title in the row: that one is there all the time, and the title is not read twice.

The bar and the list are inside a scaffold, as they would be in an app: the list fills the whole scaffold and is given the bar's height as its top inset. As the bar closes and opens the list itself stays where it is; only its inset changes. The button below takes the list back to its top and opens the bar by setting `collapsedFraction` to zero.

examples.name: TopBarInsets
examples.title: The insets the bar keeps clear
examples.description: `insets` is the room the bar keeps clear at its edges: room for the status bar and a cutout. A `PantrixScaffold` hands it to its top bar itself; here a top inset of 28dp is given by hand. The bar's fill runs behind the inset, and the title and the back button stay below it: the bar is as tall as its style's height plus the inset.

examples.name: TopBarOwnColors
examples.title: In its own colours
examples.description:
`colors` gives the bar colours of its own in place of the theme's. The first bar's fill is the colour of one of the theme's roles, and that alone is given: the theme pairs the colour of the title, the subtitle and the back button with it.

The second bar is in a colour the theme does not have, the app's own purple: the colour that reads on it is given with `content`. The title, the subtitle and the back button take the `content` colour. The icon button has colours of its own: the colour that reads on the fill is given to it separately.

appNames.name: ownColors
appNames.description: The "app's own colour" of the examples: a purple that is in none of the theme's roles. It is there to show what changes when a component is given `colors`; given one of the theme's roles, nobody could tell whether the colour came from the component's tone or from the parameter.

pages.title: Alert
pages.summary:
A message about what the user is doing, beside the thing it is about: the form that was just sent, the row about to be deleted, the field that needs a second look.

The alert stands in the content, is as wide as what holds it, and stays until the screen takes it away. What the app has just done, said for a few seconds over the whole screen, is a snackbar.
features: **Six tones.** `tone` chooses the alert's colour, its icon and how it is announced. The four semantic tones, `Info`, `Success`, `Warning` and `Danger`, say how something went in three ways: a colour alone fails whoever cannot see it. `Primary` and `Neutral` say nothing of that, and have no icon of their own.

**Three variants.** `variant`: `Soft` is the tone's pale fill, `Outline` an edge with no fill, and `Accent` the fill with a bar down its leading edge: on the left in a left-to-right layout, on the right in a right-to-left one.
**A message with a link.** `message` can be an `AnnotatedString` too: a `LinkAnnotation` in it becomes a link, underlined, in the alert's text colour.
**Title and icon.** `title` is a line above the message, in a heavier type. `icon` puts another icon in place of the tone's own, or takes the icon away with null.
**Action.** `action` puts one or two small buttons under the message, at the trailing edge.
**Dismissal.** With `onDismiss` the alert has a close button. An alert does not go away by itself: it stays until the caller stops showing it.

**Screen reader.** The title and the message are read as one, and the action and the close button after them. The alert is announced when it appears or changes: assertively for `Danger`, politely for the rest. `announce = false` turns this off.
**First line.** The icon and the close button stand on the text's first line, however large the type is set. An alert with an icon and one without are as tall as each other.
**Platform.** The corners are medium on Android and iOS, and small on desktop and the web; the padding is 12dp and 10dp, and the bar 4dp and 3dp (`AlertStyle`).
**Text.** `textStyle` changes the type of the message, and of the title in its bold; the icon and the close button stand on that type's first line.

**Colours of its own.** `AlertColors` gives the fill, the colour of the text and of what marks the tone, and `border` the colour of an edge apart from the icon's; the tone still decides the icon and the way the alert is announced.
**Automation.** With `tagKey` the alert is `Alert_<tagKey>` and its close button `AlertClose_<tagKey>`. A dismissal is reported with its tone and its variant, and never with its message.
api: com.pantrixui.components.container.alert.PantrixAlert(String, Modifier, AlertTone, AlertVariant, String?, ImageVector?, (@Composable RowScope.() -> Unit)?, (() -> Unit)?, Boolean, AlertStyle?, AlertColors?, String?, TextStyle)

com.pantrixui.components.container.alert.PantrixAlert(AnnotatedString, Modifier, AlertTone, AlertVariant, String?, ImageVector?, (@Composable RowScope.() -> Unit)?, (() -> Unit)?, Boolean, AlertStyle?, AlertColors?, String?, TextStyle)

examples.name: AlertPlain
examples.title: Message and title
examples.description:
The least it takes is `message` alone: the tone is then `Info` and the variant `Soft`, and the icon comes from the tone. The alert fills the width it is given.

`title` puts a line in a heavier type above the message: it says in a few words what the alert is about. A screen reader hears the title and the message as one.
examples.code:
PantrixAlert(message = "Your profile photo has been updated", tagKey = "plain")
PantrixAlert(
    message = "We have sent a verification link to your new address",
    title = "Verify your email",
    tagKey = "titled"
)

examples.name: AlertTones
examples.title: Six tones
examples.description:
`tone` is one of the theme's colour roles; it chooses the alert's colour, its icon and how it is announced to a screen reader, all at once. The four semantic tones reach the user three ways: as a colour, as an icon and in the way they are announced. `Danger` is the one tone announced assertively.

`Primary` and `Neutral` do not say how something went, and have no icon. An alert in one of them is a note set apart from the text around it: a feature to try, something to know that does not ask for the eye.
examples.code:
PantrixAlert(message = "A new version is ready to install", tagKey = "info")
PantrixAlert(message = "Your changes have been saved", tone = AlertTone.Success, tagKey = "success")
PantrixAlert(message = "Your storage is almost full", tone = AlertTone.Warning, tagKey = "warning")
PantrixAlert(message = "The message could not be sent", tone = AlertTone.Danger, tagKey = "danger")
PantrixAlert(message = "Try the new editor", tone = AlertTone.Primary, tagKey = "primary")
PantrixAlert(message = "Last opened: yesterday", tone = AlertTone.Neutral, tagKey = "neutral")

examples.name: AlertVariants
examples.title: Three variants
examples.description:
`variant` chooses how the alert is drawn: a pale fill, an edge alone, or the fill with a bar down its leading edge. `Soft` is the default, and what a page wants. `Accent` tells alerts one under another apart at a glance.

`Outline` is for a card or a dialog: a pale fill would be lost on their own fill. The one here is inside a filled card: it has no fill of its own, so the card's fill shows, and its text is written in the colour that reads on the card. This alert's `announce` is false as well: a note that was there before the user came is not announced when it appears.
examples.code:
PantrixAlert(
    message = "A pale fill: this is how it looks on a page",
    title = "Soft",
    tagKey = "soft"
)
PantrixCard(modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(), variant = CardVariant.Filled) {
    PantrixAlert(
        message = "Archived records cannot be changed",
        variant = AlertVariant.Outline,
        title = "Outline: read-only",
        // It was already here when the user came: a screen reader gets to it in its own time.
        announce = false,
        tagKey = "outline"
    )
}
PantrixAlert(
    message = "Alerts one under another are told apart at a glance",
    tone = AlertTone.Success,
    variant = AlertVariant.Accent,
    title = "Accent",
    tagKey = "accent"
)

examples.name: AlertIcons
examples.title: Changing and removing the icon
examples.description:
`icon` is the mark before the text: the tone's own unless one is given, and none when null. The `Primary` and `Neutral` tones have no icon of their own; here each of them was given one. The icon is never read out: the message says what it stands for.

An alert with an icon and one without are as tall as each other: the text's first line takes the room of an icon, with one beside it or without.
examples.code:
PantrixAlert(message = "An info note with its icon removed", icon = null, tagKey = "no_icon")
PantrixAlert(
    message = "Added to your favourites",
    tone = AlertTone.Primary,
    icon = PantrixIcons.Star,
    tagKey = "star_icon"
)
PantrixAlert(
    message = "The meeting is at 10.00 tomorrow",
    tone = AlertTone.Neutral,
    icon = PantrixIcons.Calendar,
    tagKey = "calendar_icon"
)

examples.name: AlertActionAndDismiss
examples.title: Action and dismissal
examples.description:
A warning with two actions and a close button. `action` puts the buttons under the message, at the trailing edge. A text button's own colour is the brand's; `buttonColors(ButtonVariant.Text)`, taken from the tone's role, draws it in the tone's colour, which reads on the tone's fill.

There is a close button because `onDismiss` is given. Press the cross or "Later": it is the screen's state that takes the alert away, not the alert; the button that brings it back takes its place. Someone using a screen reader can also close the alert with the dismiss action, without finding the button.

examples.name: AlertFormError
examples.title: Form error
examples.description: A form that fails when it is sent. Press "Send": the error alert appears above the button at once. Because its tone is `Danger`, it is announced to a screen reader straight away, interrupting what it is saying. The cross takes it away.

examples.name: AlertWithALink
examples.title: A message with a link
examples.description: The message can be an `AnnotatedString` too: to set a word in bold, or to put a link in it. A link is a `LinkAnnotation`; the alert draws it in its text's colour, underlined. A `LinkAnnotation.Clickable` does the app's own work when it is pressed, a `LinkAnnotation.Url` opens its address in the browser.

appNames.name: LocalExampleEvents
appNames.description: Where an example tells its card what happens in it: a button pressed, a row chosen, a dialog closed. The card writes the last thing told under the example, on its "Last event" line.

examples.name: AlertOwnColors
examples.title: In its own colours
examples.description: An alert whose fill, text and marks are in colours the caller gives. `AlertColors` takes three colours: the fill (`container`), the text (`content`) and what marks the tone (`accent`): the icon, the edge of `Outline` and the bar of `Accent`. A colour that is left out stays the tone's. The tone still gives the alert its icon and the way it is announced: only what it is painted in changes.
examples.code:
val own = ownColors()
PantrixAlert(
    message = "The colours of its fill, its text and its marks were given by the caller",
    variant = AlertVariant.Accent,
    colors = AlertColors(container = own.container, content = own.onContainer, accent = own.color),
    tagKey = "own"
)
PantrixText(
    text = "Colours are given with AlertColors; a colour that is left out stays the tone's.",
    style = PantrixTheme.typography.footnote,
    color = PantrixTheme.colors.textSecondary
)

appNames.name: ownColors
appNames.description: The "app's own colour" of the examples: a purple that is in none of the theme's roles. It is there to show what changes when a component is given `colors`; given one of the theme's roles, nobody could tell whether the colour came from the component's tone or from the parameter.

examples.name: AlertOwnStyle
examples.title: In its own style
examples.description:
`style` changes the alert's geometry: its corners, its padding, the room between its parts, and how thick the edge of `Outline` and the bar of `Accent` are. Only the fields that are set change; the rest comes from the platform's style.

The third is a note: its fill and its icon are the tone's, its edge a colour apart from them (`AlertColors(border = …)`), its padding one across and another up and down (`horizontalPadding`, `verticalPadding`), and its text the theme's `label` (`textStyle`): the icon and the close button stand on that text's first line, and its colour is still the alert's.
examples.code:
PantrixAlert(
    message = "Square corners, bar 8dp",
    tone = AlertTone.Success,
    variant = AlertVariant.Accent,
    style = AlertStyle(shape = ShapeSpec.Fixed(RectangleShape), accentWidth = 8.dp),
    tagKey = "own_style_accent"
)
PantrixAlert(
    message = "Padding 20dp, edge 2dp",
    tone = AlertTone.Warning,
    variant = AlertVariant.Outline,
    style = AlertStyle(padding = 20.dp, borderWidth = 2.dp),
    tagKey = "own_style_outline"
)
PantrixAlert(
    message = "An edge in a colour apart from the fill and the icon; padding of 14 across and 10dp up and down; text the size of a label",
    tone = AlertTone.Warning,
    style = AlertStyle(horizontalPadding = 14.dp, verticalPadding = 10.dp),
    colors = AlertColors(border = PantrixTheme.colors.warning.color.copy(alpha = 0.45f)),
    tagKey = "own_style_note",
    textStyle = PantrixTheme.typography.label
)

pages.title: Breadcrumb
pages.summary:
The trail of pages above the one on screen: each a link back to it, the last the page on screen itself. In a path of folders, in the sections of a document or in a catalogue, it tells the reader where they are and how to go up one. The row at the top of this page is a `PantrixBreadcrumb` too.

A trail is one line, and never wraps. When it does not fit its row it folds by itself: the pages after the first go behind a button, as few of them as it takes, and the button opens them as a menu.
features: **Links and the page on screen.** The pages above are links, each underlined; when one is pressed, `onSelect` reports its key. The last page is the page on screen: it is a text, it is not pressed, and its key is never reported.

**It folds by itself.** Where the row is too narrow, the trail keeps its first page and its last ones, and those between them go into the menu that the three-dot button opens. Where the first page and the last do not fit beside the button either, the long names are cut to one width, and a short one stays as it is.
**The most pages.** With `maxItems` the row shows no more pages than that, even where it has room. It has to be at least two: a trail always shows its first page and its last.
**Icons.** `BreadcrumbItem.icon` stands before the page's name; with `iconOnly` it takes the name's place, and the page is a button that says its name to a screen reader.

**Type and sizes.** `textStyle` is the names' type, the theme's `label` where it is not given. `BreadcrumbStyle` gives the room between the names and the marks, and the size of the mark and of the icon; these are the same on every platform. `minHeight` makes the row lower than the touch target, and `linkUnderline` says when the links are underlined.
**Colours.** `BreadcrumbColors` paints the links, the page on screen and the marks one by one. On a fill, all of a trail that is given no colour is in the colour that is written on the fill.

**Screen reader.** The row is a group named "Breadcrumb", the last page is read with the state "Current page", and the marks in between are not read. On iOS the group has no name: a screen reader there reads a group's name after what the group holds.
**Right to left.** In languages read from right to left the trail starts on the right, and the marks turn round.
**Automation.** In a trail that is given a `tagKey`, the pages and the button for the folded pages are named inside it: `Breadcrumb_docs.Item_components`, `Breadcrumb_docs.More_pages`.

examples.name: BreadcrumbFolders
examples.title: Navigating folders
examples.description:
At its plainest: the trail's pages (`items`) and what happens when one of them is pressed (`onSelect`). Which page the app is on is the screen's state; the trail does not hold it, and only reports the key of the page that was pressed.

Press a folder above: the app goes up to it, and the trail ends in that folder. "Go deeper" makes the path longer again. The last page is not pressed: that is where the app already is.

examples.name: BreadcrumbMaxItems
examples.title: A row that shows three pages at the most
examples.description:
`maxItems = 3`: the row shows no more than three pages, even where it has room. The first page and the last two stay; those between them are behind the three-dot button.

Press the button: the folded folders open as a menu, in the order of the trail. A folder chosen in the menu is reported through `onSelect` as one pressed in the row is, and the app goes up to it. When the path is down to three pages the button goes.

examples.name: BreadcrumbIcons
examples.title: Icons: before the name or in its place
examples.description:
`icon` stands before the page's name, in the name's colour. The icon and the name are one link: a press on the icon is a press on the name, and the icon is no second stop for the keyboard and no second thing for a screen reader.

In the first trail the first page is shown by its icon alone, with `iconOnly`: it is a button that says its name to a screen reader. A page without an icon is written by its name whatever `iconOnly` says.

In the second trail two pages that are shown by their icons alone are folded away. Press the three-dot button: the menu writes each page's name beside its icon.
examples.code:
PantrixBreadcrumb(
    items = listOf(
        BreadcrumbItem(key = "files", label = "Files", icon = PantrixIcons.Folder, iconOnly = true),
        BreadcrumbItem(key = "starred", label = "Starred", icon = PantrixIcons.Star),
        BreadcrumbItem(key = "schedule", label = "Calendar", icon = PantrixIcons.Calendar)
    ),
    onSelect = {},
    tagKey = "icons"
)
PantrixBreadcrumb(
    items = listOf(
        BreadcrumbItem(key = "files", label = "Files", icon = PantrixIcons.Folder, iconOnly = true),
        BreadcrumbItem(key = "starred", label = "Starred", icon = PantrixIcons.Star, iconOnly = true),
        BreadcrumbItem(key = "schedule", label = "Calendar", icon = PantrixIcons.Calendar, iconOnly = true),
        BreadcrumbItem(key = "today", label = "Today")
    ),
    onSelect = {},
    maxItems = 2,
    tagKey = "icons_folded"
)

examples.name: BreadcrumbFoldsByItself
examples.title: A path too long for its row folds by itself
examples.description:
No `maxItems` is given: the trail folds to the width that is left to it. First the pages after the first go behind the button, as few of them as it takes; the trail keeps its first page, where it began, and its last ones, where it is. Where the first page and the last do not fit beside the button either, the long names are cut to one width, and a short one stays as it is.

The same path at three widths: the first as wide as the example, the others in frames 480dp and 240dp wide at the most. In the middle frame the page in between is behind the button; in the narrow frame the last page's name is cut as well. Narrow the window: the first trail folds in the same order.

examples.name: BreadcrumbOnAFill
examples.title: On a fill
examples.description: A trail on a fill that is not one of the theme's grounds. No colour is given: the fill says what is written on it, and all of the trail, its links, the page on screen and the marks, is written in that colour. The theme's link and text colours are for the theme's own grounds; here a link is told from the page on screen by its underline.

examples.name: BreadcrumbTextStyleAndSizes
examples.title: Text style and sizes
examples.description:
`textStyle` is the type the names are set in: a trail that is given none is written in the theme's `label` style. `style` gives the sizes: `itemGap` is the room between a name and the mark beside it, and between an icon and its name; `separatorSize` is the size of the mark and of the button for the folded pages; `iconSize` is the size of a page's own icon. Only the fields that are set change.

The middle trail is as it is with nothing given: 16dp marks and icons, 4dp from the names. The one above it is the same trail set small, and the one below it the same trail set large. The rows of all three are at least as tall as the platform's touch target.
examples.code:
PantrixBreadcrumb(
    items = PLACES,
    onSelect = {},
    textStyle = PantrixTheme.typography.footnote,
    style = BreadcrumbStyle(itemGap = 2.dp, separatorSize = 12.dp, iconSize = 12.dp),
    tagKey = "small"
)
PantrixBreadcrumb(items = PLACES, onSelect = {}, tagKey = "usual")
PantrixBreadcrumb(
    items = PLACES,
    onSelect = {},
    textStyle = PantrixTheme.typography.callout,
    style = BreadcrumbStyle(itemGap = 8.dp, separatorSize = 20.dp, iconSize = 20.dp),
    tagKey = "large"
)

private val PLACES = listOf(
    BreadcrumbItem(key = "files", label = "Files", icon = PantrixIcons.Folder),
    BreadcrumbItem(key = "starred", label = "Starred", icon = PantrixIcons.Star),
    BreadcrumbItem(key = "schedule", label = "Calendar", icon = PantrixIcons.Calendar)
)

examples.name: BreadcrumbOverATitle
examples.title: Over a title, low and without lines
examples.description:
The trail over a documentation page's title: as low as a line of text, and not underlined. `minHeight` is the row's least height; where it is not given, it is the platform's touch target. In a lower row a touch beside a page still reaches it: the theme gives a small target room for a touch that takes no room in the layout.

`linkUnderline = LinkUnderline.OnHover` underlines the links only under a pointer and while they hold the focus: a trail does not stand in a sentence, and its marks already tell its links from the page on screen. Where the platform is used by touch they are still underlined always.

examples.name: BreadcrumbOwnColors
examples.title: With its own colours, a small type and small marks
examples.description:
`colors` takes the colour of the links (`link`), of the page on screen (`current`) and of the marks (`separator`) one by one; one that is left out stays the theme's. Here the links and the marks are in the app's own purple, which is in none of the theme's roles; the page on screen is given no colour, and stays in the theme's text colour.

The type is `footnote`, and the marks are 12dp and 6dp from the names: the colour, the text style and the sizes are given independently of each other.
examples.code:
val own = ownColors()
PantrixBreadcrumb(
    items = FOLDERS.take(3),
    onSelect = {},
    textStyle = PantrixTheme.typography.footnote,
    style = BreadcrumbStyle(itemGap = 6.dp, separatorSize = 12.dp),
    colors = BreadcrumbColors(link = own.color, separator = own.color),
    tagKey = "own"
)

private val FOLDERS = listOf(
    BreadcrumbItem(key = "home", label = "Home"),
    BreadcrumbItem(key = "documents", label = "Documents"),
    BreadcrumbItem(key = "projects", label = "Projects"),
    BreadcrumbItem(key = "pantrix", label = "Pantrix"),
    BreadcrumbItem(key = "design", label = "Design")
)

appNames.name: ownColors
appNames.description: The "app's own colour" of the examples: a purple that is in none of the theme's roles. It is there to show what changes when a component is given `colors`; given one of the theme's roles, nobody could tell whether the colour came from the component's tone or from the parameter.

pages.title: Navigation Bar
pages.summary:
The app's top-level destinations along the bottom of the screen: three to five of them, one of them where the app is now. It is the navigation of a phone and of a narrow window. This app's own navigation is a `PantrixNavigationBar` too, in a window narrower than 600dp.

Here the bars stand inside the page, in a bordered frame. On a real screen the bar is the bottom bar of a `PantrixScaffold`: it takes the insets the scaffold gives it, and its fill runs behind the system's navigation bar.
features: **The state is the screen's.** The bar is given the key of the current destination (`selected`), and reports the key of a destination that is pressed (`onSelect`). A press on the current destination is reported too: an app commonly takes that destination back to its top. With `selected` null, no destination is marked.
**A pill, or colour alone.** The current destination is marked by a pill behind its icon; by its colour alone where the `indicator` field of `NavigationBarStyle` is `NavigationIndicator.None`.
**Badge.** `NavigationBadge` puts a count or a dot on the destination's icon. The badge's top is level with the icon's: it does not run out of the bar. The count is capped as a badge's is: "99+".
**Another icon while selected.** `NavigationItem.selectedIcon` is drawn in place of `icon` while the app is at that destination.
**A destination that cannot be pressed.** `enabled = false` draws the destination in the theme's disabled text colour; the destination takes no press.
**The same on every platform.** 64dp tall, under a hairline; a pill of 56×28dp, a 20dp icon and a label set in `footnote`. `style` changes the sizes, `labelStyle` the label's type.

**Colours.** `NavigationColors` takes the fill, what is written on it, the pill, the icon on the pill and the colour that marks where there is no pill, each on its own. `PantrixNavigationRail` takes the same colours and the same list of destinations.
**System bar.** `insets` is the room the bar keeps clear along the bottom edge and at its sides: the fill runs behind that room, and the destinations stay out of it.

**Upright bar.** `orientation = NavigationBarOrientation.Vertical` lays the destinations one above another in a capsule of the bar's fill: as the tabs in the system's vertical bar on the iPhone Duo's outer screen. `PantrixScaffold` puts it at the bottom of the column there by itself. In an upright bar the destinations have their icons alone; `showLabels = true` writes their names too. Along the bottom, `showLabels = false` leaves the icons alone as well.

**Destination without a label.** Its name is told to a screen reader and shows in a tooltip while a pointer rests on it, while it has the keyboard's focus and after a long press: above the destination along the bottom, at its start in an upright bar.
**Screen reader.** A destination is read as a tab: its name, what its badge says, and whether it is selected. "Inbox, 3 unread".
**Automation.** The destinations of a bar that is given a `tagKey` are named inside it: `NavigationBar_main.Item_inbox`.

examples.name: NavigationBarThreeDestinations
examples.title: Three destinations
examples.description:
At its plainest: the list of destinations (`items`), the key of the current destination (`selected`) and `onSelect`, which is told the key of the destination that is pressed. The bar selects nothing by itself; the screen holds where the app is. The destinations share the bar's width.

Press a destination, then press the same one again: that is reported too. The line above counts it; a real app takes that destination back to its top.

examples.name: NavigationBarBadge
examples.title: Three destinations, with a count on one
examples.description:
The three destinations of a mail app. The badge on "Inbox" counts the unread: `NavigationBadge(contentDescription, count)`. When the destination is opened the count goes to zero and the badge goes away: with nothing left to count, `badge` is given null. "Starred" has a `selectedIcon`: while it is selected, that is drawn in place of the star. An app gives the icon's filled form there; `PantrixIcons` has no filled forms, so another icon stands here.

The badge's `contentDescription` is required and is read after the destination's name: "Inbox, 3 unread". A number alone does not say what it counts; giving null is a decision, made where the name says it already.

examples.name: NavigationBarPill
examples.title: With a pill: five destinations, one that cannot be pressed
examples.description:
Five destinations: the most a bar takes. The current destination is marked by the pill behind its icon (`NavigationIndicator.Pill`): that is the default on every platform, written out here. The press and the focus ring are drawn in the pill's room too, not over the whole destination.

The badge on "Folders" is a dot (`count` was not given); the 128 on "Profile" is more than the largest number that is written, and becomes "99+". "Calendar" cannot be pressed: `enabled = false`.
examples.code:
var where by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf("search") }
PantrixSurface(modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(), border = PantrixTheme.colors.divider) {
    PantrixNavigationBar(
        items = FIVE,
        selected = where,
        onSelect = { where = it },
        style = NavigationBarStyle(indicator = NavigationIndicator.Pill),
        tagKey = "pill"
    )
}

private val FIVE = listOf(
    NavigationItem(key = "starred", label = "Starred", icon = PantrixIcons.Star),
    NavigationItem(
        key = "folders",
        label = "Folders",
        icon = PantrixIcons.Folder,
        badge = NavigationBadge(contentDescription = "New files")
    ),
    NavigationItem(key = "search", label = "Search", icon = PantrixIcons.Search),
    NavigationItem(key = "calendar", label = "Calendar", icon = PantrixIcons.Calendar, enabled = false),
    NavigationItem(
        key = "profile",
        label = "Profile",
        icon = PantrixIcons.Person,
        badge = NavigationBadge(contentDescription = "128 notifications", count = 128)
    )
)

examples.name: NavigationBarTint
examples.title: By colour alone
examples.description: The same bar with `NavigationIndicator.None`: no pill is drawn, the current destination's icon and label are in the theme's `primary` colour, and the others in the secondary text colour. A tab bar on iOS marks its destination this way; no platform's preset chooses it, and whoever wants it gives a style.
examples.code:
var where by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf("search") }
PantrixSurface(modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(), border = PantrixTheme.colors.divider) {
    PantrixNavigationBar(
        items = FIVE,
        selected = where,
        onSelect = { where = it },
        style = NavigationBarStyle(indicator = NavigationIndicator.None),
        tagKey = "tint"
    )
}

private val FIVE = listOf(
    NavigationItem(key = "starred", label = "Starred", icon = PantrixIcons.Star),
    NavigationItem(
        key = "folders",
        label = "Folders",
        icon = PantrixIcons.Folder,
        badge = NavigationBadge(contentDescription = "New files")
    ),
    NavigationItem(key = "search", label = "Search", icon = PantrixIcons.Search),
    NavigationItem(key = "calendar", label = "Calendar", icon = PantrixIcons.Calendar, enabled = false),
    NavigationItem(

examples.description:
`style` changes the bar's sizes, `labelStyle` the type the labels are set in. The preset bar is 64dp tall on every platform; Android's own bar is 80dp with a larger pill, and a tab bar on iOS is 49pt with no pill. Neither is the preset, but a style can ask for either.

The bar above is 80dp, with a pill of 64×32dp and a 24dp icon. The one below is 49dp, has no pill, has its labels set in `caption` and less room between an icon and its label (`labelGap = 2.dp`). Only the fields that are given change. A destination is never lower than the platform's touch target.

            indicatorHeight = 32.dp,

It is there to show what changes when a component is given `colors`; given one of the theme's roles, nobody could tell whether the colour came from the component's tone or from the parameter.

examples.name: NavigationBarInsets
examples.title: Behind the system bar
examples.description:
`insets` is the room the bar keeps clear along the bottom edge and at its sides: the fill runs behind that room, and the destinations stay out of it. On a real screen `PantrixScaffold` gives the insets (`bottomBar = { insets -> … }`) and the system's navigation bar sits over the bar's fill. That is how the app's own bottom bar gets its insets.

There is no scaffold here: 24dp stand in for the insets, and the line inside them for the system's gesture bar. The destinations stay above the line, and the bar's fill goes down under it.

examples.name: NavigationBarUpright
examples.title: Upright bar
examples.description:
The bar stands upright: the destinations one above another, in a capsule of the bar's fill with a thin line around it. On the iPhone Duo's outer screen the system keeps a column for such bars along the right edge; `PantrixScaffold` puts the navigation at the bottom of that column and tells it `ScaffoldNavigationPlacement.VerticalBar` (the "Scaffold" page has an example).

The one on the left has its icons alone, as UIKit's tabs in that column: rest on a destination or press it long, and its name shows in a tooltip at its start; a screen reader says the name too. The one on the right writes the names as well, with `showLabels = true`, and is as wide as its longest name. The two share one state: press a destination in one and the other marks it too.
examples.code:
var where by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf("search") }
Row(horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.xxl)) {
    PantrixNavigationBar(
        items = FIVE,
        selected = where,
        onSelect = { where = it },
        orientation = NavigationBarOrientation.Vertical,
        tagKey = "upright_icons"
    )
    PantrixNavigationBar(
        items = FIVE,
        selected = where,
        onSelect = { where = it },
        orientation = NavigationBarOrientation.Vertical,
        showLabels = true,
        tagKey = "upright_labels"
    )
}

pages.title: Navigation Rail
pages.summary:
The app's top-level destinations down the start edge of a wide window, one under another: the navigation bar's place on a tablet, an open foldable and a desktop window. The rail takes a bar's destinations and its colours: a screen that shows the bar in a narrow window and the rail in a wide one gives both the same list.

Here the rails stand inside the page, in a bordered frame of a set height. On a real screen the rail is the side bar of a `PantrixScaffold`: it is as tall as the window, and its fill runs behind the system bars.
features: **The same destinations as a bar.** `items` is a list of `NavigationItem`: the icon, the label, the badge, another icon while selected and a destination that cannot be pressed are as in a bar. A rail takes three to seven destinations.

**The state is the screen's.** `selected` is the key of the current destination, and `onSelect` reports that of the one that is pressed; a press on the current destination is reported too. With `selected` null, no destination is marked.
**Header.** `header` stands over the destinations, in the middle of the rail: a button that opens the menu, or the screen's main action.
**Destinations that scroll.** Where the destinations are taller than the rail they scroll by themselves; the header stays where it is.
**Height.** The rail is as tall as the room it is given, and that room has to have an end: a scaffold's side bar has one; inside a page that scrolls it takes a box of a set height.
**A pill, or colour alone.** The current destination is marked by the pill behind its icon; by its colour alone where the `indicator` field of `NavigationRailStyle` is `NavigationIndicator.None`.
**The same on every platform.** 80dp wide, with a hairline along its end edge; the destinations are 56dp tall and 4dp apart. `style` changes the sizes, `labelStyle` the label's type.
**Colours.** `NavigationColors` is the same class as the bar's: one set of colours paints both components.
**System bars.** `insets` is the room the rail keeps clear at its top, its bottom and its start edge: the fill runs behind that room, and the destinations stay out of it.

**Screen reader and right to left.** A destination is read as a tab: its name, what its badge says, and whether it is selected. In languages read from right to left the rail is at the right edge, and its line moves to its left edge.

examples.name: NavigationRailThreeDestinations
examples.title: Three destinations
examples.description:
At its plainest: the list of destinations (`items`), the key of the current destination (`selected`) and `onSelect`, which is told the key of the destination that is pressed. The destinations stand one under another from the top; each is as wide as the rail, so a press beside the icon is a press on the destination too.

The rail is as tall as the frame (240dp): in a place that has no height of its own, inside a page that scrolls, it has to be given one.

examples.name: NavigationRailHeader
examples.title: Three destinations under a menu button
examples.description:
`header` stands over the destinations, in the middle of the rail: here, a button that opens the menu. Press it and the area beside the rail counts.

The destinations are a mail app's. The badge on "Inbox" counts the unread: when the destination is opened the count goes to zero and the badge goes away. A screen reader reads the badge after the destination's name: "Inbox, 3 unread".

examples.name: NavigationRailScrolls
examples.title: The destinations scroll in a short rail
examples.description:
Seven destinations in a rail of 220dp: the most a rail takes, in a place too short to show them all. The destinations scroll by themselves; the button in the header does not scroll, it stays where it is. Scroll the rail up: it goes down as far as "About".

The badge on "Folders" is a dot, the 128 on "Profile" becomes "99+", and "Calendar" cannot be pressed.

examples.name: NavigationRailTint
examples.title: By colour alone
examples.description:
With `NavigationIndicator.None` no pill is drawn: the current destination's icon and label are in the theme's `primary` colour, and the others in the secondary text colour. The press and the focus ring are still drawn in the pill's room.

The frame is 440dp: the seven destinations fit at their preset sizes and the rail does not scroll.

examples.name: NavigationRailStyles
examples.title: Style: width, gaps and the label's type
examples.description:
`style` changes the rail's sizes, `labelStyle` the type the labels are set in; only the fields that are given change. The first rail is the preset: 80dp wide, its destinations 56dp tall and 4dp apart. The second is 96dp wide, its destinations 64dp tall and 12dp apart, 16dp in from the top and the bottom; its labels are set in `caption`.

The second rail has no line along its end edge either: `divider = false`.
examples.code:
val destinations = SEVEN.take(4)
var where by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf("search") }
PantrixSurface(modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth().height(340.dp), border = PantrixTheme.colors.divider) {
    Row {
        PantrixNavigationRail(
            items = destinations,
            selected = where,
            onSelect = { where = it },
            tagKey = "usual"
        )
        PantrixNavigationRail(
            items = destinations,
            selected = where,
            onSelect = { where = it },
            labelStyle = PantrixTheme.typography.caption,
            style = NavigationRailStyle(
                width = 96.dp,
                itemMinHeight = 64.dp,
                itemSpacing = 12.dp,
                verticalPadding = 16.dp,
                divider = false
            ),
            tagKey = "wide"
        )
    }
}

The icon and the text in the header name no colour either: on the theme's own fill they would be in their own default colours, and here they are in the colour that is written on the rail.

appNames.name: ownColors
appNames.description: The "app's own colour" of the examples: a purple that is in none of the theme's roles. It is there to show what changes when a component is given `colors`; given one of the theme's roles, nobody could tell whether the colour came from the component's tone or from the parameter.

examples.name: NavigationRailInsets
examples.title: Behind the system bars
examples.description:
`insets` is the room the rail keeps clear at its top, its bottom and its start edge: the fill runs behind that room, and the header and the destinations stay out of it. On a real screen `PantrixScaffold` gives the insets to its side bar, and the rail runs behind the system bars.

There is no scaffold here: the 24dp strip at the top stands in for the system's status bar. The rail's fill goes on behind the strip, and the menu button starts under it.

pages.title: Sidebar
pages.summary:
The column of destinations down the side of an app: groups, sections with destinations inside them, and the rail of icons it takes when room runs short. It is the navigation of a wide window: this app's own side menu, in a window wider than 600dp, is a `PantrixSidebar` too.

A sidebar is as tall as the room it is given. On a real screen it is `PantrixScaffold`'s side bar: it is as tall as the window, and keeps its rows clear of the system bars with the `insets` the scaffold gives it. Here it stands inside a page that scrolls, so each example is in a box of a set height; the area beside it says which destination is open.
features: **Two levels.** Rows are given in groups (`SidebarGroup`) and a line is drawn between groups; a group with a name has it written over its rows. A row with children is a section, not a destination: a press opens or closes it in place. There is nothing deeper: a child's children are not drawn.

**The state is the app's.** The current destination (`selected`) and the open sections (`expanded`) are the caller's state; a press on a row only asks (`onSelect`, `onExpandedChange`). A sidebar that kept its own state would fight the back button, a deep link and a restored process.

**One section open.** With `singleExpanded`, which is the default, opening a section closes the one that was open: a sidebar of six sections stays the height of six rows. Given false, more than one section can stay open.

**Icon rail.** `collapsed` reduces the sidebar to a rail of icons: a destination's icon carries its name, and shows a tooltip. A section opens what it holds beside the rail (`flyout`): in a card, or in a column that moves the page over. A top-level row without an icon is drawn as a chevron on the rail: give every one an icon.
**Narrows by itself.** With `adaptive`, which is the default, the sidebar takes the rail by itself where its column would leave the page less than 840dp.

**Header, pinned destinations, footer.** `header` stands above the rows, `footerItems` and `footer` below them; none of them scrolls. The header and the footer learn which shape they are in through `SidebarSlotScope.collapsed`.

**Where the app is.** The current destination is told three ways: its fill, its heavier label, and its selected state for a screen reader. The name of the section that holds it is written heavier too; on the rail that section carries the fill and the bar on the edge.

**Height and scrolling.** The rows take the room left between the header and the pinned destinations, and scroll inside it when they do not fit, with Pantrix's scroll bar along the edge on the desktop and the web. A row is never lower than the platform's touch target, and grows with a larger type.

**Colours and style.** `SidebarColors` paints the fill, the text, the selected row, the lines and the bar on the rail; `SidebarStyle` gives the width, the rows and the corners. The column is 248dp wide on every platform. `textStyle` gives the rows' type and `titleTextStyle` the groups' titles'; the current destination is a step heavier than the type given.
**Screen reader and keyboard.** A section says whether it is open; a closed one composes nothing of what it holds. The column a rail opens closes with Escape, and focus returns to the section's row.

examples.name: SidebarGroupsAndSections
examples.title: Groups and sections
examples.description:
At its plainest: the rows in groups (`groups`), the key of the current destination (`selected`), the keys of the open sections (`expanded`), and two callbacks that ask for those two to change. The sidebar changes nothing by itself; here the state is kept with `rememberSaveable`, and is not lost when the screen rotates.

"Quality" and "Releases" are sections: a press opens them in place, and opening one closes the other. Pick "Crashes" and close "Quality": the section's name stays heavier, so even closed it says where the app is. "Archive" and "Invoices" cannot be pressed.

`adaptive = false` is given: the sidebar stands inside a box here, and with the default it would take the rail; the "Narrows by itself" example shows that. The box is 480dp tall: a sidebar is as tall as the room it is given.

examples.name: SidebarManySections
examples.title: More than one section can stay open
examples.description:
`singleExpanded = false`: opening one section does not close the other. Open "Releases": "Quality" stays open too.

When its rows do not fit in its box, the sidebar scrolls them inside itself: on a phone that is what happens in the 480dp box once both sections are open.

examples.name: SidebarTitledGroups
examples.title: Groups with names
examples.description:
A group's name stands over its rows: `SidebarGroup(items, title = "Guides")`. The name is written small, in capitals and in the quiet colour, and a screen reader hears it as a heading: as a documentation's "Getting started" and "Guides" sections are. A group without a name is set apart by a line alone.

A rail has no room for names: press "Switch to rail", and the groups are still set apart by a line.

examples.name: SidebarDisabledRows
examples.title: Rows that cannot be pressed
examples.description:
`enabled = false` writes the row in the theme's disabled text colour; the row takes no press. "Invoices" is a destination that cannot be pressed.

"Reports" is a section that cannot be pressed: it does not open or close, and stays as `expanded` has it; here it is open. Each destination inside it follows its own `enabled`: "Weekly" can be pressed, "Monthly" cannot.

examples.name: SidebarHeaderAndFooter
examples.title: Header, pinned destinations and footer
examples.description:
`header` stands above the rows and does not scroll: the app's mark, a workspace switcher. `footerItems` are destinations pinned under the rows: settings, help. They are no sections: one that has children is refused. `footer` stands at the very bottom: an account, a plan. A line sets each of them off; the rows in between take the room that is left.

The header and the footer are the caller's. The text in them is in the sidebar's text colour unless it gives a colour of its own. Both are drawn in a `SidebarSlotScope`, and learn which shape the sidebar is in through `collapsed`: here a name in the column, and only initials on the rail. The next example shows the rail.

examples.name: SidebarRail
examples.title: Icon rail: a section opens a card beside it
examples.description:
`collapsed` reduces the sidebar to a rail of icons. A destination's icon carries its name: a pointer resting on it, keyboard focus or a long press shows the name in a tooltip. A section opens what it holds beside the rail; with `SidebarFlyout.Popup` that is a card. It comes when the pointer rests on the section and goes when the pointer leaves; where there is no pointer, a press by a finger, the keyboard or a screen reader opens it, and it stays until it is dismissed. It closes once a destination in it is chosen.

A row's `detail` ("87 open") is written only here, where there is room for it; the section's ("3 warnings") is at the top of the card, beside its name. It is not written in the column: the column is a list of places to go, and a run of figures down its side would read as data.

"Switch to column" turns the same sidebar into a column: the shape changes at once, the width follows it over the theme's motion, and the page beside it moves with it. On the rail the header and the footer draw only a letter or two.

examples.name: SidebarPanel
examples.title: Icon rail: a section opens a column beside it
examples.description:
With `SidebarFlyout.Panel` the section's destinations open beside the rail, in a column of their own: the column's width and the rail's height. The sidebar grows wider by that much; the page is not covered but moved over.

Press "Quality". The column opens at a press, and not as a pointer passes. Pressing the section again, choosing a destination and Escape close it; pressing another section shows that one's. When it is opened with the keyboard, focus goes to the column's first destination, and returns to the section's row when it closes.

examples.name: SidebarAdaptive
examples.title: Narrows by itself: a rail in a narrow space, a column in a wide one
examples.description:
`adaptive`, whose default is true, makes the sidebar take the rail by itself where its column would crowd the page: where the width it is given, less the column's 248dp, is under 840dp. 840dp is the width below which a page has no room for two panes. So where the sidebar gets less than 1088dp the rail shows, and otherwise the column.

The selector changes the width of the box the sidebar stands in: the 1200dp box shows the column, the 700dp box the rail. The sidebar looks at the room it is given, not at the window: the window stays the same, only the box narrows, and the sidebar takes the rail. When the box does not fit on the page it scrolls sideways, and a scrollbar appears under it.

The app's own side menu is an `adaptive` `PantrixSidebar` too: narrow the window and it takes the rail; under 600dp the bar along the bottom edge takes its place.

In the other examples `adaptive = false`: `collapsed` alone decides the shape. That is right for a sidebar in a drawer too: a drawer covers the page and does not crowd it. An `adaptive` sidebar measures the room it is given; it must be turned off under a parent that asks for its size with `IntrinsicSize`.

appNames.name: HorizontalScrollFrame
appNames.description: A frame that scrolls sideways: where its content does not fit its room, it draws a scrollbar under it.

examples.name: SidebarRoleColors
examples.title: The selected row in a role's colour
examples.description: Only the selected row's fill is given: `selectedContainer`. It is the colour of one of the theme's roles, so the theme knows what reads on it: the role's paired colour comes without `selectedContent` being given. Every colour that is not given stays the theme's.

examples.name: SidebarOwnColors
examples.title: In its own colours
examples.description:
A sidebar filled with the app's own colour. The theme does not know this colour and cannot tell what reads on it: along with the fill (`container`), the colour of the text (`content`) and the colours of the selected row's fill and text are given too.

The lines are not given: on the fill they are drawn as a share of the text's colour. Rows that cannot be pressed are written in a share of that colour too. The card and the column a rail opens are drawn in the same colours.

appNames.name: ownColors
appNames.description: The "app's own colour" of the examples: a purple that is in none of the theme's roles. It is there to show what changes when a component is given `colors`; given one of the theme's roles, nobody could tell whether the colour came from the component's tone or from the parameter.

examples.name: SidebarStyles
examples.title: Style: width, rows and corners
examples.description:
`style` changes the sidebar's geometry; only the fields that are set change, and the rest come from the platform's preset style. Here the column is 216dp, the rows 52dp, the rows inside a section 48dp, and the corners of a row's fill fully rounded.

In the preset style the column is 248dp on every platform; the rows are 44dp on Android and iOS, 36dp on desktop and 40dp on the web. A row is never lower than the platform's touch target. The colours are not part of the style: the theme and `SidebarColors` give them.

examples.name: SidebarOwnText
examples.title: In a type of its own
examples.description: In a type of its own: the rows in the theme's `body` type, semibold (`textStyle`), the groups' titles in `footnote`, extra bold (`titleTextStyle`). The current destination is set a step heavier than the type given; the text's colour is its row's.

examples.name: SidebarInsets
examples.title: Behind the system bars
examples.description:
`insets` is the room the sidebar keeps clear at its edges: the fill runs behind it, while the header and the rows stay clear of it. On a real screen `PantrixScaffold` gives its side bar that room (`sideBar = { insets -> … }`), and the rows stand clear of the system bars. The app's own side menu takes its insets from the scaffold too.

There is no scaffold here: the 24dp strip at the top stands in for the system's status bar. The sidebar's fill runs on behind the strip, and its header starts below the strip.

pages.title: Dialog
pages.summary:
A window that stops the app to ask the user for a decision, or to give news that must not go unseen. It sits in the middle of the app's window, above a scrim, and is modal on every platform: nothing behind it takes a press, and Tab never leaves it.

The dialog never closes itself. It is shown while `visible` is true; a click on the scrim, back and Escape call `onDismissRequest`, and the actions' buttons call their own `onClick`. What closes it is the calling code, which sets `visible` to false.
features: **Title, message, actions.** `title` is a short question or statement, and `message` the explanation under it. `actions` are end-aligned buttons; they wrap onto another line when they do not fit side by side.

**The safe choice first.** In a dialog opened with a keyboard the focus starts on the first control, usually the first action; so "Cancel" is written before "Delete". When it is opened by touch the focus stays where it is.
**Icon.** `icon` stands above the title and centres it. It is decorative: a screen reader does not read it.
**Its own content.** `content` puts a form field or a list of choices under the message.

**Width.** A dialog of a title, a message and actions is as wide as its widest part, between the style's two widths: a short question is narrow, and a long message wraps at the widest. A dialog that holds content is as wide as it may be.
**A long body.** In a short window only the message and the content scroll; the title and the actions stay where they are.
**A dialog that cannot be dismissed.** With `dismissible = false` the scrim, back and Escape do nothing; the actions are the only way out.

**It stays in the tree as it closes.** A dialog that is closed composes nothing: it stays in the tree with `visible = false` and leaves with the theme's motion. An open one that is taken out of the composition is gone at once, without the motion.

**Colour and style.** `colors` changes the fill, the title, the message, the icon and the scrim; `style` the corners, the widths, the margin to the window, the shadow and the icon's size. The dialog looks the same on every platform; what differs is in the style: the corners are large on Android and iOS and medium on desktop and the web, and there is no shadow on iOS.

**Screen reader.** The title is announced when the dialog opens and is the heading of what it holds. On Android TalkBack stays inside the dialog. In a dialog that can be dismissed the scrim is a single "Close" action, read after the content.

examples.name: DialogConfirm
examples.title: Confirmation
examples.description:
The confirmation of something that cannot be undone: a title, a message and two actions. The dialog never closes itself: a click on the scrim, back and Escape call `onDismissRequest`, and the actions call their own `onClick`; in all three it is the `open = false` line that closes it. The card's "Last event" line says which of them happened last.

The safe choice comes first: "Cancel" is written before the `Destructive` "Delete". When the dialog is opened with a keyboard, the focus is on "Cancel".

appNames.name: LocalExampleEvents
appNames.description: Where an example tells its card what happens in it: a button pressed, a row chosen, a dialog closed. The card writes the last thing told under the example, on its "Last event" line.

examples.name: DialogWithIcon
examples.title: With an icon
examples.description:
`icon` stands above the title, and the title is centred. The icon is decorative: the title carries the meaning, and a screen reader does not read the icon.

A notice with a single action: news important enough to interrupt. A click on the scrim, back and Escape close it too.

appNames.name: LocalExampleEvents
appNames.description: Where an example tells its card what happens in it: a button pressed, a row chosen, a dialog closed. The card writes the last thing told under the example, on its "Last event" line.

examples.name: DialogWithForm
examples.title: Form
examples.description:
`content` puts the caller's content under the message: here a field that takes the file's new name. A dialog that holds content is as wide as it may be, even with a short title: the field fills that room. "Save" is disabled while the name is empty.

When the dialog is opened by touch the focus does not move to the field: the keyboard does not come up by itself. When it is opened with a keyboard the focus starts on the first control.

appNames.name: LocalExampleEvents
appNames.description: Where an example tells its card what happens in it: a button pressed, a row chosen, a dialog closed. The card writes the last thing told under the example, on its "Last event" line.

examples.name: DialogRequiredChoice
examples.title: A required choice
examples.description:
`dismissible = false`: the scrim, back and Escape do nothing, and `onDismissRequest` is not called. A screen reader is not offered the scrim's "Close" action either.

The user has to choose one of the actions, so there is an action for every way out: someone who does not accept the terms presses "Sign out". Use it only where the user must choose.

appNames.name: LocalExampleEvents
appNames.description: Where an example tells its card what happens in it: a button pressed, a row chosen, a dialog closed. The card writes the last thing told under the example, on its "Last event" line.

examples.name: DialogLongBody
examples.title: Long content
examples.description: A body that does not fit the window: release notes of forty lines. Only the body scrolls; the title and the action stay where they are, in view. The message scrolls with the content too.

appNames.name: LocalExampleEvents
appNames.description: Where an example tells its card what happens in it: a button pressed, a row chosen, a dialog closed. The card writes the last thing told under the example, on its "Last event" line.

examples.name: DialogWidth
examples.title: A short question, a long message
examples.description:
A dialog of a title, a message and actions is as wide as its widest part, between the style's two widths. A short question is at its narrowest (`DialogStyle.minWidth`); a long message wraps at the widest (`maxWidth`).

Open the two in turn: the difference shows in a wide window. The first is also the dialog with the least to write: a title and actions.

examples.name: DialogOwnColors
examples.title: Its own colours
examples.description:
The colours given with `colors` change, and one that is not given stays the theme's: here the fill, the title, the message and the icon are in the app's own purple, and the scrim is the theme's.

This purple is in none of the theme's roles, so the colour that reads on it, for the title and the message, is the caller's to give too. Had the fill been one of the theme's role colours, the title, the message and the icon would have taken the colour paired with that role by themselves.

appNames.name: LocalExampleEvents
appNames.description: Where an example tells its card what happens in it: a button pressed, a row chosen, a dialog closed. The card writes the last thing told under the example, on its "Last event" line.

appNames.name: ownColors
appNames.description: The "app's own colour" of the examples: a purple that is in none of the theme's roles. It is there to show what changes when a component is given `colors`; given one of the theme's roles, nobody could tell whether the colour came from the component's tone or from the parameter.

examples.name: DialogOwnStyle
examples.title: Its own style
examples.description: `style` changes the geometry of this call alone: the corners have the theme's smallest rounding (`ShapeRole.ExtraSmall`), the widest width is 360dp and the icon 40dp. The fields that are not set, the narrowest width, the margin to the window and the shadow, come from the platform's style.
examples.code:
var open by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf(false) }
PantrixButton(
    text = "Share folder…",
    onClick = { open = true },
    variant = ButtonVariant.Outline,
    tagKey = "open_share_folder"
)
PantrixDialog(
    visible = open,
    onDismissRequest = { open = false },
    title = "Share the folder?",
    message = "Anyone with the link can see the files in the Reports folder.",
    icon = PantrixIcons.Folder,
    style = DialogStyle(shape = ShapeRole.ExtraSmall, maxWidth = 360.dp, iconSize = 40.dp),
    actions = {
        PantrixButton(
            text = "Cancel",
            onClick = { open = false },
            variant = ButtonVariant.Text,
            tagKey = "cancel_share_folder"
        )
        PantrixButton(text = "Share", onClick = { open = false }, tagKey = "confirm_share_folder")
    },
    tagKey = "share_folder"
)

examples.name: DialogInTheOtherTheme
examples.title: In a part in another theme
examples.description: A part in the opposite colours to the page, and a dialog opened from inside it. The part is a second theme (`PantrixTheme(darkTheme = …)`); the dialog is called inside that theme too, so it is in its colours: a dark dialog opens on a light page, and a light one on a dark page.

appNames.name: LocalExampleEvents
appNames.description: Where an example tells its card what happens in it: a button pressed, a row chosen, a dialog closed. The card writes the last thing told under the example, on its "Last event" line.

examples.name: DialogLeaving
examples.title: A dialog that stays in the tree as it closes
examples.description:
A dialog that is closed composes nothing; so it stays in the tree with `visible = false`, and leaves with the theme's motion as it closes. The first dialog is like this.

The second is inside an `if`: when it closes it leaves the composition and is gone at once, without the motion. The exit motion is all that is lost. Close the two in turn and watch them leave; in a theme with reduced motion both are gone at once.
examples.code:
var kept by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf(false) }
var removed by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf(false) }
FlowRow(
    horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.sm),
    verticalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.sm)
) {
    PantrixButton(
        text = "Stays in the tree",
        onClick = { kept = true },
        variant = ButtonVariant.Outline,
        tagKey = "open_kept"
    )
    PantrixButton(
        text = "Taken out of the tree",
        onClick = { removed = true },
        variant = ButtonVariant.Outline,
        tagKey = "open_removed"
    )
}
PantrixDialog(
    visible = kept,
    onDismissRequest = { kept = false },
    title = "Leaves with motion",
    message = "In the tree while closed too: once visible = false, it leaves with the theme's motion.",
    actions = { PantrixButton(text = "Close", onClick = { kept = false }, tagKey = "close_kept") },
    tagKey = "kept"
)
if (removed) {
    PantrixDialog(
        visible = true,
        onDismissRequest = { removed = false },
        title = "Gone at once",
        message = "Leaves the composition when it closes: the exit motion does not play.",
        actions = { PantrixButton(text = "Close", onClick = { removed = false }, tagKey = "close_removed") },
        tagKey = "removed"
    )
}

pages.title: Modal
pages.summary: A modal layer of the app's own: a scrim over the whole window, and over it content the app draws. It is the layer the dialog and the command palette stand on, for a layer neither of them draws: a search with filters of its own, a picture shown large, an editor that fills a phone's screen.
features: **It never closes itself.** Back, Escape and a press on the scrim call `onDismissRequest`; the caller turns `visible` off. The content enters and leaves with the theme's motion; once it has closed, nothing of the modal is drawn.

**The focus stays inside.** Opened from the keyboard, the focus moves to the content's first control, and Tab goes round inside it and never reaches the app under it; opened by touch, the focus stays where it was, and no software keyboard opens unasked. Once it closes, the focus is back where it was.

**Its place.** `position` puts the content in the middle of the window or at its top: `Top`, for a search whose field stays where it is. `margin` is the room left between the content and the window's safe area; it is part of the scrim.
**A page of its own.** A `margin` of none, content that fills itself and a `scrimColor` that is the theme's background make the modal a page on a phone.
**Screen reader.** `paneTitle` is read as the modal opens; the scrim is one "Close" action, after the content.
**A fold.** Where a fold divides the window in two, the content keeps to the half it was opened from; a modal opened inside a picture of a window takes that picture for its window.

examples.name: ModalSearch
examples.title: A search at the top
examples.description: A search of your own, at the top of the window: the field stays where it is, and the results grow and shrink under it. Escape, back or a press on the scrim closes it; so does a press on a result.

examples.name: ModalPage
examples.title: A page of its own
examples.description: A page on a phone: a `margin` of none, a scrim in the theme's background and content that fills itself. Behind the window's bars stays the background's colour too.

examples.name: ModalDecision
examples.title: One that asks for a decision
examples.description: A modal that does not close before a decision is made: a press on the scrim and back do nothing (`dismissOnScrimClick` and `dismissOnBack` are off); one of the two buttons in it is chosen.

pages.title: Sheet
pages.summary:
A panel over the app for a short task that belongs to the current screen: choosing how to sort, filling in a field or two, picking from a list, looking at the details of what was pressed. It opens from the bottom edge, where a drag moves it, or from the end edge as a side sheet. It is modal either way: nothing behind it takes a click, and Tab never leaves it.

The sheet never closes itself. A click on the scrim, back, Escape, a drag towards its edge and the side sheet's close button call `onDismissRequest`; what closes it is the calling code, which sets `visible` to false.
features: **Along the bottom edge.** The default edge is `SheetEdge.Bottom`: the sheet is as wide as the window, up to the style's `maxWidth`, and as tall as what it holds. A drag moves it: a drag down closes it.

**Side sheet.** With `edge = SheetEdge.End` the sheet stands at the end edge, on the left in a language written right to left: it runs the length of the window, is as wide as the style's `sideWidth` and has a close button. A drag towards the edge closes it. `SheetEdge.Start` opens the same sheet from the start edge: an app's menu in a narrow window.

**Edge-to-edge content.** The content spans the sheet's width: the rows of a list reach its edges, and a form brings its own horizontal padding. Content that does not fit in the sheet scrolls under the title.

**Half open.** With `halfOpen` a sheet whose content is taller than half the window first opens half open, its top at the middle of the window. A drag up, or focus moving into it, opens it fully; a drag down from half open closes it.
**Full screen.** With `fullScreen` the fully open sheet is as tall as the window under the status bar, however short its content. `coverStatusBar` takes it under the status bar too.

**A list that scrolls itself.** A long list belongs in a `LazyColumn`, with `scrollContent = false`. `overscrollMovesSheet = false` makes the list do nothing but scroll: once it is at its top it does not pull the sheet down, and the handle and the title still drag the sheet.

**A sheet that cannot be dismissed.** With `dismissible = false` a drag, the scrim, back and Escape do nothing; a side sheet has no close button, and a sheet that does not open half open has no handle either. The way out is a control in the content.

**It stays in the tree as it closes.** A closed sheet composes nothing: it stays in the tree with `visible = false` and leaves with the theme's motion. A sheet taken out of the composition while it is open is gone at once, without the motion.

**Keyboard and screen reader.** When the sheet is opened with the keyboard, focus starts on the first control; when it is opened by touch, focus stays where it was. `title` is announced when the sheet opens and is the heading of what it holds. A screen reader cannot drag, so it is offered actions that open a half-open sheet fully and bring it back.

**Colour and style.** `colors` changes the fill, the title, the handle, the close icon and the scrim; `style` the corners that face the app, the widths, the margin kept for the scrim, the shadow and the handle. The corners are large on Android and iOS and medium on desktop and the web; there is no shadow on iOS.

examples.name: SheetSorting
examples.title: Sorting
examples.description:
At its plainest: a title and content. A choice is the whole task: the sheet closes as soon as it is made, and there is no need for a separate "OK" button.

The sheet never closes itself: a drag down, a click on the scrim, back and Escape call `onDismissRequest`; in every case it is the `open = false` line that closes it. The card's "Last event" line says what happened last.

examples.title: Form
examples.description:
A field and a button. The content reaches the sheet's edges, so the form brings its own horizontal padding: `Modifier.padding(horizontal = …)`. "Save" is disabled while the note is empty.

When the sheet is opened by touch, focus does not move to the field. Once the field is pressed, the sheet stays above the keyboard.

appNames.name: LocalExampleEvents
appNames.description: Where an example tells its card what happens in it: a button pressed, a row chosen, a dialog closed. The card writes the last thing told under the example, on its "Last event" line.

examples.name: SheetOverTheKeyboard
examples.title: With the keyboard open
examples.description:
A sheet opened while typing in a field of the page. Focus stays wherever it is on the page, and is there again when the sheet closes; where that is depends on the platform. On Android and iOS a tap on the button takes no focus: focus stays in the field that was typed in. On desktop and the web a press on the button moves focus to the button: when the sheet closes, focus is on the button.

While the sheet is open, what is typed on the keyboard goes to the sheet, not to the field underneath; meanwhile the field is drawn at rest, without its caret. On Android and iOS the on-screen keyboard closes when the sheet opens; when the sheet closes, the caret and the keyboard return to the field.

Type in the field first, then press the button: what was typed in the field stays as it is on every platform.

examples.name: SheetHalfOpenList
examples.title: Half-open list
examples.description:
A long list that starts half open: the top of it is usually enough. With `halfOpen` the sheet opens up to the middle of the window; a drag up, or focus moving into it, opens it fully. `fullScreen` makes the fully open sheet as tall as the window under the status bar.

The list scrolls itself: it is in a `LazyColumn`, and `scrollContent = false` turns off the sheet's own scroll area. The list is given `Modifier.fillMaxWidth()`: without it, a drag beside its rows would not scroll it. With `overscrollMovesSheet = false` a list that has reached its top does not pull the sheet down; the handle and the title still drag the sheet.
