examples.title: Full screen
examples.description:
Like a screen of its own: with `fullScreen` the fully open sheet is as tall as the window under the status bar, however short its content. With `coverStatusBar` it reaches under the status bar too and is as tall as the whole window: its top corners square off there, and its handle and title stay below the bar.

The files are filtered as you type in the field; the sheet's height does not change even when the list gets shorter. The search starts empty each time the sheet opens.

No role of the theme has this purple, so the colour that reads on it is the caller's to give too: the title's through `colors`, and that of the text in the content through its own `color`. Had the fill been one of the theme's role colours, the title, the handle and the close icon would have taken the colour paired with that role by themselves.

pages.title: Menu
pages.summary:
A list of actions for one element, in a panel that opens beside it: what a "more" button opens, or the actions of a row. There is no scrim, and the page stays in view around it; the panel sits beside its anchor (`anchor`) and follows it as the content moves.

The menu does not close itself. Choosing a row, a press outside, back and Escape call `onDismissRequest`; it is the caller that closes the menu, by setting `visible` to false. The `onClick` of the row that was chosen is called after the menu has been asked to close: a row says only what it does, and gives no thought to closing the menu. The first press outside only closes it: what is under it is not pressed.
features: **Rows.** `PantrixMenuItem` takes a label, an icon before it (`icon`), a shortcut at its end (`shortcut`) and a second, smaller line under it (`supportingText`, its type `supportingTextStyle`). A `PantrixDivider` goes between groups.

**A row that deletes, and one that cannot be chosen.** `destructive` draws the label and the icon in the menu's destructive colour: the theme's `danger` colour unless another is given. `enabled = false` draws the row faded: it takes no press and no focus.

**Side and alignment.** `side` says which side of the anchor the panel opens on, and `alignment` how it lines up along that side: unless told otherwise it is below the anchor, hanging from its start edge. Where the side asked for has no room it takes the opposite side.
**Inside the window.** The panel never comes closer than the style's `margin` to the edges of the window, its system bars or the keyboard: at an anchor near an edge it shifts inwards.

**Width and height.** The panel is as wide as its longest row, between the style's narrowest and widest widths; a longer label is cut at one line. More rows than fit the tallest height scroll inside the panel.

**Keyboard.** When the menu is opened by the keyboard, the focus is on its first row. The arrow keys walk the rows and go round from the last to the first, Home and End go to the first row and the last, and Tab walks the rows as well; Enter and the space bar choose the row, and Escape closes the menu. Once it has closed, the focus is back on the control that opened it. While the menu is open the page under it shows no focus.
**Touch and mouse.** When the menu is opened by a touch or a click, no row shows the focus; the first arrow key, Home or End brings the keyboard into use. The row a mouse is over is filled faintly.

**Colours and style.** `colors` (`MenuColors`) gives the colour of the panel and of its rows, and `style` (`MenuStyle`) the corners, the widths, the tallest height and a row's dimensions. Only the fields that are set change, and the rest stay the theme's.

**Platforms.** The menu looks the same on every platform; what differs is in the style. The style's row height is 48 dp on Android, 44 on iOS, and 32 on desktop and the web; a row is never shorter than the platform's touch target.
**Screen reader.** The icon is not read: a screen reader is told the row's label alone. A shortcut is shown and read out, but never bound: binding the keys is the app's job.

**Chosen row.** Among rows that each choose one thing, a language or an order, the one in effect is `selected`: a check stands at its end, in the label's colour, and a screen reader is told it is selected.

**A sheet in a narrow window.** `presentation`'s default is `OverlayPresentation.Adaptive`: in a narrow (`Compact`) window the menu is a sheet from the bottom, in a wider one a panel beside the anchor. In the sheet the rows are as wide as the sheet and as tall as the touch target, there is no title, and a drag down closes it; on a platform used by touch the shortcuts are not written. `Popover` and `Sheet` choose one of the two in every window. It is chosen as the menu opens, and does not change until it closes.

examples.name: MenuRowActions
examples.title: Row actions
examples.description:
At its plainest: a file's "more" button opens the menu. Whether the menu is open is the screen's state (`visible`). The menu does not close itself: when it wants to close it calls `onDismissRequest`, and it is this code that sets `visible` to false. The row that deletes is under a `PantrixDivider` and, with `destructive`, in the theme's `danger` colour.

Pick a row: the menu is first asked to close, then the row's `onClick` is called; the card's "Last event" line says what happened last. A press outside, back and Escape only close it. When the menu is opened by the keyboard, the focus is on its first row; once it has closed, the focus is back on the button.

The rows of a menu given a `tagKey` are named inside it for automation: the test tag of the "Delete" row here is `Menu_row_actions.MenuItem_delete`, and it cannot be mixed up with another menu's "Delete" row.

examples.name: MenuIconsAndShortcuts
examples.title: Icon and shortcut
examples.description:
`icon` draws an icon before the label: in the label's colour and at the style's icon size. The icon is a picture of what the label says; a screen reader reads the label alone. `shortcut` shows the keys that do the same thing at the end of the row. A shortcut is only shown and read out: binding the keys is the app's job.

`enabled = false` draws the row faded: "Move to folder" takes no press, and the keyboard skips it. `destructive` draws both the label and the icon in the destructive colour.

var open by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf(false) }
val report = LocalExampleEvents.current
PantrixMenu(
    visible = open,
    onDismissRequest = {
        open = false
        report("File menu closed")
    },
    anchor = {
        PantrixButton(
            text = "File",
            onClick = { open = true },
            variant = ButtonVariant.Outline,
            tagKey = "open_file"
        )
    },
    tagKey = "file"
) {
    PantrixMenuItem(
        text = "Search",
        onClick = { report("Search chosen") },
        icon = PantrixIcons.Search,
        shortcut = "Ctrl+F",
        tagKey = "search"
    )
    PantrixMenuItem(
        text = "Refresh",
        onClick = { report("Refresh chosen") },
        icon = PantrixIcons.Refresh,
        shortcut = "F5",
        tagKey = "refresh"
    )
    PantrixMenuItem(
        text = "Move to folder",
        onClick = { report("Move to folder chosen") },
        icon = PantrixIcons.Folder,
        enabled = false,
        tagKey = "move"
    )
    PantrixDivider()
    PantrixMenuItem(
        text = "Delete",
        onClick = { report("Delete chosen") },
        icon = PantrixIcons.Close,
        shortcut = "Del",
        destructive = true,
        tagKey = "delete"
    )
}

examples.description: A menu whose rows each choose one thing: the list's order. The one in effect is `selected`: a check stands at its end, in the label's colour, and a screen reader is told it is selected. Choose another order: the check moves to its row, and the button writes the new order.

examples.name: MenuSupportingText
examples.title: Second line
examples.description: `supportingText` puts a second, smaller line under the label: what the choice leads to. Here, under each language, the site's address in it, set in the code type (`supportingTextStyle`); its colour is the row's. The row grows to hold it; a screen reader hears the second line after the label. The second line runs to two lines at the most, and the rest is cut.

examples.name: MenuSideAndAlignment
examples.title: Side and alignment
examples.description:
`side` says which side of the anchor the panel opens on, and `alignment` how it lines up along that side. Unless told otherwise the menu is below its anchor and hangs from the anchor's start edge: `PopoverSide.Bottom` and `PopoverAlignment.Start`. The two enums are the popover's; the menu shares them.

Start and End follow the reading direction: in a left-to-right layout Start is the left. While the panel is beside the anchor (Start or End) the alignment is vertical: Start makes the top edges meet, and End the bottom edges.

Where the side asked for has no room the menu takes the opposite side: pick Top and open the menu while the button is near the top edge of the window. With room on neither side the menu keeps the side asked for and slides inside the window, over its anchor.

`presentation = OverlayPresentation.Popover`: the menu is a panel in a narrow window too, not a sheet; its side and alignment show on a phone as well.

examples.name: MenuAtTheEdge
examples.title: At the edge
examples.description:
A "more" button near the end edge of the window. A menu hangs from the start edge of its anchor; with the button near the edge, the panel would run out of the window. It does not: it shifts to stay the style's `margin` in from the edge. In a narrow window the menu would be a sheet; `presentation = OverlayPresentation.Popover` keeps it a panel in every window.

Try it in a narrow window: the one to narrow is the app's own window. A menu picks its place by the real window, not by the window a card's window selector gives its example; that is why this card has no such selector. In a window that is wide enough there is room for the panel beside the card; there the panel does not shift, and hangs from the start edge of the button.

`presentation = OverlayPresentation.Popover`: a panel in a narrow window too. In a sheet the rows scroll inside the sheet, which is as tall as the window at the most.

examples.description:

The labels of the "Short" menu are shorter than the narrowest width: the panel stays at that width. The first label of the "Long" menu does not fit the widest panel: it is cut at one line.

examples.name: MenuOwnStyle
examples.title: Its own style
examples.description:
`style` changes this menu's geometry alone: the fields of `MenuStyle` that are set change, and the rest comes from the theme's and the platform's style. Here the panel's corners are the theme's large corner (`ShapeRole.Large`), the panel is at least 240dp wide, its rows are 56dp tall and their icons 28dp.

The style given to a menu draws its rows too; `PantrixMenuItem` takes no style of its own. The width and the height that are given scale with the theme's density; the corners and the icon's size do not.

`presentation = OverlayPresentation.Popover`: a sheet's corners and width are the sheet's, and there the panel's style draws only the rows; the menu is a panel so that the style shows in a narrow window too.

examples.name: MenuOwnColors
examples.title: Its own colours
examples.description:
`colors` gives the menu the colours that are set in place of the theme's: here the app's own purple, which is in none of the theme's roles. Only the fields of `MenuColors` that are set change, and the rest stay the theme's: the row that deletes is still in the theme's `danger` colour.

The theme's secondary and disabled text colours are for the theme's own grounds alone. On this fill the shortcut is drawn in the row's colour, and a row that cannot be chosen in a share of that colour. The line between the groups is given no colour: on the fill it too is a share of the row's colour.

On a fill that no role has, `content` is given too: the theme does not know what reads on that fill. Where the fill is the colour of one of the theme's roles, such as `PantrixTheme.colors.primary.container`, the rows take the colour the theme pairs with it by themselves.

var open by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf(false) }
val report = LocalExampleEvents.current
val own = ownColors()
PantrixMenu(
    visible = open,
    onDismissRequest = {
        open = false
        report("Pro menu closed")
    },
    anchor = {
        PantrixButton(
            text = "Pro",
            onClick = { open = true },
            variant = ButtonVariant.Outline,
            tagKey = "open_pro_menu"
        )
    },
    colors = MenuColors(container = own.container, content = own.onContainer, border = own.color),
    tagKey = "pro_menu"
) {
    PantrixMenuItem(
        text = "Upgrade plan",
        onClick = { report("Upgrade plan chosen") },
        icon = PantrixIcons.Star,
        shortcut = "Ctrl+U",
        tagKey = "upgrade"
    )
    PantrixMenuItem(
        text = "Invoices",
        onClick = { report("Invoices chosen") },
        icon = PantrixIcons.Folder,
        enabled = false,
        tagKey = "invoices"
    )
    PantrixDivider()
    PantrixMenuItem(
        text = "End subscription",
        onClick = { report("End subscription chosen") },
        icon = PantrixIcons.Close,
        destructive = true,
        tagKey = "cancel_plan"
    )
}

pages.title: Popover
pages.summary:
A layer that opens beside an element and shows more about it than the element itself can: what a status means, what a field expects, a few controls for one row. There is no scrim, and the page stays in view around it; the popover sits beside its anchor (`anchor`) and moves with it as the content scrolls.

The popover does not close itself. A press outside it, back and Escape call `onDismissRequest`; what closes it is the caller, setting `visible` to false. The first press outside only closes: what is under it is not pressed, so a press on the anchor closes the popover and does not open it again.

A closed popover composes nothing but its anchor: it stays in the tree with `visible = false`, and enters and leaves with the theme's motion. A popover that is taken out of the composition while it is open goes at once, without motion.
features: **Title.** `title` stands at the top of the popover and stays in place while the content scrolls. Every popover of more than a line is given one.
**Content.** `content` is a column under the title: a text, a link, a few buttons.

**Side and alignment.** `side` says which side of the anchor the popover opens on, `alignment` how it lines up along that side: left unsaid, it opens below the anchor and is centred on it. Where the side that is asked for has no room, it takes the opposite side.

**Inside the window.** It comes no closer than the style's `margin` to the edges of the window, the system bars and the keyboard, and is no larger than that room: its content wraps, and what does not fit scrolls under the title.
**A popover that cannot be dismissed.** With `dismissible = false`, a press outside it, back and Escape do not ask it to close: only for a popover that something inside it closes.

**Keyboard.** Opened by the keyboard it takes the focus: its first control does, or the popover itself where it has none. Then the arrow keys, Page Up and Page Down, the space bar, Home and End scroll the content. Tab stays inside it; once it has closed, the focus goes back to the anchor, the control that opened it.
**Touch and mouse.** Opened by a touch or a click it leaves the focus where it was; once the keyboard comes into use the popover takes the focus. While it is open the page under it shows no focus.

**Colours and style.** `colors` (`PopoverColors`) gives the fill and the colours of the title and of the line around it; `style` (`PopoverStyle`) gives the corners, the widths, the tallest height, the shadow and the distance to the anchor. Only the fields that are given change; the rest stay the theme's.

**Platforms.** The popover looks the same on every platform; the difference is in the style. At its widest it is 320 dp on Android and iOS, and 360 dp on desktop and the web; its corners are the theme's medium corner on Android and iOS, and its small one on desktop and the web.

**Screen reader.** The popover's title is announced as it opens; the title is the heading of the content. Since there is no scrim around it to press, a screen reader closes it with its own dismiss action.

The popover does not close itself: when it wants to close it calls `onDismissRequest`, and it is this code that sets `visible` to false. A press on a control inside it does not ask it to close: the link closes the popover in its own `onClick`.

A press outside it, back and Escape close it. Opened by the keyboard, the focus is on the link; once it has closed, the focus is back on the button. The card's "Last event" line says what happened last.

pages.title: Tooltip
pages.summary:
The short label that sits beside the control it names: the name of an icon-only button, a truncated label in full. It shows what the control already says: a screen reader reads the control itself, and the label is hidden from it. So the control's `contentDescription` or its text has to be the same words; a tooltip is no place to say anything new.

It comes up by itself and takes nothing from the app: no focus and no key, and the control goes on working. It takes no press from the control but the long press that asks for the name.
features: **Mouse.** The label comes up once the pointer has rested on the control for the style's `pointerRestMillis`, and goes as the pointer leaves. The pointer may cross onto the label and rest there. A click on the control puts the label away; it does not come up again until the pointer has left and come back.
**Keyboard.** The label comes up at once when the keyboard brings the focus to the control, and goes as the focus leaves. Escape puts it away, and the focus stays on the control.

**Touch.** A long press on the control brings the label up, and it stays until something is pressed. The long press that asks for the name does not press the control; a tap only presses the control and brings no label up.

**Side.** `side` says which side of the control the label sits on: the top by default. The label is centred on the control on that side; where there is no room it takes the opposite side, and it comes no closer to the window's edges than the style's `margin`.

**State.** Whether the label is up is one state (`state`): the mouse, the keyboard and a long press change it. A screen can change it too: it holds the state with `rememberPantrixTooltipState()` and calls `show()` and `dismiss()`.
**Can be turned off.** `enabled = false` puts the label away and keeps it from coming up: for a control whose name is already in view.
**Puts itself away.** The label is put away while its control is under a dialog, a sheet or an open popover, when the control scrolls out of view, and when the window changes size.
**One label.** A window has one label up at a time: when a new one comes up, the one before it goes. Escape puts away the label that is up, wherever the focus is, and goes no further.

**Colours and style.** The label is in the tone opposite the theme's: dark in the light theme, light in the dark. `colors` (`TooltipColors`) gives it a colour of its own; `style` (`TooltipStyle`) gives the corners, the spacing, the maximum width and the mouse's wait.

**On which control.** The anchor is a control that is pressed, a button or an icon, or a text that is only read. A control with a long press of its own, a text field or text that can be selected, loses that press to the tooltip on a touch screen.

examples.name: TooltipToolbar
examples.title: Toolbar
examples.description:
At its plainest: `PantrixTooltip` wraps the control it names. Four buttons show only an icon: the tooltip shows each one's name and `contentDescription` says it to a screen reader. The two are the same words.

Rest the mouse on a button, focus it with the keyboard or long-press it with a finger: its name comes up. A click and a tap press the button; the long press that asks for the name does not. The card's "Last event" line says which button was pressed last.

examples.title: Side
examples.description: `side` says which side of the control the label sits on; the label is centred on the control on that side. By default it sits above the control: `PopoverSide.Top`. Start and End follow the reading direction: in a left-to-right layout Start is the left. Where the side asked for has no room, the label takes the opposite side.

examples.name: TooltipCutLabel
examples.title: Truncated label
examples.description:
A file name cut short on one line because it does not fit its column: the tooltip shows the name in full. The tooltip's label is never wider than the style's maximum width (`TooltipStyle.maxWidth`); the long name wraps inside it.

The anchor here is not a control that is pressed but a text that is only read: the label comes up when the mouse rests on it or a finger long-presses it.

examples.name: TooltipHintFromTheScreen
examples.title: A hint the screen brings up
examples.description:
Whether the label is up is a state, and the screen can hold it itself: `rememberPantrixTooltipState()`. `hint.show()` brings the label up without anyone touching the control: a hint on the first run, the name of a control that has just changed. `hint.dismiss()` puts it away, and so does a press anywhere else.

The mouse, the keyboard and a long press change that same state too: `hint.visible` always tells the truth about whether the label is up.

examples.description: While `enabled = false` nothing brings the label up, and a label that is already up is put away. It is for a control whose name is already in view. Turn the switch on: the button's tooltip starts working.

examples.name: TooltipOwnStyle
examples.title: Its own style
examples.description:
`style` changes the geometry of this tooltip alone: the fields of `TooltipStyle` that are set change, and the rest comes from the theme's and the platform's style. The first button's label comes up the moment the mouse is over it: `pointerRestMillis = 0`. The second's label has fully rounded corners (`ShapeRole.Full`) and more room around its text, and sits 12dp from the button.

`pointerRestMillis` is the mouse's wait alone: keyboard focus brings the label up at once, and a finger's long press after the platform's long-press time. The style's wait is 400 milliseconds on Android and iOS, 500 on desktop and the web.

examples.name: TooltipOwnColors
examples.title: Its own colours
examples.description:
Given no colours, the label is in the tone opposite the theme's: dark in the light theme, light in the dark. `colors` gives the label colours of its own: here the app's own purple, which is in none of the theme's roles. Only the fields of `TooltipColors` that are set change.

On a fill that has no role, `content` is given too: the theme does not know what reads on that fill. Where the fill is the colour of one of the theme's roles, such as `PantrixTheme.colors.primary.color`, the text by itself takes the colour the theme pairs with that role.
examples.code:
val report = LocalExampleEvents.current
val own = ownColors()
PantrixTooltip(
    text = "Pro feature",
    colors = TooltipColors(container = own.color, content = own.onColor),
    tagKey = "own"
) {
    PantrixIconButton(
        imageVector = PantrixIcons.Info,
        contentDescription = "Pro feature",
        onClick = { report("Pro feature button pressed") },
        tagKey = "own"
    )
}

examples.name: TooltipIconWhereItIsNarrow
examples.title: Icon where it is narrow, text where it is wide
examples.description:
An icon alone where it is narrow, a button with text where it is wide. The button learns its own room from `BoxWithPantrixWindow`: where it is narrow a tooltip shows its name; where it is wide the name is written on the button and there is no tooltip.

This box composes its content while it measures, and when its room crosses a breakpoint it throws the old branch away inside the measuring pass. The label's layer is composed at the window's root, so nothing breaks even if the label is up at that moment; the label is also put away whenever the window changes size.

examples.name: TooltipRoomThatNarrows
examples.title: Room that narrows while the window stays the same
examples.description:
Room that narrows while the window stays the same: as with a pane that is dragged or a sidebar that slides open. Press the button: three seconds later the box widens or narrows. Within those three seconds bring up the icon's label or open the popover: when the room changes, the branch that holds them is thrown away, and the label and the popover go with it.

The box is a layout that composes its content while it measures (`BoxWithConstraints`): when it crosses the breakpoint it throws away the branch inside it, in the middle of the measuring pass. The layers of an open label and an open popover are composed at the window's root, so once the branch is thrown away they close in the next frame.

pages.title: Snackbar
pages.summary:
A short message about something the app has just done: "Conversation archived", "Changes saved". It has at most one action, never takes focus and never blocks the app.

A snackbar is not drawn, it is asked for: `PantrixSnackbarState.show` puts it in the queue, and a `PantrixSnackbarHost` puts it on screen when its turn comes. There is usually a single host, at the root of the app; a `PantrixScaffold` that is given the queue sets the host up itself, and provides the queue to every screen inside it through `LocalPantrixSnackbars`.
features: **In turn, one at a time.** One snackbar is on screen at a time; the others wait in the order they were asked for. `show` is a suspending function: once the snackbar has left, it returns how it left.
**One action.** `actionLabel` gives the snackbar a single action: "Undo". The result is `SnackbarResult.ActionPerformed` if the action was pressed, and `Dismissed` if not.

**Duration.** A snackbar without an action leaves after four seconds (`Short`); `Long` is ten. One with an action stays until the action is taken or it is closed (`UntilDismissed`), and has a close button. The time waits while the pointer is over the snackbar and while focus is inside it, and then starts again.

**Six tones.** `tone` picks the colour, the icon and the way it is announced together. The four semantic tones (`Info`, `Success`, `Warning`, `Danger`) have an icon; `Primary` and the default, `Neutral`, have none.

**Ways to leave.** Its time runs out, its action or its close button is pressed, it is swiped sideways, Escape is pressed with focus inside it, a screen reader's dismiss action is used, or the app dismisses it (`SnackbarData.dismiss`).

**Placed by platform.** It appears in the middle of the bottom edge on Android, at the top on iOS, and in the bottom end corner on desktop and the web: `SnackbarStyle.placement`. It stays inside the window's safe area.
**The colour is the host's.** `SnackbarColors` is given to the host, not to the snackbar, and paints every snackbar of that host; the icon and the way it is announced still come from the tone.
**Screen reader.** A snackbar is announced without interrupting what is being read; only the `Danger` tone interrupts.
**Under a dialog and a sheet.** A snackbar belongs to the app: a dialog or a sheet opened over the host covers it.

examples.name: SnackbarMessage
examples.title: A message
examples.description:
The least there is to write: a message. The queue does not come here as a parameter; the scaffold provides it to every screen inside it through `LocalPantrixSnackbars`. `show` is a suspending function, so it is called in a coroutine. A snackbar without an action leaves by itself after four seconds.

The scope is this example's (`rememberCoroutineScope`): it is cancelled when the page is left, and takes the snackbar on screen with it. A snackbar that must stay even when the screen changes is asked for in a scope that outlives the screen. Outside a scaffold, where nothing provides the queue, `LocalPantrixSnackbars.current` is null and the button does nothing.
examples.code:
val snackbars = LocalPantrixSnackbars.current
val scope = rememberCoroutineScope()
PantrixButton(
    text = "Save draft",
    onClick = { scope.launch { snackbars?.show(message = "Draft saved", tagKey = "draft_saved") } },
    variant = ButtonVariant.Outline,
    tagKey = "save_draft"
)

examples.name: SnackbarTones
examples.title: Tones
examples.description:
The snackbar's six tones: each button asks the app's queue for a snackbar in that tone. `tone` picks the colour of one of the theme's roles, an icon in the four semantic tones, and how the snackbar is announced: `Danger` interrupts what a screen reader is saying, and the others are announced without interrupting. A snackbar is filled in every tone: from the role's `color` and `onColor`, not its pale `container`.

Those with an action stay until the action is taken or they are closed; those without one leave by themselves after four seconds. The snackbars of buttons pressed one after another come in turn, one at a time. How each one left is written under the buttons.

examples.name: SnackbarUndo
examples.title: An action and its result
examples.description:
`actionLabel` gives the snackbar a single action. Once the snackbar has left, `show` returns how it left: `SnackbarResult.ActionPerformed` if the action was pressed; `Dismissed` if its time ran out, it was closed or the app dismissed it. Pressing "Undo" puts the conversation back in the inbox.

A snackbar with an action does not leave by itself: a few seconds are not enough for some users to reach the action. That is why its default duration is `UntilDismissed`, and it has a close button.

examples.name: SnackbarDurations
examples.title: Duration and close button
examples.description:
`duration` says how long the snackbar stays when nobody acts on it: `Short` is four seconds, `Long` ten; `UntilDismissed` is until it is closed. The platform may make this longer for a user who needs more time. A snackbar that stays until it is closed has a close button; `closeButton = true` puts one on a short snackbar too.

Hold the pointer over the snackbar: its time waits, and starts again when the pointer moves away. It waits while keyboard focus is inside it too. Swiping the snackbar sideways sends it away without waiting for its time.

examples.name: SnackbarQueue
examples.title: Snackbars that come in turn
examples.description:
Three snackbars are asked for one after another; they come on screen in the order they were asked for, one at a time. `show` suspends until its own turn comes. The app's single queue keeps the order: a snackbar that another example asks for waits in the same line.

"Cancel the rest" cancels this example's coroutines: when the coroutine that called `show` is cancelled, the snackbar on screen leaves, and those whose turn has not come are never shown.

examples.name: SnackbarDismissedByTheApp
examples.title: A snackbar the app dismisses
examples.description:
Some snackbars are dismissed by the app, not the user: once the connection is back there is no point in saying "You're offline". `PantrixSnackbarState.current` is the snackbar on screen, or null; `dismiss()` takes it away, and `show` returns `SnackbarResult.Dismissed`. "Back online" is enabled only while this example's snackbar is on screen.

This snackbar stays until it is dismissed and has no close button (`closeButton = false`); swiping it sideways still sends it away.

examples.name: SnackbarOwnColors
examples.title: A colour given to the host
examples.description:
The colour is given not to the snackbar but to the host that shows it: `PantrixSnackbarHost(state, colors = SnackbarColors(container = …, content = …))`. The app's host stands at the root, so the switch's state is there too, in the app's settings; the host reads it. While it is on, every snackbar is drawn with the same fill; its icon and the way it is announced still come from its tone.

Flip the switch, then ask for a snackbar from here or from "Tones". The switch stands at the end away from the edge the snackbar appears at: below the button where the snackbar appears at the top (iOS), above it where it appears at the bottom.

appNames.name: LocalDemoSettings
appNames.description: The app's settings, for every screen inside it: the buttons in the top bar and the "Settings" page read and change them from here. Outside the app, on a page drawn by itself in a test, they are the default settings.

examples.name: SnackbarOwnHost
examples.title: A host of its own: placement, style and colour
examples.description:
There is usually a single host, at the root of the app. Here, to show what its parameters do, there is a second host in a box, with a queue of its own: `rememberPantrixSnackbarState` gives the queue, and `PantrixSnackbarHost` shows it. The host is the box's last child: it fills the space it is given and stands above the content.

`style` changes the placement and the geometry: `placement` picks one of four places, and `maxWidth` keeps the snackbar to 320dp. In a narrow box the snackbar fills the box; start, centre and end only differ in a wide one. `colors` paints every snackbar of this host: the fill is the app's own purple, and the icon is still the tone's.

The host stays inside the window's safe area. This box stands in the middle of the window, so it consumes those insets itself (`consumeWindowInsets`); a host at the root does not need to.

The snackbar the queue shows is its `current` (`SnackbarData`): the line under the box writes its message, and "Remove" closes it with `dismiss()`, without waiting out its time.

appNames.description: The "app's own colour" of the examples: a purple that is in none of the theme's roles. It is there to show what changes when a component is given `colors`; given one of the theme's roles, nobody could tell whether the colour came from the component's tone or from the parameter.

pages.title: Command Palette
pages.summary: Every command of the app in one place, found by its name and run from the keyboard: the panel Cmd+K or Ctrl+K opens. In this demo too, Cmd+K (on a Mac) or Ctrl+K opens, on every page, a palette that lists all the pages.
features: **A modal panel.** As a dialog is: a scrim behind it, the focus inside; back, Esc and a click on the scrim ask to close. Whether it is shown is the screen's state (`visible`, `onDismissRequest`); the palette does not close itself. `onRun` is where the palette is closed before the command does its work.

**It stands at the top.** At the top of the window, in the middle: as you type, the list under it shrinks and grows, and the field stays where it is. On a phone it is as wide as the margins leave, and ends above the keyboard.

**Commands.** A `PantrixCommand`'s `key` is the same in every language; `label` gives the name read, `group` the heading it stands under, `icon` the icon before it, `shortcut` the shortcut at its end, `keywords` other words that find it, and `supportingText` the second line under the label.

**Search.** Each word typed is looked for in the label, the group, the keywords or the second line; capitals and small letters are compared as the theme's language has them (in Turkish İ with i, I with ı). The groups keep their order; inside each group, those matched from the start, and from the start of a word, come first; the letters found are set in bold.

**Keyboard.** The field keeps the focus; the down and up arrows go between the commands that can be run and stop at the ends, Page Down and Page Up skip a page, and the mouse highlights the row it passes over. Enter, the keyboard's action and a press on the row run the command. Each time it opens the field is empty and the highlight is on the first command that can be run.
**Disabled.** A command with `enabled = false` is listed, written faintly; the arrows pass it by and it is not run.

**Shortcuts.** A `PantrixShortcut` holds a key and what is pressed with it; `command` is Command on Apple's systems and Control elsewhere. It is written at the row's end as the system writes it: ⇧⌘K or Ctrl+Shift+K. `Modifier.onShortcut` binds one shortcut and `Modifier.commandShortcuts` every command's in the list; `Modifier.shortcutRoot` on the window's root makes the shortcuts heard while nothing has the focus too.

**Screen reader.** As it opens, the palette is announced by the theme's name for a list of commands. The highlighted row is selected, the groups are headings, the shortcut is read as the row's state; as you type, how many commands are left is said.

**Platform.** The panel is a dialog's, the rows the platform's list rows: 48dp on Android, 44pt on iOS, 36dp on desktop and the web. On desktop and the web the panel stands a little lower from the top.

pages.title: Diagnostics Inspector
pages.summary: What the theme's diagnostics have found, over the app: a button with the number of findings, and on its press a list; the node of the finding chosen in the list is outlined on the screen. This app is under one too: the button at the bottom right is for the app's own findings.
features: **It wraps the app.** `PantrixDiagnosticsInspector(findings) { App() }`: the content is laid out as it would be without it, and gets every press.
**Unseen while nothing is found.** The button comes with the first finding and goes when the list is cleared.
**Outline.** The node of the finding chosen in the list is outlined until the screen is next pressed; a finding without a node says that it is not on the screen.
**Where it stands.** `alignment` chooses the button's corner; the default is the bottom of the end edge.

pages.summary:
Slides one beside another, one of them on screen: featured items, a picture gallery, a step-by-step introduction. A swipe turns the slide; the dots under it say where the carousel is.

Which slide is on screen is the screen's state: the carousel is given the slide's index (`currentPage`), and a swipe reports back where it ended (`onPageChange`). The buttons, the dots and the arrow keys turn nothing by themselves; they report the slide that is asked for.
features: **Indicators.** Dots under the slides, a count ("2 / 4") or nothing: `CarouselStyle.indicator`.

**Previous and next buttons.** They show where the platform is not used by touch, on desktop and in a browser on a desk, and not in a phone's browser. What decides is the pointer the screen is used with, not whether the screen can be touched: they show on a laptop with a touch screen too. `CarouselStyle.controls` shows them everywhere or never.
**Neighbouring slides.** With `peek` the edges of the slides at the two sides show: what a swipe will bring is already in sight.
**Slides that go round.** With `loop` the first comes after the last.

**Turning by itself.** With `autoAdvanceMillis` the carousel turns by itself; it waits while the reader holds a slide, while the mouse is over it and while the keyboard's focus is in it. The button beside the dots stops it and starts it again. Where the theme's motion is reduced it does not turn by itself.
**Over the slide.** `CarouselPlacement.Overlaid` puts the buttons and the dots over the slide, on a fill of their own: in a gallery they take no room.

**Height.** In a carousel given a height, the slides fill the room the dots leave. A carousel given none is as tall as the slide on screen, and its height changes without a jump on the way from one slide to another.
**Keyboard.** The slides are one stop: the arrow keys turn them, and Home and End go to the first and the last.
**Touch.** For a finger the dots are one target: its left half goes one slide back and its right half one slide forward; in a right-to-left layout the halves change places.
**Screen reader.** It says where the carousel is at every change: "Slide 2 of 4". A carousel that turns by itself does not break in at every turn.

examples.name: CarouselFeatured
examples.title: Featured: with dots
examples.description:
Its plainest form: four slides with dots under them. The slide's index is the screen's state; the carousel takes it with `currentPage` and reports it back with `onPageChange` when a swipe ends. The line below reads the same state.

The height was given to the carousel (180dp): the slides fill the room the dots leave. On desktop and in a browser on a desk the previous and next buttons show at the two sides as well; on a phone, in its browser too, a swipe is enough.

examples.name: CarouselOffers
examples.title: Cards whose neighbours show, with a count and buttons
examples.description: With `peek = 24.dp` a slide's neighbours show at its two sides: what a swipe will bring is already in sight. `indicator = CarouselIndicator.Count` writes a count in place of the dots; `controls = CarouselControls.Always` shows the buttons on a phone too.

examples.name: CarouselIntroduction
examples.title: An introduction that goes on by its own button
examples.description: An introduction that cannot be swiped: `swipeEnabled = false`, with the indicator and the buttons off too. The steps go on only with "Continue". Which step it is on is the screen's own state; the button adds one to it, and the carousel turns there.

examples.name: CarouselOnAFill
examples.title: On a fill
examples.description: A carousel on a fill that is not one of the theme's grounds. No colour was given: the fill says what colour is written on it. The dot of the slide on screen and the buttons are in that colour, and the other dots in a share of it.

examples.name: CarouselGallery
examples.title: A gallery that goes round by itself
examples.description:
Like a picture gallery: with `loop` the slides go round, and with `autoAdvanceMillis` the carousel turns by itself every six seconds. `placement = CarouselPlacement.Overlaid` puts the buttons and the dots over the slide, on the carousel's own fill (dark in the light theme, light in the dark one); they take no room.

The button beside the dots stops the turning and starts it again. While a slide is held, while the mouse is over the carousel and while the keyboard's focus is in it, the carousel waits by itself.

examples.name: CarouselNotes
examples.title: Slides of different heights
examples.description: The slides differ in height, and the carousel was given no height. The carousel is as tall as the slide on screen; on the way from one slide to another its height changes along with it, without a jump. The line below shows this: it moves down and up with the slide.

examples.name: CarouselOwnColors
examples.title: In its own colours
examples.description: In its own colours: `CarouselColors` paints the dots, the dots' track, the buttons and the scrim over the slide. Here the dots are in the colour of success, not the brand's; every colour not given is the theme's.

pages.title: Code Block
pages.summary:
Code set out to be read: in the theme's code type, a line to a line, each part of it in the colour of what it is, and ready to be copied. A usage example in a document, a file under review, a command and the difference between two versions are shown this way.

The block does not know the language it shows. What colours the code are the tokens its caller gives (`tokens`): which letters of the text are a keyword, which a string, which a comment. On this page the app's own reader of Kotlin gives them; code given no tokens is written in one colour.
features: **Two forms.** The form that takes `code` shows a text. The form that takes `lines` takes the lines one by one: each line carries its own tokens and what is said about it. `codeLines` gives the lines of a text; a screen starts from there and marks the lines it wants.

**Tokens.** There are eight kinds of token: plain text, comment, keyword, type, string, number, punctuation, and the names written before something (`@Composable`). Their colours come from the theme's roles; a comment is slanted as well. Where two tokens lie over the same letters, the one given later colours them.

**Header.** Over the code a header stands while there is something to say: `title`, mostly a file's name; `language`, the language's name; `icon`; what the screen puts at its start with `leading` and at its end with `trailing`. The copy button is at the header's end; when there is nothing else to say there is no header, and the button stands over the code, in a strip of its own.

**Copying and selecting.** The button copies all of the code, whatever part of it is on the screen. After a copy it shows a tick for two seconds and tells a screen reader too; `onCopy` reports whether the code got to the clipboard. The lines on the screen can be selected as well, by dragging a mouse or by a long press. `copyable = false` takes the button away, and `selectable = false` turns selection off.

**Line numbers.** `lineNumbers` writes each line's number before it; `firstLineNumber` gives the first line's number: a part taken out of a file starts where it started there. The numbers are not selected and not read to a screen reader.
**Scrolling sideways.** A line that does not fit the block is not broken: the code scrolls sideways and the line numbers stay where they are. A line of code that has lost its indent cannot be read.
**Lines that go on under themselves.** With `softWrap` a long line goes on under itself: for a narrow screen where the words matter more than the columns.

**Height.** In a block given a height the code scrolls in that height, under a header that stays, and only the lines on the screen are built. A block given no height is, in a page that scrolls, as tall as its lines where it has no more than 300; with longer code it is no taller than the window, and scrolls in it.

**Scroll bars.** Where it scrolls the block has a bar of its own: at its side, and along its foot for code that scrolls sideways. For a reader with a pointer it is there while there is something to scroll, and a mouse drags it; under a finger it shows only while the code moves.

**Keyboard.** Where there is a pointer and something to scroll, the lines are a stop for Tab. With the focus there the arrow keys scroll by a line and, sideways, by a step; Page Up and Page Down by a screen; Home and End go to the first line and to the last.

**Marks on lines.** A line's mark (`CodeMark`) draws the soft fill of its tone's role behind the line and a bar in the role's colour down its left edge; with a `message`, the message stands under the line. There are six tones: `Primary`, `Info`, `Success`, `Warning`, `Danger` and `Neutral`. All of a marked line is written in the one colour the theme pairs with that fill.
**The code's type.** `textStyle` sets the code in another style than the theme's `code`: smaller on a phone's page.
**Reading direction.** Code is written from left to right in every language; the header and a mark's message follow the app's direction.

**Colour.** On the theme's own grounds each kind of token has a colour of its own. On one of the theme's role colours all of the code is written in the one colour that reads there. A colour given with `CodeBlockColors` is used, and one that is not stays the theme's.

**Platform.** Lines of code stand close: nothing in them is pressed. A line of the theme's code type is 20dp tall; Android leaves 2dp over and under its words, iOS 1dp, and the desktop and the web none. The corners are the card's.
**Screen reader.** The code is read a line at a time; the line numbers are passed over. A mark's message is read after its line, as one thing.

**Automation.** With `tagKey` the block is `CodeBlock_<tagKey>`, a line of it `CodeBlock_<tagKey>.Line_<number>`, the message under a line `CodeBlock_<tagKey>.Note_<number>`, the window a keyboard scrolls `CodeBlock_<tagKey>.Lines_window`, and the button that copies `CodeBlock_<tagKey>.Button_copy`. A copy is reported as `copy`, with whether it got to the clipboard. Nothing of the code is reported.
api: com.pantrixui.components.data.codeblock.PantrixCodeBlock(String, Modifier, List<CodeToken>, String?, String?, ImageVector?, Boolean, Int, Boolean, Boolean, Boolean, ((copied: Boolean) -> Unit)?, (@Composable () -> Unit)?, CodeBlockStyle?, CodeBlockColors?, String?, (@Composable RowScope.() -> Unit)?, TextStyle?)

com.pantrixui.components.data.codeblock.PantrixCodeBlock(List<CodeLine>, Modifier, String?, String?, ImageVector?, Boolean, Int, Boolean, Boolean, Boolean, ((copied: Boolean) -> Unit)?, (@Composable () -> Unit)?, CodeBlockStyle?, CodeBlockColors?, String?, (@Composable RowScope.() -> Unit)?, TextStyle?)

examples.name: CodeBlockSnippet
examples.title: A snippet of code
examples.description:
At its plainest: a text of code, the tokens that colour it, and the language's name. The block knows no language; `tokens` says what is a keyword, what a string and what a comment. Here the app's own reader of Kotlin gives them.

Keywords are in the colour of the theme's `primary` role, types in `info`, strings in `success`, numbers in `warning`, and names that start with `@` in `danger`; a comment is written in `textSecondary`, and slanted. The button in the header copies all of the code and shows a tick for two seconds.

examples.name: CodeBlockFile

A file: `title` gives its name, `icon` the icon before it, `lineNumbers` the line numbers. The block was given a height: the code scrolls in it, under a header that stays, and only the lines on the screen are built.

A line that does not fit is not broken. Scroll the code sideways: the line numbers stay where they are, and the lines pass under them. On a screen with a pointer both of the block's scroll bars show, and a mouse drags them; once Tab has come to the lines, the arrow keys scroll the code.

examples.name: CodeBlockWrapped
examples.title: Lines that go on under themselves
examples.description:
A long command. With `softWrap` the line goes on under itself where it does not fit the block, and the block does not scroll sideways; without it the command is one line, and the code scrolls sideways. Turn the switch and compare the two.

A line that goes on under itself loses its indent: `softWrap` suits a command or a line of a log, not code whose indent carries meaning.

examples.name: CodeBlockCopy
examples.title: Copying, and the end of the header
examples.description:
`onCopy` is called after the button was pressed, with whether the code got to the clipboard: a screen that says so in its own way listens here. `trailing` puts something of the screen's own at the end of the header, before the button that copies: here, the number of lines.

In the second block `copyable` and `selectable` are off and nothing else stands in the header: it has no header, and its code is not selected.
examples.code:
val report = LocalExampleEvents.current
PantrixCodeBlock(
    code = DEPENDENCIES,
    title = "build.gradle.kts",
    onCopy = { copied -> report(if (copied) "Code copied to the clipboard" else "The code could not be copied") },
    trailing = { PantrixText(text = "4 lines", style = PantrixTheme.typography.caption) },
    tagKey = "copied"
)
PantrixCodeBlock(code = DEPENDENCIES, selectable = false, copyable = false, tagKey = "plain")

private val DEPENDENCIES =
    """
    dependencies {
        implementation("com.pantrixui:foundation:0.1.0")
        implementation("com.pantrixui:components:0.1.0")
    }
    """.trimIndent()

appNames.name: LocalExampleEvents
appNames.description: Where an example tells its card what happens in it: a button pressed, a row chosen, a dialog closed. The card writes the last thing told under the example, on its "Last event" line.

examples.title: Tabs in the header
examples.description:
`leading` puts the screen's own thing at the header's start, before the icon and the title: here two tabs that choose between two forms of the same line, as a documentation's setup step does. They are written in the header's text colour.

`textStyle` sets the code in another style than the theme's `code`: here at the size of `caption`, in the code's family, for a narrow column. The `style`'s `headerLineWidth` is the width of the line under the header; `headerHorizontalPadding` keeps what the header holds nearer the side than the lines are.

examples.name: CodeBlockInACard
examples.title: In a card, in colours of its own
examples.description:
The block has a fill and an edge of its own: the fill is the theme's `surface`, the edge the theme's `divider`. In a card that has both, `colors` makes both transparent. A colour that is given is used, and one that is not stays the theme's.

`style` changes the block's geometry; only the fields it is given change. Here `horizontalPadding` is zero, so that the lines start where the card's own padding ends.

examples.name: CodeBlockHandTokens
examples.title: Tokens written by hand
examples.description: The block carries no reader of a language; the app gives the tokens. For a short text with no reader the tokens can be written by hand: each `CodeToken` is what a run of the line is (`CodeTokenKind`), from `start` up to `end`. Here a shell command's lines are built as `CodeLine`s directly: the comment `Comment`, the command `Keyword`, the task `StringLiteral`, the option `Type`.

pages.title: Data Table
pages.summary:
A table that shows records row by row and their values column by column: orders, users, invoices. Its header orders the rows, its boxes choose them, its rows open, its columns stay in place or scroll sideways; on a narrow screen it becomes a list of records.

The rows are the caller's. The table shows the rows given with `rows` in the order they are given, and changes nothing by itself: a press on a header reports the order that is asked for with `onSortChange`, a press on a box the rows to be chosen with `onSelectionChange`, a press on a chevron the rows to be open with `onExpandedChange`. One table thus shows both the rows a screen holds and orders itself, and the rows a server orders and sends a page at a time.
features: **Columns.** A column is described with a `DataTableColumn`: its key (`key`), its header (`header`) and what a row shows in that column (`cell`). A column of plain text is written shortly with `DataTableColumn.text`: a long text is cut with an ellipsis. A cell can be any content: a badge, a button, an avatar.

**Width.** A column given a `width` is that wide. Those given none share what is left by their `weight`, and are no narrower than `minWidth` or, where that is not given either, the style's `columnMinWidth`. `alignment` sets the header and the values at one side of the column: numbers stand at its end, so that their digits line up.

**Scrolling sideways.** Where the columns do not fit the table even at their least widths, the table scrolls sideways: by a drag of a finger, by the wheel, by the bar under the rows where there is a pointer, and by the keyboard: the cell that takes the focus is brought into view.

**Pinned columns.** `pin = DataTablePin.Start` keeps a column at the table's start, `DataTablePin.End` at its end: the others scroll under them. Where more than half of a table that scrolls would stay in place, the pinned columns scroll with the others, and only the boxes stay.

**Sorting.** The header of a column with `sortable = true`, or one given a `comparator`, is a button. The first press orders smallest first, the second largest first, and the third takes the order away. An arrow that points up means the smallest comes first. `multiSort = true` adds the pressed column to the order: the rows are put in the first column's order, and the next settles the ones it holds equal; a header shows its column's place in the order. Ordering the rows is the caller's work: `sort.comparator(columns)` makes one comparator out of the columns' own. A column of text takes a `textOrder` to be ordered by the language's alphabet: `rememberTextOrder()` gives the one of the theme's language.

**Selection.** A table given `onSelectionChange` has a box in every row; the keys of the chosen rows are given with `selected`. The box in the header chooses every row that is shown or lets them all go, and leaves what was chosen on other pages alone; it shows a dash while some are chosen. `DataTableSelection.Single` puts radio buttons in the boxes' place: choosing a row lets the other go.

**Rows that open.** A table given `rowDetail` and `onExpandedChange` has a chevron in every row: a press opens the row's detail under it, as wide as the table. The keys of the open rows are given with `expanded`. The chevron stands at the row's end and stays there while the columns scroll; `DataTableStyle(expander = DataTableExpander.Start)` puts it at the start.
**Rows that are pressed.** `onRowClick` makes every row a button as wide as the table.

**Closed rows.** `rowEnabled` closes a row: it is drawn fainter, cannot be chosen or pressed, and the box in the header neither chooses it nor lets it go. Its chevron opens it all the same; closing the buttons in its cells is the caller's work.

**Tones.** `rowTone` lays a row on the soft fill of one of the theme's roles and turns its text to the colour paired with that fill; a column's `tone` paints its header. What the colour says should be written in the row in words too.

**Height.** A table told no height is as tall as its rows and builds them all: that is for a page of rows, in a page that scrolls, and its header scrolls with the page. A table told a height keeps its header in place, scrolls its rows under it and builds only the ones in view: it holds thousands of rows. A table whose header is to stay in place is told a height.

**State.** Where the rows and the columns are scrolled to and the widths the columns were dragged to are kept in a `DataTableState`. A screen that holds it itself, with `rememberDataTableState()`, reads the widths, keeps them, resets them (`columnWidths`) and scrolls to a column (`animateScrollToColumn`).

**Narrow.** A table of `DataTableLayout.Auto` is a list of records where its own width is narrower than the style's `compactWidth` (600dp): each row a block, each value with its column's name before it. The boxes, the chevrons and the order stay. `showInList = false` keeps a column out of the list; `listContent` draws a record its own way.
**Loading and empty.** `loading = true` puts skeleton rows in the rows' place, in the table's columns. A table without rows shows the theme's words, "No rows", or what is given with `empty`.
**Toolbar and footer.** `toolbar` stands over the header and `footer` under the rows, inside the table's edge: a title and what is done with the chosen rows; a `PantrixPagination`.

**Variants.** `DataTableVariant.Plain` draws a line between the rows, `Bordered` an edge around the table as well, and `Grid` a line between the columns too. `striped = true` lays every other row on a faint fill.

**Columns whose width changes.** The end of the header of a column with `resizable = true` is dragged with a pointer. The keyboard comes there with Tab after the column's name, and the arrow keys along the row make the column wider or narrower; a screen reader is told the width as a value that can be changed. On screens used with a finger there is no handle to drag.
**Choosing the columns.** Which columns are shown, and in which order, is the `columns` list itself: a screen that hides a column or moves one gives the table another list.

**The headers' type.** `headerTextStyle` is the type the headers are written in. The headers are written as they are given: a table that wants small capitals set apart gives the type and writes its headers in capitals.
**Colours.** `DataTableColors` paints the table's fill, its text, the header's band and its text, the stripe, the fill of a chosen row and the lines one by one; what is not given is the theme's.

**Keyboard.** Tab goes through the headers that sort, the boxes, the chevrons, the rows that are pressed and whatever the cells hold; the arrow keys move the focus to the nearest of them that way. A cell that holds nothing to press is no stop: this is a table to read and to act on, and not a grid to walk cell by cell. Where there is a pointer, the rows' window is a stop too while the table scrolls: there the arrow keys, Page Up, Page Down, Home and End scroll the table.

**Screen reader.** A header says that it is a header and how the rows are ordered by its column. Where `rowLabel` is given a row's box is read by the row's name: "Select Ada Lovelace". A cell says which row and column it is in.

**Automation.** A table given a `tagKey` is `DataTable_<tagKey>`, and its parts are named inside it: `Header_<column>`, `Row_<row>`, `Cell_<row>/<column>`, `Select_<row>`, `Toggle_<row>`, `Detail_<row>`. Presses are reported as a `DataTable` event: `sort`, `select`, `selectAll`, `expand`, `collapse`, `open`.

examples.name: DataTablePlain
examples.title: Rows and columns
examples.description:
At its plainest: the rows (`rows`) and the columns (`columns`). All four columns are plain text and are written with `DataTableColumn.text`; the items and the total stand at the end of their columns, so that their digits line up.

The columns are given no width: they share the table's width evenly. On a narrow screen, a phone held upright, the table becomes a list of records by itself: each order is a block, and each value has its column's name before it.
examples.code:
PantrixDataTable(
    rows = TABLE_ORDERS.take(5),
    columns = remember {
        listOf(
            DataTableColumn.text(key = "customer", header = "Customer") { it.customer },
            DataTableColumn.text(key = "city", header = "City") { it.city },
            DataTableColumn.text(key = "items", header = "Items", alignment = Alignment.End) { "${it.items}" },
            DataTableColumn.text(key = "total", header = "Total", alignment = Alignment.End) { "${it.total} ₺" }
        )
    },
    tagKey = "plain"
)

examples.name: DataTableSorted
examples.title: Sorting by a press on a header
examples.description:
The header of a column with `sortable = true` is a button. Press a header: the rows are put in that column's order, smallest first, and an arrow that points up appears beside the header. Press again: largest first. A third press takes the order away, and the rows are as they were given.

The order is the screen's state (`sort`); the table only reports the order that is asked for (`onSortChange`). Ordering the rows is the screen's work too: `sort.comparator(columns)` makes one comparator out of the columns' own. The columns of text are ordered by their text, without regard to case and in the order of the language's alphabet (`textOrder`, `rememberTextOrder()`): press Customer, and "İpek Güneş" stands between "Emre Koç" and "Kerem Aksoy"; without it the name, starting with "İ", would fall to the very end, after "Zeynep Demir". The items and the total are numbers and give comparators of their own: as texts, "10" would come before "9".

examples.name: DataTablePinned
examples.title: Pinned columns and scrolling sideways
examples.description:
Each of the seven columns is given a width, and together they are wider than the table: the table scrolls sideways. Drag it with a finger, turn the wheel sideways or, where there is a pointer, drag the bar under the rows.

The customer's column is pinned at the start and the button's at the end (`pin`): the others scroll under them, and a line appears at their edges while something is under them. On a phone held upright the pinned columns would take more than half the table: there they scroll with the others.

The ends of the City and Status headers are dragged with a pointer (`resizable`): the column grows wider or narrower, and the table keeps that width. With the keyboard: come to the header's end with Tab, and make the column wider or narrower with the right and left arrow keys. Go to the buttons with Tab: a button that takes the focus under a pinned column is scrolled into view.

The screen holds the table's state (`rememberDataTableState()`). "Scroll to Total" scrolls the columns until that column is in view (`animateScrollToColumn`); "Reset the widths" lets the dragged widths go (`columnWidths`).

The example is a table at every width (`DataTableLayout.Table`): it does not become a list on a narrow screen.

val report = LocalExampleEvents.current
val table = rememberDataTableState()
val scope = rememberCoroutineScope()
FlowRow(horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.sm)) {
    PantrixButton(
        text = "Scroll to Total",
        onClick = { scope.launch { table.animateScrollToColumn("total") } },
        variant = ButtonVariant.Outline,
        size = ButtonSize.Small,
        tagKey = "to_total"
    )
    PantrixButton(
        text = "Reset the widths",
        onClick = { table.columnWidths = emptyMap() },
        variant = ButtonVariant.Text,
        size = ButtonSize.Small,
        enabled = table.columnWidths.isNotEmpty(),
        tagKey = "reset_widths"
    )
}
PantrixDataTable(
    rows = TABLE_ORDERS.take(6),
    columns = remember(report) {
        listOf(
            DataTableColumn.text(key = "customer", header = "Customer", width = 160.dp, pin = DataTablePin.Start) {
                it.customer
            },
            DataTableColumn.text(key = "id", header = "Order", width = 110.dp) { "#${it.id}" },
            DataTableColumn.text(key = "city", header = "City", width = 140.dp, resizable = true) { it.city },
            DataTableColumn.text(key = "status", header = "Status", width = 160.dp, resizable = true) { it.status },
            DataTableColumn.text(key = "date", header = "Date", width = 130.dp) { it.date },
            DataTableColumn.text(key = "items", header = "Items", width = 100.dp, alignment = Alignment.End) {
                "${it.items}"
            },
            DataTableColumn.text(key = "total", header = "Total", width = 130.dp, alignment = Alignment.End) {
                "${it.total} ₺"
            },
            DataTableColumn(key = "open", header = "", width = 112.dp, pin = DataTablePin.End, showInList = false) {
                PantrixButton(
                    text = "Open",
                    onClick = { report("#${it.id} was opened") },
                    variant = ButtonVariant.Text,
                    size = ButtonSize.Small,
                    tagKey = "open_${it.id}"

            }

    },

    state = table,

)

examples.name: DataTablePaged
examples.title: Page by page, with a skeleton while it loads
examples.description:
A list that comes from a server a page at a time: the table knows only the rows of the page on screen. In its footer (`footer`) stand which orders are shown, in the theme's words (`PantrixTheme.strings.rowRange`), and a `PantrixPagination`.

Go to another page: until the rows come the table is loading (`loading`), and skeleton rows stand in the rows' place, in the table's columns; the header and the footer stay. The waiting is imitated here with a delay of half a second; "Keep it loading" holds the skeleton in place to look at.

The table is told a height (320dp): the header stays in place, the rows scroll under it, and only the ones in view are built. The last page has two orders; the table stays as tall, and its footer does not move.
examples.code:
var page by rememberSaveable { mutableIntStateOf(1) }
var loading by remember { mutableStateOf(false) }
var shown by rememberSaveable { mutableIntStateOf(1) }
var held by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf(false) }
PantrixSwitchButton(
    checked = held,
    onCheckedChange = { held = it },
    label = "Keep it loading",
    tagKey = "hold_loading"
)
// In place of a server: the page that was asked for comes half a second later.
LaunchedEffect(page) {
    if (page != shown) {
        loading = true
        delay(LOAD_MILLIS.milliseconds)
        shown = page
        loading = false
    }
}
val first = (shown - 1) * PAGE_SIZE
val rows = TABLE_ORDERS.drop(first).take(PAGE_SIZE)
PantrixDataTable(
    rows = rows,
    columns = remember { orderColumns(sortable = false) },
    modifier = Modifier.height(320.dp),
    rowKey = { it.id },
    loading = loading || held,
    loadingRows = PAGE_SIZE,
    footer = {
        FlowRow(
            modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(),
            horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.SpaceBetween,
            itemVerticalAlignment = Alignment.CenterVertically
        ) {
            PantrixText(
                text = PantrixTheme.strings.rowRange(first + 1, first + rows.size, TABLE_ORDERS.size),
                color = PantrixTheme.colors.textSecondary,
                tagKey = "range"
            )
            PantrixPagination(
                page = page,
                pageCount = (TABLE_ORDERS.size + PAGE_SIZE - 1) / PAGE_SIZE,
                onPageChange = { page = it },
                tagKey = "pages"
            )
        }
    },
    variant = DataTableVariant.Bordered,
    tagKey = "paged"
)

examples.name: DataTableVariants
examples.title: Variants, stripes and colours
examples.description:
Three variants of one table. `Plain` draws a line between the rows and nothing around them: for a table inside a card. `Bordered` draws an edge around the table, in the style's shape. `Grid` draws a line between the columns as well: for a dense report the eye reads down as much as along.

)

)

examples.name: DataTableAsList

examples.name: DataTableTones
examples.title: Tones and closed rows
examples.description:
`rowTone` lays a row on the soft fill of one of the theme's roles: cancelled orders are in the danger tone and the ones being prepared in the warning tone, and the row's text turns to the colour the theme pairs with that fill. The tone is over the stripe; the fill of a chosen row comes over the tone too. What the colour says, the Status column says in words: a colour says nothing to someone who cannot see it.

A column's `tone` paints its header: the Total header is in the info tone.

Delivered orders are closed (`rowEnabled`): they are drawn fainter, their boxes cannot be pressed, and the box in the header neither chooses them nor lets them go. Press the box in the header: only the open rows are chosen.

val report = LocalExampleEvents.current
var chosen by remember { mutableStateOf(emptySet<String>()) }

    rows = TABLE_ORDERS.take(7),
    columns = remember { orderColumns(sortable = false, totalTone = DataTableTone.Info) },
    rowKey = { it.id },
    rowLabel = { it.customer },
    rowEnabled = {
        when (it.status) {
            "Delivered" -> false
            else -> true
        }
    },
    rowTone = {
        when (it.status) {
            "Cancelled" -> DataTableTone.Danger
            "Preparing" -> DataTableTone.Warning
            else -> null
        }
    },
    selected = chosen,
    onSelectionChange = { asked ->
        chosen = asked
        report("Rows selected: ${asked.size}")
    },
    variant = DataTableVariant.Bordered,
    striped = true,
    tagKey = "tones"
)

examples.name: DataTableProjects
examples.title: Projects: rich cells and closed rows
examples.description:
A product's projects: every cell is more than plain text. The project column has a tile with a letter, a name and a package name in monospace; the platforms are coloured dots; sampling and retention are a label each; under the date stands its age. A cell takes any content: a `DataTableColumn`'s `cell` is a composable.

The headers are small capitals set apart: the type is given with `headerTextStyle`, and the headers themselves are written in capitals (the table does not turn a header to capitals by itself: "ı" and "i" do not grow alike in every language). The band behind the header is `DataTableColors.headerContainer`.

The two inactive projects are closed (`rowEnabled`): everything the row shows is drawn fainter. A project without an API key has a warning mark beside its count; what the colour says, its name says too.

On a narrow screen the table becomes a list of records, and each project is drawn with the card given with `listContent`: the name and the status on top, the platforms and the keys under them, the labels and the date at the foot.

examples.name: DataTableCrashGroups
examples.title: Crash groups: sorting and a row's detail
examples.description:
An app's crash groups: the one seen most on top. The count, users and last seen columns sort; the arrow in the header points down for largest first and up for smallest first. The largest value of each column is written bold.

Press the chevron at the row's end: the crash's detail opens under the row, as wide as the table. The chevron stands at the row's end and stays there while the columns scroll sideways; a style says so where it is to stand at the start (`DataTableStyle(expander = DataTableExpander.Start)`). In the detail the stack frames are in a monospace block, with the message and the devices the crash is seen on most beside them: side by side where there is room, one under the other where there is not.

The title over the table and the "how many of how many" note are in the toolbar (`toolbar`). On a narrow screen each group is a card: the exception's name and place, the severity and status labels under them, and the counts at the foot.
