examples.name: DataTableRequests
examples.title: Requests: a table or cards
examples.description:
Captured network requests. The status code stands in its colour, the method in a label and the address in monospace; a long address shows its start and its end, and is cut in the middle. The duration column has a bar beside the value: a slow request is orange and one that returned an error red, and a slow one has "SLOW" written beside its address.

The "Table" and "Cards" buttons in the toolbar choose the layout (`layout`): the table is a table at every width and scrolls sideways where it does not fit; the cards are a list of records at every width. In a narrow window the example opens as cards.

As cards, each request is drawn by `listContent`: on top the status code, the method and the outcome; under them the address; under that the size, the network and the time, with the duration at the end; and at the foot a bar of the duration as wide as the record. The edge around the records, the line between them, the chevron at a record's end and the detail it opens are the table's: both layouts show the same `rowDetail`, and a request that is open in one is open in the other.

The requests sort by status, duration, size and time: a press on a header puts them in that column's order, another turns the order round, and a third takes it away. As cards they have no header; the names of the columns that sort stand in the strip over the records, and are the same buttons. That is the table's doing: the example gives only `sort`, `onSortChange` and the columns' `comparator`. Each column compares by the number behind its cell and not by the text in it: as texts, "412 KB" would come before "84.1 KB". The example opens with the newest request on top.

In the strip the arrow stands only beside the name of the column the records are ordered by. Where the names do not fit, the strip scrolls sideways, fades towards the end it goes on past, and brings the name of that column into view; on a narrow phone four names fit side by side. The source column sorts too, but in the table alone: the cards do not show the source, and with `showInList = false` its name does not stand in the strip.

The chevron at the end of a row or of a record opens the request's identifiers and the whole address; the address can be selected and copied. Opening a request closes the one that was open: with `expansion = DataTableExpansion.Single` one row is open at a time. Told nothing, the table keeps every row it opens.

pages.title: JSON View
pages.summary:
A JSON text set out to be read: one value to a line, each level set in from the one that holds it, each kind of value in a colour of its own. Objects and arrays fold away behind their first lines. A server's response, a document of settings, a long export are read this way.

What an open document shows is the document: the names and the strings in their quotes, the brackets and the commas in their places, as a pretty-printer writes them. A number is shown as the text wrote it, to its last digit. An object or an array that is folded is one line: an ellipsis between its brackets and, after them, how many things it holds.

The view keeps what is open by itself: at first as much as `expandedDepth` says, and from then on what its reader folds and unfolds, which stays so while the text changes under it. A screen that opens the document from a button of its own, or keeps what was open somewhere, holds that state itself: with the form that takes `expanded`.
features: **Folding.** A line that folds is a button with a chevron before it, which points down while the line is open and forward while it is folded. A press, Enter and the space bar fold and unfold the line.

**Guides.** A thin line runs down from every open object and array, under its chevron, past everything it holds: it tells one level from the next where the indent is narrow. Its width is `JsonViewStyle.guideWidth` and its colour `JsonViewColors.guide`; a width of zero draws none.

**Keyboard.** The document is one stop for Tab: the focus comes to the line it was on last, and the arrows walk from there. The down and up arrows go through the lines a value starts on, one after another, and Home and End go to the first line and the last. The right arrow unfolds a folded line and, on an open one, goes in to the first thing it holds; the left arrow folds an open line and, on any other, goes out to the line that opened what holds it. The button that copies is the next stop for Tab.

**Opening.** `expandedDepth` says how many levels are open at first: `1` opens the text's own value and leaves what is in it folded, and `2` opens those too. Without it every level is open. Giving another depth starts the view again from it.

**The screen's state.** In the form that takes `expanded` the paths of the objects and arrays that are open are the screen's state: when a line is pressed the new set that is to be open is reported with `onExpandedChange`, and the view changes nothing by itself.

**Paths.** A path is a JSON Pointer (RFC 6901): the text's own value is the empty string, its member `user` is `/user`, and the first of that one's `tags` is `/user/tags/0`. `jsonViewPaths` gives the paths that open a document down to a depth.

**Search.** `search` marks what it looks for in the names and the values, in capitals or in small letters; a folded value that holds some of it is marked whole. Where the view scrolls, it brings the first of what was found on the screen. A view that keeps what is open by itself also opens the values that hold some of it; what its reader folds stays folded. In the form that takes `expanded`, opening is the screen's to do: `jsonViewSearchPaths` gives the paths to open. The fill of a mark is `JsonViewColors.match`.

**Line numbers.** `lineNumbers` writes each line's number before it: the number the line has while the whole document is open. A folded value keeps the number of the line it opens with, and the line after it goes on from where the folded lines would have ended. The numbers are not selected, and a screen reader passes them over.
**Width.** The view fills the width it is given, and a line too long for it goes on under itself. However deep a line is, it is set in by no more than half the view's width.

**Lines that do not wrap.** `softWrap = false` keeps every value on one line: the view keeps its width, and the document scrolls sideways. A line that does not wrap is not held back at half the width: it is set in by its whole indent.

**Height.** In a view given a height the document scrolls inside it, and only the lines on the screen are built: that is how a document of thousands of lines is shown. A view given none, in a page that scrolls, is as tall as the lines it shows where the document, all open, has no more than 300; with a longer document it is no taller than the window, and scrolls in it.

**Scroll bars.** Where it scrolls, the view has a scroll bar of its own: at its side, and at its foot too where the document scrolls sideways. A bar shows how much of the document is on the screen, and where in it that is. Where the reader has a pointer, on desktop and in a desktop's browser, it is there while there is something to scroll, and a mouse can drag it; under a finger it shows only while the document moves.

**Copying and selecting.** The button in the view's top right corner copies the whole document as an open view writes it: a value to a line and two spaces a level, whatever is folded on the screen. After a copy it shows a tick for two seconds, and says so to a screen reader too; `onCopy` reports whether the document got to the clipboard. The lines on the screen can be selected too, by a mouse drawn over them or a long press, and copied by the system's own means: what is copied so is what the lines show. `copyable = false` takes the button away, and `selectable = false` turns selecting off.
**Reading direction.** A document is written from left to right in every language, as code is.
**A text that is not JSON.** It is shown as it is; the line over it says where the reading stopped, by line and column, in the theme's language.

**Colour.** On the theme's own grounds each kind of value has a colour of its own, from the theme's roles: a number is told from a string that holds digits before its quotes are read. On one of the theme's role colours the whole document is written in the one colour that reads there. A colour given with `JsonViewColors` is used, and one that is not stays the theme's.

**Platform.** Under a finger, on Android, on iOS and on the web, a line has 4dp over and under its words, which makes it 28dp tall in the theme's code type; on desktop it has 2dp, for a pointer. A level is set in by 16dp on desktop and the web, and by 12dp on a phone. The corners are the card's.

**Screen reader.** On a line that folds a screen reader is offered what a press does and is told whether the line is open. The line says its name, how many things it holds if it is folded, and how deep it is, the last two in the theme's words: "items, Items: 2, Level 2". The text's own value has no name: open, it says "Level 1" alone. The other lines are read as they are written; the line that closes an open value is passed over.

**Automation.** With `tagKey` the view is `JsonView_<tagKey>` and a line in it `JsonView_<tagKey>.Row_<path>`: the path is as it is written (`Row_/user/tags/0`), and the text's own value is `Row_root`. The line that closes an open value is `JsonView_<tagKey>.End_<path>`, the line over a text that is not JSON `JsonView_<tagKey>.Note_fault`, and the button that copies `JsonView_<tagKey>.Button_copy`. A press is reported as `expand` or `collapse`, with the line's level; a copy as `copy`, with whether it got to the clipboard. Nothing of the document is reported.

examples.name: JsonViewResponse
examples.title: A response
examples.description:
Its plainest form: a JSON text and an automation key. The view sets the text out to be read: one value to a line, each level set in from the one that holds it. The names and the strings keep their quotes, and the brackets and the commas their places: what an open document shows is the document. Numbers are as the text wrote them, and `249.90` keeps its last zero.

Each kind of value is in a colour of its own: strings, numbers, and `true`, `false` and `null`. The first line of an object or an array is a button: press the `"items"` line and the array folds onto one line, which says how many things it holds. Press it again and it opens.

examples.name: JsonViewDepth
examples.title: How much is open at first
examples.description:
`expandedDepth` says how many levels of the document are open at first. `1` opens the text's own value and leaves everything in it folded; `2` opens those too; without it every level is open.

The view keeps what is open by itself: what you fold or unfold by pressing a line stays so. Given another depth, the view starts again from it: press the `"customer"` line, then choose another depth.

examples.name: JsonViewLongDocument
examples.title: A long document in a height it is given
examples.description:
A document of a few hundred lines, in a room 280dp tall. The height was given to the view's `modifier`: the document scrolls inside that height, and only the lines on the screen are built. A document of thousands of lines is shown this way too.

Given no height, in a page that scrolls as this one does, the view would take the window's height with this document of more than 300 lines, and scroll in it. With a document of no more than 300 lines it would be as tall as all its lines: it is so in the other examples that are given no height. The text is read again only when it changes; here it is built once and kept with `remember`.

examples.name: JsonViewSearch
examples.title: Search
examples.description:
`search` finds what it looks for in the names and the values, in capitals or in small letters, and does three things: it marks what it finds, opens the values that hold it, and brings the first of it on the screen where the view scrolls.

The document is an array of forty-eight orders, in a room 240dp tall, with its first level alone open: each order is folded onto one line. Type `returned` into the field: the four orders that were returned open, the word is marked in all four, and the view scrolls to the first of them, the twelfth order. Empty the field: the marks go, and the orders the search opened fold again.
examples.code:
val query = rememberTextFieldState()
val orders = remember { orderExport(count = 48) }
PantrixTextField(
    state = query,
    modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(),
    placeholder = "Search the orders",
    showClearButton = true,
    contentDescription = "Search the orders",
    tagKey = "order_search"
)
PantrixJsonView(
    json = orders,
    modifier = Modifier.height(240.dp),
    expandedDepth = 1,
    search = query.text.toString(),
    tagKey = "orders"
)

private fun orderExport(count: Int): String =
    (1..count).joinToString(separator = ",", prefix = "[", postfix = "]") { n ->
        val status = if (n % 12 == 0) "returned" else "shipped"
        """{"id": ${4800 + n}, "status": "$status", "total": ${30 + n * 4}.50}"""
    }

examples.name: JsonViewLineNumbers
examples.title: Line numbers, and lines that do not wrap
examples.description:
`lineNumbers` writes each line's number before it: the number the line has while the whole document is open. Press the `"request"` line: the folded value keeps the number of the line it opens with, 4, and the line after it goes on from 9.

The `"signature"` value is too long for the card. At first its line goes on under itself, and carries one number. Turn the switch off: `softWrap = false` keeps every value on one line, the view keeps its width, and the document scrolls sideways.

examples.name: JsonViewCopy
examples.title: Copying and selecting
examples.description:
The button in the view's top right corner copies the whole document: what is folded on the screen too, as an open view writes it, a value to a line and two spaces a level. After a copy the button shows a tick for two seconds.

`onCopy` reports whether the document got to the clipboard: here it is written on the card's "Last event" line. Where the system itself shows what was copied, on Android 13 and later, a screen that tells its user says so only when nothing was copied: `rememberPantrixClipboard().traits.announcedBySystem` is true there.

In the upper view the lines on the screen can be selected too, by a mouse drawn over them or a long press, and copied by the system's own means. The lower view is the same document: `copyable = false` takes the button away, and `selectable = false` turns selecting off.

appNames.name: LocalExampleEvents
appNames.description: Where an example tells its card what happens in it: a button pressed, a row chosen, a dialog closed. The card writes the last thing told under the example, on its "Last event" line.

examples.name: JsonViewControlled
examples.title: From the screen's own buttons
examples.description:
In the form that takes `expanded` the screen holds what is open, as it does an accordion's sections: the view is given the paths of the objects and arrays that are open, and when a line is pressed the new set that is to be open is reported with `onExpandedChange`. The view changes nothing by itself.

The state was made with `jsonViewPaths(json, depth = 1)`: the text's own value alone is open. "Open all" puts all the document's paths there, and "Close all" empties the set: nothing is left open, and the document comes down to one line. Each change is written on the card's "Last event" line, with how many paths are open.

A path is a JSON Pointer: the text's own value is the empty string, its member `notifications` is `/notifications`, and the first of `shortcuts` is `/shortcuts/0`.

appNames.name: LocalExampleEvents
appNames.description: Where an example tells its card what happens in it: a button pressed, a row chosen, a dialog closed. The card writes the last thing told under the example, on its "Last event" line.

examples.name: JsonViewSearchControlled
examples.title: Search, with the screen's own state
examples.description:
In the form that takes `expanded` a search only marks; opening what it finds is the screen's to do. `jsonViewSearchPaths` gives the paths of the values that hold some of what is looked for, and the screen adds them to its own set.

Type `ctrl` into the field: the `shortcuts` array and the two objects in it open, and `Ctrl` is marked in both. While the search is there these lines do not fold: the search's paths are added to the set again each time. Empty the field: what is open is the screen's set alone again.

examples.name: JsonViewNotJson
examples.title: A text that is not JSON
examples.description:
A text with a comma left after its last member: it is not JSON. The view does not keep back a text it could not read: it shows it as it is, line by line. The line over it says, in the theme's language, where the reading stopped: a line and a column, both counted from one.

Here the reading stops at the first character of the fourth line: after the comma a name is expected, and the closing bracket comes.

examples.name: JsonViewInACard
examples.title: In a card, in colours of its own
examples.description:
The view has a fill and an edge of its own: the fill is the theme's `surface`, and the edge the theme's `divider`. In a card that has both, `colors` makes the two transparent. A colour that is given is used, and one that is not stays the theme's: the names are the theme's `textPrimary`, and the brackets and the commas its `textSecondary`; strings are in the colour of the `success` role, numbers in that of `warning`, and `true`, `false` and `null` in that of `primary`.

`style` changes the view's geometry; only the fields that are given change. Here `horizontalPadding` is zero, so that the lines start where the card's padding ends, and each level is set in by 24dp: `indent`.

pages.title: List Item
pages.summary: A row of a list: a title, what leads it and what ends it, and a line or two under it. A row of an inbox, of settings or of a search's results.
features: **Lines.** `headline` is the row's name; `supportingText` a line or two under it, smaller and quieter; `overline` a short line over it; `trailingText` a short text at the end of the title's line, on its baseline: a time, a count, a setting's value. The supporting text is cut at `supportingMaxLines` lines, two by default.

**What leads and ends it.** `leading` leads the row (an icon, an avatar, a picture) and `trailing` ends it (a badge, a tag, a switch). Both are given the row's quiet colour. `chevron` puts a chevron at the row's end, which says it leads on to another screen; it turns round where the layout is read from the right, and is not read out.

**Pressing and choosing.** A row given `onClick` is one target, at least as tall as the platform's touch target, and shows the press, a faint fill under a pointer and the focus ring inside its own edges. `selected` fills the row in the primary role's container colour and tells a screen reader it is selected.
**One node.** A screen reader hears the row as a whole: the overline, the title, the trailing text, the supporting text. A switch or a button at its end stays a node of its own.
**The line.** `divider` draws a line under the row: `Full` from one side to the other, `Inset` from where the text starts, as iOS's lists have it.

**Platform.** Material 3's rows on Android (56, 72, 88dp), iOS's on iOS (44, 60, 76), denser rows on the desktop and the web (36/52/68 and 40/56/72). The title is set in the body type on a phone and in the label type on the desktop and the web; `headlineStyle`, `supportingTextStyle` and `trailingTextStyle` change them.

examples.name: ListItemInbox
examples.title: An inbox
examples.description: An inbox: who wrote, when, and about what. A press on a row chooses it; the chosen row is filled. The lines are drawn from where the text starts, and leave the column of avatars whole.

examples.name: ListItemSettings
examples.title: Settings
examples.description: Settings: the rows that lead on to another screen have their values and a chevron at their end. The notifications' row is not pressed; the switch at its end is a control of its own. A row that is turned off takes no press and is written faintly.

var notify by remember { mutableStateOf(true) }
Column {
    PantrixListItem(
        headline = "Downloads",
        trailingText = "Wi-Fi only",
        leading = { PantrixIcon(PantrixIcons.Download, contentDescription = null) },
        chevron = true,

        divider = ListItemDivider.Full,
        tagKey = "downloads"
    )
    PantrixListItem(
        headline = "Notifications",
        supportingText = "When a new message comes",
        leading = { PantrixIcon(PantrixIcons.Inbox, contentDescription = null) },
        trailing = {
            PantrixSwitchButton(
                checked = notify,
                onCheckedChange = { notify = it },
                contentDescription = "Notifications",
                tagKey = "notify"
            )
        },
        divider = ListItemDivider.Full,
        tagKey = "notifications"
    )
    PantrixListItem(
        headline = "Backup",
        supportingText = "Not in your plan",
        leading = { PantrixIcon(PantrixIcons.Upload, contentDescription = null) },
        chevron = true,
        onClick = {},
        enabled = false,
        tagKey = "backup"
    )
}

examples.name: ListItemThreeLines
examples.title: Three lines
examples.description: Three lines, read and not pressed: the date over it, up to two lines of supporting text under it, a tag at its end. In a row of three lines what leads and ends it stands at its top.
examples.code:
Column {
    PantrixListItem(
        headline = "Order 1042",
        overline = "28 October",
        supportingText = "Two books and a notebook. Shipped, and expected to arrive tomorrow.",
        trailing = { PantrixTag(text = "On its way", tone = TagTone.Info) },
        divider = ListItemDivider.Full,
        tagKey = "order_1042"
    )
    PantrixListItem(
        headline = "Order 1039",
        overline = "21 October",
        supportingText = "A pair of headphones.",
        trailing = { PantrixTag(text = "Delivered", tone = TagTone.Success) },
        tagKey = "order_1039"
    )
}

examples.name: ListItemFound
examples.title: What a search found
examples.description: A search's results: the word searched for is set in bold in the title (the overload that takes an `AnnotatedString`), and the supporting text says where it was found.

examples.name: ListItemOwn
examples.title: A style and colours of its own
examples.description: A style and colours of its own: denser rows (`ListItemStyle`), the title in the theme's `callout` role, the selected row in a success colour (`ListItemColors`), the supporting text in the `footnote` type (`supportingTextStyle`), the price in the code type (`trailingTextStyle`).
examples.code:
val success = PantrixTheme.colors.success
var chosen by remember { mutableStateOf(0) }
Column {
    listOf("Weekly" to "29 ₺", "Monthly" to "99 ₺", "Yearly" to "990 ₺").forEachIndexed { index, (plan, price) ->
        PantrixListItem(
            headline = plan,
            supportingText = if (index == 2) "Two months on us" else null,
            trailingText = price,
            selected = chosen == index,
            onClick = { chosen = index },
            style = ListItemStyle(oneLineHeight = 40.dp, twoLineHeight = 52.dp, headlineRole = TypeRole.Callout),
            colors = ListItemColors(selectedContainer = success.container, selectedContent = success.onContainer),
            supportingTextStyle = PantrixTheme.typography.footnote,
            trailingTextStyle = PantrixTheme.typography.code,
            tagKey = "plan_$index"
        )
    }
}

pages.title: Pagination
pages.summary:
The row that moves between the pages of a long list or a table: previous, the pages by their numbers, and next. It stands under the results of a search, a table of orders or an archive.

Which page is on screen is the screen's state: the row is given the number of the page on screen (`page`, counted from one) and how many pages there are (`pageCount`); when a page is asked for, its number is reported through `onPageChange`. The row changes nothing by itself: it shows the page that was asked for once `page` says so.

The numbers stay as long as they fit in the row. In a place too narrow for them the row shows fewer numbers first; where no row of numbers fits, on a phone held upright or in a table's narrow foot, it is laid out as previous, "Page 3 of 10" and next; with its numbers again once it has the room.

In a table's foot its two companions stand beside it: `PantrixPageSize` chooses how many rows a page shows, and `PantrixPageJump` goes to the page whose number is typed.
features: **Numbers and gaps.** The first and the last `boundaryCount` pages are shown, and `siblingCount` pages on each side of the page on screen; those between them fold into a gap of three dots. Each is one unless given. A gap stands for two pages at the least: where a single page is left in between, that page itself is shown. Once there are enough pages to fold, the row has as many items whichever page is on screen: near an end, more pages stand on that side.

**In a narrow place.** A row too narrow for its numbers folds step by step: first it shows fewer pages beside the page on screen, as many as fit; if that does not fit either, fewer pages at its ends, down to one. Where no row of numbers fits it is laid out as previous, "Page 3 of 10" and next. The room is asked for the page on which the row is widest: the row folds the same way on every page, and its layout does not change as the page moves. How it is laid out is decided by the width left to the row, not by the window. `PaginationLayout.Compact` asks for the short row at every width. In a place narrower even than its buttons the short row is drawn smaller: its buttons are not cut.

**First and last page.** `firstAndLast = true` puts one more button outside previous and outside next: one goes to the first page, the other to the last. On the first page the two buttons at the start cannot be pressed, nor the two at the end on the last page. Four buttons leave less room for the numbers.
**The page on screen.** It is told by its fill and is no button: a press on it reports nothing.

**The ends.** Previous cannot be pressed on the first page, nor next on the last. A `page` outside the pages is taken as the nearest page. A `pageCount` under one is taken as one: a list with nothing in it has one page, an empty one, and the row's arrows cannot be pressed.

**A row that cannot be pressed.** `enabled = false` turns the whole row off: no part of it can be pressed, and the row is drawn in the theme's disabled colours. If the row is turned off while a keyboard's focus is on one of its parts, the focus stays there; when the row is turned on again, the keyboard goes on from where it was.

**Keyboard.** The numbers and the arrows are each a stop for Tab; Enter and Space press them. The page on screen is a stop too, and keeps the focus a keyboard put on it: on a page opened by the keyboard the focus stays where it is. When the row comes to one of its ends, the page on screen takes the focus of the button that can no longer be pressed; in the short row the button on the other side takes it.

**Sizes.** `PaginationStyle.itemSize` is the size of a number, of previous and of next: 40dp on Android, 36dp on iOS, 32dp on desktop and the web. A number too long for it makes its item wider; the icon of previous and of next is 4dp more than half the item. `itemShape` gives the corners: fully round on Android and iOS, small on desktop and the web. `itemGap` is the room between two neighbours, and follows the density. The platform's touch target is kept free around every item; the row is as wide as its items, and at least as tall as that target.

**Type.** `textStyle` is the text style of the numbers and of the short row's words, the theme's `label` style unless given. A style that makes an item larger does not make its text larger: a large item is given a large type too.

**Digits.** The numbers, the numbers in the short row's words and the numbers in the names said to a screen reader are written in the digits of the theme's language (`PantrixStrings.digits`): in Arabic digits in the Arabic pack. `onPageChange` reports the same number in every language.

**Colours.** `PaginationColors` paints the numbers and the short row's words (`content`), previous, next and the gaps' marks (`control`), and the fill and the number of the page on screen (`selectedContainer`, `selectedContent`) one by one. On a fill, all of a row that is given no colour is in the colour that is written on the fill; the page on screen is told by its fill, a share of that colour.

**Screen reader.** A number is a button named by the page it opens: "Page 4". The page on screen is no button and offers the reader nothing to press: it is read with the state "Current page". The gaps are not read. The buttons that go to the first and the last page are named "First page" and "Last page". The short row's words are told to the reader each time they change. The row is a group named "Pagination". On iOS the group has no name: the reader there reads a group's name after what it holds.
**Right to left.** In languages read from right to left the row starts on the right, and the arrows turn round.

**Page size.** `PantrixPageSize` is the words "Per page" and, beside them, a select of sizes. The size that is chosen is its caller's: it is given with `pageSize`, and when another size is chosen it is reported through `onPageSizeChange`; choosing the chosen size again reports nothing. The sizes are 10, 25, 50 and 100 unless given (`DefaultPageSizes`); `pageSizes` gives others. A `pageSize` that is none of the sizes is shown as chosen too, and stands in the list before the first size larger than itself. The select is as wide as the longest size needs: the row stands still as the choice changes.

**Go to page.** `PantrixPageJump` is the words "Go to page" and, beside them, a short field. Enter, or the action of a keyboard on the screen, reports the page that was typed through `onPageChange` and empties the field; the focus stays in the field. A number outside the pages is taken as the nearest page; an empty field reports nothing. The field takes digits alone, the Western ones and those of the theme's language, and holds as many digits as the last page's number has.

**The companions' words.** In both the words stand before the control, on the side where the row starts, and are for the eye: a screen reader is given one control, named by those words. `label` changes the words. In a narrow place the words give way and the control does not. `enabled = false` writes the words in the disabled text colour and turns the control off.

**Automation.** A row given a `tagKey` is `Pagination_<tagKey>`, and its parts are named inside it: `Pagination_orders.Page_4`, `Pagination_orders.Step_previous`, `Pagination_orders.Step_next`, `Pagination_orders.Step_first`, `Pagination_orders.Step_last`, and the short row's words `Pagination_orders.Text_position`. Every page that is asked for is reported as `select`, with its number and with what asked for it (`page`, `previous`, `next`, `first`, `last`). The companions are `PageSize_<tagKey>` and `PageJump_<tagKey>`; the select in one carries the tag `Select_<tagKey>_page_size`, the field in the other `TextField_<tagKey>_page_jump`.

examples.name: PaginationPlain
examples.title: Moving between pages
examples.description:
At its plainest: the page on screen (`page`), how many pages there are (`pageCount`) and what happens when a page is asked for (`onPageChange`). Which page the app is on is the screen's state; the row does not hold it: it reports the number of the page that was asked for, and shows it once `page` says so.

Press a number, or one of the arrows at the two ends: the page that was asked for is written on the card's "Last event" line. The page on screen has a fill and is no button: a press on it reports nothing. Previous cannot be pressed on the first page, nor next on the last.

There are ten pages: the row shows the first and the last, the one on screen and the ones on its two sides, and folds those between into a gap of three dots. On a phone held upright that much does not fit. There the row, by the phone's width, either shows fewer numbers or is in its short form: previous, "Page 1 of 10" and next.
examples.code:
val report = LocalExampleEvents.current
var page by rememberSaveable { mutableIntStateOf(1) }
PantrixPagination(
    page = page,
    pageCount = 10,
    onPageChange = { asked ->
        page = asked
        report("Page $asked was asked for")
    },
    tagKey = "plain"
)

appNames.name: LocalExampleEvents
appNames.description: Where an example tells its card what happens in it: a button pressed, a row chosen, a dialog closed. The card writes the last thing told under the example, on its "Last event" line.

examples.name: PaginationOrders
examples.title: A list shown a page at a time
examples.description:
A list of forty-eight orders, five to a page: that makes ten pages, with three orders left for the last. The number of pages is worked out from the list itself. The row only reports which page was asked for; showing that page's orders is the screen's work.

Press next, or a number where the numbers fit: the list goes to that page's orders, and the text under it says which orders are shown. Go to the last page: there are three orders there, and next cannot be pressed.

The list is five orders tall on every page: on the last page the two rows that have no order stand empty. Had the list grown shorter, the row under it would have moved up, out from under the finger that pressed it.

examples.name: PaginationSiblings
examples.title: How many pages beside the one on screen and at the ends
examples.description:
`siblingCount` says how many pages are shown on each side of the page on screen, and `boundaryCount` how many at each end of the row; each is one unless given. Four rows of twenty pages show the same page: press a page in one of them, and all four go there.

The first row is given neither. The second shows two pages on each side of the page on screen, and the third two pages at each end. In the last one both are zero: only the page on screen is left in the middle, and the others are reached by the arrows.

A row has as many items whichever page is on screen. Press 1 in the first row: at an end one of the gaps goes, and the pages at that end take its place; in the last row the second page stands beside the first.

The rows are in a frame that scrolls sideways: there the width has no end, and the rows keep their numbers on a narrow screen too.
examples.code:
var page by rememberSaveable { mutableIntStateOf(10) }
val secondary = PantrixTheme.colors.textSecondary
HorizontalScrollFrame(tagKey = "around") {
    Column(verticalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.sm)) {
        PantrixText(text = "Neither is given: one page on each side, one at each end", color = secondary)
        PantrixPagination(page = page, pageCount = 20, onPageChange = { page = it }, tagKey = "around_usual")
        PantrixText(text = "siblingCount = 2", color = secondary)
        PantrixPagination(
            page = page,
            pageCount = 20,
            onPageChange = { page = it },
            siblingCount = 2,
            tagKey = "around_siblings"
        )
        PantrixText(text = "boundaryCount = 2", color = secondary)
        PantrixPagination(
            page = page,
            pageCount = 20,
            onPageChange = { page = it },
            boundaryCount = 2,
            tagKey = "around_boundaries"
        )
        PantrixText(text = "siblingCount = 0, boundaryCount = 0", color = secondary)
        PantrixPagination(
            page = page,
            pageCount = 20,
            onPageChange = { page = it },
            siblingCount = 0,
            boundaryCount = 0,
            tagKey = "around_none"
        )
    }
}

appNames.name: HorizontalScrollFrame
appNames.description: A frame that scrolls sideways: where its content does not fit its room, it draws a scrollbar under it.

examples.name: PaginationFirstLast
examples.title: With buttons that go to the first and the last page
examples.description:
`firstAndLast = true` puts one more button outside previous and outside next: one goes to the first page, the other to the last. It is for going from one end to the other in one press, in a list of many pages such as an archive.

Press the last page button: the row goes to the fortieth page; there neither next nor the last page button can be pressed. The first page button goes to the first page, and there the two buttons at the start cannot be pressed. The page that was asked for is written on the card's "Last event" line.

Four buttons leave less room for the numbers: at the same width this row folds before one with two buttons does. On a phone held upright it is in its short form: two buttons, "Page 12 of 40" and two buttons. On the narrowest phones, where four buttons leave no room for the words, the end of the words is cut and the buttons are not.
examples.code:
val report = LocalExampleEvents.current
var page by rememberSaveable { mutableIntStateOf(12) }
PantrixPagination(
    page = page,
    pageCount = 40,
    onPageChange = { asked ->
        page = asked
        report("Page $asked was asked for")
    },
    firstAndLast = true,
    tagKey = "ends"
)

appNames.name: LocalExampleEvents
appNames.description: Where an example tells its card what happens in it: a button pressed, a row chosen, a dialog closed. The card writes the last thing told under the example, on its "Last event" line.

examples.name: PaginationNarrow
examples.title: Where it is too narrow for the numbers
examples.description:
The same row at three widths: the first as wide as the example, the second in a frame of 320dp, the third in one of 240dp. The row fits its place step by step. The first frame is too narrow for the seven items of ten pages: there the row gives up the pages beside the page on screen, and stands with five items. In the second frame that does not fit either: the row is laid out as previous, "Page 3 of 10" and next. Nothing was given for this: the row looks at the width left to it, not at the window.

The three show the same page: press next in one of the frames, and all three go to that page. A row folds the same way on every page: none of them changes its layout as the page moves. Make the window narrower: the row at the top also shows fewer numbers first, and then goes to its short form.

The frames' widths were chosen for the 32dp items of desktop and the web. On a phone the items are larger, and the touch target is kept free around them: there both frames are too narrow for the numbers, and the short row stands in both. The row at the top, by the phone's width, either shows fewer numbers or is short too.

examples.name: PaginationCompact
examples.title: The short row at every width
examples.description:
`PaginationStyle(layout = PaginationLayout.Compact)` asks for the short row at every width: where the numbers would fit, too, the row is previous, the page's place and next. It is for a place where people step from page to page and do not jump to a number, such as the foot of a table.

Press next: the words become "Page 2 of 5"; a screen reader is told the changed words without being asked. Next cannot be pressed on the fifth page, nor previous on the first.
examples.code:
var page by rememberSaveable { mutableIntStateOf(1) }
PantrixPagination(
    page = page,
    pageCount = 5,
    onPageChange = { page = it },
    style = PaginationStyle(layout = PaginationLayout.Compact),
    tagKey = "compact"
)

examples.name: PaginationDisabled
examples.title: A row that cannot be pressed while the list loads
examples.description:
`enabled = false` turns the whole row off: the numbers, previous and next cannot be pressed, and the row is drawn in the theme's disabled colours. It is used so that a second page is not asked for while one is loading: `enabled = !loading`.

While the switch is on, the list counts as loading: press next or, where the numbers fit, a number; the card's "Last event" line does not change. Turn the switch off and press again: the page that was asked for is reported. The page on screen is told in a row that cannot be pressed too: by its fill in a row of numbers, by its words in the short row.

If the list starts loading while the keyboard is on a number or an arrow, the focus stays there: what it is on cannot be pressed, but once the list has come the keyboard goes on from where it was.
examples.code:
val report = LocalExampleEvents.current
var loading by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf(true) }
var page by rememberSaveable { mutableIntStateOf(4) }
PantrixSwitchButton(
    checked = loading,
    onCheckedChange = { loading = it },
    label = "The list is loading",
    tagKey = "list_loading"
)
PantrixPagination(
    page = page,
    pageCount = 10,
    onPageChange = { asked ->
        page = asked
        report("Page $asked was asked for")
    },
    enabled = !loading,
    tagKey = "while_loading"
)

appNames.description: Where an example tells its card what happens in it: a button pressed, a row chosen, a dialog closed. The card writes the last thing told under the example, on its "Last event" line.

examples.name: PaginationFoot
examples.title: In a table's foot: page size and go to page
examples.description:
A table's foot: `PantrixPageSize` chooses how many orders a page shows, `PantrixPagination` moves between the pages, and `PantrixPageJump` goes to the page whose number is typed. The three are in a `FlowRow`: where there is room they stand side by side, and in a narrow place the one that does not fit goes down to the next line; on a phone held upright the three stand one under another. A `Row` does not take what does not fit down a line: it squeezes the last one into the room that is left. The three may not be the same height: `itemVerticalAlignment` lines them up by their middles.

All three read the screen's state, and none knows of the others. Change the page size: forty-eight orders make sixteen pages three at a time, and five pages ten at a time; the row's numbers and the number of digits the field takes follow the new number of pages. As the size changes the first order shown stays on screen: the page that is opened is the one that order falls on at the new size. On the fourth page, with orders 16–20 shown, choose 10: the second page comes, orders 11–20. For forty-eight orders the sizes are small: 3 and 5, before the first of the ready sizes (`DefaultPageSizes`), 10.

Type a number in the field and press Enter: that page is opened, the field is emptied and the focus stays in the field. A number larger than the last page opens the last page; the field takes nothing but digits. The page that was asked for, whatever asked for it, is written on the card's "Last event" line.

appNames.description: Where an example tells its card what happens in it: a button pressed, a row chosen, a dialog closed. The card writes the last thing told under the example, on its "Last event" line.

examples.name: PaginationArabic
examples.title: In Arabic: a row that starts on the right, and Arabic digits
examples.description:
The same row in an Arabic section: the inner theme is given `locale` alone, `PantrixLocale.Arabic`. The row starts on the right: previous is on the right, the arrows turn round, and the numbers grow towards the left. The numbers are written in Arabic digits: the language's pack carries its digits too (`PantrixStrings.digits`). The one below is the short row: its words are Arabic, and its numbers are written in the same digits.

Press a page: the card's "Last event" line writes the page that was asked for in the app's language. The digits change the writing alone: `onPageChange` reports the same number in every language. The names said to a screen reader are Arabic too, and are written in the same digits.

On a phone held upright the row at the top, by the phone's width, also shows fewer numbers or is short.

appNames.description: Where an example tells its card what happens in it: a button pressed, a row chosen, a dialog closed. The card writes the last thing told under the example, on its "Last event" line.

examples.name: PaginationOwnColors
examples.title: With its own colours, and on a fill
examples.description:
`colors` takes the colour of the numbers and of the short row's words (`content`), of previous, next and the gaps' marks (`control`), and of the fill and the number of the page on screen (`selectedContainer`, `selectedContent`) one by one; one that is left out stays the theme's. In the first row the arrows and the fill of the page on screen are in the app's own purple, which is in none of the theme's roles. The theme cannot know what reads on a fill it does not have: the colour of its number is given too. The other numbers are given no colour, and stay in the theme's text colour.

The second row is on a fill that is not one of the theme's grounds, and no colour is given: the fill says what is written on it, and all of the row is written in that colour. The page on screen is told by its fill, a share of the same colour.
examples.code:
val own = ownColors()
var page by rememberSaveable { mutableIntStateOf(2) }
PantrixPagination(
    page = page,
    pageCount = 3,
    onPageChange = { page = it },
    colors = PaginationColors(control = own.color, selectedContainer = own.color, selectedContent = own.onColor),
    tagKey = "own"
)
PantrixSurface(
    modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(),
    color = PantrixTheme.colors.primary.color,
    shape = PantrixTheme.shapes.md
) {
    PantrixPagination(
        page = page,
        pageCount = 3,
        onPageChange = { page = it },
        modifier = Modifier.padding(horizontal = PantrixTheme.spacing.md),
        tagKey = "filled"
    )
}

appNames.name: ownColors
appNames.description: The "app's own colour" of the examples: a purple that is in none of the theme's roles. It is there to show what changes when a component is given `colors`; given one of the theme's roles, nobody could tell whether the colour came from the component's tone or from the parameter.

examples.name: PaginationSizes
examples.title: Sizes and shape
examples.description:
`style` gives the row's sizes; only the fields that are set change. `itemSize` is the size of a number, of previous and of next, `itemShape` their corners, and `itemGap` the room between two neighbours. The arrows' icon grows and shrinks with its item: it is 4dp more than half of it.

The middle row is as it is with nothing given. The one above it is built with 24dp items, fully round and with no room put between them; the one below it with 48dp items, medium corners and 8dp between them. The platform's touch target is kept free around the small items too: the items shrink, but come no closer to each other than that target.

A larger item is not written larger by itself: the bottom row is also given the theme's `title` style, with `textStyle`.
examples.code:
var page by rememberSaveable { mutableIntStateOf(2) }
PantrixPagination(
    page = page,
    pageCount = 3,
    onPageChange = { page = it },
    style = PaginationStyle(itemSize = 24.dp, itemShape = ShapeRole.Full, itemGap = 0.dp),
    tagKey = "small"
)
PantrixPagination(page = page, pageCount = 3, onPageChange = { page = it }, tagKey = "usual")
PantrixPagination(
    page = page,
    pageCount = 3,
    onPageChange = { page = it },
    textStyle = PantrixTheme.typography.title,
    style = PaginationStyle(itemSize = 48.dp, itemShape = ShapeRole.Medium, itemGap = 8.dp),
    tagKey = "large"
)

pages.title: Tree View
pages.summary:
A hierarchy whose branches open and close: folders and files, categories, a document's headings.

Which branches are open is the screen's state: the tree is given the keys of the open branches (`expanded`), and when a branch is opened or closed it hands back the new set that is to be open (`onExpandedChange`). So is which rows are chosen (`selected`, `onSelectionChange`). The tree changes nothing by itself.
features: **Nodes.** A `TreeNode`'s `key` is the same in every language, and no two nodes of a tree have one key. A row has its `icon` first, then its `label`, and at its end a short text (`trailing`: a number, a file's size).

**Choosing.** `TreeSelection.None` opens or closes a branch when its row is pressed. `Single` chooses the row pressed; `Checkbox` checks the row's checkbox. While rows are chosen, the chevron at a row's start opens and closes the branch by a press of its own. A branch's checkbox checks everything under it that can be checked, and clears it where all of it is checked; a branch with only some of what is under it checked shows a dash. `onSelectionChange` gives every checked node.
**Disabled.** A node with `enabled = false` cannot be chosen or checked and is written faint; its branch still opens and closes.

**Loading when opened.** A node with `hasChildren = true` and no children yet has its chevron drawn; when it is opened, the screen loads its children. While its key is in `loading`, a spinner stands in the chevron's place.

**Filtering.** While `filter` holds more than spaces, the tree shows the rows whose labels hold it and the branches they stand in; the letters found are marked, and capital and small letters are compared in the theme's language (in Turkish İ with i, and I with ı). These branches are open while the filter is given, and the reader can still close them. Everything under a node that holds what is looked for shows. Where nothing is found the tree shows no row; what to say then is the screen's.
**Guides.** `guides` draws a faint line down from each open branch's chevron along what stands under it.

**Keyboard.** The tree is one stop for Tab. The arrows down and up go from row to row, Home and End to the first and the last row. The arrow along the row opens a branch, and on an open branch goes to its first child; the other arrow closes an open branch, and on another row goes to the branch over it. A letter goes to the next row that starts with it, and `*` opens every branch beside it. Enter and Space press the row.

**Screen reader.** A row says its name, what stands at its end, how many children a closed branch has and at which level it stands, in the theme's words; what a press will do (choose, check, open or close) is offered, and a branch says whether it is open.

**Size.** The tree is as wide as the room it is given and as tall as its open rows, and does not scroll: it stands in a page that scrolls. Every open row is composed; a tree with thousands of open rows wants a list of its own. A branch's children come and go with the theme's motion.

**Platform.** A row is the platform's list row: 48dp on Android, 44pt on iOS, 32dp on desktop and the web; it is never lower than the platform's touch target, and on a desktop or a web page used by touch it takes a finger's. Each level steps in by 24dp on Android, 20pt on iOS, and 16dp on desktop and the web.

**Colour.** `TreeViewColors` gives the fill, the text, the chosen row, the guides and the ground of the letters found. A tree with no fill stands on what is behind it, and on a fill it is written in the colour that fill gives.

**Automation.** With `tagKey` the tree is `TreeView_<tagKey>`, a row `TreeView_<tagKey>.Node_<key>`, and its chevron `TreeView_<tagKey>.Twisty_<key>`. Presses are reported with the node's key as `expand`, `collapse`, `select`, `check` and `uncheck`.

examples.name: TreeViewFiles
examples.title: Folders and files
examples.description: A project's folders and files, one of them chosen. A press on a row chooses it; the chevron before a folder opens it or closes it. Each file's size is written at the row's end. The open folders and the chosen file are the screen's state and are kept with `rememberSaveable`.

    onSelectionChange = { chosen = it },
    tagKey = "files"

PantrixText(

    style = PantrixTheme.typography.footnote,
    color = PantrixTheme.colors.textSecondary

examples.name: TreeViewOwnColors
examples.title: In its own colours
examples.description: In its own colours: `TreeViewColors` paints the tree's ground, its text, the selected row, the indent guides and the text a search found. Here the selected row is in the colour of information, not the brand's.

pages.title: Tag
pages.summary: A short label on a piece of data: a status, a category, a version. A tag is read, not pressed: something that is pressed, removed or chosen is a chip, and a count or a dot on another element is a badge.
features: **Six tones.** `tone` draws the tag in one of the theme's roles: `Primary`, `Info`, `Success`, `Warning`, `Danger` and the default `Neutral`. When the brand's colour changes, every tag changes with it.

**Three variants.** `Soft` is the role's pale fill and the default; `Solid` is the role's full colour, for the state a row is about; `Outline` has no fill, and its edge and its words are in the role's full colour. The theme picks that colour to read on its grounds in both of its modes.
**Icon and dot.** `icon` stands before the words, in their colour. `dot` puts a small disc in the role's full colour before the words: the state a row is in. Where an icon is given, no dot is drawn.

**Words, not colour.** The words carry the meaning: a red "Overdue" says the same to someone who cannot see red. A screen reader hears the tag as one thing, its words; `contentDescription` takes their place.
**Not pressed.** A tag takes no focus, has no touch target and is lower than a chip on every platform: it stands inside a row without taking it over.

**Type.** The words are one line, set in the theme's `footnote` unless `textStyle` is given, and are cut with "…" where the room ends. A larger type makes the tag taller; their colour is always the tag's.

**On a fill.** `Soft` and `Solid` bring their own grounds and are drawn in their role's colours everywhere. On a fill that is not the theme's ground, an `Outline`'s edge and words are in what is written there.
**Colours of its own.** `colors` takes the place of the tone's colours: those given are used, the rest stay the tone's. A role's fill given brings the colour the theme pairs with it.

**Platform.** 24dp tall on Android, 22 on iOS, on desktop and on the web. On iOS its ends are round, as iOS's own labels are; on the other platforms its corners are only a little round, which tells it from a chip.

examples.name: TagTonesAndVariants
examples.title: Tones and variants
examples.description: One variant to a row, six tones in each: `Soft`, `Solid` and `Outline`. Each tag's words say what its tone means; the colour only backs them up.

examples.name: TagIconsAndDots
examples.title: Icon and dot
examples.description: The icon stands before the words, in their colour, and says nothing to a screen reader. The dot is in the role's full colour and tells a state: online, outage, offline. Where both are given, the icon is drawn.

examples.name: TagInARow
examples.title: The state of a row
examples.description: A tag's own place is at the end of a row: an invoice's state. The row does not shrink to the tag; the tag stands inside it without taking it over, and is not pressed. Where a press on the row does something, the row does it.

examples.name: TagTopics
examples.title: Beside a title
examples.description: An article's topics, beside its title: tags with no fill, which do not shout on a page in colour. The tags that do not fit go to the next line; `FlowRow` does that, not the tag. The last tag has little room, and its words are cut with "…".

examples.name: TagOnAFill
examples.title: On a fill
examples.description: On a fill that is not the theme's ground, here the primary role's full colour: `Soft` and `Solid` bring their own grounds and are drawn in their role's colours. The `Outline`, with no fill, is written in what is written there, white here: the role's own colour may not read on that fill.

examples.name: TagOwnColors
examples.title: Colours of its own and a description of its own
examples.description: `colors` gives a colour none of the theme's roles has: here the app's own violet. The colours not given stay the tone's. The last tag has a `contentDescription`: a screen reader says "Payment status: overdue" in place of "Overdue".
examples.code:
val own = ownColors()
FlowRow(
    horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.sm),
    verticalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.sm)
) {
    PantrixTag(
        text = "Campaign",
        colors = TagColors(container = own.container, content = own.onContainer, dot = own.color),
        dot = true,
        tagKey = "own"
    )
    PantrixTag(
        text = "Campaign",
        variant = TagVariant.Outline,
        colors = TagColors(content = own.onContainer, border = own.color)
    )
    PantrixTag(
        text = "Overdue",
        tone = TagTone.Danger,
        contentDescription = "Payment status: overdue",
        tagKey = "described"
    )
}

appNames.name: ownColors
appNames.description: The "app's own colour" of the examples: a purple that is in none of the theme's roles. It is there to show what changes when a component is given `colors`; given one of the theme's roles, nobody could tell whether the colour came from the component's tone or from the parameter.

examples.name: TagOwnStyle
examples.title: In its own style
examples.description: In its own style: `TagStyle` gives a tag's height, its padding, its corners and its dot. Here the tags are pill-shaped, 32dp high, with a 10dp dot; every field not given is the platform's preset. `textStyle` gives the type of the words: here the theme's `label`, in bold.
examples.code:
val style = TagStyle(shape = ShapeRole.Full, height = 32.dp, horizontalPadding = 14.dp, dotSize = 10.dp)
val words = PantrixTheme.typography.label.copy(fontWeight = FontWeight.Bold)
FlowRow(
    horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.sm),
    verticalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.sm)
) {
    PantrixTag(
        text = "Online",
        tone = TagTone.Success,
        dot = true,
        style = style,
        tagKey = "online_pill",
        textStyle = words
    )
    PantrixTag(
        text = "Under maintenance",
        tone = TagTone.Warning,
        dot = true,
        style = style,
        tagKey = "maintenance_pill",
        textStyle = words
    )
}

pages.title: Chart
pages.summary:
Values along a run of places: lines and filled areas through the value each series has at each place, with the axis of the places under them and the axis of the values beside them. This is how the course of a measurement over the months, or two things going side by side, is shown.

The chart takes its series, and each series carries its own rows: what it is drawn from, where a row stands and what its value is. The axes, the legend and the tooltip are parts of the chart: each is given by the value that describes it and taken away by `null`.
features: **Series.** A `LineSeries` is a line; with `fill` the room under the line is filled and it becomes an area. A `BarSeries` is a bar at each place. Each series takes a key (`key`), a name, its rows and two functions that read two things from those rows: `x` the row's place, `y` its value. A row with no value gives `null`. Series of different kinds are drawn in one chart: a line over bars.
**Stacking.** Series that name the same `stack` stand on one another at each place: bars in a single bar, areas on top of each other. A series that names none stands on zero by itself.

**Places.** A place is what a row's `x` gives: a name, a day, anything that equals itself. The chart sets out every place any of its series names, in the order they are first named. Series need not be read from one list, and need not stand at the same places either.

**Time axis.** A chart whose every place is a moment (`kotlin.time.Instant`) sets its places out by time: in the order of time whatever the order of the rows, and as far apart as their moments are. The axis is marked at round moments (hour, day, month) and a place is written as a date: by the device's clock and in the theme's language, unless the `time` of `xAxis` (`ChartTime`) says otherwise. No date library is needed.

**Axes.** `xAxis` is the axis of the places, `yAxis` of the values. A `ChartAxis` says its title, whether it is written, its line and its grid lines; the axis of values also its least, its most, whether it starts at zero and how many values are marked. Values are marked at round numbers.

**A second axis.** In a chart with two kinds of value (a count and a rate), a series that says `axis = ChartYAxis.Second` is drawn by a scale of its own; that scale's axis (`secondYAxis`) is written at the chart's other side, and its marks stand on the first axis' grid lines. Each value is written the way its own axis writes. A stack is made of the series of one axis.

**Writing.** Values are written in the theme's language: short beside the axis from ten thousand on (`12K`), in full in the tooltip. `format` says how an axis' values are written, `label` how its places are.

**Marks.** `marks` draws what the series are read against: a line at a value or at a place (`ChartReferenceLine`), a shaded band between two values or two places (`ChartReferenceBand`). A mark at a value makes its axis go far enough to show it. A mark that has a label is said to a screen reader too.
**Value labels.** A series' `labels` writes its values at their marks: over a line's point, at the end of a bar, inside a bar of a stack. A label that has no room is left out.

**Legend.** The names of the series, each beside a sample that shows how the series is drawn. A chart of one series has no legend. Pressing an entry takes the series out of the chart, pressing it again brings it back; the axis is set again for the series that stay. The legend stands on one of the chart's four sides.

**Tooltip.** The values at the place pointed at, in a small card beside the place. With `shared` the values of all the series there are shown together, and with it off only the value of the series nearest the pointer. `format` says how the card writes its values; left out, the axis' `format` writes them. `content` leaves the inside of the card to the screen. In a narrow chart with no room beside the place the card stands over the place, at the end the values are not at.

**Pointing at a place.** A pointer over the chart points at the nearest place. A finger points by touching, or drawn along the chart; a second touch on the place it points at lets go of it. The place is marked by a line; in a chart that has bars its band is shaded.

**Keyboard.** The chart is one stop for Tab. The arrow keys go from place to place, Home and End to the first and the last place, and Escape lets go; Enter and Space press the value pointed at. Where the tooltip tells the series apart, the arrows up and down go from one series' value to the next.

**State.** `ChartState` holds the series the reader has hidden and the place they point at. A screen that makes one with `rememberChartState` and gives it to the chart reads both, and says both; two charts given the same state behave as one.

**Zoom.** A chart that is given a `zoom` (`ChartZoom`) shows a part of its places as wide as the plot, and is moved along the rest. With a mouse: the wheel, while Ctrl (Command on a Mac) is held, zooms about the place under the pointer, and a wheel turned sideways and a drag move along the places; a wheel with no key is the page's. Two fingers spread apart zoom in, and moved together they take the places along; one finger points at a place, as in any chart. On the keyboard plus and minus zoom in and out, zero brings all the places back, and the arrows bring the place they go to into view. For whoever uses none of those there are the buttons (`buttons`) and, under the plot, the navigator that all the places lie on (`navigator`). The part in view is in the `ChartState` (`window`, `zoomTo`, `resetZoom`): two charts given the same state zoom together. The axes of values stay as all the values have them and hold still as you move along; `fitValues = true` makes them again for the values of the places in view, and the navigator stays on the axes of all the values. A chart that is given no `zoom` does none of this.

**Export.** A chart that is given an `export` (`ChartExport`) has an export button among its own: the reader chooses the kind (PNG, SVG, PDF), the chart makes the file and hands it to `onExport`. Where the file goes is the app's to say: a phone shares it, a window saves it, a browser downloads it. The file shows the chart as it is on the screen: a series that was taken out is out, and of a chart that is zoomed it has the part in view; the place that is pointed at, the tooltip and the buttons are not in it, and the legend stands under the plot. An SVG and a PDF are lines and shapes, sharp at any size; their words are written in a typeface of whatever opens the file. A chart that is given no `export` has no such button.

**Many points.** A line with more than two points to a pixel is thinned (`decimation`, `ChartDecimation`): the default `DecimationAlgorithm.MinMax` goes through the first, the highest, the lowest and the last point of each column of pixels, covers the same pixels and does far less work; `DecimationAlgorithm.Lttb` keeps one point to a pixel and keeps the line's shape. `threshold` says after how many points it is thinned; `decimation = null` draws every point. A thinned line is drawn straight, and its points have no marks. A chart that is looked at closer draws only the places in view.

**Size.** The chart fills the width it is given. A height given with `modifier` is the whole chart's; given none, the plot is as tall as the style says and a legend above or under it adds to that. Place names that have no room left to be written are left out by a rule: every second, every third.

**Motion.** The chart comes in drawn from the side where the places start; when the values change, each goes from where it was to where it is. Where the system asks for reduced motion none of it moves.

**Colour.** A series that does not say its colour takes the one at its place among the theme's chart colours; a hidden series keeps its place and its colour. The grid lines and the words are the theme's; where the chart stands on a fill they come from the colour that is read there.

**Patterns.** `ChartStyle(patterns = true)` tells series apart by more than their colours: the first series stays plain, the others have a texture cut into their fills in turn (`ChartPattern`), lines are drawn dashed and dotted in turn, and after the fourth line their points are marked. A step of a waterfall that takes away and a candle that falls take a texture too. The legend, the tooltip and an exported file show the same texture. Left out, the system's setting is followed: the patterns are on where iOS's "Differentiate Without Color" or Android's colour correction is. A series says its own texture with `pattern` and its own dashes with `dash`; what it says always holds.
**Reading direction.** In a language written from right to left the places start at the right and the values are written at the right.

**Screen reader.** The chart first says its description, given with `description`, then each place with the values the series have there. The legend's entries are switches. A chart of more than two hundred places is read by its description alone.

**Automation.** With `tagKey` the chart is `Chart_<tagKey>`, the plot `Chart_<tagKey>.Plot`, a place `Chart_<tagKey>.Point_<number>`, a series' legend entry `Chart_<tagKey>.Legend_<the series' key>`, and the tooltip `Chart_<tagKey>.Tooltip`. The zoom buttons are `Chart_<tagKey>.Zoom_in`, `.Zoom_out`, `.Zoom_all`, `.Zoom_back` and `.Zoom_on`, the navigator is `Chart_<tagKey>.Navigator`, and the export button `Chart_<tagKey>.Export`. A press on a value is reported as `select`, a press on a legend entry as `toggle`, a press of a zoom button or key as `zoom`, and a file that is made as `export` with its kind; nothing of the values is reported.

examples.name: ChartTwoSeries
examples.title: Two series
examples.description:
At its plainest: two series read from the same rows. Each `LineSeries` takes its key, its name, the rows, and the two functions that read the place (`x`) and the value (`y`) from those rows.

The rest comes by itself: the axis of the months under the chart and of round values beside it, grid lines at the values, a legend since there are two series, and the tooltip of the place pointed at. Move the pointer over the chart, or draw a finger along it; press a name in the legend to take its series out.
examples.code:
val series: List<ChartSeries> = listOf(
    LineSeries("desktop", "Desktop", VISITS, x = { it.month }, y = { it.desktop }),
    LineSeries("mobile", "Mobile", VISITS, x = { it.month }, y = { it.mobile })
)
PantrixChart(
    series = series,
    description = "Desktop and mobile visits by month",
    tagKey = "two_series"
)

private data class Visits(
    val month: String,
    val desktop: Int,
    val mobile: Int,
    val tablet: Int
)

    Visits("Aug", desktop = 310, mobile = 210, tablet = 83),

examples.name: ChartOwnRows
examples.title: Series from their own rows
examples.description:
Series need not be read from one list. Here the measured values come from one list and the forecast from another, and the two meet only in September. The chart sets out every place any of its series names, in the order they are first named; where a series gives no value it has no line.

The forecast is drawn in dashes (`dash`) and its points are marked (`marker`): it is told from the measured by more than its colour.
examples.code:
PantrixChart(
    series = listOf(
        LineSeries("measured", "Measured", MEASURED, x = { it.first }, y = { it.second }),
        LineSeries(
            key = "forecast",
            name = "Forecast",
            data = FORECAST,
            x = { it.first },
            y = { it.second },
            marker = ChartMarker.Circle,
            dash = ChartDash.Dashed
        )
    ),
    description = "The year's measured and forecast sales",
    tagKey = "own_rows"
)

private val MEASURED = listOf(
    "Jan" to 42,
    "Feb" to 48,

    "Apr" to 57,
    "May" to 61,
    "Jun" to 58,
    "Jul" to 66,
    "Aug" to 71,
    "Sep" to 69
)

examples.name: ChartBarsAndLine
examples.title: A line over bars
examples.description:
Kinds mix in one chart: each month's orders are a bar (`BarSeries`), and their three-month average is a line (`LineSeries`). In a chart that has bars each place has a band, and the line goes through the middles of the bands. A series given later is drawn over an earlier one: give the line after the bars.

The tooltip writes the two values of the place together; in the legend a bar is a patch, and the line a short line with its mark.
examples.code:
PantrixChart(
    series = listOf(
        BarSeries("orders", "Orders", HALF_YEAR, x = { it.first }, y = { it.second }),
        LineSeries(
            key = "average",
            name = "Three-month average",
            data = HALF_YEAR,
            x = { it.first },
            y = { it.third },
            marker = ChartMarker.Circle
        )
    ),
    description = "Orders by month and their three-month average",
    tagKey = "bars_and_line"
)

private val HALF_YEAR = listOf(
    Triple("Jan", 310, 298),
    Triple("Feb", 285, 302),
    Triple("Mar", 342, 312),
    Triple("Apr", 398, 342),
    Triple("May", 371, 370),
    Triple("Jun", 426, 398)
)

examples.name: ChartTwoAxes
examples.title: Two axes
examples.description:
Two kinds of value in one chart: each month's orders are a count, and the return rate is a share. Drawn against one axis, the rate would lie flat on zero. A series that says `axis = ChartYAxis.Second` is read by the second axis; that axis is written at the chart's other side (`secondYAxis`), and its marks stand on the first axis' grid lines.

Each value is written the way its own axis writes: in the tooltip the orders are a number and the rate a percentage, and a screen reader says them so. `secondYAxis = null` does not draw the axis; the series still stands by its own scale.
examples.code:
val strings = PantrixTheme.strings
PantrixChart(
    series = listOf(
        BarSeries("orders", "Orders", RETURNS, x = { it.first }, y = { it.second }),
        LineSeries(
            key = "returned",
            name = "Return rate",
            data = RETURNS,
            x = { it.first },
            y = { it.third },
            marker = ChartMarker.Circle,
            axis = ChartYAxis.Second
        )
    ),
    yAxis = ChartAxis(title = "Orders"),
    secondYAxis = ChartAxis(title = "Return rate", format = { strings.percent(it, fractionDigits = 1) }),
    description = "Orders and return rate by month",
    tagKey = "two_axes"
)

private val RETURNS = listOf(
    Triple("Jan", 310, 0.042),
    Triple("Feb", 285, 0.051),
    Triple("Mar", 342, 0.038),
    Triple("Apr", 398, 0.036),
    Triple("May", 371, 0.047),
    Triple("Jun", 426, 0.031)
)

examples.name: ChartMarks
examples.title: A target line and bands
examples.description:
Series are read against something: a target, a usual range, the months of a campaign. `marks` takes the marks the chart draws besides its series.

- `ChartReferenceLine(y = …)` is a line across the plot at a value, and `ChartReferenceLine(x = …)` a line up it at a place.

- `ChartReferenceBand(y1 = …, y2 = …)` is a shaded band between two values, and `ChartReferenceBand(x1 = …, x2 = …)` one between two places. A band given one end goes on to the end of the axis.

Lines are drawn over the series and bands behind them; `inFront` changes that. A mark at a value stretches its axis far enough to show it: the target here is at 450, which none of the visits reach. A mark with a label is read to a screen reader after the chart's description.

A mark's words are written over the series, on a plate in the tooltip's colour: they read over a line or a bar as well. `labelPosition` says where along the mark they stand: a line's words are at its end by default, a band's at its start. Here "Usual" is at the end of its band and "New site" at the foot of its line.

How thick the lines are and how deep the bands' tint is belongs to the style: two dp and a fifth of the colour here (`markLineWidth`, `markBandAlpha`).
examples.code:
val marks: List<ChartMark> = listOf(
    ChartReferenceBand(y1 = 200, y2 = 300, label = "Usual", labelPosition = ChartMarkLabelPosition.End),
    ChartReferenceBand(x1 = "Jun", x2 = "Aug", label = "Summer campaign"),
    ChartReferenceLine(
        x = "Oct",
        label = "New site",
        dash = ChartDash.Dotted,
        labelPosition = ChartMarkLabelPosition.Start
    ),
    ChartReferenceLine(y = 450, label = "Target", color = PantrixTheme.colors.success.color)
)
PantrixChart(
    series = listOf(LineSeries("desktop", "Desktop", VISITS, x = { it.month }, y = { it.desktop })),
    marks = marks,
    description = "Desktop visits by month",
    style = ChartStyle(markLineWidth = 2.dp, markBandAlpha = 0.2f),
    tagKey = "marks"
)

private data class Visits(
    val month: String,
    val desktop: Int,
    val mobile: Int,
    val tablet: Int
)

    Visits("Apr", desktop = 173, mobile = 190, tablet = 51),
    Visits("May", desktop = 209, mobile = 130, tablet = 66),

    Visits("Jul", desktop = 280, mobile = 170, tablet = 76),
    Visits("Aug", desktop = 310, mobile = 210, tablet = 83),
    Visits("Sep", desktop = 268, mobile = 232, tablet = 90),
    Visits("Oct", desktop = 342, mobile = 250, tablet = 96),
    Visits("Nov", desktop = 390, mobile = 286, tablet = 91),

examples.name: ChartAxes
examples.title: Axes
examples.description:
An axis is described by a `ChartAxis`. Here the axis of values has a title and writes its values short, in the theme's language (`format`); the axis of places has a title too.

The axis of a chart of lines does not start at zero: what is read is the line's rise and fall. `startFromZero` takes the axis down to zero; turn the switch and see how the same values look on the two axes. A chart with a filled series starts at zero by itself: an area's height is read as an amount.
examples.code:
var fromZero by remember { mutableStateOf(false) }
val strings = PantrixTheme.strings
PantrixSwitchButton(
    checked = fromZero,
    onCheckedChange = { fromZero = it },
    label = "Start the value axis at zero",
    tagKey = "chart_from_zero"
)
PantrixChart(
    series = listOf(LineSeries("revenue", "Revenue", REVENUE, x = { it.first }, y = { it.second })),
    xAxis = ChartAxis(title = "2026"),
    yAxis = ChartAxis(title = "Revenue (TL)", startFromZero = fromZero, format = { strings.compact(it) }),
    description = "Monthly revenue of 2026",
    tagKey = "axes"
)

    "Feb" to 1_310_000,
    "Mar" to 1_285_000,
    "Apr" to 1_420_000,
    "May" to 1_390_000,
    "Jun" to 1_510_000,
    "Jul" to 1_640_000,
    "Aug" to 1_585_000,
    "Sep" to 1_720_000,

examples.name: ChartLegendPlace
examples.title: Where the legend stands
examples.description:
The legend stands on one of the chart's four sides. Above and under it the entries are set in a row and go on to the next row where they do not fit; at the sides they stand under one another. `alignment` says where the legend stands along its own side.

Each entry is a switch for its series: pressed, the series leaves the chart and the axis is set again for the ones that stay, while the entry stays in place, drawn faint. A series that is out keeps its colour; the others' colours do not change either.

examples.name: ChartTooltipKinds

The tooltip reads in two ways. With `shared` on, the values of all the series at the place pointed at come together: that is how a chart is read at a place, and a finger need not aim. examples.name: ChartOwnTooltip
examples.title: Your own tooltip
examples.description:
The inside of the card can be the screen's: `content` takes the values at the place pointed at and draws what it wants from them. Here the two series' values are added up and mobile's share is written as a percentage, both in the theme's number format.

The card itself, its fill, its edge and where it stands remain the chart's.

val strings = PantrixTheme.strings
PantrixChart(
    series = listOf(

        LineSeries("mobile", "Mobile", VISITS, x = { it.month }, y = { it.mobile })
    ),
    tooltip = ChartTooltip(
        content = { points ->
            val total = points.sumOf { it.value }
            val mobile = points.firstOrNull { it.series == "mobile" }?.value ?: 0.0
            PantrixText(text = points.first().label, style = PantrixTheme.typography.footnote)
            PantrixText(text = "${strings.decimal(total)} visits", style = PantrixTheme.typography.label)
            PantrixText(
                text = "Mobile's share ${strings.percent(mobile / total)}",
                style = PantrixTheme.typography.caption,
                color = PantrixTheme.colors.textSecondary

        }
    ),
    description = "Total visits and mobile's share by month",
