examples.name: ChartSharedState
examples.title: Two charts that share a state
examples.description:
`ChartState` holds the series the reader has hidden and the place they point at. A screen that makes one with `rememberChartState` and gives it to the chart reads both: the row underneath writes the month pointed at from the state.

Two charts given the same state behave as one. Point at a month in the upper one: the lower one marks the same month. A series hidden in the legend of one is hidden in the other too, since the two charts' series carry the same keys.

The state is written from the screen too: the button gives `state.selection` a `ChartSelection(x = "Mar")`, and both charts show March.
examples.code:
val state = rememberChartState()
PantrixChart(
    series = listOf(
        LineSeries("desktop", "Desktop", VISITS, x = { it.month }, y = { it.desktop }),
        LineSeries("mobile", "Mobile", VISITS, x = { it.month }, y = { it.mobile })
    ),
    modifier = Modifier.height(200.dp),
    state = state,
    description = "Visits by month",
    tagKey = "shared_visits"
)
PantrixChart(
    series = listOf(
        LineSeries(
            key = "desktop",
            name = "Desktop",
            data = VISITS,
            x = { it.month },
            y = { it.desktop * 3 / 100 },
            fill = ChartFill.Solid
        ),
        LineSeries("mobile", "Mobile", VISITS, x = { it.month }, y = { it.mobile * 2 / 100 }, fill = ChartFill.Solid)
    ),
    modifier = Modifier.height(160.dp),
    legend = null,
    state = state,
    description = "Orders by month",
    tagKey = "shared_orders"
)
PantrixText(
    text = state.selection?.let { "Month pointed at: ${it.x}" } ?: "No month is pointed at",
    style = PantrixTheme.typography.footnote,
    color = PantrixTheme.colors.textSecondary
)
PantrixButton(
    text = "Show March",
    onClick = { state.selection = ChartSelection(x = "Mar") },
    variant = ButtonVariant.Outline,
    size = ButtonSize.Small,
    tagKey = "show_march"
)

examples.name: ChartMissingValues
examples.title: Missing values
examples.description:
`missing` says what the line does at a row that has no value. This sensor gave no reading in April and in August. `Gap` breaks the line there: what is missing is seen to be missing. `Connect` goes on from the point before to the point after. `Zero` counts the row as zero.

A value with no point before it and none after it is drawn as a dot though no mark was asked for: a line through a single point has nothing to show.

var missing by remember { mutableStateOf(ChartMissing.Gap) }

    onSelect = { missing = it },

            data = SENSOR,

            y = { it.second },
            marker = ChartMarker.Circle,
            missing = missing

    ),
    description = "The sensor's mean temperature by month",
    tagKey = "missing"
)

examples.name: ChartWithNoData

examples.description: A chart with no value writes the theme's words ("No data") in the middle of its plot. `empty` puts content of its own in their place: here a line that says what is going on and a button that brings the data. A screen reader is not told "No data" either; the content speaks for itself. Once there are values, the content goes.

examples.name: ChartManyPlaces
examples.title: Many places
examples.description:
Ninety days. The days' names do not fit side by side; the chart leaves them out by a rule, every sixth or every tenth, and sets the same rule again as the window narrows and widens. All the values stay where they are: the value of every day is shown with a pointer or a finger.

The line goes through smoothly (`ChartCurve.Smooth`): it stays between its points, and shows no peak or dip that the values do not have.
examples.code:
PantrixChart(
    series = listOf(
        LineSeries(
            key = "sessions",
            name = "Sessions",
            data = DAILY,
            x = { it.first },
            y = { it.second },
            curve = ChartCurve.Smooth,
            fill = ChartFill.Gradient
        )
    ),
    xAxis = ChartAxis(label = { "Day $it" }),
    description = "Daily sessions of the last ninety days",
    tagKey = "many"
)

private val DAILY: List<Pair<Int, Int>> = List(DAYS) { day ->
    (day + 1) to BASE + day * GROWTH + WEEK[day % WEEK.size]
}

private const val DAYS = 90

private const val BASE = 320

private const val GROWTH = 3

private val WEEK = listOf(40, 62, 55, 70, 48, -90, -120)

examples.name: ChartTimeAxis
examples.title: Time axis
examples.description:
A chart whose places are moments: a server's response time, measured at uneven intervals over a day. Since the rows' `x` gives a `kotlin.time.Instant`, the chart sets them out by time: the hours measured often stand close together and those measured seldom far apart, and the axis is marked at round hours, not at the measurements.

The line and the band stand at moments too, whether a row has that moment or not: when the deployment went out and the maintenance window. A mark after the measurements, the next morning's maintenance, stretches the axis as far as itself, as a target line stretches an axis of values. The hours are read by UTC (`ChartTime`'s `offset`); left out, they are read by the device's clock.

Moments are written as the app writes them too (`ChartTime`'s `format`): the axis's marks on the hour as "14h", a measurement's moment in the tooltip to its minute. The `ChartTimeUnit` given to `format` says what is written: the axis's marks are asked for by the unit between them, a place by the finest unit the places are told apart by.
examples.code:
PantrixChart(
    series = listOf(
        LineSeries(
            key = "response",
            name = "Response time (ms)",
            data = RESPONSE_TIMES,
            x = { momentAt(it.first) },
            y = { it.second },
            marker = ChartMarker.Circle
        )
    ),
    xAxis = ChartAxis(time = ChartTime(format = ::clockOfUtc, offset = { Duration.ZERO })),
    marks = listOf(
        ChartReferenceBand(x1 = momentAt("02:00"), x2 = momentAt("04:00"), label = "Maintenance"),
        ChartReferenceLine(x = momentAt("13:20"), label = "Release"),
        ChartReferenceLine(x = Instant.parse("2026-10-14T03:00:00Z"), label = "Next maintenance")
    ),
    description = "A server's response time over a day, at the moments it was measured",
    tagKey = "time"
)

private val RESPONSE_TIMES = listOf(
    "00:10" to 182,
    "01:40" to 176,
    "02:30" to 240,
    "03:30" to 262,
    "05:00" to 190,
    "08:00" to 205,
    "09:00" to 231,
    "09:30" to 248,
    "10:00" to 236,
    "10:30" to 259,
    "11:00" to 244,
    "12:00" to 228,
    "13:00" to 252,
    "13:30" to 171,
    "14:00" to 158,
    "15:00" to 149,
    "17:30" to 144,
    "21:00" to 139,
    "23:30" to 133
)

private fun momentAt(time: String): Instant = Instant.parse("2026-10-13T$time:00Z")

private fun clockOfUtc(moment: Instant, unit: ChartTimeUnit): String {
    val minute = moment.epochSeconds.floorDiv(SECONDS_IN_A_MINUTE).mod(MINUTES_IN_A_DAY)
    val hour = (minute / MINUTES_IN_AN_HOUR).toString().padStart(2, '0')
    val ofTheHour = (minute % MINUTES_IN_AN_HOUR).toString().padStart(2, '0')
    return if (unit >= ChartTimeUnit.Hour) "${hour}h" else "$hour:$ofTheHour"
}

private const val SECONDS_IN_A_MINUTE = 60

private const val MINUTES_IN_AN_HOUR = 60

private const val MINUTES_IN_A_DAY = 24 * 60

examples.name: ChartZoomed
examples.title: Zoom
examples.description:
`zoom = ChartZoom()` lets the chart be looked at closer: a part of the ninety days fills the whole plot, and the rest is moved along. The buttons over the plot scroll back and forward, zoom out, zoom in and bring all the days back, in that order; a button with nothing to do is drawn faint.

With a mouse, turn the wheel while Ctrl (Command on a Mac) is held: the day under the pointer stays where it is. Once it is zoomed, drag the chart. On a touch screen spread two fingers, then move them together; one finger still points at a day. With the keyboard, go to the chart and press plus, minus and zero: zoomed in, more of the days' names find room to be written.
examples.code:
PantrixChart(
    series = listOf(
        LineSeries("sessions", "Sessions", DAILY, x = { it.first }, y = { it.second }, marker = ChartMarker.Circle)
    ),
    xAxis = ChartAxis(label = { "Day $it" }),
    zoom = ChartZoom(),
    description = "The daily sessions of the last ninety days, which can be looked at closer",
    tagKey = "zoomed"
)

private val DAILY: List<Pair<Int, Int>> = List(DAYS) { day ->
    (day + 1) to BASE + day * GROWTH + WEEK[day % WEEK.size]
}

private const val DAYS = 90

private const val BASE = 320

private const val GROWTH = 3

private val WEEK = listOf(40, 62, 55, 70, 48, -90, -120)

examples.name: ChartNavigated
examples.title: Navigator
examples.description:
The navigator (`navigator = true`) lies under the plot and holds all the places: the series are drawn small on it, and the part in view is marked. Take the marked part by its middle and drag it; widen or narrow it by the grips at its two ends; press somewhere else on the strip, and the part comes there. With the keyboard, on the strip the arrows move the part, and Home and End take it to the start and the end.

The places here are moments: the hourly measurements of sixty days. As you zoom in the axis' marks go from months to days and from days to hours. A screen reader says the strip as the "range in view", with the first and the last moment in view.
examples.code:
PantrixChart(
    series = listOf(
        LineSeries(
            key = "load",
            name = "Load (%)",
            data = HOURLY,
            x = { hourAt(it.first) },
            y = { it.second },
            fill = ChartFill.Gradient
        )
    ),
    xAxis = ChartAxis(time = ChartTime(offset = { Duration.ZERO })),
    yAxis = ChartAxis(min = 0.0, max = 100.0),
    zoom = ChartZoom(navigator = true),
    description = "A server's hourly load over sixty days",
    tagKey = "navigated"
)

private val HOURLY: List<Pair<Int, Int>> = List(HOURS) { hour ->
    val weekend = (hour / A_DAY) % WEEK.size >= WEEK.size - 2
    hour to (if (weekend) 36 else 52) + (wave(hour, A_DAY) * 26).toInt() + hour * 7 % 9
}

private const val HOURS = 24 * 60

private const val A_DAY = 24

private fun hourAt(hour: Int): Instant = Instant.parse("2026-08-15T00:00:00Z") + hour.hours

private val WEEK = listOf(40, 62, 55, 70, 48, -90, -120)

private fun wave(
    step: Int,
    period: Int
): Double = sin(step * 2 * PI / period)

examples.name: ChartZoomedTogether
examples.title: Two charts zoomed together
examples.description:
Two charts that are given the same `ChartState` zoom together: the part in view is kept in the state, and both show it. Zoom the upper chart, or drag the lower one's navigator: the other shows the same days. Pointing at a day is shared too.

The buttons are on the upper chart and the strip on the lower: `ChartZoom(buttons = false, navigator = true)`. The two charts have the same places, so the same part is the same days.
examples.code:
val state = rememberChartState()
PantrixChart(
    series = listOf(LineSeries("sessions", "Sessions", DAILY, x = { it.first }, y = { it.second })),
    modifier = Modifier.height(220.dp),
    xAxis = ChartAxis(label = { "Day $it" }),
    zoom = ChartZoom(),
    state = state,
    description = "Daily sessions of the last ninety days",
    tagKey = "together_sessions"
)
PantrixChart(
    series = listOf(
        LineSeries(
            key = "conversion",
            name = "Conversion (%)",
            data = CONVERSION,
            x = { it.first },
            y = { it.second },
            fill = ChartFill.Solid
        )
    ),
    modifier = Modifier.height(220.dp),
    xAxis = ChartAxis(label = { "Day $it" }),
    zoom = ChartZoom(buttons = false, navigator = true),
    state = state,
    description = "The daily conversion rate of the last ninety days",
    tagKey = "together_conversion"
)

private val DAILY: List<Pair<Int, Int>> = List(DAYS) { day ->
    (day + 1) to BASE + day * GROWTH + WEEK[day % WEEK.size]
}

private val CONVERSION: List<Pair<Int, Double>> = List(DAYS) { day ->
    (day + 1) to 3.2 - WEEK[day % WEEK.size] / 100.0 + day / 120.0
}

private const val DAYS = 90

private const val BASE = 320

private const val GROWTH = 3

private val WEEK = listOf(40, 62, 55, 70, 48, -90, -120)

examples.name: ChartZoomFromScreen
examples.title: The screen's own buttons
examples.description:
The screen can say the part in view too: `ChartState.zoomTo` takes two shares of the way along the places, from zero to one, and `resetZoom` brings them all back. The three options here stand in for the chart's own buttons (`ChartZoom(buttons = false)`); the mouse, the fingers and the keyboard still work.

The state is read as well: the line underneath writes `state.window`. The part in view is kept, with the hidden series, when the screen is rotated (`rememberChartState`).
examples.code:
val state = rememberChartState()
var span by remember { mutableStateOf(DAYS) }
PantrixSegmentButton(
    options = SPANS,
    selected = span,
    onSelect = { days ->
        span = days
        // The days stand at even steps from the chart's start to its end: the last `days` days start that far from the end.
        if (days == DAYS) state.resetZoom() else state.zoomTo(1f - (days - 1f) / (DAYS - 1f), 1f)
    },
    fullWidth = false,
    tagKey = "zoom_span"
)
PantrixChart(
    series = listOf(
        LineSeries("sessions", "Sessions", DAILY, x = { it.first }, y = { it.second }, marker = ChartMarker.Circle)
    ),
    xAxis = ChartAxis(label = { "Day $it" }),
    zoom = ChartZoom(buttons = false),
    state = state,
    description = "Daily sessions of the last ninety days",
    tagKey = "zoom_from_screen"
)
val from = (state.window.start * PERCENT).toInt()
val to = (state.window.endInclusive * PERCENT).toInt()
PantrixText(
    text = if (state.zoomed) "In view: $from% – $to%" else "All the days are in view",
    style = PantrixTheme.typography.footnote,
    color = PantrixTheme.colors.textSecondary
)

examples.name: ChartManyPoints
examples.title: Tens of thousands of points
examples.description:
Fifty thousand points: what a sensor measured once a minute for thirty-five days. The plot is a few hundred pixels wide, so the line goes through the first, the highest, the lowest and the last point of each column of pixels: the line on the screen covers the same pixels as one through every point, and no peak or dip is lost.

Zoom in: only the minutes in view are drawn, and once there are fewer than two points to a pixel each point is drawn itself. `closest` says how close the chart may be looked at, at the most: here a thousand times, which is fifty minutes.

"Thin with LTTB" (`ChartDecimation(algorithm = DecimationAlgorithm.Lttb)`) draws the line through one point to a pixel and keeps its shape; a minute's flicker between two kept points is not drawn, and the line looks smoother. "Fit the axis to the part in view" (`ChartZoom(fitValues = true)`) makes the axis of values for the minutes in view alone as you zoom in: a degree or two over a few hours fills the plot. Turned off, the axis stays as all the days have it and holds still as you move along.

examples.name: ChartExported
examples.title: Export
examples.description:
`export = ChartExport(...)` puts an export button among the chart's own. Press it and choose the kind: the chart makes the file and hands it to `onExport`. Where the file goes is the app's to say: this example says its name, its type and its size, shows the picture again underneath when it is a PNG, and "Save the file" hands it over in the platform's window for saving (`rememberFileSaver`): the window for a new document on Android, Files on iOS, the save dialog on the desktop, a download on the web.

The file shows the chart as it is on the screen: take a series out from the legend and export again. The place that is pointed at and its tooltip are not in the file; the legend stands under the plot. An SVG and a PDF are sharp at any size, and a few kilobytes.

examples.name: ChartExportedPart
examples.title: The part in view, one kind
examples.description:
Given one kind alone the button opens no choice: a press makes that file. Here only a PNG, at three pixels to a dp (`scale = 3f`) and on a white ground (`background`); with no ground given it is the theme's, dark in the dark theme.

The chart can be zoomed: zoom in and export. The file has the part in view, and neither the navigator nor the buttons. The picture that was made is shown underneath; the room around the chart is the file's own (`padding`).

examples.name: ChartPatterns
examples.title: Patterns for colour blindness
examples.description:
Patterns for colour blindness (`ChartStyle(patterns = true)`): the first series stays plain, the others have a texture cut into their bars in turn, and lines are drawn dashed and dotted in turn; the legend and the tooltip show the same texture. Turn the switch off: the patterns go, and the series are told apart by their colours alone.

A series can say its own texture with `pattern` (`ChartPattern`); a texture it says is drawn with the switch off too: here the dots in the tablet's bars.

pages.title: Line Chart
pages.summary:
A line chart of rows that are given once: a line for each value read from the rows (`values`), along the places the rows name (`x`).

It is the short way of writing a `PantrixChart` whose series are all lines and all read from the same rows: it does everything a chart does. The axes, the legend, the tooltip, the state, the keyboard and the screen reader are as told on the "Chart" page.
features: **Rows and values.** `data` gives the rows, `x` a row's place. Each `ChartValue` is a series: its key, its name and the function that reads its value from a row.

**How the line goes.** `curve` says how the line goes from one point to the next: straight, smooth or stepped. A smooth line stays between two points; it shows no peak or dip that the values do not have.
**More than colour.** A series' `dash` draws its line in dashes or in dots, and its `marker` puts a shape on its points. Both show in the series' sample in the legend and in the tooltip.
**Missing values.** `missing` says what the line does at a row that has no value: it breaks, connects, or counts it as zero.

**Numeric axis.** Where the places are numbers and `xAxis = ChartAxis(numeric = true)`, the points stand as far apart as their numbers and the axis is marked at round numbers; otherwise numbers are names too, set out at even steps.
**Value labels and marks.** `labels` writes the values over the points; `marks` draws a target line or the band of a range.
**When `PantrixChart`.** For a chart whose series come from different lists, are of different kinds or are read by a second axis: each series takes its own `LineSeries`.
**Automation.** The chart is tagged as the `PantrixChart` it is: `Chart_<tagKey>`.

Three series take the theme's first three chart colours. Press a name in the legend: its series goes, and the ones that stay keep their colours.

pages.title: Area Chart
pages.summary:
An area chart of rows that are given once: a line for each value read from the rows, and an area that fills the room between the line and zero. It is for amounts read by their height: a revenue, a traffic, a stock.

It is the short way of writing a `PantrixChart` whose series are all filled lines and all read from the same rows. The axes, the legend, the tooltip, the state, the keyboard and the screen reader are as told on the "Chart" page.
features: **Fill.** `fill` says what the room under the line is filled with: `Gradient` is the series' colour fading from the line towards zero, `Solid` an even tint of the colour.

**Zero.** An area chart's value axis starts at zero: an area's height is read as an amount, and an area cut off above zero shows less than there is. The axis can say otherwise with `startFromZero = false`. Where values go below zero the area fills downwards from the zero line.

**Areas over one another.** Each area is drawn over the one before it, and all from zero: a later series covers an earlier one where it is larger. The fading fill shows the one underneath; give the larger series first.

**Stacked areas.** With `stacked` each area stands on the one before it, and the topmost line is the total: the parts of a whole are shown so. The tooltip writes each series' own value, and then the total. With `stacking = ChartStacking.Percent` each place's total counts as a hundred percent and the areas show the shares.
**Line.** `curve`, `missing`, and a series' `dash` and `marker` are as in the line chart.
**Automation.** The chart is tagged as the `PantrixChart` it is: `Chart_<tagKey>`.

pages.title: Range Chart
pages.summary:
A chart that shows what lies between two values at each place: the lowest and the highest temperature of a day, the least and the most a price went to, the hour a shift starts and ends at.

It is the short way of writing a `PantrixChart` with a single `RangeSeries`. The axes, the tooltip, the state, the keyboard and the screen reader are as told on the "Chart" page.
features: **A band or bars.** `RangeKind.Area` draws the range as a band that goes from place to place: two lines, and a tint of the series' colour between them. `RangeKind.Bar` puts a bar at each place, from the lower value to the higher; both ends of the bar are round, because it stands on nothing.

**The band's look.** `lines = false` does not draw the two lines, and the band stays as its tint alone; `dash` draws the lines dashed or dotted, `marker` puts a mark on each point, and `fillAlpha` says how much of the series' colour the tint between them takes (about a sixth where it is not given). A bar reads none of these.

**Zero.** Nothing of a range stands on zero: the value axis does not start at zero unless the axis says so, and is set out around the range's values. What is read is how far apart the two values are and where they lie.
**A missing value.** A row with no lower or no higher value has neither: the band stops before it and starts again after it. A place left by itself is a line from its lower value to its higher.
**Tooltip and screen reader.** The two values are written with a dash between them: "9 – 17". A press is handed the higher value as the point's `value` and the lower as its `from`.
**Value labels.** `labels` writes the two values at the two ends of the range: the higher over it, the lower under it.
**Horizontal.** `horizontal = true` sets the places down the side of the chart, and the ranges go along it: like the shifts of a timetable. The values are written under the chart.

**With other series.** A chart that wants a line over the band (a forecast within its bounds), or two ranges in one chart, is a `PantrixChart`: it takes a `RangeSeries` for the range and a `LineSeries` for the line.
**Automation.** The chart is tagged as the `PantrixChart` it is: `Chart_<tagKey>`. Its one series has the key `range`.

pages.title: Bar Chart
pages.summary:
A bar chart of rows that are given once: at each place the rows name, a bar for each value read from the rows. It is for amounts compared place by place: the sales of the months, the shares of the channels.

It is the short way of writing a `PantrixChart` whose series are all bars and all read from the same rows. The axes, the legend, the tooltip, the state, the keyboard and the screen reader are as told on the "Chart" page.
features: **Side by side or stacked.** A place's bars stand side by side; with `stacked` they stand on one another, in the order of `values`. Side by side suits a few values compared at each place; stacked suits the parts of a whole: the whole reads as well. A stack's tooltip writes the total after the values.

**Shares.** `stacking = ChartStacking.Percent` counts every stack as a hundred percent: the parts' shares read, not the whole. The axis writes percentages, the tooltip adds each value's share beside it, and a label writes the share.
**Zero.** A bar chart's value axis starts at zero: a bar's length is read as an amount. A value below zero goes down from zero; in a stack, under the others that go down.

**Band.** Each place has a band of the chart's width, and its bars stand in the middle of that band. A bar is no wider than a set width however much room it has (`ChartStyle.barMaxWidth`); where there is little room the bars get thinner.

**Horizontal.** `horizontal = true` sets the places down the side of the chart, and the bars go from the left (from the right in a language read from the right): for a ranking, or for places with long names. Each name is written across, on its own line; a name wider than a third of the box is cut short. The values are written under the chart, a second axis over it. The arrows down and up go from place to place, right and left from value to value. A horizontal chart that is looked at closer (`zoom`) goes up and down its places; its navigator stands upright beside the chart, at the side lines end at.

**The place pointed at.** The band of the place under the pointer or the finger is shaded, and the tooltip shows the values of that place. Where the tooltip tells the series apart (`shared = false`) a ring is drawn around the bar under the pointer.
**With a line.** A chart that wants a line over its bars is a `PantrixChart`: it takes a `BarSeries` for each run of bars and a `LineSeries` for the line. Its example is on the "Chart" page.

**Value labels.** `labels` writes the values at the ends of the bars, and inside stacked bars; `position` names another place, and `total` writes a stack's total past its end. A label with no room is left out.
**Marks.** `marks` draws a target line or the band of a range, as told on the "Chart" page.
**Automation.** The chart is tagged as the `PantrixChart` it is: `Chart_<tagKey>`.

examples.name: BarChartLongRanking
examples.title: A long ranking
examples.description:
The number of stores in forty provinces, from the most to the fewest: this many rows do not fit in the chart's height. In a horizontal chart that is looked at closer (`zoom`) the first ten provinces fill the plot (`ChartState.zoomTo`); the navigator (`navigator = true`) stands upright at the chart's right and shows all the provinces, and the part in view is dragged along it or made larger by its ends.

Drag the chart up and down with the mouse, turn the wheel, or slide two fingers along it; the wheel with Ctrl, and two fingers moved apart or together, look closer or further off. The buttons go up and down, look further off and closer, and show all the provinces again. With the keyboard the arrow down goes to the next province; reaching one that is out of view moves the part in view.
examples.code:
val state = rememberChartState()
LaunchedEffect(state) { state.zoomTo(start = 0f, end = 0.25f) }
PantrixBarChart(
    data = PROVINCES,
    x = { it.first },
    values = listOf(ChartValue("stores", "Stores") { it.second }),
    modifier = Modifier.height(360.dp),
    horizontal = true,
    zoom = ChartZoom(navigator = true),
    state = state,
    description = "The number of stores in forty provinces, from the most to the fewest",

examples.name: BarChartLabels
examples.title: Values over the bars
examples.description:
Values are written beside the bars (`labels`): over the end of a bar that stands by itself, under a bar that goes below zero. Turn the switch: in stacked bars a value is written inside its bar, in the black or white that reads better on the bar's colour, and the stack's total over its end (`total`). The line marks a target no month reaches (`marks`); where it runs through a label, the label is written on a plate that covers the line there. The target's words stand at the line's start (`labelPosition`): at its end they would take the place of the highest months' labels.

Pick where the labels go with the buttons (`position`): "Auto" is wherever there is room; the others are past the bar's end, inside its end, its middle and its base. Past the end of a stacked bar is the next bar: there the label is written inside the end of its own bar.

A label is written where it has room: one that would stand on another label, reach out of the chart or not fit its bar is left out; the value is still in the tooltip and with the screen reader. `ChartDataLabels(format = …)` says how a value is written; left out, the axis' way of writing is used.

var stacked by remember { mutableStateOf(false) }
var position by remember { mutableStateOf(ChartDataLabelPosition.Auto) }
PantrixSwitchButton(

    onCheckedChange = { stacked = it },
    label = "Stacked",

    fullWidth = false,
    tagKey = "label_place"

pages.title: Waterfall Chart
pages.summary:
A chart that shows how an amount comes about, step by step: each bar starts where the one before it ended, and goes up by what the row adds and down by what it takes away. It is for a period's cash flow, the items of a budget, what comes into a stock and goes out of it.

It is the short way of writing a `PantrixChart` with a single `WaterfallSeries`. The axes, the tooltip, the state, the keyboard and the screen reader are as told on the "Chart" page.
features: **Steps.** A row's value is the amount it adds; below zero, what it takes away. A step that adds is drawn in the chart's `rising` colour and one that takes away in its `falling` colour: the theme's `success` and `danger` colours, unless `colors` says otherwise.

**Totals.** A row that `total` says is a total stands on zero and shows what the steps before it come to; its own value is not asked for. A total with a value of its own is where the count starts again: like the opening amount before the first step. Totals are drawn in the series' own colour (`color`).
**Connecting lines.** A thin line goes from the end of each bar to where the next begins (`connectors`).
**Zero.** The value axis takes zero in: the totals stand on it.

**Tooltip and screen reader.** A step is written as what it adds, with its sign ("+310"); a total as what it comes to. A press is handed the step as the point's `value` and the level the step starts from as its `from`.
**Value labels.** `labels` writes what each bar stands for at its end: over one that goes up, under one that goes down.

**Horizontal.** `horizontal = true` sets the items down the side of the chart; each bar starts where the one above it ended, and one that adds goes right, one that takes away left (the other way about in a language read from the right). The values are written under the chart.
**Automation.** The chart is tagged as the `PantrixChart` it is: `Chart_<tagKey>`. Its one series has the key `steps`.

pages.title: Candlestick Chart
pages.summary:
A chart that shows, at each place, what something opened at, what it closed at, and the highest and the lowest it reached between: a price's trading day, a temperature's day, a measurement's shift.

It is the short way to write a `PantrixChart` that has a single `CandlestickSeries`. The axes, the tooltip, the state, the keyboard and the screen reader are as the "Chart" page tells.
features: **Candle.** Each place has a body from its opening to its close, and a thin wick through the body's middle from the lowest to the highest. A candle that closes over its opening is drawn in the chart's `rising` colour and one that closes under it in its `falling` colour: the theme's `success` and `danger`, unless `colors` says otherwise. A candle that closes where it opened is a line across, in the series' own colour (`color`).

**OHLC bar.** `kind = CandleKind.Ohlc` draws a line in place of the body: from the lowest to the highest, with a tick at the opening on the side lines come from and one at the close on the side they go to. It stays apart where candles would crowd.

**Hollow candle.** `hollow = true` draws the body of a candle that closed higher as its outline alone, with the wick outside the body: the way it went is read without its colour too. A candle that closed lower stays filled.
**A candle's own colour.** `colorOf` gives a row's candle a colour of its own (a day of news); the candle of a row that gives `Color.Unspecified` stays in the colour of its way.
**Legend.** In the legend a series of candles is a sample of two halves: the rising colour and the falling one.

**Volume.** A `BarSeries` with `behind = true` stands behind the candle at each place, as wide as it: the day's trading volume. It is read by the second axis, and that axis' top keeps the bars low in the chart.
**Four values.** A row has all four values, or it has no candle. The wick is no shorter than the body: a highest given under the close is taken for the close.
**Nought.** The axis of values does not take nought in by itself: what is read is how the value moves, not how large it is.

**Tooltip and screen reader.** A candle is written as its four values, each by its name in the theme's language: open, high, low, close. A press is handed the close in the point's `value`, the opening in its `from`, and the two ends of the wick in its `high` and `low`.
**With other series.** Candles stand together with lines in a `PantrixChart`: a moving average, a target.

**Time axis.** When the rows' `x` gives a moment (`kotlin.time.Instant`), the candles stand where their moments are: a day with no row is a gap, and the axis is marked at round dates, not at the days.
**Automation.** The chart is tagged as the `PantrixChart` it is: `Chart_<tagKey>`. Its one series has the key `candles`.

pages.title: Pie Chart
pages.summary:
The parts of a whole as the slices of a disc: each slice takes as much room as its value is of the total. With its middle cut out (`hole`) it is a ring, and the hole has room for a total or a title.

The chart is given its slices: each `PieSlice` is a key, a name and a value. The slices lie in the order they are given, clockwise from twelve o'clock; each is drawn in the theme's next chart colour unless it names its own. The legend, the tooltip and the state are the same parts a chart with axes has, and are given as the "Chart" page tells.
features: **Angle.** `startAngle` is where the first slice begins, in degrees clockwise from twelve o'clock; `sweepAngle` is how much of a turn the slices take together: 360 a whole pie, 180 a half pie. A half pie is as wide as its box allows.

**Order and small slices.** `sort` lays the slices out as given, largest first or smallest first. `others` gathers the slices smaller than a share of the whole into one slice at the end; that slice's tooltip and what a screen reader hears of it name each one it holds.
**Values.** A slice's value is an amount; the chart works out its share. A slice with no value, or one that is not over nought, has no place in the pie, and its name stays in the legend.

**Ring.** `hole` says how much of the radius is cut out: nought is a whole pie, six tenths a ring with room to write in. `center` stands in the hole, in the largest box the hole holds; in a half ring, in the hole of the half that is drawn.

**The slice pointed at.** The slice under the pointer, or the one that is touched, stands out past the pie's rim and the tooltip writes its value and its share. With a finger, another touch on the slice that is pointed at lets go of it.

**Keyboard.** The pie is one stop for Tab: the arrows go from slice to slice, and after the last slice back to the first; Home and End go to the first and the last slice, Escape lets go, Enter and Space press the slice that is pointed at. On desktop and on the web a press on the pie gives it the focus: the arrows that follow go round this pie.
**Legend.** The names of the slices, each beside its colour. Pressing an entry takes the slice out of the pie; the slices that are left share the whole anew.

**Labels.** `labels` writes each slice's share on the slice, in black or white, whichever reads better on its colour; its value, where `format` is given. A label that does not fit on its slice is written outside it with the slice's name, and a line in the slice's colour links it to the slice. `position` changes this: `Outside` writes all of them outside, `Center` only inside. The pie makes room at its two sides for the words outside it; where that room would leave the pie less than half its size, the words stay inside only.
**Screen reader.** The chart says its `description` first, then each slice with its name, its value and its share.
**Direction.** The pie turns clockwise in a language read from right to left too; its legend follows the reading direction.

**Export.** `export` puts a button over the chart: the chart is made, as it is on the screen and without the part that is pointed at or its tooltip, into a PNG, an SVG or a PDF file and handed to the app.
**Automation.** The chart is `PieChart_<tagKey>`; the pie `.Plot`, the slices `.Slice_<number>`, the legend's entries `.Legend_<the slice's key>`, the tooltip `.Tooltip`.

examples.title: The shares of a whole
examples.description:
At its plainest: the slices, each with its key, its name and its value. The first slice starts at twelve o'clock and the others follow it clockwise; the legend stands under the chart.

examples.name: PieChartRing

examples.description:
A pie with its middle cut out is a ring: six tenths of the radius are cut out (`hole`) and the total is written in the hole (`center`).

Take a slice out from the legend: the number in the middle becomes the total of the slices that are left. The screen keeps the chart's state itself (`rememberChartState`) and reads the hidden slices from it.

pages.title: Gauge
pages.summary:
One value on a scale: it is read by how much of an arc it fills. A speed, a load, the used share of a quota: a measure read against its least and its most.

The scale turns clockwise along three quarters of a turn: `min` at the lower left, `max` at the lower right; both are written under the ends. The value fills the arc from where the scale begins up to itself, and is written in the middle of the gauge.
features: **Scale.** `min` and `max` are the ends of the scale. A value past an end stands at that end and is written as it is. A gauge with no value (`null`) shows only its scale.

**Ranges.** `segments` gives parts of the scale a colour and a name: the range that is fine, the range that is too much. Each `GaugeSegment` says where it ends (`upTo`); the first begins where the scale does, the others where the one before ends. The arc fills in the colour of the range the value has reached; the ranges themselves stay under it in their faint colours.

**Needle.** With `needle` a hand reaches from the middle to the value, and the value is written under it. In a gauge with both a needle and ranges the ranges are drawn in their full colours and the arc is not filled: the hand is read against them.

**Writing.** `format` says how the value and the two ends of the scale are written; left out, they are written as numbers in the theme's language. `center` puts your own content in place of the value's writing.
**Screen reader.** The gauge is one thing: its `description`, then the value as it is written and, where it has one, the name of the range it is in.

**Size and motion.** The gauge is as wide as the room it is given and as tall as the chart's style says; the arc is the largest that fits there. When the value changes the arc and the hand go to the new value; where the system asks for reduced motion they do not go, they are there.
**Direction.** The scale turns the same way in a language read from right to left too.

**Export.** `export` puts a button over the chart: the chart is made, as it is on the screen and without the part that is pointed at or its tooltip, into a PNG, an SVG or a PDF file and handed to the app.
**Automation.** `Gauge_<tagKey>`.

    tagKey = "plain"

pages.title: Progress Circle
pages.summary: A ring that fills as a piece of work goes on: how much of an upload has gone, how many steps of a set-up are behind, how much of a quota is used. It shows a share of a whole whose end is known; for work whose end is not known there is the spinner.
features: **Value.** The ring starts at twelve o'clock and fills clockwise by `value` over `max`; a faint ring shows the whole. A value under nought is nought, and one past `max` is the whole.
**Middle.** `content` stands in the middle of the ring: the share as a number, an icon.

**Colour.** The ring is drawn in `color`, or else in the content colour of where it stands (as on a filled card), or else in the primary colour; its track is a faint share of the same colour (unless `trackColor` says otherwise).
**Sizes.** `ProgressCircleStyle` gives the ring's size and thickness; a size on the modifier is the ring's too.
**Motion.** When the value changes the ring goes to the new value; where the system asks for reduced motion it does not go, it is there.

**Screen reader.** It is a progress bar whose name is `contentDescription` and which says the share it has reached. A number written in its middle is read too; it is better hidden from the screen reader, which already hears the share.
**Direction.** The ring fills clockwise in a language read from right to left too.

**Export.** `export` puts a button over the chart: the chart is made, as it is on the screen and without the part that is pointed at or its tooltip, into a PNG, an SVG or a PDF file and handed to the app.
**Automation.** `ProgressCircle_<tagKey>`.

pages.title: Meter Group
pages.summary:
Several amounts of one whole, side by side on one bar: what a storage is filled with, where a budget goes. The parts are read against each other and against what is left.

The bar is as long as `max`. Each `MeterItem` takes as much of the bar as its value; the parts are set out in order from the start of the line, each drawn in the theme's next chart colour unless it names its own. What no part takes shows the bar's track.
features: **Values.** A part's value is counted in what `max` is counted in. A part with no value, or one that is not over nought, takes none of the bar, and its name stays in the legend. What the parts come to past `max` is cut off at the bar's end.

**Legend.** It writes each part's name, then its value, beside its colour. It stands above the bar or under it: a legend at the start counts as above, one at the end as under. Its entries are no switches here: the bar shows what it is given.
**Writing.** `format` says how a value is written in the legend; left out, it is written as a number in the theme's language.
**Screen reader.** The bar is a picture with its `description`; the legend's entries say the parts. A bar with no legend says its parts itself.
**Direction.** In a language read from right to left the first part stands at the right.

**Export.** `export` puts a button over the chart: the chart is made, as it is on the screen and without the part that is pointed at or its tooltip, into a PNG, an SVG or a PDF file and handed to the app.
**Automation.** `MeterGroup_<tagKey>`; the bar `.Bar`, the legend's entries `.Legend_<the part's key>`.

pages.title: Status Tracker
pages.summary:
A run of steps as a row of blocks: each block in the colour of what was the case at that step. The days a service was up, the builds that passed: where the bad ones are is seen at a glance, and which they are is read by going over them.

Each `StatusBlock` is a name and a colour. The blocks are set side by side from the start of the line, each with an even share of the width. A block that is given no colour is drawn in the colour of the chart's grid: a step of which nothing is known.
features: **The block pointed at.** The name of the block under the pointer, or of the one that is touched, is written under the row beside its colour; the others are drawn faint. With a finger, another touch on the block that is pointed at lets go of it.
**The line under the row.** With `caption` off the name is not written. The line's room is kept whether a block is pointed at or not: the row does not move.

**Keyboard.** The row is one stop for Tab: the arrows go from block to block and stop at the ends, Home and End go to the first and the last block, Escape lets go, Enter and Space press the block that is pointed at.
**Pressing.** `onSelect` gives the place of the block that is pressed, counted from nought.
**State.** The block that is pointed at is kept in `ChartState`, as a selection whose `x` is the block's place.
**Screen reader.** The row says its `description`, then each block by its name. A row of more than two hundred blocks is told by its description alone.
**Direction.** In a language read from right to left the first block stands at the right, and the arrows go the way they point.

**Export.** `export` puts a button over the chart: the chart is made, as it is on the screen and without the part that is pointed at or its tooltip, into a PNG, an SVG or a PDF file and handed to the app.
**Automation.** `StatusTracker_<tagKey>`; the row `.Blocks`, the blocks `.Block_<number>`, the line under the row `.Caption`.

pages.title: Sparkline
pages.summary: The run of a number in the room of a word: it stands beside the number it belongs to. It has no axes, no legend and nothing to point at: it shows which way the number has gone, and a chart shows the rest.
features: **Values.** The values are set out at even steps from the start of the line to its end. A line and an area are drawn between the least and the most of the values: the run fills the height it has. Bars are drawn from nought.

**Ends.** `min` is the value at the foot of the height and `max` the one at its top: several runs read on one scale. A value past the ends is cut off at the box's edge. An end not given comes from the values and the reference line.
**Curve.** `curve` says how a line and an area go from one value to the next (`ChartCurve`): straight, rounded without going past the values, or in steps. Bars have no curve.
**Last value.** `markLast = true` marks the last value: a dot on a line and an area, and on bars the last bar in full colour and the others fainter. The last value is the last one that is a number.
**Reference line.** `reference` draws a dashed line behind the values, in the colour charts write in: a target, or where the run began.
**Style.** `style` goes over the theme's sizes: the line's width (`lineWidth`), the gap between bars (`barGap`), the last value's dot (`markerSize`) and the reference line's width (`markLineWidth`).
**Kind.** `SparklineKind.Line` is a line, `Area` a line faintly filled under it, `Bar` a bar for each value.
**A missing value.** A value that is `null`, or no number, is a gap in a line and an empty place among bars.
**Size and colour.** It is 96dp wide and 32dp tall unless the modifier says otherwise; it is drawn in `color`, or else in the theme's first chart colour.
**Screen reader.** With a `contentDescription` it is a picture of that name; with none it is not read at all: that suits a run beside a number that says the same.
**Direction.** In a language read from right to left the first value stands at the right.

**Export.** `export` puts a button over the chart: the chart is made, as it is on the screen and without the part that is pointed at or its tooltip, into a PNG, an SVG or a PDF file and handed to the app.
**Automation.** `Sparkline_<tagKey>`.

        values = SPARK_TEMPERATURE,
        contentDescription = "Today's temperature, in steps",
        tagKey = "steps",

pages.title: Scatter Chart
pages.summary:
Points set out by two values: one along the chart, the other up it. It shows how two things go together: do sales rise with the temperature, does what costs more rate higher too. Give each point a size by a third value and it is a bubble chart.

The chart is given its series; each `ScatterSeries` carries its own rows: where a row stands along the chart (`x`), where up it (`y`) and, for bubbles, how large it is (`size`). Both axes are of values: each goes from a round number under its values to one over them, and marks the round values between.
features: **Bubbles.** The points of a series that is given `size` are bubbles. A bubble's area is as much as its size is of the largest size in the chart: twice the value, twice the area. How large the smallest and the largest bubble are is in the chart's style (`bubbleMinSize`, `bubbleMaxSize`). A chart with bubbles keeps room for the largest at the ends of its axes.
**A point's name.** `label` says what a point is called: a country, a product. It is the tooltip's heading and what a screen reader says.

**Axes.** `xAxis` and `yAxis` are the `ChartAxis` of a chart with places: title, format, ends, grid lines. The titles are what the values are called in the tooltip. `sizeAxis` says what the size is called (`title`), how it is written (`format`) and the value the largest bubble stands for (`max`); nothing of it is drawn.
**Marks.** `marks` draws a line at a value or a band between two; here a mark's `x` is a value of the axis along the chart.

**The point pointed at.** The point under the pointer, or near it, or touched by a finger, is pointed at: a ring about it, two lines through it and the tooltip that writes its values. Of points that lie on one another, the smallest is pointed at.

**Keyboard.** The chart is one stop for Tab: the right and left arrows go along the chart between the points of a series, the up and down arrows to the series before and after, Home and End to the series' first and last point, Escape lets go, Enter and Space press the point that is pointed at.

**State and pressing.** The point that is pointed at is kept in `ChartState`, as a selection whose `x` is the row's place in its series and whose `series` is the series' key. `onSelect` gives the pressed point with the same place.
**Screen reader.** The chart says its `description`, then each point, series by series, with its name and its values. A chart of more than two hundred points is told by its description alone.
**Direction.** In a language read from right to left the values along the chart start from the right, and those up it are written at the right.

**Export.** `export` puts a button over the chart: the chart is made, as it is on the screen and without the part that is pointed at or its tooltip, into a PNG, an SVG or a PDF file and handed to the app.

**Zoom.** With `zoom` the reader looks closer at both values at once: a wheel (with Ctrl or Command), two fingers, the plus and minus keys and the buttons look closer; a drag moves what is in view every way.
**Automation.** `ScatterChart_<tagKey>`; the plot is `.Plot`, the points `.Point_<series>_<number>`, the legend's entries `.Legend_<series>`, the tooltip `.Tooltip`.

examples.name: ScatterChartPlain
examples.title: Two values, two groups
examples.description:
Fifty days of a café: the day's temperature and the cold drinks sold that day. Weekdays and weekends are separate series; the points go up with the temperature, and the weekends higher still.

Move the pointer near a point, or touch one: the tooltip writes the day's two values under the titles of the axes. Pressing an entry of the legend takes that series out of the chart.
examples.code:
PantrixScatterChart(
    series = listOf(
        ScatterSeries("weekdays", "Weekdays", cafeDays(weekend = false), x = { it.heat }, y = { it.sold }),
        ScatterSeries("weekend", "Weekend", cafeDays(weekend = true), x = { it.heat }, y = { it.sold })
    ),
    xAxis = ChartAxis(title = "Temperature (°C)"),
    yAxis = ChartAxis(title = "Cold drinks"),
    description = "Cold drinks sold by temperature",
    tagKey = "plain"
)

internal fun cafeDays(weekend: Boolean): List<CafeDay> = List(50) { it }
    .filter { (it % 7 >= 5) == weekend }
    .map { day ->
        val heat = 12.0 + (day * 7 % 19) + (day % 4) * 0.5
        val wobble = (day * 37 % 29) - 14
        val busy = if (weekend) 45 else 0
        CafeDay(
            heat = heat,
            sold = (heat * 6.5 - 40 + wobble + busy).toInt().coerceAtLeast(4),
            hot = (190 - heat * 4.5 + wobble).toInt().coerceAtLeast(4),
            food = 85 + wobble + busy / 3
        )
    }

internal class CafeDay(
    val heat: Double,
    val sold: Int,
    val hot: Int,
    val food: Int
)

pages.title: Radar Chart
pages.summary:
Several measures of one thing are set out on spokes about a middle and joined into a web: its shape is read at a glance, and two things are told apart by theirs. The skills of two people, a product and its rival, this year and the last.

The chart is given its series; each `RadarSeries` carries its own rows: the spoke a row stands on (`x`) and its value there (`y`). The spokes are set out in the order the series name them, clockwise from twelve o'clock. All the spokes are read by one axis of values: out from the middle, from nought to a round number over the values.
features: **Web.** Each series is a web: its line, its fill with a share of its colour (`filled`; the share is `fillAlpha`, a fifth where left out) and a mark at each of its values (`marker`). The line can be dashed or dotted (`dash`): to tell a target from what was measured. Every fill lies under every line.
**Rings.** `grid` says whether the rings of the values are drawn straight from spoke to spoke (as a web) or round.

**Axes.** `xAxis` is the spokes: whether their names are written (`labels`), how they are written (`label`), whether the spokes are drawn (`line`). `yAxis` is the axis of values: its ends, how many values it marks, how they are written, whether the values are written (`labels`) and whether the rings are drawn (`grid`). The axis of values starts at nought unless it is told otherwise.

**The spoke pointed at.** The spoke nearest the pointer, or the one that is tapped, is pointed at: the spoke stands out, the values on it grow, and the tooltip writes the values the series have there. With `ChartTooltip(shared = false)` the tooltip writes only the value of the series nearest the pointer.

**Keyboard.** The chart is one stop for Tab: the arrows go from spoke to spoke round the chart, and after the last back to the first; Home and End go to the first and the last spoke, Escape lets go, Enter and Space press the value that is pointed at.
**Screen reader.** The chart says its `description`, then each spoke with the values the series have there.
**Direction.** The chart turns the same way in a language read from right to left too.

**Export.** `export` puts a button over the chart: the chart is made, as it is on the screen and without the part that is pointed at or its tooltip, into a PNG, an SVG or a PDF file and handed to the app.
**Automation.** `RadarChart_<tagKey>`; the plot is `.Plot`, the spokes `.Point_<number>`, the legend's entries `.Legend_<series>`, the tooltip `.Tooltip`.

pages.title: Polar Chart
pages.summary:
Bars set out round a middle: each as long from the middle out as its value. It suits what comes round again: the hours of a day, the months of a year, the points of a compass; and what is to be compared at a glance by how far each reaches.

The chart is given its series; each `PolarSeries` carries its own rows: the sector a row stands in (`x`) and its value there (`y`). The sectors are set out in the order the series name them, clockwise from twelve o'clock, each an equal part of the turn. The axis of values goes out from the middle: from nought to a round number over the values.
features: **Side by side and stacked.** The bars of several series stand side by side in a sector; the series that name the same `stack` share one bar there, each further out than the one before it.
**The hole in the middle.** With `hole` the bars start from a ring: the shortest shows too. No more than nine tenths of the radius.

**Rings.** The value rings are round: so are the bars' ends, which are read against them. With `grid = RadarGrid.Polygon` the rings are drawn straight from one side of a sector to the other, and the bars' ends are straight too. The marked values are written over the line at the start of the first sector, over the bars.
**Fill.** `fillAlpha` says how much of its colour a series' bars are filled with: under one, the rings behind show. The legend and the tooltip show the whole colour.

**Axes.** `xAxis` is the sectors: their names (`labels`, `label`) and the lines between them (`line`). `yAxis` is the axis of values: its ends, how many values it marks, how they are written, the values (`labels`) and the rings (`grid`).
**The sector pointed at.** The sector the pointer is over, or the one that is tapped, is shaded, and the tooltip writes the values the series have there.

**Keyboard.** The chart is one stop for Tab: the arrows go from sector to sector round the chart, and after the last back to the first; Home and End go to the first and the last sector, Escape lets go, Enter and Space press the value that is pointed at.
**Screen reader.** The chart says its `description`, then each sector with the values the series have there.
**Direction.** The chart turns the same way in a language read from right to left too.

**Export.** `export` puts a button over the chart: the chart is made, as it is on the screen and without the part that is pointed at or its tooltip, into a PNG, an SVG or a PDF file and handed to the app.
**Automation.** `PolarChart_<tagKey>`; the plot is `.Plot`, the sectors `.Point_<number>`, the legend's entries `.Legend_<series>`, the tooltip `.Tooltip`.

pages.title: Heatmap
pages.summary:
A grid of cells: each cell in a shade that says how much its value is. It suits what has two names and a number: the hours of the days of a week, the months of several years, one list set against another. What is much and what is little is seen at a glance; a table of the same numbers has to be read.

The chart is given its data and three ways to read a datum: the column it stands in (`x`), its row (`y`) and its value (`value`). The columns and the rows are those the data name, in the order they are first named. A datum with no value fills no cell; a cell that no datum fills is drawn faint.
features: **Scale.** `HeatmapScale` says how a value becomes a shade: its two ends (`min`, `max`; left out, the least and the most of the values), how many shades it has (`steps`; at nought each value has its own) and its colour (`color`). With one colour, a shade is a share of the colour on what the chart stands on: it reads in a light theme and a dark one. Given `low`, the scale goes from the least's colour `low` to `color`; the shades between are the two colours mixed in Oklab, each step changing as much as the one before.
**The value in a cell.** With `labels` each cell has its value written in it, in the one of black and white that reads better on its shade; it is not written in a cell it has no room in.
**Scale bar.** `legend` says where the scale of shades stands: the least and the most of the values are written at its ends.
**Names.** `xAxis` is the names of the columns and `yAxis` of the rows: whether they are written (`labels`) and how (`label`). A name that has no room is left out by a rule.
**The cell pointed at.** The cell under the pointer, or the one that is tapped, is ringed, and the tooltip writes its column, its row and its value.

**Keyboard.** The chart is one stop for Tab: the arrows go from cell to cell, past the blank cells; Home and End go to the first and the last cell, Escape lets go, Enter and Space press the cell that is pointed at.

**State and pressing.** The cell that is pointed at is kept in `ChartState`, as a selection whose `x` is the datum's place in the list. `onSelect` gives the cell that is pressed: `label` is its column, `name` its row, `value` its value.
**Screen reader.** The chart says its `description`, then each cell, row after row, with its column, its row and its value. A chart of more than two hundred cells is told by its description alone.
**Direction.** In a language read from right to left the columns start from the right, and the rows' names are written at the right.

**Export.** `export` puts a button over the chart: the chart is made, as it is on the screen and without the part that is pointed at or its tooltip, into a PNG, an SVG or a PDF file and handed to the app.
**Automation.** `Heatmap_<tagKey>`; the cells are `.Plot`, a cell `.Cell_<number>`, the scale `.Legend`, the tooltip `.Tooltip`.

    value = { it.visits },

)

internal fun weekVisits(): List<SlotVisits> {
    val days = listOf("Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun")
    val hours = listOf("09", "11", "13", "15", "17", "19")
    val visits = listOf(
        listOf(12, 18, 34, 22, 41, 30),
        listOf(10, 16, 31, 20, 38, 28),
        listOf(14, 21, 36, 25, 44, 33),
        listOf(11, 19, 35, 27, 47, 36),
        listOf(16, 24, 42, 31, 58, 52),
        listOf(28, 45, 61, 66, 72, 57),
        listOf(22, 39, 54, 60, 49, 26)
    )
    return days.flatMapIndexed { day, name -> hours.mapIndexed { slot, at -> SlotVisits(name, at, visits[day][slot]) } }
}

internal class SlotVisits(
    val day: String,
    val hours: String,
    val visits: Int
)

examples.title: Five shades, with the values written

    data = examScores(),
    x = { it.subject },
    y = { it.student },

    labels = ChartDataLabels(),
    legend = ChartLegend(position = ChartLegendPosition.End),
    description = "Students' scores by subject",
    tagKey = "steps"
)

internal fun examScores(): List<ExamScore> {
    val subjects = listOf("Maths", "Physics", "Chemistry", "History", "Language")
    val scores = mapOf(
        "Ada" to listOf(92, 85, 78, 64, 88),
        "Lin" to listOf(71, 58, null, 90, 95),
        "Can" to listOf(45, 62, 70, 81, 39),
        "Ece" to listOf(84, 97, 91, 55, 73)
    )
    return scores.flatMap { (student, row) ->
        subjects.mapIndexed { at, subject -> ExamScore(student, subject, row[at]) }
    }
}

internal class ExamScore(
    val student: String,
    val subject: String,
    val score: Int?
)

pages.title: Treemap
pages.summary:
A box cut into tiles: each tile as large as its value is of the whole. It suits a whole of many parts, where a pie would have too many slices to read: the folders of a disk, a budget by its lines, a market by its companies. What is large is seen at once, and the small parts have their place too.

The chart is given its items. Each `TreemapItem` is a tile, or a group whose own items are its tiles (`children`). A group's tiles lie together in a block, in the group's colour, with the group's name over them where there is room. The blocks are set out from the largest on, and so are the tiles in each block.
features: **What is written in a tile.** With `labels` each tile has its name written in it and under it its value, in the one of black and white that reads better on its colour. A tile with no room for its name has neither; the tooltip and a screen reader say both.
**Groups.** An item that gives `children` is a group: its value is the sum of its tiles, and a value given to it is not read.
**Colour.** Each item given takes the one of the theme's chart colours that falls to its place; a group's tiles are in the group's colour. `color` gives an item or a tile a colour of its own.

**Shaded by value.** Given a `scale`, every tile is drawn in its value's shade on the scale, as a heatmap's cells are (`HeatmapScale`): a large tile lies nearer the scale's end. The item's and the group's colours are not read then; the blocks and the groups' names stay. The scale bar stands where `legend` says.
**The tile pointed at.** The tile under the pointer, or the one that is tapped, is ringed, and the tooltip writes its group, its name, its value and its share of the whole.

**Keyboard.** The chart is one stop for Tab: an arrow goes to the nearest tile the way it points; Home and End go to the largest tile and the last, Escape lets go, Enter and Space press the tile that is pointed at.
**State and pressing.** The tile that is pointed at is kept in `ChartState`, as a selection whose `x` is the item's key. `onSelect` gives the tile that is pressed.

**Screen reader.** The chart says its `description`, then each tile from the largest block on, with its group, its name, its value and its share. A chart of more than two hundred tiles is told by its description alone.
**Direction.** In a language read from right to left the largest tile lies at the right.

**Export.** `export` puts a button over the chart: the chart is made, as it is on the screen and without the part that is pointed at or its tooltip, into a PNG, an SVG or a PDF file and handed to the app.
**Automation.** `Treemap_<tagKey>`; the tiles `.Plot`, a tile `.Tile_<number>`, the scale `.Legend`, the tooltip `.Tooltip`.

pages.title: Funnel Chart
pages.summary: A chart that shows the stages of a way that fewer and fewer get through: the stages stand one under another, each as wide as the number that reached it. It shows where the others were lost: of those who visited, those who signed up; of those, the ones who tried; of those, the ones who paid.
features: **Shape.** The largest stage is as wide as the chart; each stage narrows to the width of the one after it, and the stages make one funnel. The last keeps its width. A stage larger than the one before it does not narrow but widens: the chart draws what it is given. `shape = FunnelShape.Bars` draws each stage as a bar as wide as its value; `horizontal` lays the stages side by side from where lines start, each as tall as its value.

**Words.** A stage's name and value are written in it; beside the value stands its share: of the first stage, of the one before, or both (`rate`). A stage too narrow for its words has its name and value beside it, under it in a horizontal funnel; where there is room for neither, only the name is left. `labels = null` writes nothing.

**The stage pointed at.** The stage whose row the pointer or a finger is on is ringed, and the tooltip writes its name, its value and its share. On the keyboard the arrows go from stage to stage: up and down, right and left in a horizontal funnel.
**Colours.** Each stage takes one of the theme's chart colours, by its place; the `color` field of `FunnelStage` gives a stage its own.

**Screen reader.** First the chart's description, then each stage in its order: its name, its value and its shares. A share of the first stage written alone is read bare; otherwise each share is read with what it is a share of.

**Export.** `export` puts a button over the chart: the chart is made, as it is on the screen and without the part that is pointed at or its tooltip, into a PNG, an SVG or a PDF file and handed to the app.
**Automation.** The chart is tagged `Funnel_<tagKey>`, and a stage `Funnel_<tagKey>.Stage_<number>`. A press on a stage is reported as a `select` event with the stage's key.

pages.title: Sankey Chart
pages.summary: A chart that shows what flows from where to where, and how much. The nodes stand in columns; between them lie bands as wide as what flows: where the visitors of a site come from and what they go on to, what a budget is made of and what it is spent on.
features: **Nodes and links.** The chart takes its nodes (`SankeyNode`) and the links between them (`SankeyLink`); a link names its two nodes by their keys. Links between the same two nodes are one flow.

**Columns.** The columns come from the links: a node nothing flows into stands in the first column, the others a column past the last of those that flow into them, and a node nothing flows out of in the last. `align` chooses where a node that could stand in more than one column stands: `Justify`, `Left`, `Right`, `Center`. The nodes of a column are put in the order that keeps their flows from crossing as far as it can; `order = SankeyOrder.Given` leaves them in the order they were given.

**Size.** A node is as tall as the greater of what flows into it and what flows out of it; a band is as wide as what flows. A node's width and the room between two nodes of a column are `ChartStyle`'s `nodeWidth` and `nodeGap`.

**The node pointed at.** The node under the pointer or a finger is ringed, its flows stand out and the others fade. The tooltip writes the node and each of its flows, with the name of the node at its other end. On the keyboard the arrows go to the nearest node the way they point.

**The flow pointed at.** Where the pointer or a finger is on a flow, the flow stands out, the others fade, and the tooltip writes its two nodes the way it flows ("Search → Signed up"). The keyboard stays on the nodes.
**What is refused.** A link from a node to itself, links that lead back to where they started, and a link that names a node the chart does not have are refused.
**Screen reader.** First the chart's description, then each node, column by column: what it counts for, and each of its flows with where it comes from or goes to.

**Export.** `export` puts a button over the chart: the chart is made, as it is on the screen and without the part that is pointed at or its tooltip, into a PNG, an SVG or a PDF file and handed to the app.

**Automation.** The chart is tagged `Sankey_<tagKey>`, a node `Sankey_<tagKey>.Node_<number>`. A press on a node is reported as a `select` event with the node's key, and a press on a flow with the keys of its two nodes (`source>target`).

pages.title: Gantt Chart
pages.summary: A chart that shows the tasks of a plan: each task in a row, a bar from the moment it starts to the moment it ends. It shows what runs when, what overlaps, and how much of each task is done.
features: **Tasks.** The chart takes its tasks (`GanttTask`) in the order of their rows; each task has a key, a name, and the moments it starts and ends. Moments are `kotlin.time.Instant`: no date library is needed.

**Time.** Time runs along the chart, from the start of the first task to the end of the last. Its axis is marked at round moments (day, week, month), as many as have room, and at each mark a line goes up through the rows. Moments are read by the device's clock and written in the theme's language, unless `time` (`ChartTime`) says otherwise.
**Progress.** A task that gives `progress` has that much of its bar in full colour and the rest faint.
**Milestone.** A task that ends when it starts is a moment, and is drawn as a diamond.

**Today.** Where `today` is given and lies in the chart's time, a line runs over the bars at it and "Today" is written on a line of its own over the rows. The chart has no clock of its own: the moment it is read at is the caller's to give.

**Groups.** Tasks that give a `group` gather under a row of the group's own: the group's bar runs from the start of its first task to the end of its last, with its ends pointing down; the tasks' names stand a little in from the group's. The group's name is the heading of its tasks' tooltip, and a screen reader says it too.

**Rows.** Tasks that give the same `row` share a row, side by side in time, and the row is called by that name: a person's work in a row of their own. Tasks whose times overlap stand one under another in the row, and the row grows by a row's height for each. Within the row the pointer goes to the task it is over; the tasks share the row halfway between them.
**Rings.** Tasks that follow one another cannot close a ring: a task that follows a task that follows it is refused.

**Dependencies.** `after` holds the keys of the tasks a task follows: from where each ends to where this one starts an arrow is drawn, turning at right angles; where the task starts too soon the arrow goes round below or above. A key the chart does not have, or the task's own, is refused.
**Weekends.** `weekends = true` shades the Saturdays and Sundays faint by the chart's clock; where a day is narrower than two pixels it shades none.

**Names.** The tasks' names stand in a column at the start of the rows, no wider than two fifths of the chart; a name that does not fit is cut short with three dots. `names = false` takes the column away.

**The task pointed at.** The bar of the task whose row the pointer or the finger is in is ringed, and the tooltip writes its name, the moments it starts and ends and, where it is said, how much of it is done. With the keyboard the arrows up and down go from task to task.
**Size.** Given no height, the chart is as tall as its rows need, group headers among them: thirty-two dp a row, and one more over them where "Today" is written.

**Screen reader.** First the chart's description, then where the today line is drawn "Today" and its day, then each task in the tasks' order: its group and row where it has them, its name, its start, its end and its progress.

**Export.** `export` puts a button over the chart: the chart is made, as it is on the screen and without the part that is pointed at or its tooltip, into a PNG, an SVG or a PDF file and handed to the app.

**Zoom.** With `zoom` a part of the time is shown as wide as the chart: a wheel (with Ctrl or Command), two fingers, the plus and minus keys and the buttons look closer; a drag and the buttons move along the time.
**Automation.** The chart is tagged `Gantt_<tagKey>` and a task `Gantt_<tagKey>.Task_<number>`. A press on a task is reported as a `select` event with the task's key.

examples.name: GanttChartPlain
examples.title: The plan of a release
examples.description:
The plan of a release: four tasks and two milestones. The tasks that are finished are in full colour; of those under way the part that is done is in full colour and the rest faint. The upright line shows today (`today`): what is to its left is past.

Move the pointer over a row, or touch the row: the bar is ringed and the tooltip writes the task's start, its end and how far it is. The days are days of UTC, so the chart is read by UTC too (the `offset` of `ChartTime`).
examples.code:
PantrixGanttChart(
    tasks = RELEASE_PLAN,
    time = ChartTime(offset = { Duration.ZERO }),
    today = dayAt("04-14"),
    description = "The plan of the spring release: from research to release",
    tagKey = "plain"
)

private val RELEASE_PLAN = listOf(
    GanttTask("research", "Research", start = dayAt("03-02"), end = dayAt("03-14"), progress = 1f),
    GanttTask("design", "Design", start = dayAt("03-09"), end = dayAt("03-28"), progress = 1f),
    GanttTask("build", "Development", start = dayAt("03-23"), end = dayAt("04-25"), progress = 0.55f),

)

var named by remember { mutableStateOf(true) }

        GanttTask(task.key, task.name, task.start, task.end, task.progress, color)

pages.title: Platform and system
pages.summary: The platform the code runs on and the system's accessibility settings. The theme reads them itself and tells the components; the app can read them from the same place.
features: **Platform.** `currentPlatformType()` is Android, iOS, desktop or web; `currentOperatingSystem()` is the operating system, in a browser the one the browser runs on.

**The platform's conventions.** `PantrixPlatform` is accessibility decisions: the smallest touch target, the focus ring's width and whether it is shown for the keyboard alone, whether it is used by touch. `rememberPantrixPlatform()` gives this device's, `PantrixPlatform.forType(…)` a platform's; `PantrixTheme(platform = …)` gives them to what is in it.
**System settings.** Reducing motion, high contrast, telling apart by marks other than colour, a touch pointer, the system's language and its clock's offset from UTC: each is a `system…` function.
**Pointer shapes.** `PantrixPointerIcons` is the pointer over a control that makes something larger or smaller when it is dragged: across, and up and down. Compose's own four pointers do not have it.

examples.name: PlatformThisDevice
examples.title: This device
examples.description: This device: the platform the code runs on, the operating system and the platform's conventions (`rememberPantrixPlatform()`). The platform the theme says (`PantrixTheme.platform`) can be another: another platform's look can be chosen in this app's "Settings"; the device itself does not change.

examples.name: PlatformSystemSettings
examples.title: System settings
examples.description: The system's settings, as they are when read: reducing motion, increasing contrast, telling apart by marks other than colour ("Differentiate Without Color" on iOS), whether the pointer is a finger, the system's language and its clock's offset from UTC. When a setting changes the lines change too.

examples.name: PlatformOtherRules
examples.title: Another platform's conventions
examples.description: Another platform's conventions, on this device: the inner theme was given `PantrixPlatform.forType(…)`. The components are drawn with that platform's look and touch target: 44dp on iOS, 48dp on Android, 32dp on a desktop used with a mouse. Choose a platform and look at the text field's and the button's height.

examples.name: PlatformResizePointer
examples.title: Resize pointer
examples.description: Making a panel wider by dragging its edge and taller by dragging its bottom edge. Over a handle the pointer is the one that says what a drag will change: `pointerHoverIcon(PantrixPointerIcons.ResizeHorizontal)` and `ResizeVertical`. The pointer shows on a desktop, on the web, and on Android under a mouse; on iOS Compose does not change the pointer at all, and under a finger there is no pointer. A real handle is open to a keyboard and a screen reader too: the handle of `PantrixListDetailScaffold(resizable = true)` is.

pages.title: Haptics
pages.summary: Haptic feedback: a component asks not for a vibration pattern but for what it means: a selection, a switch turned on or off, a success, an error. The platform plays its own pattern for that meaning.
features: **Meanings.** `HapticType` is the name of what is said: `Selection`, `ToggleOn`, `ToggleOff`, `Success`, `Warning`, `Error`, `Impact`, `LongPress`.
**The platform's patterns.** `rememberPlatformHaptics()` is the device itself on Android and iOS; on the desktop and the web it plays nothing (`PantrixHaptics.NoOp`).
**The theme's.** `PantrixTheme(haptics = …)` gives the components' haptics somewhere else: to turn them off from a setting, or to count them in a test. `PantrixTheme.haptics` is the nearest theme's.

examples.name: HapticsOfComponents
examples.title: The components' haptics
examples.description: The haptics the components ask for. The inner theme takes a `PantrixHaptics` that plays the device's patterns but writes their name first: change the switch and the checkbox, and the line underneath says what the component asked for. On the desktop and the web the line is written, but nothing vibrates.

examples.name: HapticsOfTheApp
examples.title: The app's own haptic
examples.description: The app's own haptic: when a job is done or an error happens the app asks from the same place, `LocalPantrixHaptics.current.perform(…)`. On a phone each button plays the pattern of its own meaning.

pages.title: Clipboard
pages.summary: The clipboard, for plain text. Compose's clipboard takes another type on each platform; `PantrixClipboard` puts a text there the same way on every platform and says whether it got there.
features: **Copying.** `rememberPantrixClipboard()` gives the clipboard; `copyText(text, label)` puts the text there and returns `true` if it got there. The `label` is carried on Android alone.

**The clipboard's traits.** `ClipboardTraits` says what the clipboard is like: whether it can be written (`writable`), whether the system shows what was copied itself (`announcedBySystem`). A web page that is not secure and a JVM with no display have no clipboard; Android 13 and later show what was copied themselves and ask the app not to say it again.
**In a test.** `LocalClipboardTraits` gives the clipboard's traits: a test or a preview gives another platform's.

examples.name: ClipboardCopyText
examples.title: Copying a text
