examples.description: Copying a text. The button puts the IBAN on the clipboard and writes the outcome on the card's "Last event" line. Where the system shows what was copied itself (Android 13 and later) the app says nothing: announcing a success twice is noise. The line above describes this platform's clipboard (`currentClipboardTraits()`).

appNames.name: LocalExampleEvents
appNames.description: Where an example tells its card what happens in it: a button pressed, a row chosen, a dialog closed. The card writes the last thing told under the example, on its "Last event" line.

examples.name: ClipboardNotWritable
examples.title: A clipboard that cannot be written
examples.description: A clipboard that cannot be written: the inner section gave `LocalClipboardTraits` a `ClipboardTraits(writable = false)`, as on a web page that is not secure. Press the code block's copy button: the block says it could not copy, and shows no success.

pages.title: Files
pages.summary: Files, without a component: the platform's own file picker and files dropped on a place. `PantrixFileDrop` is built on these two; a screen that wants a look of its own uses them directly.
features: **Picker.** `rememberFilePicker()` gives the platform's picker (`FilePicker`); `pick(request) { files -> … }` opens it and hands over what was chosen. `FilePickRequest` says what is shown (`accept`) and whether several files can be chosen (`multiple`). Where only pictures are asked for, Android and iOS open their photo picker.

**Dropping.** `Modifier.fileDropTarget(onOver, onFiles)` takes the files dropped on an element: on the desktop and the web, from another app or another window. `onOver` says `true` while files are over it.

**Saving.** `rememberFileSaver()` gives the platform's window for saving a file (`FileSaver`); `save(file) { result -> … }` writes the file where the user chooses and says what became of it (`FileSaveResult`): the window for a new document on Android, Files on iOS, the save dialog on the desktop, the browser's download on the web.
**File.** `PantrixFile` carries its name, size and type; its content is read when it is asked for.

**A screen's picker.** Where `LocalFilePicker` gives a picker, `rememberFilePicker()` returns it in the place of the platform's: a preview or a test gives every picker of a screen the same one at once. `LocalFileSaver` does the same for the saver.

examples.name: FilesPick
examples.title: Having a file chosen
examples.description: The platform's own picker: "Choose PDFs" shows only PDFs and lets several files be chosen (`FilePickRequest(accept = listOf(PantrixFileType.Pdf), multiple = true)`). The chosen ones are written underneath with their names and sizes; on a cancel the list comes empty.

examples.name: FilesDrop
examples.title: Files dropped on a place
examples.description: Files dropped on a place: the box carries `fileDropTarget`. On the desktop or the web, drag a file over the box: the box takes a colour while it is over it, and on a drop the files are written underneath. On a phone files are not dropped; the picker is used there.

examples.name: FilesGivenPicker
examples.title: A screen with sample files
examples.description: Giving a screen its picker from outside: while "Sample files" is on, the screen gets a sample picker through `LocalFilePicker`, and "Choose an offer" gives two sample files without opening the platform's picker; while it is off, the platform's picker opens. The screen itself does not change, it calls `rememberFilePicker()`: a preview or a test checks it this way. `PantrixFileDrop` takes its default picker from here too.

examples.name: FilesSave
examples.title: Having a file saved
examples.description: Handing the user a file the app made: "Save the note" opens the platform's window for saving, the file is written where the user chose, and what became of it is written underneath: saved, cancelled, or on the web the download started.

examples.name: FilesGivenSaver
examples.title: A screen with a sample saver
examples.description: Giving a screen its saver from outside: while "Sample saver" is on, the screen is given a saver through `LocalFileSaver`, and "Save the report" takes the file without opening a window and says it was saved; while it is off, the platform's window opens. A preview or a test checks a screen this way, without changing it.

pages.title: Keyboard shortcuts
pages.summary: Keyboard shortcuts: a key and what is held with it. With Command on Apple's systems and with Ctrl on the others: `⌘S` and `Ctrl+S` are the same shortcut.
features: **Shortcut.** `PantrixShortcut(Key.S, command = true)` says the key and what is held; `writtenOn(system)` gives it as that system writes it (`⌥⇧⌘K`, `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+K`), `keysOn(system)` key by key.
**Listening.** `Modifier.onShortcut(shortcut) { … }` listens for the shortcut while the focus is on the element or inside it, before the control inside.
**The focus's root.** `Modifier.shortcutRoot()` holds the focus itself while nothing in it does: a screen's shortcuts are heard without a field being pressed.
**System.** `currentOperatingSystem()` says the system; `LocalOperatingSystem` gives another system in a preview or a test.

examples.name: ShortcutsOnAScreen
examples.title: A screen's shortcut
examples.description: A shortcut: the box listens for the save shortcut with `onShortcut`, and with `shortcutRoot` holds the focus itself while no field in it does. Press the box once, then press the shortcut: the count goes up. It is heard while typing in the field too, before the field. On a phone it works with a keyboard attached.

examples.name: ShortcutsOnOtherSystems
examples.title: On another system
examples.description: The same shortcut on three systems. Each line gives another system with `LocalOperatingSystem` and writes the shortcut as that system writes it: with symbols on Apple's systems, with names on the others. The top line is this device's system (`currentOperatingSystem()`).

pages.title: Accessibility
pages.summary: Accessibility helpers for the app's own control: the ones the library's components use.
features: **Focus ring.** `Modifier.focusRing(interactionSource, shape, color, width)` draws the ring around the element; `rememberFocusRingVisible(interactionSource)` says whether the ring is to be seen right now: the element is focused, no modal is over it, and where the platform shows the ring only for the keyboard, the focus came by the keyboard.

**Touch target.** `Modifier.minTouchTarget(min)` reserves at least `min` in the layout without changing what is drawn: a 24dp icon is pressed in a 48dp area. The value comes from the platform, `PantrixTheme.platform.minTouchTarget`.
**Compose's slop.** The theme fits Compose's touch slop to the platform's: `PantrixViewConfiguration` gives it to `LocalViewConfiguration`.

examples.name: AccessibilityOwnControl
examples.title: Your own control's focus and touch target
examples.description: Your own control's focus ring and touch target. The star is 24dp; `minTouchTarget` makes it pressable in the platform's touch target. `focusRing` draws the ring, in the theme's `focusRing` colour and the platform's width. Come to the star with Tab: the ring shows, and the line beside it writes what `rememberFocusRingVisible` says; on a mouse press the ring does not show.

examples.name: AccessibilityViewConfiguration
examples.title: Compose's touch slop
examples.description: Where an element is small, Compose gives it a touch in the room around it too; `LocalViewConfiguration` says how much. The theme fits this value to the platform's touch target: `PantrixViewConfiguration` wraps Compose's configuration and gives the smallest touch target as the platform's. The line underneath reads it.
examples.code:
val configuration = LocalViewConfiguration.current
val target = configuration.minimumTouchTargetSize
PantrixText(
    text = "The theme's configuration: ${if (configuration is PantrixViewConfiguration) "yes" else "no"} · " +
        "smallest touch target ${target.width.value.toInt()} × ${target.height.value.toInt()} dp",
    style = PantrixTheme.typography.footnote
)

pages.title: Language and words
pages.summary: What the components say by themselves: "Close", "Loading", "Per page", everything said to a screen reader. The theme takes them from its language; the app's own texts are the app's.
features: **Language.** `PantrixLocale` is a language and the direction of its script; `forLanguageTag("ar-EG")` works the direction out from the tag. `PantrixTheme(locale = …)` gives the language to what is in it, and `PantrixTheme.locale` is the nearest theme's.

**Words.** `PantrixStrings` is the components' words. Turkish, English and Arabic packs come with it (`PantrixStrings.forLocale(locale)`); another language is given by a pack's `copy`: `PantrixTheme(strings = …)`.
**The words of time.** `PantrixTimeWords` is the words that count time: "Last 15 minutes", "~ 2 hours ago", "in 3 days"; a pack's `timeWords`.

examples.name: LanguagePacks
examples.title: Three packs
examples.description: The words of three packs: each line is a pack's "Close", its "Loading" and how it writes a number. Arabic writes in its own digits. The pack is found from the language: `PantrixStrings.forLocale(PantrixLocale.forLanguageTag("ar-EG"))` is Arabic's.
examples.code:
val packs = listOf(
    "tr" to PantrixStrings.Turkish,
    "en" to PantrixStrings.English,
    "ar-EG" to PantrixStrings.forLocale(PantrixLocale.forLanguageTag("ar-EG"))
)
packs.forEach { (tag, strings) ->
    PantrixText(
        text = "$tag · ${strings.close} · ${strings.loading} · ${strings.number(1_234_567)}",
        style = PantrixTheme.typography.footnote
    )
}

examples.name: LanguageOwnPack
examples.title: A language Pantrix does not know
examples.description: A language Pantrix has no pack for: German. The inner theme was given `PantrixLocale.forLanguageTag("de-DE")` and a copy of the English pack translated into German. The page size picker reads its word from the new pack. The line underneath reads the language and "Close" straight from the locals (`LocalPantrixLocale`, `LocalPantrixStrings`).

examples.name: LanguageTimeWords
examples.title: The words of time
examples.description: The words of time in three languages: a range ("last 15 minutes"), an approximate past ("~ 2 hours ago") and a future ("in 3 days"). After a number the noun stays singular in Turkish, takes the plural in English, and changes with the number in Arabic.
examples.code:
listOf(PantrixTimeWords.Turkish, PantrixTimeWords.English, PantrixTimeWords.Arabic).forEach { words ->
    PantrixText(
        text = "${words.last(15, PantrixTimeUnit.Minutes)} · " +
            "${words.ago(2, PantrixTimeUnit.Hours, approximate = true)} · " +
            words.fromNow(3, PantrixTimeUnit.Days, approximate = false),
        style = PantrixTheme.typography.footnote
    )
}

pages.title: Analytics
pages.summary: The components' events: a press, a change, a menu that opened. An event is told by identity, not by content: which component, what happened, the test tag, the screen's name. A text typed or read does not go into the event; something chosen goes in by the key the app gave it.
features: **Event.** A `PantrixUiEvent` has a `component`, an `action`, a `testTag`, a `screen` and optional `props`.

**Where it goes.** `PantrixTheme(analytics = PantrixAnalytics { event -> … })` gives the events somewhere: to the app's analytics library, to a log. Left out, the events are dropped (`PantrixAnalytics.NoOp`).
**The app's own event.** `LocalPantrixAnalytics.current` gives the same place: the app sends its own event there too.

**The app's keys.** A table's row, an option's value, a tree's node goes into the event by its key: the key must not be personal data. Which component sends which key is in docs/guide/analytics/ANALYTICS_GUIDE.md.

examples.name: AnalyticsOfComponents
examples.title: The components' events
examples.description: The components' events. The inner theme gives the events to a list: press the button and turn the switch, the last events are written underneath, the newest on top. An event has the component's name, what happened and the test tag, and Pantrix's own values too, such as the button's variant and whether the switch was turned on.

examples.name: AnalyticsOfTheApp
examples.title: The app's own event
examples.description: The app's own event. The share button reads the theme's event sink with `LocalPantrixAnalytics.current` and sends its own event there: its component, what happened, its screen and some `props`. It goes to the same place as the components' events.

pages.title: Analytics connector
pages.summary: The class with which an app connects Pantrix's events to its analytics product: the connector given to `PantrixTheme(analytics = …)`. Under which name the events go, when they are sent, what happens while there is no network and what is never in them are its decisions. The connector on this page is `ProductAnalytics`, from the samples/pantrix-analytics sample.
features: **Tracking plan.** `TrackingPlan` gives the product's names to the events told by a component's tag and action, and says which values each of them carries.

**Generic event.** Every event the plan does not name goes as one `ui_interaction`: with its component, its action, its screen, the tag built from its key and Pantrix's own values. The app's keys and the tags built from where a component is called do not go in.
**Consent.** Until the user says yes, no event is collected; when consent is taken back, what waits is dropped.

**Sending.** `track` puts the event in the queue and returns. The events go in batches and off the UI thread: when a batch is full, when its first event has waited long enough, or when the app calls `flush()`.
**Offline.** The events wait; the send is tried again at ever longer intervals, and the events reach the product in the order they happened. When the queue is full the oldest is dropped.

**No text.** A text that was typed goes into no Pantrix event, nor into anything the connector sends. The sample is described in samples/pantrix-analytics/README.md, and every event in docs/guide/analytics/ANALYTICS_GUIDE.md.

examples.name: AnalyticsConnectorPlan
examples.title: Tracking plan
examples.description: The events the plan names. A press of the pay button becomes `checkout_pay_tapped` and carries only the button's variant. A choice of shipping becomes `shipping_chosen` and carries the key of the shipping chosen: the plan says it is no personal data. Make a choice or press the button: the events the product heard are written underneath, the newest on top.

examples.name: AnalyticsConnectorGenericEvent
examples.title: The generic event
examples.description: Every event the plan does not name goes as `ui_interaction`: with its component, its action, its screen, its tag and Pantrix's own values, such as whether the switch is on. The plan is empty: the shipping choice's key does not go in, as it is the app's key and may be personal data. Nor does the tag of the button with no `tagKey`: it is built from where the button is called, and changes when the code does.

examples.name: AnalyticsConnectorConsent
examples.title: Consent
examples.description: Until the user says yes, the connector collects no event. Once they do, the events wait in the queue and go when five of them wait, or with "Send now". When consent is taken back, what waits is dropped. Underneath is the connector's log, the newest on top.

examples.name: AnalyticsConnectorOffline
examples.title: Offline
examples.description: Turn the network off and press the button a few times: a send is tried every three events, fails, and is tried again after one, two, four seconds. The queue keeps six events; when it is full the oldest is dropped. Turn the network on: what waits goes at the next try, in the order it happened.

pages.title: Test tags
pages.summary: The tag automation finds a component by: `Section.Component_key`. The tag comes from a key that is the same in every language, not from the visible text: the tests do not break when the app opens in another language.
features: **Key.** A component's `tagKey`, and in a form-bound component the field's `id`: `PantrixButton(tagKey = "pay")` becomes `Button_pay`. Left out, a key is derived from the place of the call.
**Section.** `TestScope("Checkout") { … }` puts the section's name in front of the tags in it; nested sections join: `Checkout.Payment.Button_pay`. `LocalTestScope` is the section at that point.
**Policy.** `TestTagPolicy.Stable` tags, `Off` tags nothing; `PantrixTheme(testTagPolicy = …)` or `LocalTestTagPolicy`.
**Your own component.** `rememberPantrixTestTag(component, tagKey)` gives a tag by the same rule, `Modifier.pantrixTestTag(tag)` sets it. The key of a control built on a component is `derivedTagKey`.

**What a test looks for.** `pantrixTestTagOf(component, tagKey, scope)` gives the tag a component carries with a key and in a section, without building the screen: a test or a device automation flow looks for this tag.

examples.name: TestTagsInAScope
examples.title: A button in a section
examples.description: A button's tag inside two sections. The button was given only `tagKey = "pay"`; the sections (`TestScope`) put their names in front of the tag. The line underneath builds the same tag with `rememberPantrixTestTag("Button", "pay")`, and reads the section from `LocalTestScope` and the policy from `LocalTestTagPolicy`.

examples.name: TestTagsOwnComponent
examples.title: Your own component's tag
examples.description: The app's own component is tagged by the same rule: `PriceRow` builds its tag with `rememberPantrixTestTag` and sets it with `pantrixTestTag`. The button in it is built on the row: its key is `derivedTagKey("total", "edit")`, `total_edit`. The line underneath writes the tags.

examples.name: TestTagsOff
examples.title: A release with no tags
examples.description: A release with no tags: a theme given `TestTagPolicy.Off` puts no tag in the tree. A component still knows its tag, and its events go with it: `rememberPantrixTestTag` builds the tag, `Modifier.pantrixTestTag` does not put it in the tree. A `Modifier.testTag` the app sets itself still stays: for the few tags an outside tool expects.

examples.name: TestTagsLookedFor
examples.title: The tag a test looks for
examples.description: The tag a test looks for, without building the screen: `pantrixTestTagOf("Button", "Save draft", scope = "Editor")`. The key goes into the tag in small letters, with `_` in the place of what is not a letter or a digit: `Editor.Button_save_draft`. It is the tag the button carries on the screen too.

pages.title: Diagnostics
pages.summary: Defects only a running screen can show: a theme whose diagnostics are on looks for them and hands what it finds to a sink. Pantrix does not know what kind of build it runs in; the app turns the diagnostics on in its own debug build. In this app the diagnostics are on, and they are turned off in "Settings".
features: **Sink.** `PantrixTheme(diagnostics = …)`: `PantrixDiagnostics.Off`, the default, looks for nothing; `PantrixDiagnostics.Log` writes to the platform's log; `PantrixFindings` keeps the findings for tests and for the inspector. A theme inside can take a sink of its own; `LocalPantrixDiagnostics` is the sink at that point.
**Six checks.** `PantrixCheck`: one tag on two nodes, colours that do not read, a squeezed touch target, a blank name, a theme with no strings for its language and a shadowed shortcut.
**Finding.** `PantrixFinding`: its check, component, tag, section, English message and the values it measured.

**When.** A finding is reported once while it lasts; one the layout finds once it has lasted half a second, a repeated tag once it has lasted a second and a half: a page transition shows two pages with the same tags together.
**Your own component.** `Modifier.checkName` and `Modifier.checkContrast` (`ContrastPair`, `ContrastNeed`) bring a component into the checks; `contrastRatio` is the WCAG ratio of two colours.

examples.name: DiagnosticsLowContrast
examples.title: Colours that do not read
examples.description: A brand's pale colour with white written on it: the button's words are hard to read. The example's own theme keeps what it finds in a sink of its own and writes it underneath: the ratio, the ratio needed and the two colours.

examples.name: DiagnosticsMissingName
examples.title: A blank name
examples.description: A name that came blank from a source: the icon button has nothing to tell a screen reader. Every component of Pantrix that takes a name says so when its name is blank.

examples.name: DiagnosticsSmallTouchTarget
examples.title: A squeezed touch target
examples.description: The checkbox's row, squeezed into a box 24 dp high: lower than every platform's touch target. What the layout finds is reported once it has lasted half a second: a row that opens squeezes what it holds for a moment.

examples.name: DiagnosticsDuplicateTag
examples.title: One tag on two nodes
examples.description: Two buttons with the same key: both are tagged `Button_save`, and a test cannot tell which one it found. Each is given a key of its own, or a section of its own (`TestScope`).

examples.name: DiagnosticsNoStrings
examples.title: A theme with no strings for its language
examples.description: A German theme: Pantrix has no German strings, and the components speak English. Once the app gives that language's strings with `PantrixTheme(strings = …)`, the finding goes away.

examples.name: DiagnosticsShadowedShortcut
examples.title: A shadowed shortcut
examples.description: A screen's root and a field inside it listen for the same shortcut: when the key is pressed the outer one runs, and the inner one never does.

examples.name: DiagnosticsOwnComponent
examples.title: Checking a component of your own
examples.description: A component of the app's own takes part in the checks too: `Swatch` tells its name with `checkName`, and the pair of its text and its ground with `checkContrast`. The line under it writes the ratio of the two colours with `contrastRatio`.

examples.name: DiagnosticsLog
examples.title: To the log and to a test
examples.description: For a test or a log: `PantrixFindings(then = PantrixDiagnostics.Log)` both keeps the findings and writes them to the log. `LocalPantrixDiagnostics` is the theme's sink at that point; a finding's fields are read one by one.

pages.title: Building blocks
pages.summary: The building blocks the library's components are built on: an app that writes its own layer, its own hint or its own control uses them too.
features: **Portal.** `PantrixPortal { … }` composes its content at a root of the window, not where it is called: for a `Popup` or a `Dialog`. A layout that throws its content away while it measures cannot close the layer in the middle of a measurement.
**Modal layer.** `PantrixModalLayer { … }` says its content is a layer that takes the keys and the presses until it closes: the focus rings under it are hidden (`PantrixTheme.isUnderModal`).

**Comes up by itself.** `PantrixTransient(shown, onDismiss)` says something came up that no one opened, as a hint does: Escape puts it away wherever the focus is. A layer hears Escape inside itself with `pantrixTransientsRoot()`.

**Automation root.** `Modifier.pantrixAutomationRoot()` opens the tags under it to the platform's automation. The theme does so for the app's window, and Pantrix's overlays for their own windows; the root of a `Popup` or a `Dialog` of your own, a window of its own on Android, carries it too.

**Press indication.** `pantrixPressIndication()` draws a light veil in the content colour while pressed, `pantrixPressIndicationWithColor(color)` in the colour given; both are a `PantrixPressIndication`.
**Conditional modifier.** `thenIfElse(condition, ifTrue, ifFalse)` goes on with a modifier chain by a condition.
**Scroll bar.** `Modifier.pantrixVerticalScroll(state)` scrolls a column with Pantrix's scroll bar, and `Modifier.pantrixScrollBar(listState)` gives a lazy list its bar.

examples.name: BuildingBlocksOwnLayer
examples.title: Your own layer
examples.description:
Your own layer: the button opens a `Popup` in the middle of the window. The popup is composed through a portal (`PantrixPortal`), its content is a modal layer (`PantrixModalLayer`), and it hears Escape inside itself (`pantrixTransientsRoot()`). While the layer is open the page's focus rings under it are not shown: the line under the button writes that the page is under a modal (`PantrixTheme.isUnderModal`). The layer's own content is not under it.

On Android the popup is a window of its own: the theme's mark that opens the tags to automation does not reach it. The layer's root says so itself (`pantrixAutomationRoot()`): a Maestro flow finds the "Close" button as `Button_close_layer`.

examples.name: BuildingBlocksTransient
examples.title: A hint that comes up by itself
examples.description: A hint that comes up by itself. "Show the hint" brings up a hint, and `PantrixTransient` tells the window it is up: press Escape, the hint goes wherever the focus is, and the key goes to nothing else.

examples.name: BuildingBlocksPressAndModifier
examples.title: Press indications and a conditional modifier
examples.description: Press indications and a conditional border. The three squares are pressed with three indications: in the content colour (`pantrixPressIndication()`), in the brand's colour (`pantrixPressIndicationWithColor`), and with a `PantrixPressIndication` built by hand, red and stronger. Press a square: it is selected and its border thickens with `thenIfElse`.

examples.name: BuildingBlocksScrollColumn
examples.title: A column with a scroll bar
examples.description:
A column taller than its window: a page's text, a settings screen. `Modifier.pantrixVerticalScroll(state)` scrolls it as `verticalScroll` does, and puts Pantrix's scroll bar beside it: the bar Pantrix's own views of documents draw. Its thumb is as long as the share on the screen, and stands where that share is.

Where the reader has a pointer, the bar is there while there is something to scroll; it darkens under the pointer and a mouse drags it. Under a finger it shows only while the content moves, and fades after. It is drawn over the content: the content keeps its width.
examples.code:
val scroll = rememberScrollState()
Column(
    modifier = Modifier
        .fillMaxWidth()
        .height(240.dp)
        .border(1.dp, PantrixTheme.colors.border, PantrixTheme.shapes.md)
        .pantrixVerticalScroll(scroll)
        .padding(PantrixTheme.spacing.md),
    verticalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(PantrixTheme.spacing.sm)
) {
    repeat(times = 24) { index ->
        PantrixText(text = "Paragraph ${index + 1}: the scroll bar stands at the edge of this column's window.")
    }
}

examples.name: BuildingBlocksScrollList
examples.title: A list with a scroll bar
examples.description: A lazy list scrolls itself, by its own state, and takes its bar on its own modifier: `Modifier.pantrixScrollBar(listState)`. The list knows the rows on the screen and how many there are, not how tall the others are: the thumb takes them to be as tall as the ones it sees.

pages.title: Window classes
pages.summary:
The window the theme gives: the width class and the height class of the window the content is drawn in, its size and how its device is folded. Nothing is set up for it: `PantrixTheme` provides it, and every composable inside the theme reads it with `PantrixTheme.window`.

It is the window, not the device and not the screen: an app in half of a split screen, in a resized desktop window or in a browser tab is as wide as that. A layout asks the class rather than the size. The examples on this page show the window's answer as it is now: the values change when you turn the phone, or narrow and widen the window on the desktop and in a browser. The window selector in the card of most examples shows the same answers without touching the window: "Narrow", "Medium", "Short" and "Wide" give that example a fixed window, and "Real" the app's. The four are in four different width classes: `Compact`, `Medium`, `Expanded` and `Large`. On the selector of the examples that look at the fold, "Book" and "Table" stand too: the inner screen of a phone that folds, held half open; the fold is upright in one and lying across in the other.
features: **Five width classes.** `widthClass`: `Compact` is narrower than 600 dp, `Medium` is from 600 dp, `Expanded` from 840, `Large` from 1200 and `ExtraLarge` from 1600. The classes are in order: "from this width on" is a comparison, `widthClass >= WindowWidthClass.Expanded`.

**Three height classes.** `heightClass`: `Compact` is shorter than 480 dp, `Medium` is from 480 dp and `Expanded` from 900. A layout follows the width first; the height says when there is no room left to stack things.
**Yes or no.** `isNarrow` says the width class is `Compact`, and `isShort` that the height class is: a phone held upright is narrow, one on its side is short.

**A value by class.** `byWidth`, `byHeight` and `byPosture` pick a value by the window's class or its posture: a number of columns, a spacing, a type style. A class left out takes the value of the class below it.
**The short form.** `responsive(...)` is `byWidth` of the theme's window: one word, for a composable that does not need the window itself.

**The page's measures.** `PantrixTheme.layout` gives the page's margin (`margin`), the gutter between columns (`gutter`), how many columns its grid has (`columns`) and how wide its content grows at the most (`maxContentWidth`) by the window's class; the theme's density scales the air, and neither the columns nor the widest.
**Spanning columns.** `layout.spanWidth(available, span)` is the width of a part a few columns wide; `Modifier.maxContentWidth()` keeps content to the theme's widest, at the start or in the middle.
**A threshold of your own.** `rememberWindowIsAtLeast(width)` asks about a width none of the classes begins at, and recomposes only when the window crosses that width.
**Recomposition.** Whoever reads the class is recomposed only when the class changes; whoever reads `size`, at every change.

**Fold posture.** `posture` says how the device is folded: like a book (`isBook`), like a laptop on a table (`isTabletop`), or flat. It is read from the system on Android, in the browsers that report it and, from iOS 27.1 on, on an iPhone that folds; the desktop reports no fold, and the posture there is flat.

**Vertical bar.** `verticalBar` is the column the system keeps along one edge of the window for bars that stand upright: on the iPhone Duo's outer screen, from iOS 27.1 on. On every other screen it is null. `rememberVerticalBarInNode()` gives the column in a node's own coordinates; `PantrixScaffold` puts the navigation and the top bar's buttons there.

**Breakpoints of your own.** Where the classes begin is `PantrixBreakpoints`; the default is Android's window size classes. A product gives the theme its own breakpoints with `rememberPantrixWindow(breakpoints = ...)`.

examples.name: AdaptiveWindowClasses
examples.title: Width class and height class
examples.description:
`PantrixTheme.window` gives the window; a layout asks its class. On a phone held upright the width is `Compact`; on most phones turned on their side the width becomes `Expanded` and the height `Compact`. A desktop window is `Large` from 1200 dp and `ExtraLarge` from 1600 dp: take it by the edge and narrow it, and the classes change one after another. In the card's window selector "Narrow" shows a `Compact` width, "Medium" a `Medium` one, "Short" an `Expanded` one and "Wide" a `Large` one; the height is `Compact` in "Short", `Expanded` in "Medium" and `Medium` in the other two.

A composable that reads the class is composed again only when the class changes: while the window grows and shrinks inside a class, this example stays as it is. The last line looks at the height class: a `WindowHeightClass.Compact` window has no room for a bar at the bottom.
examples.code:
val window = PantrixTheme.window
PantrixText(text = "Width class: ${window.widthClass.name}", tagKey = "width_class")
PantrixText(text = "Height class: ${window.heightClass.name}", tagKey = "height_class")
val bars = if (window.heightClass == WindowHeightClass.Compact) "no bar at the bottom" else "a bar at the bottom"
PantrixText(text = "By the height: $bars", tagKey = "bars_by_height")

examples.name: AdaptiveWindowNarrowAndShort
examples.title: Is it narrow, is it short?
examples.description:
`isNarrow` says the width class is `Compact`, as a phone held upright is: it is the question of the layout of one pane, with its navigation along the bottom. `isShort` says the height class is `Compact`, as a phone on its side is; such a window is often wide, but has no height to stack bars in along the bottom.

On a phone held upright the first says yes and the second no; turn the phone on its side and on most phones it is the other way round. On the desktop the answer changes when the window is made narrower than 600 dp or shorter than 480 dp. In the card's window selector "Narrow" says yes to the first and "Short" to the second; "Medium" and "Wide" say no to both. For "from this width on", compare the class: `widthClass >= WindowWidthClass.Expanded`.
examples.code:
val window = PantrixTheme.window
PantrixText(text = "isNarrow: ${if (window.isNarrow) "yes" else "no"}", tagKey = "is_narrow")
PantrixText(text = "isShort: ${if (window.isShort) "yes" else "no"}", tagKey = "is_short")

examples.name: AdaptiveWindowColumns
examples.title: Number of columns by class
examples.description:
`byWidth` picks a value by the window's width class. Here it is the number of columns: with `byWidth(compact = 2, medium = 4)` the boxes stand two to a row in a narrow window, and all four side by side from 600 dp on. A class left out takes the value of the class below it: `Expanded` and those after it are 4 too. Try "Narrow" and "Wide" in the card's window selector, turn the phone, or narrow the window to under 600 dp: the arrangement changes.

The gap between the boxes, at their sides and under them alike, is the theme's gutter: `PantrixTheme.layout.gutter`.

examples.name: AdaptiveWindowBarHeight
examples.title: A value by height
examples.description: `byHeight` does the same with the height class: it makes a value smaller where height is scarce. Here it is a bar's height: 44 dp in a short window, 56 dp in the others. Pick "Short" in the card's window selector, turn the phone on its side or make the window shorter than 480 dp, and the bar gets lower.

examples.name: AdaptiveWindowResponsive
examples.title: The short form: responsive
examples.description:
`responsive(...)` is `byWidth` of the theme's window, in one word: it is for a composable that wants a single value and does not need the window itself. Here it is the number of columns of a form: 1 in `Compact`, 2 from `Medium` on, 3 from `Large` on. `Expanded` is left out and takes the value of `Medium`, and `ExtraLarge` that of `Large`. In the card's window selector "Narrow" says 1 column, "Medium" and "Short" 2, and "Wide" 3.

It goes by the width alone and is called only inside a composable; for the height, ask the window. The caller is recomposed when the class changes, and not as the window is resized within it.
examples.code:
val formColumns = responsive(compact = 1, medium = 2, large = 3)
PantrixText(text = "responsive: a $formColumns-column form", tagKey = "responsive")

examples.name: AdaptiveWindowMeasures
examples.title: Layout measures
examples.description:
`PantrixTheme.layout` gives the page's measures for this window's class; they are not chosen by hand. `margin` is the room at the page's sides: 16 on a phone, 24 from 600 dp, 32 from 1200 dp. Every page of this app pads its content by it; as the window grows, the page's edges open. `gutter` is the room between columns and between panes side by side: 16, and 24 from 840 dp. `columns` is how many columns the grid has: 4, 8 from 600 dp, 12 from 840 dp. `maxContentWidth` is how wide the content grows at the most: without a bound up to 1200 dp, then 1040 dp. Try "Narrow" and "Wide" in the card's window picker: the numbers grow.

The margin and the gutter are air: the theme's density scales them with the spacing scale. The columns are a count and the widest is a measure of the content; the density does not change them. Change the density in "Settings": the first two numbers change. The reader is composed again when the window's class changes.

examples.name: AdaptiveWindowGrid
examples.title: A grid of columns
examples.description: The page's grid: each strip a column, the theme's gutter between them. `layout.columns` is 4 on a phone, 8 from 600 dp and 12 from 840 dp; the columns share the room inside the page's margins. Try "Narrow", "Medium" and "Wide" in the card's window picker: the number of strips changes.

examples.name: AdaptiveWindowSpans
examples.title: Parts spanning columns
examples.description: `layout.spanWidth(available, span)` gives the width of a part a few columns wide: its columns, and the gutters between them. Here an article and the links beside it. On a phone both are 4 columns, one above the other; from 600 dp 5 and 3 columns, and from 840 dp 8 and 4 columns, side by side. Two parts side by side and the gutter between them fill the row exactly. `byWidth` chooses how many columns each part has.

examples.name: AdaptiveWindowContentWidth
examples.title: The content's widest
examples.description: `Modifier.maxContentWidth()` keeps content to the theme's widest: 1040 dp in a window wider than 1200 dp, and no bound in a narrower one. A line that runs across a desktop window is not read; the rest of the room is left empty beside the content. The content is aligned at the start or in the middle: at the start, in line with its title; in the middle, with as much room on either side. Pick "Wide" in the card's window picker: the text stops at 1040 dp and the frame reaches past it. In "Medium" the text is as wide as the frame.

examples.name: AdaptiveWindowOwnThreshold
examples.title: A threshold that fits none of the classes
examples.description:
`rememberWindowIsAtLeast(1000.dp)`: whether the window is at least 1000 dp wide. It is for a threshold of one screen's own, which neither `Expanded`, beginning at 840, nor `Large`, beginning at 1200, meets. On the desktop, drag the window's edge to either side of 1000 dp: that is where the answer changes. In the card's window selector "Narrow", "Medium" and "Short" say no, and "Wide" says yes.

This composable is recomposed only when the window crosses 1000 dp; asking the same as `window.size.width >= 1000.dp` would recompose it at every size.
examples.code:
val threeColumns = rememberWindowIsAtLeast(1000.dp)
PantrixText(
    text = "rememberWindowIsAtLeast(1000.dp): ${if (threeColumns) "yes, three columns" else "no, two columns"}",
    tagKey = "at_least_1000"
)

examples.name: AdaptiveWindowSize
examples.title: The window's size
examples.description:
`size` is the window's size. Whoever reads it follows every change: it is recomposed at each frame of a rotation and at each pixel of a dragged window edge. So it is not read for a layout decision. Here it is only shown; since this example reads it in a composable of its own, the rest of the page is left alone while the window is dragged.

`isSizeKnown` is false until the platform has told the size. Android and iOS tell the size from the start; on the desktop and on the web the content is first composed before the window has a size, and at that moment the window reads as `Compact` both ways. A decision that is made once and kept, such as a start page, waits for this.

The "Narrow", "Medium", "Short" and "Wide" windows of the card's window selector are fixed sizes: here that size is shown, and it is known from the start.

examples.name: AdaptiveWindowPosture
examples.title: Fold posture
examples.description:
`posture` says how the device is folded. A layout is written for two postures: `isBook` is half open with the fold upright (two panes side by side, split at the fold), `isTabletop` is half open with the fold lying across (what is looked at above, controls below). A single-screen foldable opened flat has a fold, but it separates nothing; the hinge of a two-screen device separates the window even when it is opened flat (`separatingFold`).

`byPosture` picks a value by posture; a posture left out takes the value of `flat`, so nothing changes on a device that does not fold. On a phone that does not fold and on the desktop it says "Flat" and "one piece" here; the others are seen on a foldable Android device or its emulator, and on the iPhone Duo of iOS 27.1. Pick "Book" and "Table" in the card's window selector: both are fixed windows with a fold held half open. The last line still says what is real: what the system says does not depend on the window the example is given.

Each fold is a `WindowFold`: its orientation, whether it is half open, whether it separates the window, whether it occludes something. The theme's window reads the posture from the system, `systemWindowPosture()`; the last line asks it directly.
examples.code:
val window = PantrixTheme.window
val posture: WindowPosture = window.posture
val named = when {
    posture.isBook -> "Book (half open, fold upright)"
    posture.isTabletop -> "Tabletop (half open, fold lying across)"
    posture.separatingFold != null -> "Flat, two screens (the hinge separates the window)"
    posture.folds.isNotEmpty() -> "Flat (there is a fold, the screen is one piece)"
    else -> "Flat"
}
// How the two halves lie, by posture: side by side in a book, one above the other on a table, one piece otherwise.
val halves = window.byPosture(flat = "one piece", book = "two halves side by side", tabletop = "two halves, one above the other")
PantrixText(text = "Posture: $named", tagKey = "posture")
PantrixText(text = "byPosture: $halves", tagKey = "by_posture")
posture.folds.forEach { fold: WindowFold ->
    PantrixText(
        text = "Fold: ${fold.orientation.name}, half open: ${if (fold.isHalfOpened) "yes" else "no"}, " +
            "separating: ${if (fold.isSeparating) "yes" else "no"}, occluding: ${if (fold.isOccluding) "yes" else "no"}",
        style = PantrixTheme.typography.footnote
    )
}
PantrixText(
    text = "Folds the system reports: ${systemWindowPosture().folds.size}",
    style = PantrixTheme.typography.footnote,
    color = PantrixTheme.colors.textSecondary
)

examples.name: AdaptiveWindowVerticalBar
examples.title: The system's vertical bar
examples.description:
On the iPhone Duo's outer screen, from iOS 27.1 on, the system keeps a column along one edge of the window for bars that stand upright: the status bar at its top and the app's bars below it. The window tells of it with `verticalBar`, a `WindowVerticalBar`: the column itself (`bounds`) and the bars' place (`barBounds`), in the window's pixels. On every other screen it is null. Pick "Cover" in the card's window selector.

A layout asks where the column is beside it with `rememberVerticalBarInNode()`: it puts its `modifier` on its node, and `verticalBar` comes in that node's coordinates; it is null where the node does not reach the column. In the box the column is drawn in a faint fill and the bars' place in a frame. `PantrixScaffold` puts the navigation and the top bar's buttons there this way.

The last line asks the system directly, `systemVerticalBar()`: it does not depend on the window the example is given, and tells of a column only on the Duo's outer screen. A preview or a test builds a screen with a column with `PantrixWindow(size, verticalBar = WindowVerticalBar(...))`; the card's "Cover" is built so.

examples.name: AdaptiveWindowLayoutChoice
examples.title: What a layout would pick in this window
examples.description:
The helpers put together: what a layout would pick in this window. Where the navigation goes, how many panes there are and where the main action goes. The rules are in this example's code and are an example for a product's layout; they are not the library's rule.

On a phone held upright the answer is a tab bar at the bottom, one pane and a fixed action bar at the bottom. With the phone on its side the navigation moves to the side and the action goes up into the header: in a short window no bars are stacked along the bottom. From 840 dp the list and the detail come side by side; from 1200 dp the navigation becomes a sidebar and the layout that of a web page. Try "Narrow", "Medium", "Short" and "Wide" in the card's window selector: each of the four gives a different layout. In the book posture the two panes part exactly at the fold; the upright hinge of a two-screen device parts the panes there even when it is opened flat.

examples.name: AdaptiveWindowBreakpoints
examples.title: A window classed by breakpoints of its own
examples.description:
The breakpoints of the classes are `PantrixBreakpoints`. The default is Android's window size classes: 600, 840, 1200 and 1600 dp in width, 480 and 900 dp in height. A product whose layouts change at other widths gives the theme its own breakpoints, `PantrixTheme(window = rememberPantrixWindow(breakpoints = ...))`, and every helper follows them.

Here the same width is classed by two sets of breakpoints: those of the theme's window, and those of a product whose `Medium` begins at 360 dp. A phone held upright that is at least 360 dp wide is `Compact` by the first and `Medium` by the second; from 600 dp on the two give the same answer. In the card's window selector "Narrow" is such a phone; in "Wide" both lines say `Large`.

examples.name: AdaptiveWindowOwnLayouts
examples.title: Your own breakpoints and layout measures
examples.description:
A product's own breakpoints and own layout measures, in a theme. The inner theme was given a window whose `Medium` starts at 360 dp, with `rememberPantrixWindow(breakpoints = …)`, and margins of its own with `PantrixLayouts(…)`: a 360 dp phone is `Medium` there, and the page's margin is 28 dp. The last line reads the library's own measures (`rememberPantrixLayouts()`) and the theme's measures directly (`LocalPantrixLayouts`).

This example's card has no window picker: the inner theme reads the window itself, from the device.
examples.code:
val library = rememberPantrixLayouts()
val window = rememberPantrixWindow(breakpoints = PantrixBreakpoints(medium = 360.dp))
PantrixTheme(window = window, layouts = OWN_LAYOUTS) {
    PantrixText(text = "Width class: ${PantrixTheme.window.widthClass.name}", tagKey = "own_width_class")
    PantrixText(text = "The page's margin: ${PantrixTheme.layout.margin.value.roundToInt()} dp", tagKey = "own_margin")
    PantrixText(
        text = "The library's Medium margin: ${library.medium.margin.value.roundToInt()} dp · this theme's: " +
            "${LocalPantrixLayouts.current.medium.margin.value.roundToInt()} dp",
        style = PantrixTheme.typography.footnote,
        color = PantrixTheme.colors.textSecondary
    )
}

private val OWN_LAYOUTS = PantrixLayouts(
    compact = PantrixLayout(margin = 20.dp, gutter = 12.dp),
    medium = PantrixLayout(margin = 28.dp, gutter = 16.dp),
    expanded = PantrixLayout(margin = 32.dp, gutter = 20.dp)
)

pages.title: Show and hide
pages.summary:
Case study: a part that shows only in some windows, on some platforms or with some inputs. A plain `if` is enough to show and to hide. The one thing to watch is state: a part inside an `if` leaves the composition when it is hidden, and drops what it remembers.

There are three separate questions, and they are not to be mixed up: how much room the window gives, which platform the code runs on, and what the app is used with. The card of an example that looks at the window has a window selector: "Narrow", "Medium", "Short" and "Wide" give that example a fixed window, and "Real" the app's; on examples that look at the fold, "Book" and "Table" too. That is how a wide window is seen on a phone, a narrow one on the desktop, and a foldable one on a device that does not fold, without touching the window.
features: **How much room does the window give?** `window.isNarrow`, `window.isShort`, `window.widthClass >= ...`. The answer is the same on a phone and in a narrowed desktop window: this is what "the mobile view" most often is.

**Which platform does the code run on?** `PantrixTheme.platform.type`. It has nothing to do with the window's size: a "download the app" banner makes sense only on the web, and "rate in the store" only on Android and iOS.
**What is it used with?** `PantrixTheme.platform.isTouch`: a finger or a mouse. The platform does not tell this: a phone's browser is the web too, but is used with a finger.

**Changing instead of hiding.** Where the same component is in both layouts, it is not hidden and called from another place; the value it is given changes. A modifier that depends on a condition is written with `Modifier.thenIf`.

**The state of what is hidden.** Where the same content is called from two separate places, Compose counts it as two separate contents: when the window changes class, one goes and the other starts from zero. Call it from one place, and give what changes as a parameter.
**Moving.** Where what the content stands in has to change, one under another in a narrow window and side by side in a wide one, `movableContentOf` moves it together with what it remembers.

**Saved state.** State that has to stay is kept with `rememberSaveable`: when Android recreates an Activity, what `remember` held is gone, and what was saved comes back by the place it is called from.

**A window of its own for a part.** `LocalPantrixWindow` gives a part of the screen another window: the way to set up a preview or a test at a given size, and what the cards' window selector does too.

examples.name: AdaptiveVisibilityByWindow
examples.title: By window
examples.description:
Parts that come and go with the room the window gives. `isNarrow` holds only in a narrow window, `!isNarrow` in every window that is not narrow. The classes are in order: `widthClass >= WindowWidthClass.Expanded` holds from a class on, `widthClass in Medium..Expanded` between two classes. `isShort` holds only in a short window. A hidden part is not in the composition: it takes no room and is not read.

On a phone held upright only the "in a narrow window" line appears; on most phones turned on their side, the other four do. In a desktop window wider than 1200 dp the "not narrow" and "From Expanded on" lines remain.

The card's window selector gives this example a window of its own: "Narrow" is a fixed window of 360 × 800 dp, "Medium" one of 768 × 1024, "Short" one of 880 × 400 and "Wide" one of 1280 × 800; "Real" is the app's. The line under it says which window the example is looking at right now. "Medium" is a tablet held upright and is `Medium`: the "not narrow" and "in Medium and Expanded" lines appear. "Short" is a phone on its side, `Expanded` at 880 dp and short at 400 dp: all four lines but the "in a narrow window" one appear.

examples.name: AdaptiveVisibilityByPlatform
examples.title: By platform
examples.description:
Parts that come and go with the platform: `PantrixTheme.platform.type`. It has nothing to do with the window's size: a wide Android tablet is still Android, and a narrowed browser window is still the web. Saying "show it on mobile" means deciding which of the two is meant: most often the window, sometimes the platform.

On the web the first line appears, on Android and iOS the second; in the desktop app only the platform's name is shown.

examples.name: AdaptiveVisibilityByInput
examples.title: By input
examples.description:
Whether the app is used with a finger or with a mouse: `PantrixTheme.platform.isTouch`. The platform's type does not tell this. Android and iOS are always used by touch and the desktop always with a mouse; the web may be either: a browser on a desk is used with a mouse, one on a phone with a finger. In a browser the answer is live: when the pointer changes, so does the answer.

Where the app is used by touch the pull-to-refresh hint appears, and where it is used with a mouse the keyboard shortcuts hint. The touch target depends on the same answer: 48 dp on Android and 44 on iOS; on the desktop and the web, 32 dp for a mouse and 48 for a finger. The components take it from the theme themselves; here it is only shown.

examples.name: AdaptiveVisibilitySameComponent
examples.title: The same component, a value that changes
examples.description:
A single component that is not hidden but changes with the window: the button fills the row in a narrow window and keeps its own width in a wide one. The component is the same call; only the value it is given changes. `Modifier.thenIf` adds its block to the chain when the condition holds.

Try "Narrow" and "Wide" in the card's window selector, or turn the phone: the button stays where it is and its width changes.
examples.code:
val window = PantrixTheme.window
PantrixButton(
    text = "Continue",
    onClick = {},
    modifier = Modifier.thenIf(window.isNarrow) { fillMaxWidth() },
    tagKey = "continue"
)

examples.name: AdaptiveVisibilityState
examples.title: What happens to state when a part is hidden
examples.description:
Two counters, the same job, written two ways. The first is called from two separate places, one for a narrow window and one for a wide one: Compose counts them as two separate counters, and when the window changes class one goes and the other starts from zero. The second is called from a single place and only its label changes: its count stays.

Increase both, then switch between "Narrow" and "Wide" in the card's window selector: the one called from two places goes back to zero, and the other stays. For an extra, such as a hint or a banner, that is no problem; content that is in both layouts is called from one place.

The counter remembers its count with `rememberSaveable`: when Android recreates an Activity, what a plain `remember` held is gone, wherever it was called from. A saved value, too, comes back by the place it is called from: the counter called from one place always finds its count. The one called from two finds it where the window is still narrow, or still wide, when the Activity is recreated: the same branch is composed. Where it has gone from narrow to wide or from wide to narrow, as on a phone that is turned, it does not.

examples.name: AdaptiveVisibilityMovedContent
examples.title: The same content, another arrangement
examples.description:
The same content in another arrangement: one under another in a narrow window, side by side in a wide one. `Column` and `Row` are two separate call sites: had the content passed from one to the other by a plain call, it would have dropped what it remembers. `movableContentOf` moves the content: the same composition goes to its new place, and the counters keep their counts. It is for when a single call site is not enough, that is, when what the content stands in has to change.

Increase the counters, then switch between "Narrow" and "Wide" in the card's window selector: the arrangement changes, the counts stay.

examples.name: AdaptiveVisibilityOwnWindow
examples.title: A window of its own for a part
examples.description:
What the cards' window selector does, in its plainest form: `LocalPantrixWindow` gives a part of the screen another window. Every `PantrixTheme.window` and `responsive(...)` inside it asks that window. A fixed window is made with `PantrixWindow(size, breakpoints)` and is classed by the real one's breakpoints: where a product has given the theme breakpoints of its own, it follows them too.

The first line shows the window the example sees: the app's, or the one the card's selector has given it. Each of the two parts under it is given a fixed window: one always picks the narrow layout and the other always the wide one, whatever the window around them. Try "Narrow" and "Wide" in the card's window selector: the first line changes, the two under it do not. The same technique is also used to set up a preview or a test at a given size. The platform and the input are not affected by it.

pages.title: Sign-in screen
pages.summary:
Case study: a screen with a marketing panel on the left and a sign-in form on the right. In a narrow window the marketing panel goes and the form stays.

This is a screen, so it asks the window (`PantrixTheme.window`). Its most important rule: the form is called from a single place. The marketing panel comes and goes with an `if`, while the form is the same `SignInForm()` call in every layout. That is why the text typed into the email field stays where it is as the window narrows and widens, or as the phone is turned. Calling the form from two separate places, for the narrow layout and for the wide one, would wipe what was typed when the class changes.

In a real app this screen fills the whole window; here it stands inside the page, in a frame. The library gives this layout ready-made too: `PantrixShowcaseScaffold` (the "Showcase Scaffold" page). This page shows building it by hand, by asking the window.
features: **The marketing panel only where there is room.** `if (!window.isNarrow) MarketingPanel()`: the marketing panel is shown only in a window that is not narrow. For an extra that comes and goes and has nothing to remember, a plain `if` is enough.

**The form from one place.** Compose ties what a composable remembers to the place it is called from: since the form is always called from the same place, its state stays while the marketing panel comes and goes.
**Share and type style by class.** `window.byWidth(compact = 1f, large = 1.25f)`: the marketing panel's share grows from `Large` on. The type style of its title is a value picked by class too.
**Padding.** `responsive(compact = 16.dp, medium = 24.dp, large = 40.dp)`: the padding grows with the class. It is the short form of `byWidth`, for a composable that does not need the window itself.

**A short window.** The marketing panel's items are inside `if (!window.isShort)`: one `Benefit(...)` for each item of the `BENEFITS` list. A phone on its side has enough width but not enough height; there is no room for the items, and the title stays.
**A value by height.** `window.byHeight(compact = 300.dp, medium = 460.dp)`: the screen's height shrinks in a short window, and so does the spacing between the form's rows.

**The form does not widen.** `widthIn(max = 360.dp)`: the form is 360 dp wide at most and stands in the centre of the room set aside for it; where that room is short, it scrolls within itself. Not everything is settled by a class.
**Saved state.** The form's fields remember with `rememberSaveable`: what was typed comes back when Android recreates the Activity too, since the call site has stayed the same.

examples.name: AdaptiveLoginScreen
examples.title: Marketing panel and sign-in form
examples.description:
The whole screen, in a frame. A narrow window has the form alone. In a window that is not narrow the marketing panel comes beside the form: with a share equal to the form's up to `Large`, and from `Large` on wider and with a larger title. In a short window, that is a phone on its side, the marketing panel's items go and its title stays; the frame gets lower and the form's rows draw closer together.

Type your email, then narrow the window or turn the phone: the marketing panel comes and goes, and what you typed stays.

The card's window selector shows the same without touching the window: it gives the example a fixed window. "Narrow" is a phone of 360 × 800 dp, "Medium" a tablet held upright of 768 × 1024 dp, "Short" a phone on its side of 880 × 400 dp and "Wide" a desktop window of 1280 × 800 dp; "Real" is the app's window. The frame is laid out as wide as the window that is picked: even on a wide screen "Narrow" is as wide as a phone. The two-pane layout is not squeezed into a narrow room. A window that does not fit the card is drawn smaller and whole, as "Wide" is on the desktop, and the line under the selector says the scale; where it would have to be drawn smaller than 60%, as "Wide" would on a phone, it keeps its own size and scrolls sideways.

examples.name: AdaptiveLoginCallSites
examples.title: A field called from two places and from one
examples.description:
This screen's real lesson, with a single field. The upper field is called from two separate places, one for the narrow layout and one for the wide; Compose counts them as two separate fields. The lower one is the same call in every layout: only the marketing panel beside it comes and goes.

Type something into both fields, then switch between "Narrow" and "Wide" in the card's window selector: the field called from two places is emptied, and the one called from one place keeps what you typed. For a user, the first is the email they typed being wiped when they turn the phone.

pages.title: Table
pages.summary:
Case study: a table of orders. A plain table with columns where the room is wide, a list of cards where it is narrow.

This is a component and not a screen, so it looks at the room it is given and not at the window. The same table may be put inside a narrow pane of a wide window; had it asked the window, it would draw a table there too and would not fit. The component learns its own room from `BoxWithPantrixWindow`: the box tells its content the room it is given, as a window is told, and answers for the box everything a screen asks the window.
features: **Its own room.** `BoxWithPantrixWindow(modifier) { box -> ... }` tells its content the most room it may take: it is `BoxWithConstraints` underneath, and what it tells is that box's `maxWidth` and `maxHeight`.
**The same helpers.** `box` is a `PantrixWindow`: `box.isNarrow`, `box.byWidth(...)`, `box.widthClass >= WindowWidthClass.Expanded`. Whatever a screen asks the window, a component asks its box.
**The window's breakpoints.** The box is classed by the same breakpoints as the theme's window; a component's own thresholds are given with `breakpoints`.

**No needless recomposition.** Content that reads a class of the box is recomposed when that class changes, and not at every size as the content of `BoxWithConstraints` is. A reader of `size` follows every change.

**Height from the window.** In a page that scrolls there is no end to the height the box may take: its height class reads `Expanded` and the box is never short. Ask the box about the width and the window about the height.
**The box is flat.** A fold is the window's: ask the window about the posture. Where it crosses the box, `rememberFoldsInNode()` says; the "Two panes" page tells of it.
**The box's measures.** `PantrixTheme.layout(box)` gives the margin and the gutter by the box's class and not the window's.

**As a window for its content.** Inside the box `PantrixTheme.window` and `responsive` still ask the window; where everything is to ask the box, the box is given to the content with `LocalPantrixWindow`.
**The content's place.** `contentAlignment` places content that is smaller than the box; `propagateMinConstraints` makes the content at least as large as the least size of the box.
**Composed while it is measured.** Like `BoxWithConstraints`, it composes its content while it is measured: it does not go in a row or a column that is sized by `IntrinsicSize`.

examples.name: AdaptiveTableOwnRoom
examples.title: The same component, in two places
examples.description:
`OrdersTable` stands twice: at the page's width and in a 280 dp box. The component asks its own box rather than the window (`box.isNarrow`): it is a list in a room narrower than 600 dp and a table from 600 dp on. The date column appears from 840 dp on.

On a phone both are lists. Turn the phone or widen the window, and the upper one turns into a table once it is left with 600 dp; the lower one stays a list. The card's window selector shows the same without touching the window: in "Narrow" both are lists; in "Wide" the upper one is a table and the lower one a list. In "Real" the upper one may be a list even while the window reads `Medium`: the sidebar and the page's margins take their share of the window's width. Had it asked the window, it would have laid a table out in the narrow room that is left.

The selected order is kept outside the component, above the two views: kept inside them, it would be lost when the view changes. Press a card in the lower list: the same order is selected in the upper view too.

examples.name: AdaptiveTableBoxWidths
examples.title: A box whose width is picked
examples.description:
The component's three states, without touching the window: the box's width is picked. A list at 320 dp, a table of four columns at 700 dp, five columns with the date column at 900 dp. Where the box is wider than the screen, it scrolls sideways.

The window never changed; what changed is the room the component is given. `box.isNarrow` picks the list, and `box.widthClass >= WindowWidthClass.Expanded` the date column. Pick a row and change the width: the selection stays.

appNames.name: HorizontalScrollFrame
appNames.description: A frame that scrolls sideways: where its content does not fit its room, it draws a scrollbar under it.

examples.name: AdaptiveTableBreakpoints
examples.title: The box's breakpoints
examples.description:
The box is classed by the same breakpoints as the theme's window: where a product has given the window breakpoints of its own, its components follow them too, with nothing to write. Where a component has thresholds of its own, they are given with `breakpoints`.

Both boxes are 240 dp wide. The first is classed by the window's breakpoints and is `Compact`. The second is given breakpoints whose `Medium` begins at 200 dp: at the same width it reads `Medium` and is not narrow. The window's size changes neither of them.
examples.code:
val frame = Modifier.width(240.dp).border(1.dp, PantrixTheme.colors.border, PantrixTheme.shapes.md)
BoxWithPantrixWindow(modifier = frame) { box ->
    PantrixText(
        text = "By the window's breakpoints: ${box.widthClass.name}",
        modifier = Modifier.padding(PantrixTheme.spacing.md),
        tagKey = "box_window_breakpoints"
    )
}
BoxWithPantrixWindow(modifier = frame, breakpoints = PantrixBreakpoints(medium = 200.dp)) { box ->
    PantrixText(
        text = "If Medium begins at 200 dp: ${box.widthClass.name}",
        modifier = Modifier.padding(PantrixTheme.spacing.md),
        tagKey = "box_own_breakpoints"
    )
}

examples.name: AdaptiveTableHeight
examples.title: Width from the box, height from the window
examples.description:
Inside a page that scrolls there is no end to the height a box may take: its height class reads `Expanded` and `box.isShort` is never true. So a component asks its box about the width and the window about the height.

The first box stands in this page with no height given. The second is given a height of 72 dp: a box whose height is bounded tells its own height, and is short. The last line is the window's answer: it says yes on a phone on its side or in a window shorter than 480 dp. Pick "Short" in the card's window selector: the last line changes, and the answers of the two boxes do not.
examples.code:
val frame = Modifier.fillMaxWidth().border(1.dp, PantrixTheme.colors.border, PantrixTheme.shapes.md)
BoxWithPantrixWindow(modifier = frame) { box ->
    PantrixText(
        text = "A box with no height given: ${box.heightClass.name}, isShort: " +
            if (box.isShort) "yes" else "no",
        modifier = Modifier.padding(PantrixTheme.spacing.md),
        tagKey = "box_free_height"
    )
}
BoxWithPantrixWindow(modifier = frame.height(72.dp)) { box ->
    PantrixText(
        text = "A 72 dp box: ${box.heightClass.name}, isShort: " + if (box.isShort) "yes" else "no",
        modifier = Modifier.padding(PantrixTheme.spacing.md),
        tagKey = "box_fixed_height"
    )
}
val window = PantrixTheme.window
PantrixText(
    text = "The window: ${window.heightClass.name}, isShort: " + if (window.isShort) "yes" else "no",
    tagKey = "window_height"
)

examples.name: AdaptiveTableLayoutOfTheBox
examples.title: The box's measures
examples.description:
`PantrixTheme.layout` gives the measures by the window's class. A component that looks at its own box asks `PantrixTheme.layout(box)` and takes the measures of the box's class: the box's room is not the window's.

The box is 240 dp wide, and the gap between the two rectangles inside it is its gutter. The lines under them put the two gutters side by side: from 840 dp on the window's gutter grows and the box's stays the same. In a window narrower than that the two are equal. Try "Narrow" and "Wide" in the card's window selector: only the window's changes.

examples.name: AdaptiveTableBoxAsWindow
examples.title: Handing the box to its content as a window
examples.description:
Inside the box `PantrixTheme.window` and `responsive(...)` still ask the window. Where everything inside is to ask the box instead, as in a pane whose content is a screen of its own, the box is given to the content as its window: `CompositionLocalProvider(LocalPantrixWindow provides box)`.

The box is 240 dp wide. The first line calls `responsive` as it is: its answer is the window's. The second calls it after the box has been given: its answer is the box's, which is narrow. In a narrow window the two lines say the same; to see the difference, pick "Wide" in the card's window selector, turn the phone or make the window at least 600 dp wide.

examples.name: AdaptiveTableContentPlacement
examples.title: The content's place in the box
examples.description: `contentAlignment` places content that is smaller than the box inside the box: in the first box the text is in the centre. `propagateMinConstraints` gives the content the box's least size too: the second box is 72 dp tall, and the surface inside it fills the box although it is given no size of its own.

pages.title: Two panes
pages.summary:
`PantrixTwoPane`, which lays two panes side by side or one above the other, and the helpers that say how many panes a layout shows and where the fold of a device that folds is.

What stands side by side in a wide window is most often two things: a list and what is chosen in it, a document and its properties, a video and its controls. `PantrixTwoPane` lays the two out in one room: it gives the first the share or the width it is given, and puts the layout's gutter between them. On a device that folds, where the fold divides the room, the panes meet exactly there: one on one side of the fold, the other on the other side; nothing falls on the fold.
features: **Side by side or one above the other.** `TwoPaneOrientation.SideBySide` puts the first pane at the start and the second at the end; `TwoPaneOrientation.Stacked` the first above and the second below.

**Share or size of its own.** `PaneSize.Fraction(0.4f)` gives the first pane 40% of the room, `PaneSize.Fixed(320.dp)` 320 dp; the second takes the rest. The gap between them is `gap`, `PantrixTheme.layout.gutter` by default.

**They meet at the fold.** On a foldable held like a book, the upright fold parts panes side by side; put on a table, the fold lying across parts panes one above the other. Then neither the share nor the gap holds: the split is at the fold, and the gap is the strip the system asks to keep clear around it, `WindowFold.clearance`. On an iPhone the strip is 20 pt on each side of the fold; Android and the browsers ask for none.
**Reading direction.** In a language read from right to left, the first of two panes side by side is on the right. The fold stays where it is on the screen; the first pane is on its start side.

**How many panes.** `PantrixTheme.window.paneCount()` says how many panes the window has room for: one in `Compact` and `Medium`, two in `Expanded`, three from `Large` on; on a foldable held like a book, at least two at any width. `PantrixTwoPane` always draws both; when to show one is the layout's decision.

**Your own layout.** `rememberFoldsInNode()` gives the folds in a node's own coordinates: whoever writes a layout of their own laid out by the fold puts its `modifier` on the node and reads `folds` as they measure.

**Preview and test.** `PantrixWindowFrame` makes a box a window of its own: it tells what it holds the window it is given, and measures its fold from the box's corner. The "Book" and "Table" windows of this page's cards are drawn so.

**Where it is read from.** The fold is read on Android from WindowManager, in the browsers that report it from the screen's segments, and from iOS 27.1 on from UIKit. On the desktop and on devices that do not fold the window is flat; the panes are split by the share.

examples.name: AdaptiveTwoPaneInbox
examples.title: A list and what is opened, side by side
examples.description:
An inbox and the message opened, side by side: the list 300 dp, the message the rest. Press a message: the pane beside it shows it.

Pick "Book" in the card's window selector: the fold is in the middle and the panes part exactly there. The list is no longer 300 dp but reaches the fold; the gap is the 20 dp strip on each side of the fold. The faint strip and the line over the example are where the fold is. In the other windows the list is 300 dp and the layout's gutter stands between them. In "Narrow" there is no room left for the message: the next example shows one pane there.

examples.name: AdaptiveTwoPaneCount
examples.title: One pane or two: paneCount
examples.description:
The window says how many panes to show: `PantrixTheme.window.paneCount()`. Where there is room for two, the list and the message stand side by side. Where there is not, one shows: the list first, the message once one is pressed, and the list again with the "Inbox" button.

When the pane count changes, the list is called from another place and composed again. Its scroll position is not lost: the example remembers it, not the list, `rememberScrollState()`, and hands it to the list. Scroll the list, open a message, then switch between "Narrow" and "Wide" in the card's window selector: the opened message and the list's place both stay.

"Narrow" and "Medium" say one pane, "Short", "Wide" and "Book" two. The 951 dp of "Book" is `Expanded` anyway; a narrower foldable held like a book takes two panes as well. In "Table" the fold lies across and does not part panes side by side: the 669 dp window is `Medium` and shows one pane.

examples.name: AdaptiveTwoPaneTabletop
examples.title: On a table: the video above, the controls below
examples.description:
For a foldable put on a table: what is looked at above, the controls below. `TwoPaneOrientation.Stacked` puts the first pane above; here the upper one takes 60% of the room.

Pick "Table" in the card's window selector: the window is 669 × 951 dp and the fold lies across its middle. In the tabletop posture the layout takes the window's whole height, `byPosture(flat = 360.dp, tabletop = window.size.height)`, and the panes part exactly at the fold: the video in the upper half, the controls in the lower. In the other windows the layout is 360 dp tall and is split by the share. In "Book" the fold is upright and does not part panes one above the other: the share holds.

examples.name: AdaptiveTwoPaneSizes
examples.title: Share, size of its own, orientation and reading direction
examples.description:
The panes' size and orientation. With the selectors, change the first pane's share, the way the panes stand and the reading direction: each pane writes its own size.

- **Share.** `PaneSize.Fraction(0.3f)` gives the first pane 30% of the room left once the gap is taken out.

- **Fixed.** `PaneSize.Fixed(200.dp)` gives the first pane 200 dp; where the room is narrower, the first takes all of it.

- **One above the other.** With `TwoPaneOrientation.Stacked` the share and the fixed size are of the height.

- **Right to left.** Side by side, the first pane goes to the right; one above the other, both stay where they are. An app takes its reading direction from its language; here it was given to these two panes alone with `LocalLayoutDirection`.

examples.name: AdaptiveTwoPaneFoldsInNode
examples.title: Your own layout: rememberFoldsInNode
examples.description:
To write a layout of your own that is laid out by the fold: `rememberFoldsInNode()` gives the folds in a node's own coordinates, in pixels. Put its `modifier` on the node and read `folds` as you measure: as the node moves, the window changes and the device is folded, the layout is measured again. A fold that does not cross the node is not in the list.

The toolbar here lines its buttons up in the middle. Where an upright fold crosses it, half of the buttons go before the fold and half after it: no button falls on the fold. Pick "Book" in the card's window selector: the buttons part on both sides of the fold, and the line below says where the fold is in the bar.

examples.name: AdaptiveTwoPaneWindowFrame
examples.title: A window that folds, in a preview
examples.description:
A window that folds, in a preview or a test: `PantrixWindowFrame` makes a box a window of its own. What it holds reads the window it is given with `PantrixTheme.window` and measures the fold from the box's corner. Here a window of 280 × 160 dp was made, with a fold held half open like a book in its middle: the two panes in it part exactly at the fold, and the narrow window says two panes in the book posture.

Where the fold is, is in pixels. The `bounds` of a `WindowFold` are the fold itself: on a phone that folds, a line with no thickness. `clearance` is the strip what is touched keeps clear of: on Android the fold itself, on iOS 20 pt more on each side. In this window the strip is 12 dp on each side.

pages.title: List and detail
pages.summary:
A list and the detail of the item opened in it: side by side where there is room, one in the other's place where there is not. An inbox, settings, contacts, files: the layout of every screen with a list and its detail.

`PantrixListDetailScaffold` chooses how many panes to show by its own room, not by the window. In a narrow room the list shows first; an item opened, its detail takes the list's place, sliding in from the end. Back, Escape and the edge swipe of iOS bring the list back. In a wide room the two stand side by side; in a very wide one a third pane can open beside the detail.

What is open is kept by `ListDetailState`: remembered with `rememberListDetailState()`, it survives a rotation and the process being restarted. The list opens an item with `select(key)`, and the detail closes with `back()`.
features: **How many panes.** One in a `Compact` or `Medium` room, two from `Expanded` on, three from `Large` on where an extra pane is given. Two at any width on a foldable held like a book: the list and the detail meet at the fold.

**Back in one pane.** While the detail is open, back, Escape and the edge swipe of iOS call `back()`. Swiped from the edge, the detail moves with the finger; let go halfway, it goes back to its place. A keyboard's focus goes with the pane shown: into the detail of the item opened from the list, and back to that item.
**In two panes back is the app's.** With the list beside it the scaffold leaves back alone; the screen's own back runs.
**Empty detail.** In two panes, while no item is open, `emptyDetail` stands in the detail's place.

**What the panes are told.** Each pane is composed in a `ListDetailScope`: `isSinglePane` chooses whether to show a back button in one pane, `isExtraInSheet` whether to show the extra pane's title; `paneCount` says how many panes there is room for.
