**Extra pane.** Where `extra` is given, `showExtra()` opens it: beside the detail where there is room for three panes, elsewhere in a sheet that slides in from the end over the detail in the scaffold's own room, titled `extraTitle`. A keyboard's focus moves into the sheet and stays in it until it closes. It is one composition in both places: what it remembers stays as the room changes.
**Each pane a window.** Everything in a pane reads the pane's width as its window: `PantrixTheme.window`, its classes and `PantrixTheme.layout` answer for the pane. The posture stays the window's.
**The panes' names.** `listTitle`, `detailTitle` and `extraTitle` introduce the panes to a screen reader by name; on Android TalkBack says the name of the pane that comes into view.

**The list's width.** `resizable = true` puts a handle between the panes: it is dragged, set with the arrow keys, and a screen reader can change its value. The width stays in `ListDetailState.listWidth`.
**State is kept.** As the room changes from one pane to two the list and the detail stay where they are in the composition: a scroll, a text typed, are not lost.
**Reduce motion.** Where the system asks for less motion the detail opens and closes without sliding.
**Reading direction.** In a right-to-left language the list is on the right, and the detail slides in from the left.

examples.name: AdaptiveListDetailInbox
examples.title: Inbox
examples.description:
The most common shape: a list of messages and the message opened. The list opens a message with `inbox.select(id)`; the detail is given the key of the message opened.

Pick "Narrow" in the card's window selector and press a message: the message takes the list's place. The back button at its top, Android's back button, Escape on a desktop and a swipe from the edge of the screen on iOS bring the list back. The back button stands only in one pane: the detail shows it by `isSinglePane`. `listTitle` and `detailTitle` introduce the panes to a screen reader: TalkBack says the message's subject as it opens, and "Inbox" as the list comes back.

Pick "Short", "Wide" or "Book": the list and the message stand side by side, and while no message is open `emptyDetail` shows on the right. Open a message and switch between "Narrow" and "Wide": the message opened and the list's scroll are both kept.

examples.name: AdaptiveListDetailSettings
examples.title: Settings: the first section open in two panes
examples.description:
A settings screen: the sections on the left, the settings of the one chosen on the right. In two panes the first section stands open instead of an empty detail; in one pane the list of sections shows first.

For that `emptyDetail` draws nothing and opens the first section: `LaunchedEffect(Unit) { settings.select(...) }`. The empty detail is shown only in two panes, so in one pane this never runs.

The settings' values are kept by the example, not by the detail: `values`. Each section is composed anew as it opens; values remembered inside the detail would be lost on going to another section and back. In "Narrow" change a switch, go back, open the section again: the value is where it was.

examples.name: AdaptiveListDetailContacts
examples.title: Contacts, with their history beside them
examples.description:
A third pane beside a contact: their history. The "History" button in the detail opens it with `contacts.showExtra()`.

Pick "Wide": there is room for three panes, and the history stands beside the detail, at the end, with its title and close button inside it. Pick "Short": there is room for two, and the history shows in a sheet that slides in from the end over the detail, inside the scaffold. The sheet's title is `extraTitle` and the close button is the sheet's, so the pane leaves its own title out by `isExtraInSheet`. A press on the scrim, the back button and Escape close the sheet. In "Narrow" it opens in the sheet too.

With the sheet open, scroll the history, then switch to "Wide": the history moves beside the detail and its scroll stays. The pane is one composition in both places.

Going from one contact to another makes the history the other's; going back to the list, `back()`, closes the history too.

examples.name: AdaptiveListDetailFiles
examples.title: Files: the list's width is dragged
examples.description:
The list's width is the reader's: `resizable = true` puts a handle between the panes. Drag it with a mouse or a finger; on a keyboard come to the handle with Tab, and the arrow keys move it in steps of 16 dp, Home and End to its narrowest and widest. A screen reader reads the handle as "List width" and can change its value.

The width is kept in `files.listWidth`; the line in the detail writes it, and "Back to the default" returns it to the style's with `Dp.Unspecified`. The style here asks for a list of 280 dp, and 200 dp at the least: `ListDetailScaffoldStyle(listWidth = 280.dp, minListWidth = 200.dp)`. The list can grow as wide as leaves the detail 320 dp.

The handle stands only in two panes: pick "Short" or "Wide".

examples.name: AdaptiveListDetailFold
examples.title: On a foldable: they meet at the fold
examples.description:
On a foldable the list and the detail meet at the fold. Each pane writes its own size and its own window class; the line above it shows what it is told. A pane is a window of its own: in "Book" the window is `Expanded`, but each of the two 456 dp panes reads `Compact`.

Pick "Book": the 951 dp window is wide enough for two panes anyway, but the list is not 360 dp: it reaches the fold. The gap is the 20 dp strip on each side of the fold; nothing falls on the fold. A narrower foldable held like a book takes two panes too. There is no handle: the fold places the panes.

Pick "Table": the fold lies across and does not divide panes side by side. The 669 dp window is `Medium`: one pane.

pages.title: Supporting pane
pages.summary:
A screen's main content and a pane that supports it: a document and its comments, a chart and its filters, a map and its results. Side by side where there is room; where there is not, the supporting pane opens in a sheet over the main content, or in its place.

`PantrixSupportingPaneScaffold` looks at its own room, not the window. From `Expanded` on, where the main content does not go under the style's `minMainWidth`, the supporting pane stands at the end, 360dp wide, and the main content takes the rest. In a narrower room the supporting pane is closed, and `show()` opens it.

What is shown is kept in a `SupportingPaneState`: remembered with `rememberSupportingPaneState()`, and not lost on a rotation or when the process starts again. `show()` and `hide()` open and close the pane for the room it is in.
features: **Beside.** In a wide room the supporting pane is open from the start; `hide()` puts it away and the main content takes the whole room. Back is the app's: the scaffold leaves it alone.

**A sheet in a narrow room.** `presentation` is `Sheet` by default: the supporting pane opens in a sheet in the scaffold's own room, over the main content. On a phone (`Compact`) it comes from the bottom and closes when dragged down by its handle; in a wider room it comes from the end. Its title is `supportingTitle`, with a close button beside it; a press on the scrim, the back key, Escape and the edge swipe of iOS close it too. A keyboard's focus goes into the sheet, and back where it was as it closes.

**In the pane's place in a narrow room.** `SupportingPanePresentation.Pane` brings the supporting pane into the main content's place, sliding in from the end; back brings the main content back, and in an edge swipe the pane follows the finger.
**As the room changes.** A narrower window does not open the sheet by itself, nor cover the main content. A supporting pane open over the main content stays beside it as the window grows wider.

**What the panes are told.** Each pane is built in a `SupportingPaneScope`: `supportingPlace` says where the supporting pane is (`Beside`, `Sheet`, `InPlaceOfMain`), `isSupportingShown` whether it is in view. Beside, the pane draws its own title and hide button; in the sheet the title is the scaffold's.

**Resizable.** `resizable = true` puts a handle between the panes: it is dragged, set with the arrow keys, and a screen reader can change its value. The width stays in `SupportingPaneState.supportingWidth`.
**Foldables.** Held like a book, the two panes meet at the fold at any width; laid on a table, the main content is above the fold and the supporting pane below it.
**Each pane a window.** Everything in a pane reads the pane's width as its window.
**State is kept.** The supporting pane stays in the composition while it is hidden and as it moves from one place to another: a comment being written and a chosen filter are not lost.
**Reading direction.** In a language read from right to left the supporting pane is on the left.

examples.name: AdaptiveSupportingPaneDocument
examples.title: A document and its comments
examples.description:
A report and its comments. In a wide room the comments stand beside the report; "Hide comments" above it puts them away, and the report takes the whole room.

Choose "Narrow" in the card's window picker and press "Comments": the comments come in a sheet that opens from the bottom. Drag it down by its handle, press the scrim or press the close button: it closes. In "Medium" the sheet comes from the end.

Write something in the comment field and change the window: what you wrote stays. The supporting pane is one composition wherever it is. Beside the report the pane draws its own title and hide button (`supportingPlace == Beside`); in the sheet the title and the close button are the scaffold's.

examples.name: AdaptiveSupportingPaneChart
examples.title: A chart and its filters: the width is dragged
examples.description:
A chart and its filters. The filters' values are kept in the example (`channels`, `stacked`): both panes read them, and the chart draws itself again as a filter changes.

`resizable = true`: in a wide room drag the handle between the panes, or focus it and adjust it with the arrow keys; the left arrow widens the filters. The width stays in `supportingWidth`, and is where it was after going to "Narrow" and back. `style = SupportingPaneScaffoldStyle(minSupportingWidth = 240.dp)`: the handle makes the filters no narrower than 240dp.

examples.name: AdaptiveSupportingPaneMap
examples.title: A map and its results: in the map's place in a narrow room
examples.description:
A map and its results, with `presentation = SupportingPanePresentation.Pane`: in a narrow room the results open in the map's place, not in a sheet. The back button at their top, Android's back key, Escape and the edge swipe of iOS bring the map back; the back button stands only then (`supportingPlace == InPlaceOfMain`).

Press a result: its mark on the map grows. The choice is kept in the example, and both panes read it.

examples.name: AdaptiveSupportingPaneToggle
examples.title: Hiding and showing it beside
examples.description:
The state's two halves: `isShownBeside` keeps what a wide room shows, `isOpenOver` what a narrow room shows; `isShown` reads the one of the room as it is. They are apart: a narrower window does not open the sheet by itself.

In "Wide" press "Hide", then go to "Narrow" and press "Show": the sheet opens. Go back to "Wide": the supporting pane stands beside, and `isShownBeside` is "yes" again. `rememberSupportingPaneState(initiallyShownBeside = false)` starts it closed in a wide room too.

examples.name: AdaptiveSupportingPaneFold
examples.title: On a foldable: split at the fold
examples.description:
On a foldable the two panes are split at the fold. Each pane writes its own size and window class.

Choose "Book": the window is 951dp wide with an upright fold; the main content and the supporting pane are on each side of it, and the gap between them is the strip of 20dp each side of the fold. Choose "Table": the fold lies across, the main content above it and the supporting pane below. A window of 669dp would be one pane on a flat phone; on a foldable laid on a table it is two.

The scaffold looks for the fold in its own room. In "Table" the fold is in the middle of the 951dp window: there the example is as tall as the window, so that the fold crosses it. On a screen the scaffold takes the whole window anyway, with `Modifier.fillMaxSize()`.

pages.title: Tabletop
pages.summary:
Content that is looked at and the controls that are touched, by how a foldable is held: a video and its player's buttons, a video call and its buttons, a camera's view and its shutter.

`PantrixTabletopLayout` takes two parts: `content` and `controls`. With a foldable laid half open on a table (the hinge lying across), the content fills the half above the fold and the controls the half below: what is looked at above, the hands below. Held like a book, the two stand at each side of the fold. On a screen that does not fold, the controls are under the content or over it.
features: **Flat.** `flatControls` is `Below` by default: the controls at the bottom, as tall as they are, and the content takes the rest. `Overlay`: the content takes the whole room and the controls sit over its bottom.
**On a table.** The content fills the half above the fold and the controls the half below; the fold's strip stays clear. The controls take the whole lower half and arrange themselves.
**Like a book.** The content at the start of the fold, the controls at its other side.
**What the parts are told.** Both parts are built in a `TabletopScope`: `arrangement` is `Flat`, `Tabletop` or `Book`. The controls can choose to be drawn larger on a table.
**It looks at its own room.** Where the fold does not cross the layout's own room, the layout is flat.
**State is kept.** As the posture changes the two parts stay where they are in the composition, at once and with no motion: the video goes on from where it was.
**Each part a window.** Everything in a part reads the part's room as its window.
**Reading direction.** In a right-to-left language, held like a book, the content is at the right of the fold.

examples.name: AdaptiveTabletopPlayer
examples.title: A video player
examples.description:
A video and its player. Flat, the buttons stand under the video, as tall as they are.

Choose "Table" in the card's window picker: the video moves above the fold and the buttons below it, where they take the lower half; there `arrangement == Tabletop`, so the buttons grow and the video's name is written too. Press play and change the window: the video goes on from where it was, and neither part leaves the composition.

In the tabletop posture the fold is in the middle of the 951dp window: there the example is as tall as the window, so that the fold crosses it. On a screen the layout takes the whole window anyway, with `Modifier.fillMaxSize()`.

examples.name: AdaptiveTabletopOverlay
examples.title: Controls over the video
examples.description: The same player with `flatControls = TabletopControls.Overlay`: flat, the video takes the whole room and the buttons sit over its bottom. On a table they still move below the fold. Over the video (`arrangement == Flat`) the buttons draw a dark, see-through ground so that they can be read.

examples.name: AdaptiveTabletopCall
examples.title: A video call
examples.description:
A video call: the people above, the buttons below. Whether the microphone and the camera are on is kept in the example; the people's tiles read it.

In "Table" the people stay above the fold and the buttons grow side by side below it: with the phone on a table, the hands are there.

examples.name: AdaptiveTabletopMeasured
examples.title: On a foldable: the parts write their measures
examples.description: Each part writes its own size and window class. In "Book" the 951dp window is split in two at the fold: the content on the left, the controls on the right. In "Table" the content is above the fold and the controls below it, both 669dp wide. In a flat window the controls are as tall as they are.

pages.title: Overlays on a fold
pages.summary:
Overlays on a foldable device: a dialog, a sheet, a popover, a menu, a command palette and a snackbar stay in a half of the fold, and none lies across it.

The rules are in the overlays' shared code; the components need no new parameter. They hold while a foldable is held half open, or where a hinge stands between two screens; a foldable opened flat is a screen in one piece.
features: **Dialog.** It is in the middle of the half it was opened from: the half of the last press, or of the focused control where it was opened with the keyboard. Where neither is known, the start half in a book, and the lower half on a table: that is where the hands are.

**Sheets.** On a table a bottom sheet takes the lower half, and a full-screen sheet all of it. In a book a bottom sheet is in the half it was opened from, as wide as that half; a side sheet is exactly the end half, from the fold's strip to the window's end.

**Anchored overlays.** A popover, a menu, a tooltip and a select's list stay in the half of the control they are anchored to: where they do not fit, they first take the other side, then slide, and last get smaller and scroll.
**Command palette.** In a book it is in the half it was opened from, as a dialog is; on a table it is in the upper half, no taller than it.

**Snackbar.** In a book a snackbar keeps to a half: one in the end corner to the end half, the others to the start half. A snackbar as wide as a phone's window would reach past the fold in a corner too.

**Overlays opened in a frame.** "Book" and "Table" on this page are a window frame drawn inside the card (`PantrixWindowFrame`): an overlay opened inside it takes the frame for its window. The scrim covers the frame, a sheet comes in from the frame's edges and the fold is the frame's; in a frame drawn smaller the overlay is drawn smaller too.

**A hinge that hides.** On a device of two screens `Modifier.keepClearOfFolds()` keeps content off the strip of the hinge that hides the screen: beside a hinge near a node's edge the other side is left empty.
**Your own overlay.** `rememberOverlayWindow()` tells an overlay its window, the folds and where it was opened from: an app that shows a `Dialog` or a `Popup` of its own places it by the same rules.

examples.name: AdaptiveFoldOverlaysDialog
examples.title: A dialog in the half it was opened from
examples.description:
A button in each of two corners opens the same dialog. In "Book" the left button opens it in the left half and the right one in the right half; in "Table" the upper one in the upper half and the lower one in the lower half. In a flat window the dialog is always in the middle.

In "Book" and "Table" the example is as tall as the window: the fold crosses it, and the dialog opens in a half of the window.

examples.name: AdaptiveFoldOverlaysAnchored
examples.title: A popover and a menu beside the fold
examples.description: The popover of a button just before the fold asks to open on its right; in "Book" its right is the other side of the fold, so it opens on its left. The menu of a button just above the fold asks to open below it; in "Table" below it is the other side of the fold, so it opens above.

examples.name: AdaptiveFoldOverlaysSheets
examples.title: Sheets at the fold
examples.description: Three buttons open three sheets. In "Table" the bottom sheet and the full-screen sheet both stay below the fold, and so does the side sheet. In "Book" the bottom sheets open in the buttons' half, as wide as that half; the side sheet is exactly the right half.

examples.name: AdaptiveFoldOverlaysPalette
examples.title: A command palette and a snackbar
examples.description: In "Table" the command palette opens above the fold, no taller than the upper half: a long list scrolls. "Save" shows a snackbar; here the snackbar is in the middle of the bottom edge on every platform, and in "Book" it moves to the middle of the left half.

examples.name: AdaptiveFoldOverlaysOwn
examples.title: Your own overlay: rememberOverlayWindow
examples.description:
An app that shows a `Dialog` or a `Popup` of its own gets what Pantrix's overlays place themselves by from `rememberOverlayWindow()`: the overlay's window (here the card's frame), the folds and where it was opened from. Press the button in either corner: the text in the middle says which side of the fold the last press was on, and in which half an overlay of your own opens. Left and right in "Book", upper and lower in "Table"; a flat window has no fold.

`openedFrom()` and the places of the folds are in the same coordinates, the pixels of the app's window: the two are compared directly.

examples.name: AdaptiveFoldOverlaysKeepClear
examples.title: keepClearOfFolds on a device of two screens
examples.description: A device of two screens, with a hinge between them that hides what is under it. The order card is two thirds of the device's width and runs over the hinge. With `keepClearOfFolds()` on, the card stays on the left screen and the other side of the hinge is empty; with it off, part of the text is under the hinge.

    data: List<T>,

    modifier: Modifier = Modifier,
    curve: ChartCurve = ChartCurve.Linear,
    fill: ChartFill = ChartFill.Gradient,
    missing: ChartMissing = ChartMissing.Gap,
    stacked: Boolean = false,
    stacking: ChartStacking = ChartStacking.Normal,
    labels: ChartDataLabels? = null,
    xAxis: ChartAxis? = ChartAxis(),
    yAxis: ChartAxis? = ChartAxis(),
    secondYAxis: ChartAxis? = ChartAxis(),
    marks: List<ChartMark> = emptyList(),
    legend: ChartLegend? = ChartLegend(),
    tooltip: ChartTooltip? = ChartTooltip(),
    zoom: ChartZoom? = null,
    decimation: ChartDecimation? = ChartDecimation(),
    export: ChartExport? = null,
    empty: (@Composable () -> Unit)? = null,
    state: ChartState = rememberChartState(),
    description: String? = null,
    onSelect: ((ChartPoint) -> Unit)? = null,
    style: ChartStyle? = null,
    colors: ChartColors? = null,
    tagKey: String? = null
)
declarations.description:
An area chart of rows that are given once: for each of the `values` read from them a line, with the room between it and nought filled.

It is a `PantrixChart` whose series are all filled lines read from the same rows, written shorter. Its axis of values starts at nought unless the axis says otherwise: the height of a filled area is read as an amount, and an area cut off above nought shows less than there is.

Each area is drawn over the one before it, and all of them from nought: a later series covers an earlier one where it is the larger, which the fading `fill` lets through. Give the larger series first. Where the values are parts of a whole they are `stacked`: each area stands on the one before it, and the topmost line is the whole. Stacked by their shares, as `stacking` says, the topmost line is a hundred percent all along, and the areas show how the whole is shared out from place to place.

```
PantrixAreaChart(
    data = months,
    x = { it.name },
    values = listOf(ChartValue("revenue", "Revenue") { it.revenue }),
    curve = ChartCurve.Smooth,
    tagKey = "revenue"
)
```

parameters.description: how the stacked areas stand on one another: as their values, or as their shares of the stack. Areas that are not `stacked` have no stack for it to go by.

parameters.name: xAxis

declarations.description:
A bar chart of rows that are given once: at each place the rows name, a bar for each of the `values` read from them, side by side, or on one another where they are `stacked`.

It is a `PantrixChart` whose series are all bars read from the same rows, written shorter: it does everything a chart does. Its axis of values starts at nought unless the axis says otherwise: a bar's length is read as an amount. A chart of bars with a line over them, or of bars from different lists, is a `PantrixChart` given a `BarSeries` for each run of bars and a `LineSeries` for the line.

Side by side suits a few values that are compared at each place; stacked suits parts that make up a whole, where the whole is read as well. A value under nought goes down from nought, and in a stack under the others that do. Where the parts matter more than the whole, the `stacking` by their shares makes every bar as tall as the others. `horizontal` bars go along the chart from its side, one place under the other: a ranking, or places with long names, each written across in the room of a line.

```
PantrixBarChart(
    data = months,
    x = { it.name },
    values = listOf(
        ChartValue("online", "Online") { it.online },
        ChartValue("stores", "Stores") { it.stores }
    ),
    stacked = true,
    tagKey = "sales"
)
```

    hollow: Boolean = false,
    color: Color = Color.Unspecified,

    yAxis: ChartAxis? = ChartAxis(),

    tooltip: ChartTooltip? = ChartTooltip(),

    onSelect: ((ChartPoint) -> Unit)? = null,
    style: ChartStyle? = null,
    colors: ChartColors? = null,
    tagKey: String? = null

declarations.description:
A candlestick chart: at each place what something opened at and closed at, and the highest and the lowest it reached between the two, as a price does in a day of trading.

It is a `PantrixChart` with one `CandlestickSeries`, written shorter: it does everything a chart does. A place has a body from its opening to its close and a thin wick from its lowest to its highest. A candle that closes over its opening is drawn in the chart's `rising` colour and one that closes under it in its `falling` colour, the theme's `success` and `danger` unless `colors` says otherwise; one that closes where it opened is a line across, in `color`.

A row has all four values or none: where one is missing, the place has no candle. The axis of values does not take nought in by itself: it goes from a round number under the lowest to one over the highest.

In the tooltip and to a screen reader a candle is its four values, each called by what it is in the theme's language. A press is handed the close as the point's `value`, the opening as its `from`, and the ends of the wick as its `high` and its `low`.

Where every row's `x` is a moment, a `kotlin.time.Instant`, the candles stand where their moments are, and a day with no row is a gap: a weekend between two weeks of trading.

```
PantrixCandlestickChart(
    data = days,
    x = { it.day },
    open = { it.open },
    high = { it.high },
    low = { it.low },
    close = { it.close },
    name = "Price",
    tagKey = "price"
)
```

declarations.signature: enum class CandleKind
declarations.description: How a `CandlestickSeries` draws the four values of a place.

entries.name: Candle
entries.description: A body from the opening to the close, with a wick through its middle from the lowest to the highest.

entries.name: Ohlc
entries.description: A line from the lowest to the highest, with a tick before it at the opening and one after it at the close: an OHLC bar, which stays apart from its neighbours where candles would crowd.

declarations.name: CandlestickSeries
declarations.description:
A series of four values at a place: what something opened at there and closed at, and the highest and the lowest it reached between the two, as a price does in a day of trading.

```
CandlestickSeries(
    key = "price",
    name = "Price",
    data = days,
    x = { it.day },
    open = { it.open },
    high = { it.high },
    low = { it.low },
    close = { it.close }
)
```

A place has a body from its opening to its close, as wide as a bar, and a thin wick through the body's middle from the lowest to the highest. A candle that closes over its opening is drawn in the chart's `rising` colour and one that closes under it in its `falling` colour, which a chart's `colors` say; one that closes where it opened is a line across, in the series' own `color`. A `hollow` series draws the body of a candle that closes over its opening as its outline alone, with the wick outside it, which tells the two ways apart without their colours. `colorOf` gives a candle a colour of its own, a day of news in another, and the way it went to the others. In the legend a series of candles has a sample of two halves, the rising colour and the falling one.

A row has all four values or none: where one is missing, or is no number, the place has no candle. The wick reaches at least as far as the body does: a highest under the close is taken for the close.

In the tooltip a candle has a row for each of its four values, called by what it is in the theme's language, and a screen reader is told the same. A press is handed the close as the point's `value`, the opening as its `from`, and the two ends of the wick as its `high` and its `low`.

A chart that has candles gives each place a band of its width, as a chart with bars does. Its axis of values does not take nought in by itself: what is read is how the values move, not how large they are. The series is of no stack, and writes no values at its marks.

Two series are the same series where everything they were built from is the same, the functions among them.

parameters.description: What tells the series from the others of its chart, and stays the same while its values change: what the legend keeps a hidden series by, what a selection names, and what an event reports. Written as a test tag's key is, in small letters and digits.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: What the series is called: in the legend, in the tooltip and to a screen reader.

parameters.name: data
parameters.description: The rows.

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: Where a row stands along the chart: a moment, a day's name, anything that is equal to itself.

parameters.name: open
parameters.description: What the row opened at.

parameters.name: high
parameters.description: The highest it reached.

parameters.name: low
parameters.description: The lowest it reached.

parameters.name: close
parameters.description: What it closed at.

parameters.name: color
parameters.description: The colour of a candle that closes where it opened, and of the series in a legend. Left out, it is the theme's chart colour for the series' place among the series of the chart.

parameters.name: kind
parameters.description: Whether a place is drawn as a candle or as an OHLC bar.

parameters.name: hollow
parameters.description: Whether the body of a candle that closes over its opening is its outline alone. An OHLC bar has no body, and is drawn the same either way.

parameters.name: colorOf
parameters.description: The colour of a row's candle, or `Color.Unspecified` for the colour of the way it went. Null gives every candle the colour of its way.

parameters.name: axis
parameters.description: Which of the chart's axes of values the series is read by.

declarations.signature:
@Composable
fun PantrixChart(
    series: List<ChartSeries>,
    modifier: Modifier = Modifier,
    xAxis: ChartAxis? = ChartAxis(),
    yAxis: ChartAxis? = ChartAxis(),
    secondYAxis: ChartAxis? = ChartAxis(),
    marks: List<ChartMark> = emptyList(),
    stacking: ChartStacking = ChartStacking.Normal,
    orientation: ChartOrientation = ChartOrientation.Vertical,
    legend: ChartLegend? = ChartLegend(),
    tooltip: ChartTooltip? = ChartTooltip(),
    zoom: ChartZoom? = null,
    decimation: ChartDecimation? = ChartDecimation(),
    export: ChartExport? = null,
    empty: (@Composable () -> Unit)? = null,
    state: ChartState = rememberChartState(),
    description: String? = null,
    onSelect: ((ChartPoint) -> Unit)? = null,
    style: ChartStyle? = null,
    colors: ChartColors? = null,
    tagKey: String? = null
)
declarations.description:
A chart of values along a run of places: lines and filled areas through the values each series has at each place, and bars up to them, with an axis of the places under them and an axis of the values beside them.

The chart is given its `series`, and each of them carries its own rows: what the series is drawn from, where a row stands and what its value is. The chart sets out every place any of them names, in the order they are first named. Series of different kinds are drawn in one chart, a line over bars, and need not be read from the same rows. The series that name the same `stack` stand on one another: as their values, or, as `stacking` says, as their shares of what the stack comes to at each place, every stack as tall as every other.

Around the series stand the chart's parts, each given by what describes it and taken away by `null`: the two axes, the `legend` and the `tooltip`. Left as they are, the axes write the places and round values with lines across the chart at them, the legend lists the series from the second on, and the tooltip shows the values at the place that is pointed at.

**A second axis of values.** A series that says it is read by the second axis is set out by a scale of its own, written at the chart's other side: an amount and a share of it, a count and a price, in one chart. Its marks stand on the first axis' lines, so that one grid serves both. Each value is written as its own axis writes it, in the tooltip and to a screen reader too.

**Ranges, steps and candles.** A `RangeSeries` has two values at each place and draws what lies between them, as a band from place to place or as a bar that stands on no axis. A `WaterfallSeries` draws each of its values as a step from where the one before it ended, and its totals on nought. A `CandlestickSeries` has four values at each place: what it opened and closed at, and the highest and the lowest between.

**Places that are moments.** Where every place of the chart is a `kotlin.time.Instant`, the places are set out by time: in the order of time whatever the order of the rows, as far from each other as their moments are, so that a day with no row is a gap. The axis is marked at round moments, hours, days, months, as many as have room, and a place is written as a date. Both are read by the screen's clock (`LocalPantrixClock`) and written in the theme's language, unless the axis of places says otherwise by its `time`: see `ChartTime`. A name among the moments, and the places are names again, at even steps. Places that are gapless stand at even steps all the same, with no gap for the days a market is closed, and the axis is marked at the first place of each day, week or month.

**Places that are numbers.** Numbers are names like any other, at even steps in the order the rows name them, unless the axis of places is `numeric`: then the places are set out by their numbers, in their order and as far apart as they are, the axis is marked at round numbers that have room, and a mark stands at any number.

**Marks.** A line at a value or at a place, and a band between two, are drawn with the series for them to be read by: a target, a limit, the weeks of a campaign. In a chart whose places are moments a mark stands at any moment, a row's or not. See `ChartMark`.

**Pointing at a place.** A pointer over the chart points at the place nearest it; a finger does by a tap, or drawn along the chart, and a tap on the place it points at lets go of it. With the keyboard the chart is one stop for Tab: the arrows along the chart go from place to place, Home and End to the first and the last, and Escape lets go. Where the tooltip tells the series apart, the arrows up and down go from one series' value to the next. The place is marked, the tooltip shown for it, and it is told to `state`. A press, Enter or Space on it calls `onSelect`.

**To a screen reader** the chart is its `description`, then each place with the values the series have there, in the places' order, which a finger also finds by touching the chart; the legend's entries are switches. A chart of more than two hundred places is told by its description alone.

**Its size.** The chart is as wide as it is given room. A height on its modifier is the whole chart's, the legend's with it; given none, the plot is as tall as the chart's style says and a legend above or under it adds its own. The places that have no room to be written are left out by a rule, every second, every third: the chart's values stay where they are.

In a language read from the right the places run from the right and the values are written at the right.

```
PantrixChart(
    series = listOf(
        LineSeries("visits", "Visits", days, x = { it.day }, y = { it.visits }),
        LineSeries("orders", "Orders", days, x = { it.day }, y = { it.orders }, dash = ChartDash.Dashed)
    ),
    modifier = Modifier.height(240.dp),
    description = "Visits and orders of the last thirty days",
    tagKey = "traffic"
)
```

parameters.name: series
parameters.description: the series, in the order they are drawn and listed: a later one is drawn over an earlier. Their keys tell them apart, and two with one key are refused.

parameters.name: modifier
parameters.description: the chart's modifier. A height here is the chart's, the legend's with it.

parameters.name: xAxis
parameters.description: the axis of the places, under the chart, or beside it in a horizontal chart. `null` draws nothing of it.

parameters.name: yAxis
parameters.description: the axis of the values, beside the chart, or under it in a horizontal chart. `null` draws nothing of it.

parameters.name: secondYAxis
parameters.description: the second axis of the values, at the chart's other side, or over it in a horizontal chart: drawn where a series, or a mark at a value, is read by it, and not otherwise. `null` draws nothing of it, and what is read by it is set out by it all the same.

parameters.name: marks
parameters.description: the lines and the bands drawn in the plot besides the series.

parameters.name: stacking
parameters.description: how the series of a stack stand on one another: as their values, or as their shares of the stack.

parameters.name: orientation
parameters.description: which way the places go: along the chart's foot, as columns, or down its side, as horizontal bars, each name written across in the room of a line. Horizontal, a chart that is looked at closer moves up and down its places, and its navigator stands beside the plot.

parameters.name: legend
parameters.description: where the names of the series stand. `null` shows none.

parameters.name: tooltip
parameters.description: what is shown for the place that is pointed at. `null` shows none.

parameters.name: zoom
parameters.description: what lets the reader look closer at a part of the places and move along the rest. `null`, which it is unless the chart is given one, shows all the places and no more.

parameters.name: decimation
parameters.description: how a line with more points in view than the plot has room for is drawn through fewer of them. `null` draws every point, as many as there are.

parameters.name: export
parameters.description: what lets the reader take the chart out of the app as a file: a picture, or a drawing that is sharp at any size. `null`, which it is unless the chart is given one, and the chart has no such button.

parameters.name: empty
parameters.description: what the chart shows in its plot while it has no value to draw, in the place of the theme's words for it ("No data"), which a screen reader is then not told either. `null` writes the words. A file the chart is exported as says them.

parameters.name: state
parameters.description: what the reader has hidden and what they point at: the chart's own where none is given.

parameters.name: description
parameters.description: what the chart shows, in a few words, for a screen reader: the first thing it says of the chart. Left out, the chart is announced by the names of its series.

parameters.name: onSelect
parameters.description: called with the value that is pressed: the one pointed at, or of the series nearest the press where the place's values are pointed at together.

parameters.name: style
parameters.description: this chart's own geometry: the fields set here, with the theme's for the rest.

parameters.name: colors
parameters.description: this chart's own colours, where they are not the theme's.

parameters.name: tagKey
parameters.description: the chart's automation key: the chart is `Chart_<tagKey>`, its plot `Chart_<tagKey>.Plot`, a place of it `Chart_<tagKey>.Point_<number>` counted from one, the legend's entry of a series `Chart_<tagKey>.Legend_<series' key>` and the tooltip `Chart_<tagKey>.Tooltip`. A press on a value is reported as a `Chart` `select` event with the series' key, and a press on a legend's entry as a `toggle` event with the key and whether the series is shown. Nothing of the values is reported.

declarations.name: ChartYAxis
declarations.signature: enum class ChartYAxis
declarations.description: Which of a chart's axes of values a series, or a mark at a value, is read by.

entries.name: First
entries.description: The chart's axis of values, written where lines start: its `yAxis`.

entries.name: Second
entries.description: The chart's second axis of values, written at its other side: its `secondYAxis`.

declarations.name: ChartAxis
declarations.description:
An axis of a `PantrixChart`: what is written along it, the lines drawn from it, and, for an axis of values, how far it goes.

A chart has an axis along which its series stand, the places their rows name, and an axis of the values they have there; a chart whose series are of two kinds of value, an amount and a share of it, has a second axis of values at its other side. Each takes what applies to it and leaves the rest: the places have no least and no most, the values no `label`.

```
val strings = PantrixTheme.strings
PantrixChart(series = series, yAxis = ChartAxis(title = "Visits", format = { strings.compact(it) }))
```

`null` in the place of an axis draws nothing of it: no labels, no line, no grid. The series are set out by it all the same.

parameters.name: title
parameters.description: What the axis measures, written beside it: under the places, and turned along the side of the values. None where it is left out.

parameters.name: labels
parameters.description: Whether the places, or the values at the grid's lines, are written. Where the places do not all have room, every second, or third, is written, and the same ones as the chart's width changes little.

parameters.name: line
parameters.description: Whether a line is drawn along the axis. Left out, the places have one, under them, and the values have none.

parameters.name: grid
parameters.description: Whether a line is drawn across the chart at each of the axis' marks. Left out, the values have them and the places do not; a second axis of values has them where the first axis is not drawn, at its own marks.

parameters.name: ticks
parameters.description: About how many values are marked along an axis of values. They stand at round numbers, and no nearer each other than that many would: there may be fewer. Nought marks as many as have room. A second axis of values has its say in it only where it is marked by itself: where it names an end or is given its `values`. Otherwise its marks stand on the first's lines.

parameters.name: values
parameters.description: The values marked along an axis of values, in the place of round steps: `listOf(0.0, 6.0, 12.0, 18.0, 24.0)` for the hours of a day. Those that lie between the axis' ends are marked; an end that is not named goes as far as the farthest of them and of the values the axis shows. `ticks` is not read. A second axis of values that is given its own is marked by itself, and the grid stays the first's.

parameters.name: min
parameters.description: The least value the axis shows. Left out, it is a round number under the least of the values, or nought where `startFromZero` says so. A second axis of values that names an end is marked by itself.

parameters.name: max
parameters.description: The most the axis shows. Left out, it is a round number over the most of the values.

parameters.name: startFromZero
parameters.description: Whether an axis of values starts at nought though every value is far over it, or ends there though every value is under it. Left out, it does where a series is filled, since the height of a filled area is read as an amount, and does not for lines alone, whose rise and fall is what is read.

parameters.name: format
parameters.description: How a value of the axis is written: beside the axis, in the tooltip and to a screen reader. Left out, beside the axis a value is written short from ten thousand on (`12K`), and everywhere else in full, in the theme's language.

parameters.name: label
parameters.description: How a place is written, given what a series' `x` gave for it: under the chart, as the tooltip's heading and to a screen reader. Left out, it is written as it writes itself, and a whole number in the theme's digits. In a chart whose places are moments it says how a place is written in the tooltip and to a screen reader, and the axis' marks are `time`'s to write.

parameters.name: time
parameters.description: For a chart whose places are moments, every one a `kotlin.time.Instant`: how they are written and by which clock. Left out, in the theme's language and by the screen's clock (`LocalPantrixClock`). An axis of values reads none of it.

parameters.name: numeric
parameters.description: Whether an axis of places whose places are all numbers sets them out by their numbers: in their order, as far apart as they are, with the axis marked at round numbers, each written as `format` says, as the places are too where `label` says nothing; and a mark of the chart at any number between them. Left out, numbers are names like any other, at even steps in the order the rows name them: years, the numbers of the weeks. An axis of values reads none of it.

declarations.name: ChartMark
declarations.signature: sealed class ChartMark
declarations.description:
Something a `PantrixChart` draws in its plot besides its series, for them to be read by: a line at a value or at a place, a band between two.

```
PantrixChart(
    series = series,
    marks = listOf(
        ChartReferenceLine(y = 500, label = "Target"),
        ChartReferenceBand(x1 = "Jun", x2 = "Aug", label = "Summer")
    )
)
```

A mark at a value is drawn against the axis of values it names, and that axis goes far enough to show it. A mark at a place that no series of the chart names is not drawn. A mark that has a label is said to a screen reader after the chart's description, with the value or the place it stands at.

In a chart whose places are moments, each a `kotlin.time.Instant`, a mark at a place stands at any moment, whether a row names it or not, and a band goes from a moment to another: the hour of a release, the days of a holiday. The axis of time goes as far as a mark that stands before the rows or after them, as an axis of values goes as far as a mark at a value; one whose places stand at even steps (`ChartTime.gapless`) does not, and a mark past its rows is not drawn. On a numeric axis of places (`ChartAxis.numeric`) a mark stands at any number in the same way.

A scatter chart draws them too. Both of its axes are of values: a mark at a place stands there at a value of the axis along the chart, a number, and that axis goes far enough to show it.

members.name: label
members.description: What is written at the mark, and said of it to a screen reader. Left out, the mark has no words.

members.name: color
members.description: The colour the mark is drawn in. Left out, it is the colour the axes are written in.

members.name: axis
members.description: Which of the chart's axes of values the mark's values are read by. A mark at a place has no use for it.

members.name: labelPosition
members.description: Where the label is written along the mark.

members.name: inFront
members.description: Whether the mark is drawn over the series, and not behind them. Its label is written over the series either way, on a plate of the tooltip's colour: so that it reads on a bar and over a line.

declarations.name: ChartReferenceLine
declarations.description:
A line through the plot: across it at the value `y`, or up it at the place `x`, one of the two.

```
ChartReferenceLine(y = 500, label = "Target")
ChartReferenceLine(x = "Mar", label = "Launch", dash = ChartDash.Dotted)
```

It is drawn over the series unless it says otherwise, as wide as the style's `markLineWidth`. Its label is written over a line across the plot, or under it where it is too near the plot's top, and beside a line up the plot; at its end unless it says otherwise: at the side lines end at, and at the top of a line up the plot.

Two are the same line where everything they were built from is the same.

parameters.name: y
parameters.description: The value the line stands at.

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: The place the line stands at: what a series' `x` gives for that place.

parameters.name: label
parameters.description: What is written at the mark, and said of it to a screen reader. Left out, the mark has no words.

parameters.name: color
parameters.description: The colour the mark is drawn in. Left out, it is the colour the axes are written in.

parameters.name: dash
parameters.description: Whether the line is drawn whole, in dashes or in dots.

parameters.name: axis
parameters.description: Which of the chart's axes of values the mark's values are read by. A mark at a place has no use for it.

parameters.name: labelPosition
parameters.description: Where the label is written along the mark.

parameters.name: inFront
parameters.description: Whether the mark is drawn over the series, and not behind them. Its label is written over the series either way, on a plate of the tooltip's colour: so that it reads on a bar and over a line.

declarations.name: ChartReferenceBand
declarations.description:
A band of the plot, shaded: across it between the values `y1` and `y2`, or up it between the places `x1` and `x2`, one of the two.

```
ChartReferenceBand(y1 = 300, y2 = 450, label = "Usual")
ChartReferenceBand(x1 = "Jun", x2 = "Aug", label = "Summer")
ChartReferenceBand(y1 = 900, label = "Too many")
```

A band with one end goes from it to the end of the axis: `y1` alone up to the axis' top and `y2` alone from its foot, `x1` alone on to the last place and `x2` alone from the first. Between two places of a chart with bars it takes in the bars of both.

It is drawn behind the series unless it says otherwise, in a tint of its colour, as much of it as the style's `markBandAlpha` says. Its label is written inside it at its top: in its corner at the side lines start at unless it says otherwise.

Two are the same band where everything they were built from is the same.

parameters.name: y1
parameters.description: The value the band starts at.

parameters.name: y2
parameters.description: The value it ends at.

parameters.name: x1
parameters.description: The place the band starts at: what a series' `x` gives for that place.

parameters.name: x2
parameters.description: The place it ends at.

parameters.name: label
parameters.description: What is written at the mark, and said of it to a screen reader. Left out, the mark has no words.

parameters.name: color
parameters.description: The colour the mark is drawn in. Left out, it is the colour the axes are written in.

parameters.name: axis
parameters.description: Which of the chart's axes of values the mark's values are read by. A mark at a place has no use for it.

parameters.name: labelPosition
parameters.description: Where the label is written along the mark.

parameters.name: inFront
parameters.description: Whether the mark is drawn over the series, and not behind them. Its label is written over the series either way, on a plate of the tooltip's colour: so that it reads on a bar and over a line.

declarations.name: ChartMarkLabelPosition
declarations.signature: enum class ChartMarkLabelPosition
declarations.description:
Where a `ChartMark`'s label is written along it.

Along a line across the plot, and along any band, it goes as lines go: from the side lines start at to the side they end at. Along a line up the plot it goes as values go, from the line's foot to its top.

entries.name: Start
entries.description: At the side lines start at, or at the foot of a line up the plot.

entries.name: Center
entries.description: Half-way along.

entries.name: End
entries.description: At the side lines end at, or at the top of a line up the plot.

declarations.name: ChartOrientation
declarations.signature: enum class ChartOrientation
declarations.description: Which way the places of a chart go, and so which way its values do.

entries.name: Vertical
entries.description: The places along the chart's foot, from the side lines start at, and the values up its side: columns.

entries.name: Horizontal
entries.description: The places down the chart's side, from its top, and the values along its foot, from the side lines start at: bars. Long names have the room of a line each, written across.

declarations.name: ChartSeries
declarations.signature: sealed class ChartSeries
declarations.description:
One run of values in a `PantrixChart`: what is drawn for it, and the rows it is read from.

A series carries its own rows. Two series of one chart may be read from one list or from two, and need not stand at the same places: the chart sets out every place any of them names, in the order they are first named, and a series has no value where it names none.

The kinds of series are the kinds of mark a chart draws: a `LineSeries`, which is an area too where it is filled, a `BarSeries`, a `RangeSeries` of two values at a place, a `WaterfallSeries` of steps, and a `CandlestickSeries` of four values at a place. Kinds mix in one chart.

members.name: key
members.description: What tells the series from the others of its chart, and stays the same while its values change: what the legend keeps a hidden series by, what a selection names, and what an event reports. Written as a test tag's key is, in small letters and digits.

members.name: name
members.description: What the series is called: in the legend, in the tooltip and to a screen reader.

members.name: color
members.description: The colour the series is drawn in. Left out, it is the theme's chart colour for its place among the series of the chart: the first of them for the first.

members.name: stack
members.description: What the series is stacked with. The series of a chart that name the same stack stand on one another at each place, in the order they are given: the first on nought, and each of the others on the one before it. A value under nought goes down from nought, under the others of its stack that do. Null, a series stands on nought by itself. A stack is of the series of one axis: two that name the same stack and are read by different axes stand apart.

members.name: axis
members.description: Which of the chart's axes of values the series is read by. A series on the second is set out by a scale of its own, written at the chart's other side: for values of another kind than the first axis', or of another size, a share beside an amount.

members.name: labels
members.description: The series' values written at its marks, where it is given any: none where this is null.

declarations.name: LineSeries
declarations.description:
A series drawn as a line through its points, and as an area where the room under the line is filled.

```
LineSeries("visits", "Visits", days, x = { it.day }, y = { it.visits })
```

`x` says where a row stands along the chart: a name, a day, anything that is equal to itself, as a category; the chart writes it with its axis' `label`, and as it writes itself where that is left out. Where every row of the chart gives a moment, a `kotlin.time.Instant`, the places are set out by time: see `ChartTime`. `y` is the row's value, and null where it has none: what the line does there is `missing`'s to say. A value that is no number, or has no end, is taken as none.

Two series are the same series where everything they were built from is the same, the two functions among them: a chart whose caller builds its series anew each time is not drawn anew for it.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: What tells the series from the others of its chart, and stays the same while its values change: what the legend keeps a hidden series by, what a selection names, and what an event reports. Written as a test tag's key is, in small letters and digits.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: What the series is called: in the legend, in the tooltip and to a screen reader.

parameters.name: data
parameters.description: The rows, in the order the line goes through them.

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: Where a row stands along the chart.

parameters.name: y
parameters.description: A row's value, or null where it has none.

parameters.name: color
parameters.description: The colour the series is drawn in. Left out, it is the theme's chart colour for its place among the series of the chart: the first of them for the first.

parameters.name: curve
parameters.description: How the line goes from a point to the next.

parameters.name: fill
parameters.description: What the room between the line and nought is filled with: nothing, for a line.

parameters.name: marker
parameters.description: What marks each point. A point with none before it and none after is always marked: a line through one point has nothing to show. Where the chart's patterns are on (`ChartStyle.patterns`), a line that marks its points with none has a mark in turn from the fourth line of its chart on.

parameters.name: dash
parameters.description: Whether the line is drawn whole, in dashes or in dots: a way to tell a series by more than its colour, and what a forecast or a target is told from what was measured by. Null, it is drawn whole, and where the chart's patterns are on, whole, dashed or dotted by its place among the chart's series.

parameters.name: missing
parameters.description: What the line does where a row has no value.

parameters.name: stack
parameters.description: What the series is stacked with: the lines of a stack go through the sums of its values, and where they are filled, each is filled down to the line it stands on.

parameters.name: axis
parameters.description: Which of the chart's axes of values the series is read by.

parameters.name: labels
parameters.description: The series' values written over its points. Null writes none.

parameters.name: pattern
parameters.description: The texture the room between the line and nought is filled with besides its colour, where it is filled. Null, none, and where the chart's patterns are on, its turn by its place among the chart's series.

declarations.name: BarSeries
declarations.description:
A series drawn as a bar at each of its places, from nought to its value.

```
BarSeries("revenue", "Revenue", months, x = { it.name }, y = { it.revenue })
```

The bars of a chart's series stand side by side at a place, each in its series' colour, and the series that name the same `stack` share one bar there, each on top of the one before it. A bar goes up from nought for a value over it and down for one under it; a row with no value has no bar.

A chart that has bars gives each place a band of its width, and a line of the same chart goes through the middles of the bands. Its axis of values starts at nought unless the axis says otherwise: a bar's length is read as an amount, and a bar cut off above nought shows less than there is.

A series `behind` the others takes no bar of its own at a place: its bar is as wide as all of the place's bars side by side, and is drawn before every series that is not behind, the volume of a day under its candle. Of two series behind, the one given later is drawn over the other.

Two series are the same series where everything they were built from is the same, the two functions among them.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: What tells the series from the others of its chart, and stays the same while its values change: what the legend keeps a hidden series by, what a selection names, and what an event reports. Written as a test tag's key is, in small letters and digits.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: What the series is called: in the legend, in the tooltip and to a screen reader.

parameters.name: data
parameters.description: The rows.

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: Where a row stands along the chart: a name, a day, anything that is equal to itself.

parameters.name: y
parameters.description: A row's value, or null where it has none.

parameters.name: color
parameters.description: The colour the series is drawn in. Left out, it is the theme's chart colour for its place among the series of the chart: the first of them for the first.

parameters.name: stack
parameters.description: What the series is stacked with. The series of a chart that name the same stack stand on one another at each place, in the order they are given: the first on nought, and each of the others on the one before it. A value under nought goes down from nought, under the others of its stack that do. Null, a series stands on nought by itself. A stack is of the series of one axis: two that name the same stack and are read by different axes stand apart.

parameters.name: behind
parameters.description: Whether the series' bars stand behind those of the other series, as wide as all of them, rather than beside them. A series behind is in no `stack`.

parameters.name: axis
parameters.description: Which of the chart's axes of values the series is read by.

parameters.name: labels
parameters.description: The series' values written at the ends of its bars, and inside the bars of a stack. Null writes none.

parameters.name: pattern
parameters.description: The texture the bars are drawn with besides their colour. Null, none, and where the chart's patterns are on (`ChartStyle.patterns`), its turn by its place among the chart's series.

declarations.name: ChartStacking
declarations.signature: enum class ChartStacking
declarations.description: How the series of a stack stand on one another in a `PantrixChart`: as their values, or as their shares of what the stack comes to at each place.

entries.name: Normal
entries.description: As their values: a stack is as tall as its series' values come to.

entries.name: Percent
entries.description: As their shares: every stack is as tall as every other, a hundred percent, and each series takes its share of it, its value over what the values of its stack come to there, under nought or over it. The axis the stacks are read by writes shares, where it writes nothing of its own; the tooltip writes a value with its share after it, and a label the share. A series in no stack is drawn as its values all the same: read it by the second axis.

declarations.name: ChartTimeUnit
declarations.signature: enum class ChartTimeUnit
declarations.description: What a chart's axis of time counts in, where it writes a moment: from the finest to the coarsest.

entries.name: Second
entries.description: Seconds, the finest unit the axis counts in.

entries.name: Minute
entries.description: Minutes.

entries.name: Hour
entries.description: Hours.

entries.name: Day
entries.description: Days.

entries.name: Month
entries.description: Months.

entries.name: Year
entries.description: Years, the coarsest unit the axis counts in.

declarations.name: ChartTime
declarations.description:
How a chart whose places are moments writes them, and by which clock: what its axis of places is given as its `time`.

A chart's places are moments where every one of them is a `kotlin.time.Instant`. Such a chart sets its places out where their moments are, in the order of time, whatever the order of its rows: two days apart are twice as far from each other as one, and a day with no row is a gap. Its axis is marked at round moments, each hour, each day, each month, as many as have room, and each mark is written by what it counts in.

```
PantrixLineChart(
    data = readings,
    x = { it.at },
    series = listOf(ChartValue("temperature", "Temperature") { it.degrees }),
    xAxis = ChartAxis(time = ChartTime(offset = { Duration.ZERO }))
)
```

Nothing needs to be given: left out, moments are written in the theme's language and read by the screen's clock (`LocalPantrixClock`), the device's unless a test or a preview gives another.

A market is open on some days and not on others, and a chart of its prices has gaps where it is closed. Places that are `gapless` stand at even steps instead, one after another in the order of time as names would, and the axis is marked at the first place of each round stretch of time, each day, each week, each month, as many as have room.

parameters.name: format
parameters.description: How a moment is written, given the moment and what it is written to: a mark of the axis to the unit its marks are apart by, and a place, in the tooltip and to a screen reader, to the finest unit the chart's places are told apart by. Left out, a mark is written short, an hour as `14:00`, a day as `Oct 13`, a month by its name and a January by its year, and a place in full, `Oct 13, 2026 14:00`, all in the theme's language. An axis' `label` is asked before this for how a place is written.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.description: How far the clock the chart is read by is ahead of UTC at a moment: what says which day a moment belongs to, and where a day starts. Left out, it is the screen's clock (`LocalPantrixClock`), the device's unless a test or a preview gives another. For rows that are days of UTC it is `{ Duration.ZERO }`; an app that has a library of time zones asks it for the zone it shows.

parameters.name: gapless
parameters.description: Whether the places stand at even steps, with no gap for the time between two of them where the rows have none: the days a market is closed. A mark of the chart at a moment between two places stands between them, as far from each as it is in time; one before the first place or after the last is not drawn.

declarations.name: ChartValue
declarations.description:
One value of the rows a chart is read from, as a series of it: for the charts that take their rows once and name each series by what it reads from a row.

```
ChartValue("desktop", "Desktop") { it.desktop }
```

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: What tells the series from the others of its chart, and stays the same while its values change.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: What the series is called: in the legend, in the tooltip and to a screen reader.

parameters.name: color
parameters.description: The colour the series is drawn in. Left out, it is the theme's chart colour for its place among the chart's series.

parameters.name: dash
parameters.description: Whether its line is drawn whole, in dashes or in dots. A bar has no line. Null, whole, and where the chart's patterns are on (`ChartStyle.patterns`), as its turn among the chart's series says.

parameters.name: marker
parameters.description: What marks each of its points. A bar has none.

parameters.name: axis
parameters.description: Which of the chart's axes of values the series is read by: the second, at the chart's other side, for a value of another kind than the first's, a share beside an amount.

parameters.name: pattern
parameters.description: The texture its bars, or the room under its line where that is filled, are drawn with besides its colour. Null, none, and where the chart's patterns are on, its turn among the chart's series.

parameters.name: y
parameters.description: A row's value, or null where it has none.

declarations.name: RangeKind
declarations.signature: enum class RangeKind
declarations.description: What a `RangeSeries` draws between the two values it has at a place.

entries.name: Area
entries.description: A band from place to place, between the line through the lower values and the line through the higher.

entries.name: Bar
entries.description: A bar at each place, from its lower value to its higher: a bar that stands on no axis.

declarations.name: RangeSeries
declarations.description:
A series of two values at each place, drawn as what lies between them: the least and the most of a day, the bounds a forecast is trusted within, the hours a shift starts and ends at.

```
RangeSeries("temperature", "Temperature", days, x = { it.name }, low = { it.coldest }, high = { it.warmest })
```

As an Area it is a band between two lines, tinted in the series' colour; as a Bar a bar at each place that starts at the one value and ends at the other, round at both of its ends. A line over a band, a forecast within its bounds, is a `LineSeries` given after it in the same chart. A band is drawn as its `lines`, `dash`, `marker` and `fillAlpha` say; a bar reads none of them. Both are drawn with the texture `pattern` says.

Nothing of a range stands on nought, so its axis does not take nought in for it, and a range does not stack: its `stack` is always null. A row that has no `low` or no `high` has neither: the band stops before it and starts again after it. Which of the two is the greater does not matter to what is drawn.

The tooltip and a screen reader are given both values with a dash between them, and a press is handed the higher as the point's `value` and the lower as its `from`.

Two series are the same series where everything they were built from is the same, the three functions among them.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: What tells the series from the others of its chart, and stays the same while its values change: what the legend keeps a hidden series by, what a selection names, and what an event reports. Written as a test tag's key is, in small letters and digits.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: What the series is called: in the legend, in the tooltip and to a screen reader.

parameters.name: data
parameters.description: The rows.

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: Where a row stands along the chart: a name, a day, anything that is equal to itself.

parameters.name: low
parameters.description: A row's lower value, or null where it has none.

parameters.name: high
parameters.description: A row's higher value, or null where it has none.

parameters.name: color
parameters.description: The colour the series is drawn in. Left out, it is the theme's chart colour for its place among the series of the chart: the first of them for the first.

parameters.name: kind
parameters.description: Whether the range is a band from place to place or a bar at each place.

parameters.name: curve
parameters.description: How the two lines of a band go from a point to the next. A bar has no line.

parameters.name: lines
parameters.description: Whether the two lines of a band are drawn, or the tint between them alone.

parameters.name: dash
parameters.description: Whether the two lines are drawn whole, in dashes or in dots. Null, whole, and where the chart's patterns are on (`ChartStyle.patterns`), as its turn among the chart's series says.

parameters.name: marker
parameters.description: The mark drawn on each point of the two lines, where they are drawn or not. None by default.

parameters.name: fillAlpha
parameters.description: How much of the series' colour the tint between the lines has: from none, a band of its lines alone, to all of it. Left out, about a sixth, as a filled line's tint.

parameters.name: axis
parameters.description: Which of the chart's axes of values the series is read by.

parameters.name: labels
parameters.description: The two values written at the range's ends: the higher over it and the lower under it. Null writes none.

parameters.name: pattern
parameters.description: The texture the band or the bars are drawn with besides their colour. Null, none, and where the chart's patterns are on, its turn by its place among the chart's series.

declarations.name: WaterfallSeries
declarations.description:
A series whose values are steps: each bar starts where the one before it ended, so that the chart shows how an amount comes about, what was added to it and what was taken from it on the way.

```
WaterfallSeries("cash", "Cash", moves, x = { it.name }, y = { it.amount }, total = { it.isTotal })
```

A row's value is what the row adds, and under nought what it takes away. The steps are counted along the chart's places, in their order. A step that adds is drawn in the chart's `rising` colour and one that takes away in its `falling` colour, which a chart's `colors` say; a thin line leads from the end of each bar to where the next begins.

**Totals.** A row that `total` says is a total stands on nought and shows what the steps before it come to: its own value is not asked for. A total that does have a value is where the count starts again: an opening amount before the first step, or a count taken up again from a known figure. Totals are drawn in the series' own `color`.

A row with no value is a step of nothing, and has no bar. A waterfall does not stack, and its axis takes nought in: its totals stand on it.

In the tooltip and to a screen reader a step is what it adds, with its sign, and a total what it comes to. A press is handed the step as the point's `value` and the level it starts from as its `from`: what the count has come to after it is the two together.

Two series are the same series where everything they were built from is the same, the three functions among them.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: What tells the series from the others of its chart, and stays the same while its values change: what the legend keeps a hidden series by, what a selection names, and what an event reports. Written as a test tag's key is, in small letters and digits.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: What the series is called: in the legend, in the tooltip and to a screen reader.

parameters.name: data
parameters.description: The rows, in the order their steps are counted.

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: Where a row stands along the chart: a name, a day, anything that is equal to itself.

parameters.name: y
parameters.description: What a row adds, under nought what it takes away, or null where it has no value. For a total, the amount the count starts again from, or null for what the steps before it come to.

parameters.name: total
parameters.description: Whether a row is a total. Null, the series has none.

parameters.name: color
parameters.description: The colour the series is drawn in. Left out, it is the theme's chart colour for its place among the series of the chart: the first of them for the first.

parameters.name: connectors
parameters.description: Whether a line leads from the end of each bar to the next.

parameters.name: axis
parameters.description: Which of the chart's axes of values the series is read by.

parameters.name: labels
parameters.description: What each bar stands for written at its end: a step with its sign, a total as it is. Null writes none.

declarations.name: ChartDataLabels
declarations.description:
The values of a series written in the chart, each at its mark: over a point of a line, at the end of a bar, and inside a bar of a stack, in the one of black and white that reads better on the bar's colour.

```
BarSeries("revenue", "Revenue", months, x = { it.name }, y = { it.revenue }, labels = ChartDataLabels())
BarSeries("online", "Online", months, x = { it.name }, y = { it.online }, stack = "sales",
    labels = ChartDataLabels(position = ChartDataLabelPosition.InsideEnd, total = true))
```

A value has its label where the label has room. Placed by itself, one that would stand on another, or reach out of the chart, is written under its point instead, or inside the end of its bar; where it has no room there either it is left out, as is one that a bar is too small to hold. Placed where its `position` says, it has no other place. The tooltip and the screen reader still have the value. A chart of more than two hundred places writes none.

A line the chart draws to read the values by, through a label, is covered where the label is: the label is written on a plate, of the tooltip's colour past a bar and of the bar's colour inside it.

Its `position` and its `total` are of a chart with axes: a pie and a heatmap write their labels where they do.

Two are the same where they write a value the same way, at the same place.

parameters.name: format
parameters.description: How a value is written. Left out, it is written as the axis the series is read by writes its values, and where that says nothing in the theme's language, short from ten thousand on. In a stack that stands as shares, it is given a value's share, and left out the share is written as a share of a hundred.

parameters.name: position
parameters.description: Where on its bar a value is written. A point of a line has its label over it, or under it where it has no room over it, whatever this says.

parameters.name: total
parameters.description: Whether what a stack of the series comes to at each place is written past its end: over the stack where it comes to nought or more, and under it where it comes to less. It is written as `format` says, but in a stack that stands as shares in the theme's language, for it is no share. One series of the stack asking for it is enough.

declarations.name: ChartDataLabelPosition
declarations.signature: enum class ChartDataLabelPosition
declarations.description: Where on its bar a value's label is written. Along a bar, the end is where its value is, and the start where the bar stands: on nought, on the bar of its stack before it, at the lower value of a range.

entries.name: Auto
entries.description: Where it has room: past the end of a bar that stands by itself, or inside that end where it has none there; in the middle of a bar of a stack.

entries.name: Outside
entries.description: Past the end of the bar. In a stack, where the bar of the next value stands, it is written inside the end of its own bar instead.

entries.name: InsideEnd
entries.description: Inside the bar, at its end.

entries.name: Center
entries.description: In the middle of the bar.

entries.name: InsideStart
entries.description: Inside the bar, at its start.

declarations.name: DecimationAlgorithm
declarations.signature: enum class DecimationAlgorithm
declarations.description: How a line with more points in view than its plot has room for is drawn through fewer of them.

entries.name: MinMax
entries.description: Of the points that stand in one column of the plot's pixels, the first, the highest, the lowest and the last: the line covers every pixel the whole line would, its peaks and its dips among them.

entries.name: Lttb
entries.description: As many points as the plot is pixels wide, each the one of its share of the points that makes the largest triangle with the point kept before it and the share after it (Largest-Triangle-Three-Buckets, Steinarsson, 2013): the line keeps its shape with a point to a pixel, though a peak between two kept points is cut off.

declarations.name: ChartDecimation
declarations.description:
What a chart does with a line that has more points in view than it can draw apart: given to a chart as its `decimation`, it draws the line through some of them, straight from one to the next, and the points have no marks. A chart given none draws every point, as many as there are.

```
PantrixLineChart(data = readings, x = { it.time }, values = levels, decimation = ChartDecimation(threshold = 2000))
```

parameters.name: threshold
parameters.description: How many places of a line may be in view before it is thinned. Left out, twice as many as the plot is pixels wide.

parameters.name: algorithm
parameters.description: Which of the points are kept.

declarations.name: ChartLegend
declarations.description:
A chart's legend: where the names of its series stand, each beside a sample of how the series is drawn.
