declarations.name: rememberFocusRingVisible
declarations.signature:
@Composable
fun rememberFocusRingVisible(interactionSource: InteractionSource): Boolean
declarations.description:
Whether a focus ring should be visible right now: the element is focused, no modal overlay is shown over it, and the focus came by the keyboard, or the platform shows the ring for every focus (`PantrixPlatform.showFocusRingOnlyForKeyboard`).

How the focus came is Compose's own `androidx.compose.ui.input.InputMode`, Touch or Keyboard: a key press puts the window in keyboard mode and a touch takes it out. It says nothing of how precise the pointing device is.

Under a modal overlay the focus stays where it was, to be there again when the overlay closes, but no key reaches it: the ring is not shown there until the overlay has closed (`PantrixModalLayer`).

parameters.name: interactionSource
parameters.description: the element's interaction source: the ring follows the focus it reports.

declarations.name: focusRing
declarations.signature:
@Composable
fun Modifier.focusRing(
    interactionSource: InteractionSource,
    shape: Shape,
    color: Color,
    width: Dp,
    inset: Boolean = false
): Modifier
declarations.description:
Draws the focus ring around the element, outside its bounds.

The ring is `width` wide and leaves a gap as wide between itself and the element, so it stays apart from the element's own fill and border: a button filled in the ring's colour is still told apart from its ring. Its corners follow `shape`, grown by the gap and the ring, so a rounded element gets a ring with the same centre of curvature. A `width` of nothing draws no ring.

The ring is drawn, not laid out, so it takes no space. Put the modifier before any `clip` or layer in the element's own chain, which would cut it off, and leave the element room: an ancestor that clips cuts it off as well. `inset` draws it inside the bounds instead, for an element as wide or as tall as its container — a list row, a pane divider — whose ring outside would run past the container's edges.

Whatever scrolls the element brings it into view when it takes the focus, and no further than its own edge. As the ring appears it asks for the room it is drawn in as well, so that a row or a column that scrolls shows the ring whole and not the element with a side of its ring cut. Only what can be scrolled to is asked for: at the very end of what a scroller holds there is nothing past the element, and the scroller's content needs that room as padding, the ring and its gap, twice `width` (`PantrixPlatform.focusRingReach`). A lazy list is asked for the element alone: how far its items go on cannot be told from an item. There the room is the list's content padding, and each item says so with `scrollPadding`.

parameters.name: interactionSource
parameters.description: the element's interaction source, whose focus decides whether the ring is drawn.

parameters.name: color
parameters.description: the ring's colour: the theme's `focusRing`, or on a fill what is written on that fill, so that the ring reads there as the text does.

declarations.name: PantrixModalLayer
declarations.signature:
@Composable
fun PantrixModalLayer(content: @Composable () -> Unit)
declarations.description:
Says that `content` is a modal overlay's: something shown over the app that takes its keys and its clicks until it closes, as a dialog and a sheet do. While it is composed, `PantrixTheme.isUnderModal` is true for everything else in the window and false in `content`. An overlay opened later lies over an earlier one, whose content is under a modal from then on.

Pantrix's own modal overlays say so themselves. An app's own, built on `Dialog`, puts what it shows in this, around the `Dialog` or inside it, so that what it covers stops looking focused: under a modal the focus stays where it was, to be there again when the modal closes, and a focus ring is drawn only where a key would reach it. On Android that `Dialog` is a window of its own: `com.pantrixui.foundation.testing.pantrixAutomationRoot` on the root of what it shows lets its test tags reach the platform's automation.

The window is the one of the outermost theme around the call: a theme inside another is in the same window, and two themes side by side are in two.

declarations.name: PantrixPlatform
declarations.description: Platform conventions that are accessibility decisions rather than visual ones.

parameters.name: type
parameters.description: The platform these are the conventions of.

parameters.name: minTouchTarget
parameters.description: The smallest touch target a control has: the room it takes in the layout and the room a touch reaches it in, both. `Modifier.minTouchTarget` gives a control this room.

parameters.name: showFocusRingOnlyForKeyboard
parameters.description: Whether the focus ring appears only during keyboard navigation. True everywhere today: a ring that follows mouse clicks is noise, and the people who need it are navigating by keyboard. Kept as a flag because it is a product decision, not a law.

parameters.name: focusRingWidth
parameters.description: Ring thickness. A token rather than a constant because high contrast thickens it.

parameters.name: isTouch
parameters.description: Whether the platform is used by touch: its primary pointer is a finger. True on Android and iOS, and in a browser on a phone or a tablet; false where a mouse or a trackpad leads, on the desktop and in a desktop's browser. It is what `type` cannot tell of the web, and what decides whatever goes by the pointer and not by the platform: a hint for a gesture or for a shortcut, something that may or may not wait for a hover. Left out, it is the platform's nature: touch on Android and iOS.

members.name: focusRingReach
members.description: How far a focus ring reaches past its element: a gap as wide as the ring, and the ring. It is the room what scrolls keeps at its ends for the ring of what stands there, and what a lazy list adds to its content padding and tells its items with `Modifier.scrollPadding`.

members.name: scaled
members.description:
Density applied to the touch target: Spacious enlarges it, Compact never shrinks it.

The platform value is a floor, not a starting point. Compact exists to tighten spacing for pointer users; it must not make the region a finger — or a hand with a tremor — has to hit smaller than the platform's own minimum.

parameters.name: density
parameters.description: the interface density the theme is given.

companion.name: forType
companion.signature:
fun forType(
    type: PlatformType,
    highContrast: Boolean = false,
    isTouch: Boolean = type.isTouchByNature
): PantrixPlatform
companion.description:
`type`'s conventions. The touch target is the platform guideline's minimum on Android (48dp, Material) and iOS (44pt, Apple HIG), whatever points at them. Desktop and web, which no guideline covers, go by the pointer: 32dp for a mouse, and for a finger what a finger is given on Android, 48dp. The focus ring is 2dp, thickened to 3dp in `highContrast`.

`isTouch` says whether the platform is used by touch. Left out, it is the platform's nature: touch on Android and iOS, a pointer on the desktop and in a browser. A browser on a phone, and a desktop app on a touch screen, are told:

```
PantrixPlatform.forType(PlatformType.Web, isTouch = true)
```

`rememberPantrixPlatform` asks the system, so a theme given no platform is right in a phone's browser.

declarations.name: LocalPantrixPlatform
declarations.signature: val LocalPantrixPlatform: ProvidableCompositionLocal<PantrixPlatform>
declarations.description: The platform whose conventions are in effect, which `PantrixTheme` provides: what `PantrixTheme.platform` reads. Outside a theme, Android's.

declarations.name: rememberPantrixPlatform
declarations.signature:
@Composable
fun rememberPantrixPlatform(): PantrixPlatform
declarations.description: This device's conventions: its `PlatformType`'s, with the focus ring thickened when the system is in high contrast, and with the touch target of what points at it: in a browser, a finger's on a phone and a mouse's on a desk. Both are followed as they change.

declarations.name: scrollPadding
declarations.signature: fun Modifier.scrollPadding(padding: PaddingValues): Modifier
declarations.description:
Says what the content of a scroller keeps free at its ends, so that what is asked to be shown is shown inside it: clear of a bar the content scrolls beneath, and not at the scroller's very edge.

Whatever scrolls an element brings it into view when it takes the focus, and no further than the scroller's own edge. Where the content scrolls beneath a bar, as a scaffold's content does that is padded by the bars' share, that edge is behind the bar: the focus of a keyboard goes where it cannot be seen, and the page fails WCAG 2.2's 2.4.11, Focus Not Obscured. With this on the content, every asking to show something in it, the focus's own and any other, is made larger by `padding` as it passes, and the scroller shows the element that far from its edge: above the bar.

It goes on what is scrolled, inside the scroller, and adds no padding of its own: it says what the content has.

- On the content of a row or a column that scrolls, after the scroll and before the padding it speaks of: `Modifier.verticalScroll(state).scrollPadding(padding).padding(padding)`.

- On each item of a lazy list or grid whose `contentPadding` is `padding`.

A scroller that is asked for more than it holds scrolls nothing and hands the rest on as a drag of the user's, which moves a sheet it stands in. So in a row or a column no more is asked for than the content reaches: what is scrolled is found by its size, larger than its place, and the last element is shown as far from the edge as there is content after it. In a lazy list, and where the content fits its scroller, how far the content goes cannot be told, and all of `padding` is asked for: the content has to have that much at its ends, as it does where it was given the same padding. A scroller inside is not touched by this: it shows the element as it does by itself, and what is asked of the one around it comes through here.

A focus ring asks for its own room where the content reaches that far (`focusRing`). In a lazy list it cannot: there the list's content padding and this have the ring's room in them, `PantrixPlatform.focusRingReach`.

docs/guide/scroll-padding/SCROLL_PADDING_GUIDE.md has the whole of it, and the same for a project without this library.

parameters.name: padding
parameters.description: what the content has at each end, inside the scroller: the bars' share a scaffold hands its content, a lazy list's `contentPadding`. Start and end follow the layout's direction. Where the scroller itself ends above the keyboard, as with `imePadding`, a bar at its foot is behind the keyboard and covers none of it: there the keyboard's inset is taken off, `padding - WindowInsets.ime.asPaddingValues()`, or what is typed is shown a bar's height too high.

declarations.name: minTouchTarget
declarations.signature: fun Modifier.minTouchTarget(min: Dp): Modifier
declarations.description:
Reserves at least `min` in the layout without changing what the component draws.

This half of the problem is the easy half. The other half is hit-testing, which Compose takes from `ViewConfiguration.minimumTouchTargetSize` — a fixed value this modifier cannot reach. A component that only applies this modifier lays out at 48dp and still only *responds* within its visual bounds, which is the kind of defect that never shows up in a screenshot.

`PantrixTheme` therefore also overrides `LocalViewConfiguration` with `PantrixViewConfiguration`, so both halves use the same number. The pair is the Foundation-only equivalent of Material 3's `LocalMinimumInteractiveComponentSize`.

While the theme's diagnostics are on, a component that is given less room than `min` for half a second is reported as `PantrixCheck.SmallTouchTarget`: whatever stands around it laid it out, and lets it be pressed, in less.

declarations.name: PantrixViewConfiguration
declarations.description:
Makes Compose's hit-test expansion agree with the platform preset.

Provided by `PantrixTheme`; delegates everything except the touch target so future Compose additions to `ViewConfiguration` keep working without a change here.

parameters.name: delegate
parameters.description: The configuration everything but the touch target comes from: the one already in effect.

parameters.name: minTouchTarget
parameters.description: The touch target, the same both ways.

declarations.name: BoxWithPantrixWindow
declarations.signature:
@Composable
fun BoxWithPantrixWindow(
    modifier: Modifier = Modifier,
    contentAlignment: Alignment = Alignment.TopStart,
    propagateMinConstraints: Boolean = false,
    breakpoints: PantrixBreakpoints = LocalPantrixWindow.current.breakpoints,
    content: @Composable (box: PantrixWindow) -> Unit
)
declarations.description:
A box that tells its content the room it is given, as a window is told: for a component that changes with the room it has and not with the window. A table that is a list where it is narrow asks its own box, since inside a narrow pane of a wide window the window is still wide:

```
BoxWithPantrixWindow(modifier) { box ->
    val withDate = box.widthClass >= WindowWidthClass.Expanded
    if (box.isNarrow) OrderList(orders) else OrderTable(orders, withDate)
}
```

The box is `BoxWithConstraints` underneath, and what it tells is the most room it may take: its `maxWidth` and `maxHeight`. Whatever a screen asks the window, the `content` asks the window it is given: `isNarrow`, `byWidth`, `widthClass >= …`.

- The box is classed by `breakpoints`, which are those of the window in effect unless given: a product that classes its window by bounds of its own has its components classed by the same.

- A reader of a class of the box is composed again when that class changes, and not at every size as the content of `BoxWithConstraints` is. A reader of its `size` follows every change. The box is one object while its room changes.

- Inside a page that scrolls there is no end to the height a box may take: its height class is Expanded and it is never short. Ask the box about the width and the window about the height.

- The box is flat. A fold is the window's, and where it crosses the box is not known here: ask the window.

- `PantrixTheme.window` and `responsive` inside the box still ask the window. Where everything inside is to ask the box instead, a pane whose content is a screen of its own, hand the box on: `CompositionLocalProvider(LocalPantrixWindow provides box) { … }`.

Like `BoxWithConstraints`, the box composes its content while it is measured, so it cannot be asked its intrinsic size: it does not go in a row or a column that is sized by `IntrinsicSize`.

parameters.name: modifier
parameters.description: The box's own modifier. The room it tells is the room this leaves it.

parameters.name: contentAlignment
parameters.description: Where the content is placed in the box when it is smaller than the box.

parameters.name: propagateMinConstraints
parameters.description: Whether the content is to be at least as large as the least size of the box.

parameters.name: breakpoints
parameters.description: The bounds the box is classed by.

parameters.name: content
parameters.description: The box's content, given the room as a window.

declarations.name: keepClearOfFolds
declarations.signature: fun Modifier.keepClearOfFolds(): Modifier
declarations.description:
Keeps what this node holds off a hinge that hides a strip of the window, where one crosses the node: the side of the hinge where the node has less room is left empty, and what the node holds is laid out on the other.

A device of two screens has such a hinge between them (`WindowFold.isOccluding`), and what is drawn under it is not seen. A node that reaches a little past it, a list a little wider than one screen or a bar along a whole edge, puts what it holds on the screen it mostly lies on. A fold that hides nothing, a foldable's, which is one screen however it is held, is not kept clear of: what is drawn across it is seen.

```
Box(Modifier.fillMaxSize()) {
    Inbox()
    // A bar along the whole bottom edge keeps to one screen of the two.
    Toolbar(Modifier.align(Alignment.BottomCenter).fillMaxWidth().keepClearOfFolds())
}
```

Where a hinge runs through the middle of a node, keeping clear of it halves the node: `PantrixTwoPane` lays out what a node holds on both sides of it instead. Here the node keeps to one side, the start one where both have as much room.

The node is measured by the place it was given when it was last placed: as it is placed again after moving, across a hinge or off it, it is measured again. Along the axis a hinge it keeps clear of crosses, it takes all the room it is given, whatever its content's size: otherwise the empty side would make it larger, and so further across the hinge, at each pass. In a room that is not bounded along that axis, as in a row that scrolls, it keeps clear of nothing.

declarations.name: maxContentWidth
declarations.signature:
@Composable
fun Modifier.maxContentWidth(alignment: Alignment.Horizontal = Alignment.Start): Modifier
declarations.description:
Keeps the content no wider than `PantrixTheme.layout.maxContentWidth`: in a desktop window a page's text stays a width that is read, and the rest of the room is left beside it. Below the class that bounds it, the content takes all the room it is given.

Where the content is narrower than its room, this takes the room and lays the content in it by `alignment`: at the start, under a title that starts there, or in the middle.

```
Column(
    Modifier
        .verticalScroll(scroll)
        .padding(horizontal = PantrixTheme.layout.margin)
        .maxContentWidth()
) { … }
```

The bound is that of the window in effect, or of a component's own box handed on as the window, and follows the window as its class changes. Without a bounded width to fill, the content is measured as it is.

parameters.name: alignment
parameters.description: where the content stands in a room wider than it may be: at the start by default.

declarations.name: OverlayWindow
declarations.signature: class OverlayWindow
declarations.description:
The window an overlay opened here is shown over, as an overlay that keeps off a fold places itself by: where that window is, its folds, and where the overlay was opened from.

It is the window the app is in, or the `PantrixWindowFrame` the content is drawn in. An overlay opened inside a frame takes the frame for its window, as a dialog opened in a preview of a foldable opens in that preview: its scrim covers the frame, a sheet comes in from the frame's edges and a fold is the frame's. The room a scaffold tells one of its panes as its window is not such a window: a dialog opened in a pane is shown over the window the pane is in.

Pantrix's own overlays place themselves by it. An overlay of the app's own, a `Dialog` or a `Popup` it shows itself, does as well:

```
val overlay = rememberOverlayWindow()
// Asked as the dialog opens: where it was opened from, and the fold the window is in two pieces at.
val openedFrom = remember { overlay.openedFrom() }
val fold = overlay.folds.firstOrNull { it.isSeparating }
val onTheLeft = fold != null && openedFrom != null && openedFrom.x < fold.bounds.center.x
```

Its places are in the coordinates of the window the app is in, and in pixels: where a `Dialog` that fills that window places what it holds. An overlay that is a window of its own beside the app's, as a popup is on Android, moves them by where the app's window is on the screen.

members.name: window
members.description: The window the overlay is shown over, as what the overlay shows is to be told of it: the frame's, and otherwise the one the outermost `PantrixTheme` stands for. Not the room of a pane the overlay was opened in.

members.name: frame
members.description:
Where the frame is seen, as it is drawn: its bounds in the window the app is in, in pixels, cut to what of it is in view. A frame partly scrolled out of its page is the part still seen, and an overlay over it covers no more: not what the page's bar stands over. Null over the window the app is in, which an overlay covers whole, and until the frame has been placed.

It is where the frame is now: an overlay that follows the frame as it moves asks again.

members.name: scale
members.description: How large the frame is drawn: the share of its own size it is drawn at, less than 1 in a layer that draws it smaller. An overlay over it is drawn as much smaller, as what the frame holds is. It is 1 over the window the app is in.

members.name: folds
members.description: The window's folds, where they are in the window the app is in: their bounds and their clearance in pixels, drawn as much smaller as a frame drawn smaller is. A frame that has not been placed has none yet.

members.name: openedFrom
members.description:
Where an overlay opened now is opened from, in the window the app is in and in pixels: where the last press in the window landed, and where a key was pressed after it, the middle of the control that has the focus. Null where neither is known, as for an overlay that opens before anything has been pressed.

It is asked once, as the overlay opens: a press inside the overlay is where the next one is opened from. It is heard at the roots of the window's layers: the outermost `PantrixTheme`'s, and the node of an overlay that carries `pantrixTransientsRoot`.

declarations.name: rememberOverlayWindow
declarations.signature:
@Composable
fun rememberOverlayWindow(): OverlayWindow
declarations.description: The window an overlay opened here is shown over: the `PantrixWindowFrame` the content is drawn in, or the window the app is in.

declarations.name: paneCount
declarations.signature: fun PantrixWindow.paneCount(maxPanes: Int = 2): Int
declarations.description:
How many panes a layout lays side by side in this window, at most `maxPanes`: one in a Compact window and in a Medium one, two from Expanded on, three from Large on. A window that a fold divides upright, a foldable held like a book or a hinge between two screens, takes two at any width: one on each side of the fold.

```
if (PantrixTheme.window.paneCount() >= 2) InboxAndMessage() else Inbox()
```

The gap between the panes is the layout's gutter, `PantrixTheme.layout.gutter`, and where a fold divides the window the panes meet at it: the fold's `clearance` is the gap there.

parameters.name: maxPanes
parameters.description: the most panes the layout has: two for a list and its detail, three with a pane beside them.

declarations.name: PantrixWindowFrame
declarations.description:
A box that is a window of its own: its content is told `window` as the window it is in, and the folds of `window` are where they are in this box, its top start corner the window's. What a preview of a screen at a size, a frame of a design tool or a catalogue's window picker draws a window in.

```
val book = PantrixWindow(DpSize(951.dp, 669.dp), posture = WindowPosture(listOf(fold)))
PantrixWindowFrame(book, Modifier.size(951.dp, 669.dp)) { Inbox() }
```

The folds of the window the app is in are in that window's coordinates; within a frame they are in the frame's. A layout that splits at a fold finds it with `rememberFoldsInNode`, wherever it is drawn. A frame drawn smaller or larger, in a scaled layer, keeps its content's folds where they are in the content: the fold is scaled with them.

parameters.name: window
parameters.description: the window the content is told of; null for the window the box is in, so that a picker offering the real window beside made-up ones keeps the content where it is in the composition, its state with it, whichever is chosen.

parameters.name: modifier
parameters.description: the box's modifier. The window's top start corner is where its content starts, inside the modifier's padding and border.

parameters.name: content
parameters.description: what the window holds.

declarations.name: FoldsInNode
declarations.signature: class FoldsInNode
declarations.description:
The window's folds where they cross one node, in the node's own coordinates and in pixels: what a layout that splits its room at a fold measures by. Put `modifier` on the node; `folds` follows the node as it moves and is resized, the window as it changes and the device as it is folded.

A node the fold does not cross has none. Until the node is first placed the folds are where they would be in a node that starts at the window's corner, as one filling the window does.

members.name: modifier
members.description: Placed on the node whose folds are asked. It follows where the node is in the window, and so a node a page scrolls past the fold is measured again as it goes.

members.name: folds
members.description: The folds crossing the node, their bounds and clearance in its coordinates.

members.name: separatingFold
members.description: The fold that divides the node, if one does: the first of `folds` that separates.

declarations.name: rememberFoldsInNode
declarations.signature:
@Composable
fun rememberFoldsInNode(window: PantrixWindow = LocalPantrixWindow.current): FoldsInNode
declarations.description: The folds of `window` where they cross the node `FoldsInNode.modifier` is put on.

parameters.name: window
parameters.description: the window whose folds are asked: the one the content is told of unless given.

declarations.name: PantrixLayout
declarations.signature:
data class PantrixLayout(
    val margin: Dp,
    val gutter: Dp,
    val columns: Int = 4,
    val maxContentWidth: Dp = Dp.Infinity
)

parameters.name: margin
parameters.description: The room between the edge of the window, or of a pane, and the content: what a page pads its content by at its sides.

parameters.name: gutter
parameters.description: The room between columns of a grid, and between panes that stand side by side.

parameters.name: columns
parameters.description: How many columns a page's grid has across its room: a part of the page spans some of them, and `spanWidth` says how wide that is. A phone has 4, a tablet 8 and a wider window 12.

parameters.name: maxContentWidth
parameters.description: How wide a page's content grows at the most: past it, the room of a wide window is left beside the content, since a line of text across a desktop window is not read. `Dp.Infinity` where the content takes all the room it has. `Modifier.maxContentWidth()` keeps content to it.

members.name: scaled
members.description: These measures at an interface density: the margin and the gutter multiplied by `factor`, the columns and the content's widest as they are.

members.name: spanWidth
members.signature:
fun spanWidth(
    available: Dp,
    span: Int
): Dp

parameters.name: available
parameters.description: the room the columns share, as wide as the page's content: within its margins.

parameters.name: span
parameters.description: how many of the columns the part spans, from 1 to `columns`.

declarations.name: PantrixLayouts
declarations.signature:
data class PantrixLayouts(
    val compact: PantrixLayout = PantrixLayout(margin = 16.dp, gutter = 16.dp, columns = 4),
    val medium: PantrixLayout = PantrixLayout(margin = 24.dp, gutter = 16.dp, columns = 8),
    val expanded: PantrixLayout = PantrixLayout(margin = 24.dp, gutter = 24.dp, columns = 12),
    val large: PantrixLayout = PantrixLayout(margin = 32.dp, gutter = 24.dp, columns = 12, maxContentWidth = 1040.dp),
    val extraLarge: PantrixLayout = large
)
declarations.description:
The layout's measures for each width class of a window: what `PantrixTheme.layout` picks from.

A phone has little width to give away and a desktop window has it to spare, so the margin and the gutter grow with the window. By default the margin is 16dp, 24dp from Medium and 32dp from Large; the gutter is 16dp, and 24dp from Expanded. Every one of them is a step of the spacing scale. The grid has 4 columns, 8 from Medium and 12 from Expanded, and the content grows without a bound until Large, where it stops at 1040dp.

A product gives the theme its own for the classes it has designed, and the rest stay as they are:

```
PantrixTheme(layouts = PantrixLayouts(compact = PantrixLayout(margin = 20.dp, gutter = 12.dp))) { … }
```

A class given its own measures has the columns and the widest content it is given: left out, they are a phone's, 4 columns and no bound. A product that gives a wider class its own measures gives them too:

```
PantrixLayouts(large = PantrixLayout(margin = 40.dp, gutter = 24.dp, columns = 12, maxContentWidth = 1200.dp))
```

parameters.name: compact
parameters.description: The measures of a window narrower than 600dp: a phone held upright.

parameters.name: medium
parameters.description: The measures from 600dp: a tablet held upright, an open foldable.

parameters.name: expanded
parameters.description: The measures from 840dp: a tablet on its side.

parameters.name: large
parameters.description: The measures from 1200dp: a desktop window, a browser.

parameters.name: extraLarge
parameters.description: The measures from 1600dp. They are `large`'s unless given: few products design that width apart.

members.name: forWidth
members.description: The measures of a window whose width class is `widthClass`.

members.name: scaled
members.description: Density applies here, not at each call site, so one switch rescales the measures of every class.

parameters.name: factor
parameters.description: the interface density's scale: each class's margin and gutter are multiplied by it.

declarations.name: LocalPantrixLayouts
declarations.signature: val LocalPantrixLayouts: ProvidableCompositionLocal<PantrixLayouts>
declarations.description: The layout's measures in effect, for every class: what the nearest `PantrixTheme` was given, scaled by its density. `PantrixTheme.layout` picks the class of the window from them.

declarations.name: rememberPantrixLayouts
declarations.signature:
@Composable
fun rememberPantrixLayouts(): PantrixLayouts
declarations.description: Pantrix's layout measures.

declarations.name: PantrixWindow
declarations.signature: interface PantrixWindow
declarations.description:
The window the content is drawn in, as a layout needs to know it: how wide and how tall it is, and how its device is folded. `PantrixTheme` provides it, and `PantrixTheme.window` reads it: nothing is set up for it.

It is the window, not the device and not the screen: an app in half of a split screen, in a resized desktop window or in a browser tab is as wide as that. A layout asks the class rather than the size:

```
val window = PantrixTheme.window
val columns = window.byWidth(compact = 2, medium = 4)
if (window.widthClass >= WindowWidthClass.Expanded) ListBesideDetail() else ListAlone()
```

The window is one object for as long as the theme stands, and its values are read when asked. Whoever reads `widthClass` or `heightClass` is composed again when the class changes and not before; whoever reads `size` follows every change, each frame of a rotation and each pixel of a dragged window edge.

A component that is a pane of its own, a scaffold or a sheet, measures the room it is given rather than asking the window: inside a narrow pane the window is still wide. `BoxWithPantrixWindow` tells a component that room as a window.

On the desktop and on the web the window has no size yet when its content is first composed, and that one composition finds a Compact window; Android and iOS tell the size from the start. Read the class where it is used rather than keeping what it was at first.

members.name: size
members.description: The window's size. On Android it is the window with its system bars; on the web, the box the app is drawn in. Zero, or unspecified, until the platform has told it: the classes are Compact until then.

members.name: isSizeKnown
widthClass
members.description: The class of the window's width: what the layout is chosen by.

members.name: heightClass
members.description: The class of the window's height: `WindowHeightClass.Compact` is a phone on its side.

members.name: posture
members.description: How the window's device is folded; `WindowPosture.Flat` where there is no fold.

members.name: verticalBar
members.description: The column the system keeps along one side of the window for bars that stand upright, or null where it keeps none, as on every screen but the iPhone Duo's outer one. Its places are in the window's coordinates: a layout asks where it stands beside it with `rememberVerticalBarInNode`.

members.name: breakpoints
members.description:
Where this window's classes begin: the bounds it is classed by. A size classed by hand goes by the same bounds, as `BoxWithPantrixWindow` classes the room a component is given:

```
val pane = PantrixWindow(paneSize, breakpoints = PantrixTheme.window.breakpoints)
```

declarations.name: PantrixWindow
declarations.signature:
fun PantrixWindow(
    size: DpSize,
    posture: WindowPosture = WindowPosture.Flat,
    breakpoints: PantrixBreakpoints = PantrixBreakpoints.Default,
    verticalBar: WindowVerticalBar? = null
): PantrixWindow
declarations.description:
A window of fixed values, for where the real one is not the answer: a test or a preview of a layout at a size, and Compose embedded in a part of a native screen, where the room is that part's.

```
PantrixTheme(window = PantrixWindow(DpSize(700.dp, 900.dp))) { … }
```

A `verticalBar` given in pixels draws what a screen with the system's column looks like, the iPhone Duo's outer one, where there is none.

parameters.name: size
parameters.description: the window's size, which its width and height classes come from.

parameters.name: posture
parameters.description: how the window's device is folded: flat, as every device with no fold is, unless a fold is given.

parameters.name: breakpoints
parameters.description: the widths and heights each class starts at: Android's window size classes unless the product has its own.

declarations.name: byWidth
declarations.signature:
fun <T> PantrixWindow.byWidth(
    compact: T,
    medium: T = compact,
    expanded: T = medium,
    large: T = expanded,
    extraLarge: T = large
): T
declarations.description:
The value of this window's width class. A class left out takes the value of the class below it, so a layout names only the widths it changes at:

```
val columns = PantrixTheme.window.byWidth(compact = 2, medium = 4)
```

parameters.name: compact
parameters.description: the value in a Compact window, the narrowest class.

parameters.name: medium
parameters.description: the value in a Medium window; `compact`'s where it is left out.

parameters.name: expanded
parameters.description: the value in an Expanded window; `medium`'s where it is left out.

parameters.name: large
parameters.description: the value in a Large window; `expanded`'s where it is left out.

parameters.name: extraLarge
parameters.description: the value in an ExtraLarge window, the widest class; `large`'s where it is left out.

declarations.name: byHeight
declarations.signature:
fun <T> PantrixWindow.byHeight(
    compact: T,
    medium: T = compact,
    expanded: T = medium
): T
declarations.description:
The value of this window's height class. A class left out takes the value of the class below it:

```
val barHeight = PantrixTheme.window.byHeight(compact = 44.dp, medium = 56.dp)
```

parameters.name: compact
parameters.description: the value in a Compact window, the shortest class: a phone held sideways.

parameters.name: medium
parameters.description: the value in a Medium window; `compact`'s where it is left out.

parameters.name: expanded
parameters.description: the value in an Expanded window, the tallest class; `medium`'s where it is left out.

declarations.name: byPosture
declarations.signature:
fun <T> PantrixWindow.byPosture(
    flat: T,
    book: T = flat,
    tabletop: T = flat
): T
declarations.description:
The value of this window's posture: `book` while the device is held half open like a book, its fold upright; `tabletop` while it is held like a laptop on a table, its fold lying across; `flat` the rest of the time, which is every device with no fold and a foldable opened flat. A posture left out takes `flat`'s value, so a layout names only the postures it changes in:

```
// Two panes side by side in a book, one above the other on a table, and one pane otherwise.
val panes = PantrixTheme.window.byPosture(flat = Panes.One, book = Panes.SideBySide, tabletop = Panes.Stacked)
```

A device folded both ways at once is taken as a book. The third of a family with `byWidth` and `byHeight`.

declarations.name: isNarrow
declarations.signature: val PantrixWindow.isNarrow: Boolean
declarations.description:
Whether the window is narrow: its width class is `WindowWidthClass.Compact`, as a phone held upright is. The layout of one pane, with its navigation along the bottom.

A name for `widthClass == WindowWidthClass.Compact`, for code that reads as the rule it follows: `if (window.isNarrow) BottomBar()`. For "from this width on", compare the class: `widthClass >= Expanded`.

True as well while the window's size is not known, since the classes are Compact until then: see `PantrixWindow.isSizeKnown`.

declarations.name: isShort
declarations.signature: val PantrixWindow.isShort: Boolean
declarations.description:
Whether the window is short: its height class is `WindowHeightClass.Compact`, as a phone on its side is. Such a window is often wide, Medium or Expanded by its width, and has no height to stack bars in: the main action goes to the header and not to a bar along the bottom, and nothing opens from the bottom edge.

A name for `heightClass == WindowHeightClass.Compact`:

```
if (window.isShort) HeaderAction() else StickyBottomBar()
```

True as well while the window's size is not known, since the classes are Compact until then: see `PantrixWindow.isSizeKnown`.

declarations.name: rememberPantrixWindow
declarations.description:
The window Compose reports, classed by `breakpoints`, folded as `posture` says and with the system's `verticalBar`: what `PantrixTheme` provides when it is given none.

Give it to the theme to class by breakpoints of the product's own, or to tell a fold the system does not:

```
PantrixTheme(window = rememberPantrixWindow(breakpoints = PantrixBreakpoints(medium = 640.dp))) { … }
```

The window stays the same object while `posture` and `verticalBar` change; it is replaced when `breakpoints` are.

declarations.name: responsive
declarations.signature:
@Composable
fun <T> responsive(
    compact: T,
    medium: T = compact,
    expanded: T = medium,
    large: T = expanded,
    extraLarge: T = large
): T
declarations.description:
The value of the width class of the window in effect: `byWidth` of `PantrixTheme.window` in one word, for a composable that needs a value and not the window. A class left out takes the value of the class below it:

```
val columns = responsive(compact = 2, medium = 4)
val cardPadding = responsive(compact = 12.dp, medium = 16.dp, large = 20.dp)
```

The page's margin and the gutter between its columns need no picking: `PantrixTheme.layout` has them by class. The caller is composed again when the class changes and not as the window is resized within it. It goes by the width alone; for the height, and outside a composable, ask the window: `byHeight`, `byWidth`.

parameters.name: compact
parameters.description: the value in a Compact window, the narrowest class.

parameters.name: medium
parameters.description: the value in a Medium window; `compact`'s where it is left out.

parameters.name: expanded
parameters.description: the value in an Expanded window; `medium`'s where it is left out.

parameters.name: large
parameters.description: the value in a Large window; `expanded`'s where it is left out.

parameters.name: extraLarge
parameters.description: the value in an ExtraLarge window, the widest class; `large`'s where it is left out.

declarations.name: rememberWindowIsAtLeast
declarations.signature:
@Composable
fun rememberWindowIsAtLeast(width: Dp): Boolean
declarations.description:
Whether the window in effect is at least `width` wide: for a layout that changes at a width none of the classes begins at.

```
// A third column from 1000dp on, which is neither Expanded's 840 nor Large's 1200.
val threeColumns = rememberWindowIsAtLeast(1000.dp)
```

The caller is composed again when the window crosses `width`, either way, and not while it is resized on one side of it. `PantrixTheme.window.size.width >= width` asks the same, and its reader is composed again at every size: each frame of a rotation, each pixel of a dragged window edge.

While the window's size is not known its width counts as zero, so the answer is false. Where every layout of a product changes at the same widths, give the window those instead: `PantrixBreakpoints`.

declarations.name: LocalPantrixWindow
declarations.signature: val LocalPantrixWindow: ProvidableCompositionLocal<PantrixWindow>
declarations.description:
The window in effect: the one the nearest `PantrixTheme` provides. With no theme around, the one Compose reports, classed by the default breakpoints and flat.

`PantrixTheme.window` reads it. Provide it to give a part of the screen a window of its own without a second theme: a pane whose content is to answer to the pane's width.

declarations.name: FoldOrientation
declarations.signature: enum class FoldOrientation
declarations.description: Which way a fold runs across its window.

entries.name: Vertical
entries.description: From the top of the window to its bottom: the two halves are side by side.

entries.name: Horizontal
entries.description: From one side of the window to the other: one half is above the other.

declarations.name: WindowFold
declarations.description: A fold or a hinge in a window.

parameters.name: bounds
parameters.description: Where it is, in pixels and in the window's coordinates. A fold in one screen has no thickness: its bounds are a line, as wide as zero. A hinge between two screens is as wide as the gap.

parameters.name: orientation
parameters.description: Which way it runs.

parameters.name: isHalfOpened
parameters.description: Whether the device is held partly open, the two halves at an angle. Opened flat, it is not.

parameters.name: isSeparating
parameters.description: Whether the window is in two pieces here, with nothing to be laid across: a fold held half open, or a hinge between two screens at any angle. A fold opened flat separates nothing.

parameters.name: isOccluding
parameters.description: Whether it hides a strip of the window, as a hinge between two screens does.

parameters.name: clearance
parameters.description: The strip around it that what is touched keeps clear of, in pixels and in the window's coordinates: `bounds` and the margin the system asks for on either side. iOS asks for one, 20pt on each side of the fold of an iPhone that folds; Android and the browsers ask for none, and the strip is `bounds` itself. Two panes split at the fold leave this strip between them.

declarations.name: WindowPosture
declarations.signature: data class WindowPosture(public val folds: List<WindowFold> = emptyList())
declarations.description:
How the window's device is folded: the folds that cross the window, and none on a device that has none.

The two postures a layout is written for are `isBook` and `isTabletop`. A fold opened flat is in `folds` and changes nothing: the screen is one piece.

parameters.name: folds
parameters.description: The folds crossing the window.

members.name: isBook
members.description: Held half open with the fold upright, like a book: two panes side by side, split at the fold, with nothing across it.

members.name: isTabletop
members.description: Held half open with the fold lying across, like a laptop on a table: what is looked at goes above the fold; controls, forms and the navigation go below it.

members.name: separatingFold
members.description: The fold the window is in two pieces at, or null when it is one piece: content keeps clear of this one.

companion.name: Flat
companion.description: No fold: every phone, tablet, desktop window and browser that does not fold.

declarations.name: systemWindowPosture
declarations.signature:
@Composable
fun systemWindowPosture(): WindowPosture
declarations.description:
The posture the system reports for this window, followed as the device is folded, opened and turned.

Android tells its folds through Jetpack WindowManager, a browser through its Device Posture and Viewport Segments APIs, which Chromium has, and iOS from 27.1 on through UIKit's hinge and its reserved regions. The desktop tells of none, and neither does an iOS before 27.1 or a library built with an Xcode before 27.1: the posture there is `WindowPosture.Flat`. An app that reads a fold by its own means gives its posture to `rememberPantrixWindow` instead.

declarations.name: WindowWidthClass
declarations.signature: enum class WindowWidthClass
declarations.description:
How wide a window is, as one of five classes a layout chooses by: the shape of its navigation, the number of its panes, the columns of a grid.

The classes are in order, so a rule that holds from a width on is a comparison: `widthClass >= WindowWidthClass.Expanded`. `PantrixBreakpoints` says where each begins.

entries.name: Compact
entries.description: Narrower than 600dp: a phone held upright, a foldable's cover screen, a narrow browser window.

entries.name: Medium
entries.description: From 600dp: an open foldable, a tablet held upright, a split view.

entries.name: Expanded
entries.description: From 840dp: a tablet on its side, and most phones on theirs (see `WindowHeightClass.Compact`).

entries.name: Large
entries.description: From 1200dp: a desktop window, a browser, a large tablet.

entries.name: ExtraLarge
entries.description: From 1600dp: a wide desktop window, an external display.

declarations.name: WindowHeightClass
declarations.signature: enum class WindowHeightClass
declarations.description:
How tall a window is, as one of three classes.

A layout follows the width first. The height says when there is no room to stack things: a `Compact` window is a phone on its side, as wide as a tablet and less than half as tall, where each bar laid across the screen takes a seventh of it.

entries.name: Compact
entries.description: Shorter than 480dp: a phone on its side.

entries.name: Medium
entries.description: From 480dp: most phones held upright, a tablet on its side.

entries.name: Expanded
entries.description: From 900dp: a tablet held upright, a desktop window, and a tall phone held upright.

declarations.name: PantrixBreakpoints
declarations.description:
Where each window class begins: the least width of a Medium, Expanded, Large and ExtraLarge window, and the least height of a Medium and an Expanded one. A window narrower than `medium` is Compact, as is one shorter than `heightMedium`.

The defaults are Android's window size classes. A product whose layouts change elsewhere gives its own to `rememberPantrixWindow`.

parameters.name: medium
parameters.description: The least width of a `WindowWidthClass.Medium` window.

parameters.name: expanded
parameters.description: The least width of a `WindowWidthClass.Expanded` window.

parameters.name: large
parameters.description: The least width of a `WindowWidthClass.Large` window.

parameters.name: extraLarge
parameters.description: The least width of a `WindowWidthClass.ExtraLarge` window.

parameters.name: heightMedium
parameters.description: The least height of a `WindowHeightClass.Medium` window.

parameters.name: heightExpanded
parameters.description: The least height of a `WindowHeightClass.Expanded` window.

members.name: widthClassOf
members.description: The class of a window `width` wide: the highest one whose least width it has reached. A width not known yet, zero or unspecified, is Compact.

members.name: heightClassOf
members.description: The class of a window `height` tall: the highest one whose least height it has reached. A height not known yet, zero or unspecified, is Compact.

companion.name: Default
companion.description: 600, 840, 1200 and 1600dp wide; 480 and 900dp tall.

declarations.name: WindowVerticalBar
declarations.description:
The column a system keeps along one side of the window for bars that stand upright: its status bar at the top, and an app's toolbar buttons and tabs below it. The outer screen of the iPhone Duo has one from iOS 27.1 on, along its trailing edge, where UIKit puts a tab bar and a navigation bar's buttons; the window's safe area keeps content clear of it.

An app's own bars stand in `barBounds`: buttons at its top, under the status bar, and the navigation at its bottom, above the home indicator. `PantrixScaffold` puts its navigation and a top bar's buttons there by itself on the outer screen held upright. The inner screen, and either screen on its side, has a column too, which it leaves to the status bar.

parameters.name: bounds
parameters.description: The column, from the window's top to its bottom, in pixels and in the window's coordinates.

parameters.name: barBounds
parameters.description: Where an app's bars stand in the column: below the status bar and above the home indicator, as wide as the column. A bar narrower than it stands in its middle, which is where the system puts its own and is not always the column's middle: the screen's rounded corner takes a part of the column's outer side. In pixels and in the window's coordinates.

declarations.name: systemVerticalBar
declarations.signature:
@Composable
fun systemVerticalBar(): WindowVerticalBar?
declarations.description: The vertical bar the system keeps in this window, or null where it keeps none: the column of the iPhone Duo's outer screen from iOS 27.1 on. Android, the desktop and the browsers have none, and neither has an iOS before 27.1 or a library built with an Xcode before 27.1. It is followed as the device is turned and its screens change.

declarations.name: VerticalBarInNode
declarations.signature: class VerticalBarInNode
declarations.description:
The window's vertical bar beside one node, in the node's own coordinates and in pixels: what a layout that puts its bars in the system's column measures by. Put `modifier` on the node; `verticalBar` follows the node as it moves and is resized, and the window as its bar comes and goes.

The bar is the window's: the one the frame the node is drawn in tells of, or the one the outermost `PantrixTheme` stands for, and not the room a pane is told of as its window. A node that does not reach the column, one in a pane away from that edge, has none. Until the node is first placed the column is where it would be beside a node that starts at the window's corner, as one filling the window does.

members.name: modifier
members.description: Placed on the node whose vertical bar is asked. It follows where the node is in the window.

members.name: verticalBar
members.description: The vertical bar, its column and the place of its bars in the node's coordinates, while the node reaches across the column to the window's edge; null where it does not, and where the window has none.

declarations.name: rememberVerticalBarInNode
declarations.signature:
@Composable
fun rememberVerticalBarInNode(): VerticalBarInNode
declarations.description: The window's vertical bar beside the node `VerticalBarInNode.modifier` is put on.

declarations.name: PantrixUiEvent
declarations.description:
A UI interaction, described by identity rather than content: which component it was, what happened, and on which screen.

**Text the user typed or read never goes in here.** A field reports that it took the focus or was cleared, never what it holds, and a test of every component that takes text holds that. A value out of a closed set does go in: a selection is reported by the key of what was selected, a page by its number. Some of `props` are the app's own keys, and an app whose keys are personal data sends that data with them: `docs/guide/analytics/ANALYTICS_GUIDE.md` names the components that report them.

parameters.name: component
parameters.description: Component name, e.g. `Button`.

parameters.name: action
parameters.description: What happened, in the component's own word: `click`, `toggle`, `select`, `open`, `dismiss`, `focus`, `expand`, and others the guide lists by component.

parameters.name: testTag
parameters.description: The component's automation tag, the same identity tests bind to, whatever the `TestTagPolicy`: built from its `tagKey`, or, where it has none, from the place it was called from, which changes with the code around it. Null for an event an app reports without one.

parameters.name: screen
parameters.description: The enclosing `TestScope` chain, e.g. `Checkout.PaymentForm`, or null outside one.

parameters.name: props
parameters.description: The event's values, of three kinds: Pantrix's own words and yes-or-no values, such as `variant`, `via` and `state`; numbers, such as `index`, `page` and `count`; and keys the app gave the component, such as `row`, `option` and `destination`.

declarations.name: PantrixAnalytics
declarations.signature: fun interface PantrixAnalytics
declarations.description:
Sink for `PantrixUiEvent`.

Defaults to a no-op, so the cost of components emitting events unconditionally is one virtual call into an empty body. Products wire their own SDK in through `PantrixTheme(analytics = ...)`; Pantrix itself depends on no analytics vendor.

A component built on a Pantrix control, as a field of dates on two text fields, hears that control's events beside its own, and one press is counted twice. It gives the control a sink of its own with `LocalPantrixAnalytics`, which drops what the component reports itself and hands the rest on under the component's name: `PantrixPageSize` does so with the select it is built on.

members.name: track
members.description: Called with each `event` a component emits, as it happens, on the UI thread. A sink hands the event on and returns: what takes time, sending above all, is done off this thread.

companion.name: NoOp
companion.description: The sink that drops every event: where a theme reports to unless it is given one.

declarations.name: LocalPantrixAnalytics
declarations.signature: val LocalPantrixAnalytics: ProvidableCompositionLocal<PantrixAnalytics>
declarations.description: Where the components here report their events: `PantrixTheme(analytics = …)`. An app's own code reads it to report its own events to the same place.

declarations.name: PantrixClock
declarations.description: Where a screen reads the time: the moment it is now, and how far the clock it is shown by is ahead of UTC at a moment. `rememberToday` reads the day from it, the time field the hour its picker opens at, the elastic date picker its ranges and a chart its moments. `System` is the device's; a test or a preview gives one of its own through `LocalPantrixClock`, to see a screen on a day and at an hour it chooses.

parameters.name: clock
parameters.description: what the moment is now.

parameters.name: utcOffset
parameters.description: how far the clock is ahead of UTC at a moment: three hours in Istanbul, less than nought west of Greenwich, and summer time where it is kept.

members.name: today
members.description: The day this clock shows now.

members.name: time
members.description: The time this clock shows now, to the second.

companion.name: System
companion.description: The device's clock, in the device's time zone.

declarations.name: LocalPantrixClock
declarations.signature: val LocalPantrixClock: ProvidableCompositionLocal<PantrixClock>
declarations.description: The clock the screen is read by: `PantrixClock.System` unless a test or a preview gives another.

declarations.name: PantrixDate
declarations.description:
A day on the calendar: a year, a month and a day of the month, with no time of day and no time zone.

Pantrix takes no library of dates. A component that spoke one would put it into the API of every app that shows a date, and which one an app uses is not a design system's to choose: this is three numbers, which an app turns into its own type and back in a line, `PantrixDate(date.year, date.month.number, date.day)` from `kotlinx-datetime`'s `LocalDate` and the same from `java.time`'s. docs/guide/date-time/DATE_TIME_GUIDE.md has the lines for each.

The calendar is the one in use now, the Gregorian, and is taken back before its start as it is forwards: a year before the first is written as nought, then as less than nought.

parameters.name: year
parameters.description: The year, as it is written.

parameters.name: month
parameters.description: The month, 1 for January to 12 for December.

parameters.name: day
parameters.description: The day of the month, from 1 to the month's last.

members.name: dayOfWeek
members.description: The day of the week this day falls on, as ISO 8601 numbers it: 1 is Monday and 7 is Sunday.

members.name: epochDays
members.description: The days from the first of January 1970 to this one: nought on that day, and less than nought before it.

members.name: plusDays
members.description: The day `days` after this one, or before it where `days` is less than nought.

members.name: plusMonths
members.description: The same day `months` months after this one, or before it where `months` is less than nought. Where that month is shorter, its last day: a month after the 31st of January is the last day of February.

members.name: plusYears
members.description: The same day `years` years after this one, or before it: the 29th of February is the 28th in a common year.

members.name: at
members.signature:
fun at(
    time: PantrixTime,
    offsetAt: (Instant) -> Duration = ::systemUtcOffset
): Instant
members.description:
The moment a clock shows `time` on this day: by default the device's own clock, whose offset from UTC `offsetAt` tells for each moment, as `systemUtcOffset` does, summer time and all.

Where the clock is put back and shows the time twice, it is the first of the two, as `java.time` takes it. Where it is put forward and never shows the time, it is as far past the hour it skips as the time is into it: half past two on a night that goes from two to three is half past three.

companion.name: ofEpochDays
companion.description: The day `days` days after the first of January 1970, or before it where `days` is less than nought.

companion.name: of
companion.signature:
fun of(
    moment: Instant,
    offset: Duration = systemUtcOffset(moment)
): PantrixDate
companion.description: The day a clock `offset` ahead of UTC shows at `moment`: by default the device's own clock, as `systemUtcOffset` tells it.

companion.name: today
companion.description: The day the device's clock shows now. A screen reads `rememberToday` instead: the day the screen's clock shows, asked again at each midnight.

companion.name: parse
companion.description: The day ISO 8601 writes as `text`: `2026-10-17`, with four digits of year or more and a sign before a year less than nought, as `toString` writes it.

companion.name: daysInMonth
companion.signature:
fun daysInMonth(
    year: Int,
    month: Int
): Int
companion.description: How many days the month `month` of `year` has: 28 to 31, the 29th of February in a leap year.

companion.name: isLeapYear
companion.description: Whether `year` has a 29th of February: every fourth year, but not every hundredth, but every four hundredth.

declarations.name: PantrixDateRange
declarations.description: A stretch of days from `start` to `end`, both of them in it: a stay, a leave, the days a report is of. A stretch of one day starts and ends on it.

members.name: contains
members.description: Whether `date` is one of the stretch's days, its first and its last among them.

declarations.name: PantrixTime
declarations.description:
A time of day: an hour by a clock of twenty-four hours, a minute and a second, with no day and no time zone.

As `PantrixDate` is, it is three numbers, which an app turns into its own type and back in a line: `PantrixTime(time.hour, time.minute, time.second)` from `kotlinx-datetime`'s `LocalTime` and the same from `java.time`'s. A day and a time make a moment with `PantrixDate.at`, on the device's clock; docs/guide/date-time/DATE_TIME_GUIDE.md has the lines for each.

A time is written in twenty-four hours whatever the language: `toString` is what is kept and sent. What a screen shows is the language's, `PantrixStrings.time`, by twelve hours in English.

parameters.name: hour
parameters.description: The hour, 0 for the one after midnight to 23.

parameters.name: minute
parameters.description: The minute of the hour, 0 to 59.

parameters.name: second
parameters.description: The second of the minute, 0 to 59: a clock's own seconds, with no leap second.

members.name: secondOfDay
members.description: The seconds from midnight to this time: nought at midnight, and 86 399 at the day's last second.

companion.name: ofSecondOfDay
companion.description: The time `seconds` seconds after midnight, 0 to 86 399.

companion.name: of
companion.signature:
fun of(
    moment: Instant,
    offset: Duration = systemUtcOffset(moment)
): PantrixTime
companion.description: The time a clock `offset` ahead of UTC shows at `moment`, to the second: by default the device's own clock, as `systemUtcOffset` tells it.

companion.name: now
companion.description: The time the device's clock shows now, to the second.

companion.name: parse
companion.description: The time ISO 8601 writes as `text`: `14:05`, or `14:05:30` with its seconds, each part in two digits, as `toString` writes it.

declarations.name: PantrixTimePoint
declarations.signature: sealed interface PantrixTimePoint
declarations.description:
A point in time that can move with the clock: now, an amount of time from now, or a moment.

"The last 15 minutes" is still the last 15 minutes at the next refresh, so a range a screen is filtered by keeps its points in this form and `resolve`s them each time it is read. Date math, as Elasticsearch and Kibana write it, is their edge: `toDateMath` writes a point as a URL or a query keeps it, `now-15m`, and `parseDateMath` reads it back.

members.name: resolve
members.signature:
fun resolve(
    now: Instant = Clock.System.now(),
    asEnd: Boolean = false,
    firstDayOfWeek: Int = 1,
    offsetAt: (Instant) -> Duration = ::systemUtcOffset
): Instant
members.description:
The moment this point falls on, `now` being now, on the clock whose offset from UTC `offsetAt` tells for each moment: by default the device's, as `systemUtcOffset` tells it.

Seconds, minutes and hours are time that passes; days and longer are the calendar's, on that clock: a day back from noon is noon. A point rounded to a unit is at the unit's start, or where it ends a range (`asEnd`) at its last millisecond, as a range query's `gte` and `lte` read them: from `now/d` to `now/d` is the whole of today. A week starts on `firstDayOfWeek`, as ISO 8601 numbers the days: 1 is Monday.

members.name: toDateMath
members.description: This point as date math: `now`, `now-15m`, `now-15m/m`, `now/d`, and a moment as ISO 8601 writes it on the clock `offsetAt` tells, `2026-10-17T14:15:00+03:00`: by default the device's.

members.name: Now
members.description: The moment the point is read.

members.name: Relative
members.description: `amount` `unit`s from now, earlier where less than nought, and then rounded to the start of `roundTo`, or to its end where the point ends a range: `Relative(-15, Minutes)` is `now-15m`, and `Relative(-1, Days, roundTo = Days)` is `now-1d/d`, yesterday. With an amount of nought the unit says nothing: `Relative(0, Days, Days)` is `now/d`, today, and with no rounding either the point is now.

parameters.name: amount
parameters.description: How many units from now: less than nought before it.

parameters.name: unit
parameters.description: What `amount` counts.

parameters.name: roundTo
parameters.description: What the point is rounded to, or null for no rounding.

members.name: Absolute
members.description: A moment, the same wherever it is read: a reader in another time zone sees it on their own clock.

parameters.name: moment
parameters.description: The moment.

companion.name: parseDateMath
companion.description:
The point the date math `text` writes, or null where it is not date math these points hold.

- `now`, and one operation after it: `now-15m` and `now+2h`, the number left out as Kibana allows it, `now-d` for `now-1d`; then a rounding: `now-1d/d`, `now/w`, `/1d` as Elasticsearch allows it.

- The units `y M w d h m s`, and `H` for hours as Elasticsearch writes them. Milliseconds are not read.

- A moment as ISO 8601 writes one with its offset from UTC or a `Z`: `2026-10-17T14:15:00+03:00`.

Date math these points do not hold, two operations, `now-1d/d+8h`, or a date before `||`, is null.

declarations.name: PantrixTimeRange
declarations.description: A range of time whose ends can move with the clock: from `now-15m` to `now` is the last 15 minutes whenever it is read. It keeps no order between its ends, since a point that moves has none until it is read: `resolve` says whether they are in order at a moment.

parameters.name: start
parameters.description: Where the range starts.

parameters.name: end
parameters.description: Where it ends.

members.name: resolve
members.signature:
fun resolve(
    now: Instant = Clock.System.now(),
    firstDayOfWeek: Int = 1,
    offsetAt: (Instant) -> Duration = ::systemUtcOffset
): ClosedRange<Instant>?
members.description: The moments the range runs between, `now` being now, its start rounded down and its end up, on the clock `offsetAt` tells, its weeks starting on `firstDayOfWeek`; or null where its end falls before its start.

members.name: toDateMath
members.description: Both ends as date math: what a URL keeps, and what a range query sends as `gte` and `lte`.

parameters.name: offsetAt
parameters.description: tells the clock's offset from UTC at each moment, for an end written as a moment: by default the device's, as `systemUtcOffset` tells it.

declarations.name: PantrixTimeUnit
declarations.description:
A unit time is counted in: a point's distance from now, and what it is rounded to.

Seconds, minutes and hours are time that passes, the same length on every day. Days and longer are the calendar's, on the clock the point is read by: a day back from noon is noon, on a day the clock is put forward too, and a month on from the 31st of January is the last day of February.

Each is written in date math by the letter Elasticsearch and Kibana write it with: `s`, `m`, `h`, `d`, `w`, `M` and `y`.

entries.name: Minutes
entries.description: Minutes: `m`.

entries.name: Hours
entries.description: Hours: `h`.

entries.name: Days
entries.description: Days of the calendar: `d`.

entries.name: Weeks
entries.description: Weeks of the calendar, from the day a week starts on: `w`.

entries.name: Months
entries.description: Months of the calendar: `M`.

entries.name: Years
entries.description: Years of the calendar: `y`.

declarations.name: rememberToday
declarations.signature:
@Composable
fun rememberToday(): PantrixDate
declarations.description:
The day the screen's clock shows, as a screen that stays open past midnight has it: it turns to the next day as the clock does, and what reads it is drawn again. A calendar marks today by it. The clock is `LocalPantrixClock`'s: the device's, unless a test or a preview gives another.

It asks the clock again at each midnight of the clock's own time, and not in between: a clock set by hand or a journey into another time zone shows the next time the screen is built, or at the next midnight.

declarations.name: checkContrast
declarations.signature:
fun Modifier.checkContrast(
    component: String,
    pairs: () -> List<ContrastPair>
): Modifier
declarations.description:
Tells the theme's diagnostics, while they are on, which colours `component` draws on which: a pair that reads under what it needs is reported as `PantrixCheck.LowContrast`, once for the component and those colours however many of it show them. `pairs` is called only while the diagnostics are on, and again when they or the theme's colours change.

A background that lets through what is under it, as that of a button without a fill, is measured on the theme's background and on its surface, where the component stands on one of the theme's own grounds, and the lower of the two counts. On a fill of another colour, which gives what stands on it a content colour of its own, such a pair is not measured: what is under it is not known. Nor is a pair with an unspecified colour.

parameters.name: component
parameters.description: The component's name in a finding, e.g. `Button`.

parameters.name: pairs
parameters.description: The colours it draws on which, in the state it is in. A disabled component, which no one is asked to read, gives none.

A null name is no name given here, as for a picture that is only decoration or a control that is named by its text, and is not reported; a control that has no other name passes a blank one.

declarations.name: PantrixDiagnostics
declarations.signature: fun interface PantrixDiagnostics
declarations.description:
Where a theme's diagnostics send what they find.

`Off`, the default, turns the checks off as well: they return at their first line, and a release build pays next to nothing for them. Pantrix does not know what kind of build it runs in, so an app turns them on in its debug build: `PantrixTheme(diagnostics = if (debug) PantrixDiagnostics.Log else PantrixDiagnostics.Off)`. A test or an inspector keeps them with `PantrixFindings`.

A finding is reported once while it lasts, and again if it comes back after it was put right. A squeezed touch target, which a layout makes, is reported once it has lasted half a second: a row that opens squeezes what it holds for a moment. Two nodes with one tag are reported once they have lasted a second and a half, longer than a page transition, which shows the page that goes and the one that comes together.

members.name: report
members.description: Called with each `finding` on the UI thread, outside composition and layout.

companion.name: Off
companion.description: Turns the checks off: nothing is looked for, and nothing is reported.

companion.name: Log
companion.description: Writes each finding to the platform's log: Logcat on Android, the console on iOS and in a browser, and the standard error on the JVM.

declarations.name: LocalPantrixDiagnostics
declarations.signature: val LocalPantrixDiagnostics: ProvidableCompositionLocal<PantrixDiagnostics>
declarations.description:
Where the checks of the components inside a theme send what they find: the theme's `diagnostics`.

A theme whose diagnostics change while its content is shown turns the checks of that content on or off at once.

declarations.name: PantrixFindings
declarations.description:
Keeps what a theme's diagnostics find, for a test to read and for an inspector to show, and hands each finding on to `then` as well.

```
val findings = PantrixFindings()
setContent { PantrixTheme(diagnostics = findings) { CheckoutScreen() } }
assertEquals(emptyList(), findings.all)
```

parameters.name: then
parameters.description: Where each finding goes on to once it is kept: `PantrixDiagnostics.Log` writes it to the log too.

members.name: all
members.description: What has been found since this was made or last cleared, in the order it was found: the list as it is when read, which equals any list of the same findings. A finding that comes back after it was put right is kept once; read in a composition, the list is followed as it grows.

members.name: clear
members.description: Forgets what has been found.

members.name: boundsOf
members.description: Where the node `finding` was made on is now, in the coordinates of the window it is drawn in: what an inspector outlines. Null where that node is gone, and for a finding made on no node, as one about a theme's colours.

declarations.name: fileDropTarget
declarations.signature:
fun Modifier.fileDropTarget(
    enabled: Boolean = true,
    onOver: (Boolean) -> Unit = {},
    onFiles: (List<PantrixFile>) -> Unit
): Modifier
declarations.description:
Takes the files dropped on this element, from the platform's files, another app or another window, as `PantrixFile`s.

Compose hands a drop over in each platform's own type: a `DragEvent` whose `ClipData` holds content `Uri`s on Android, `UIDragItem`s whose providers still have to load their files on iOS, a list of file addresses on the desktop, and a `DataTransfer` on the web whose files can be read only while the drop lasts. This turns each into the same list. On Android it asks the activity for the right to read what another app dropped, which a drop that is not asked for loses; on iOS it copies each file into the app's temporary folder, as a provider's file is gone when its loading ends.

Dragging a file in is a pointer's gesture, and some platforms never have one: a phone with no other app beside it. A drop target is never the only way to give an app a file: put a `FilePicker` beside it, on the same press.

```
Box(Modifier.fileDropTarget(onOver = { over = it }) { files -> attach(files) })
```

parameters.name: enabled
parameters.description: whether a drop is taken. A target that is not does not light up either: it is never told something is over it.

parameters.name: onOver
parameters.description: told true when something that may hold files is dragged over this element, and false when it leaves, is dropped or the drag ends somewhere else.

parameters.name: onFiles
parameters.description: handed the files of a drop, on the main thread. It is not called for a drop that held none; on iOS it is called once the files are loaded, a moment after the drop.

declarations.name: FilePickRequest
declarations.description: What a picker is asked for: the kinds of file it shows, and whether the user may choose more than one.

parameters.name: accept
parameters.description: the kinds of file the picker shows. A file of none of them cannot be chosen, where the platform's picker can tell: the desktop's window on Windows cannot, and shows every file.

parameters.name: multiple
parameters.description: whether the user may choose more than one file.

members.name: accepts
members.description: Whether `file` is of a kind the picker shows.

members.name: imagesOnly
members.description: Whether only pictures are asked for: every kind is an image's. Android and iOS then open their photo picker, where a user's pictures are, in place of their files.

declarations.name: FilePicker
declarations.signature: fun interface FilePicker
declarations.description:
Opens the platform's own picker for files, and hands the app what the user chose.

`rememberFilePicker` gives the platform's: Android's documents (`ACTION_OPEN_DOCUMENT`), iOS's Files, the desktop's own window and the browser's. Where only pictures are asked for (`FilePickRequest.imagesOnly`), Android and iOS open their photo picker instead. None of them asks for a permission.

A test, or a screen shown before a picker exists, gives one of its own:

```
val picker = FilePicker { _, onPicked -> onPicked(listOf(PantrixFile("report.pdf", bytes))) }
```

members.name: pick
members.signature:
fun pick(
    request: FilePickRequest,
    onPicked: (List<PantrixFile>) -> Unit
)
members.description: Opens the picker for `request`. `onPicked` is called on the main thread with what the user chose, in the order the platform gives it, and is not called when the user chose nothing.

declarations.name: rememberFilePicker
declarations.signature:
@Composable
fun rememberFilePicker(): FilePicker
declarations.description: The platform's own picker for files: see `FilePicker`. On Android it needs an activity that keeps results, a `ComponentActivity`, as every Compose activity is. Where `LocalFilePicker` gives a picker, it is that one.

declarations.name: LocalFilePicker
declarations.signature: val LocalFilePicker: ProvidableCompositionLocal<FilePicker?>
declarations.description: The picker `rememberFilePicker` gives inside it: what a test or a preview puts in the place of the platform's, for every file drop zone of a screen at once. Null, the default, leaves the platform's.

declarations.name: FileSaveResult
declarations.signature: enum class FileSaveResult
declarations.description: What became of a file given to `FileSaver.save`.

entries.name: Saved
entries.description: The user chose a place, and the file was written there.

entries.name: Cancelled
entries.description: The user closed the platform's window without choosing a place: nothing was written.

entries.name: Started
entries.description: The file was handed to the browser, which keeps it as its user has it set to: in the downloads folder, or where it asks. A page is told no more than that.

entries.name: Failed
